eries started. Inaugurated in Mt Isa in 1978, the Mill Operators’ Conference aims to once again promote the sharing of knowledge in operating practices for mineral processing plants, including extractive metallurgy, process control and environmental issues. This conference provides the opportunity for plant operators, metallurgists, engineers and suppliers to learn, share and network with others in the minerals industry. 

Technology advances over the last 40 years have changed the way our industry operates. Previous conferences have investigated the evolution and survival of our industry through boom and bust, the experiences gained, the lessons learned and the challenges ahead. We have investigated how we can optimise our operations, achieving more with less and how technology now gives us the opportunity to measure, manage and improve. Despite 40 years of technology advancements and numerous commodity cycles the fundamentals of our operations remain largely the same, mineralogy and mineral behaviour drives grade and recovery. Throughput, recovery, grade and costs drive the profitability of our operations. The 14th Mill Operators’ Conference is about understanding and getting ‘Back to Basics’ for the good of our business. 

Once again sponsorship and exhibition booth opportunities have been well supported by industry. We would like to thank these companies because without their support conferences such as this would not be possible. Collaboration is fundamental to our industry and we would encourage you to take the time to visit booths and talk with our exhibitors, to find out about changes in technology, what is available in our industry and what they can do for your operation. 

This year we received over 100 potential abstracts and papers. While not all of the proposed papers could be given the opportunity to be included in the program we are confident that with the assistance and generous support of many peer reviewers the committee has been able to deliver a program that, over the next three days, captures the best of our industry. 

Following the highly successful 13th Mill Operators’ Conference format we have once again kept presentation times short and implemented an expertly moderated discussion session at the end of each session. This was found to maximise the impact of each session by allowing exploration and clarification of concepts via robust discussion. This year we have also reintroduced a morning panel discussion on education and professional development in our industry. The panel aims to investigate the state of education, especially after its battering by the boom and bust cycle, and what we need to do as an industry to move forward. It is a timely reminder that these areas are fundamental to the longevity and success of our industry and at the heart of our conference theme of getting ‘Back to Basics’. 

The conference sits in the middle of a full week of metallurgical development as many delegates choose to visit mine sites

and laboratory facilities, participate in the MetSoc Plant Operators Forum, attend the Delprat Distinguished Lecture or take a course. I encourage participants to make full use of these opportunities, to learn from their peers and to allow others to learn from them. 

Thank you to all the committee members who have all taken on their share of responsibility to make this event what it is. Thank you also to the AusIMM staff whose professional expertise and hard work is unfailing, especially through a period of upheaval within the AusIMM structure. It is this group of professionals who pull the conference together and make it the success that it has become. Without their expertise the Mill Operators’ conferences could never exist. 

Our theme of getting ‘Back to Basics’ reminds us to think about what we are doing and why, to understand the fundamentals of our business. Many of our papers address this concept directly while others introduce us to new ideas. The committee has pulled together a program that will help to remind us what the basics are and, perhaps, challenges us to reassess the fundamentals of our industry. I 

commend this volume to your bookshelf and digital storage and trust it will become a valuable resource for years to come.

Email Jean-Paul.Franzidis@uct.ac.za ###### **ABSTRACT** When, in 1985, Marty McFly is accidentally sent back to 1955 in a DeLorean ‘time machine’ in _Back to the Future_ , he encounters young versions of his parents, and must make sure they fall in love or he will cease to exist. This Conference celebrates 40 years since the inaugural Mill Operators’ Conference in Mt Isa in 1978; over this period, great technological advances have been made in almost all aspects of mill operation, resulting in considerable improvements in grades and recoveries from ever-more complex ores. However, in 2018, the mining industry is facing challenges that might have been difficult to predict in 1978 (or were they?). The computer revolution, the information revolution, and the bio-technology revolution have all contributed to the increase in operating efficiencies, but, combined with the social revolution, they also call into question the existence of the mining industry as we know it. This presentation looks back at the ‘way things were’ in the 1970s, and at what was then considered to be the ‘basics,’ and attempts to sketch what the mining industry might be like in 2058. As _Back to the Future Part II_ demonstrates so vividly, it is much easier to review the past than predict the future. It is difficult to know what form the mining industry will have in 40 years’ time. Nevertheless, as this presentation will argue, it is important to take action now, to ensure that it (like Marty McFly) does not cease to exist. Some courses of action are proposed, including going back to the basics of a very different p

ast. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### Mill Operators’ conferences – a 40-year retrospective and a vision for the future 

###### _P D Munro_<sup>_1_</sup> 

1. FAusIMM, Position title, Principal Consultant, Mineralis Consultants Pty Ltd, Taringa Queensland 4068. Email: pmunro@mineralis.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

On the occasion of the 14<sup>th</sup> Mill Operators’ Conference and marking 40 years since the first one was held in Mount Isa in 1978, it is fitting to review the history of the Conference and its development over that time. 

The first 10 Conferences were irregularly held at three to four year intervals, with 9 of these in regional centres of Australasia. It is only since 2012 that the Mill Operators’ Conference has become a regular biennial event, alternating with the MetPlant Conference. 

The number of people attending the Conference has more than doubled to 470 delegates at the 13<sup>th</sup> one in 2016. It has outgrown its regional beginnings. 

Papers presented to the previous Conferences have been analysed according to commodity, country of origin, technology and theme plus the affiliation of the authors to discern any trends that may assist in planning the future events. 

Suggestions are made as to how the AusIMM might wish to arrange its mineral processing/metallurgical conferences. 

Recent changes to the structure of the Conference providing a more meaningful experience for the delegates and increasing their interaction and involvement should be vigorously pursued. 

###### **THE BEGINNING AND EARLY YEARS** 

###### **Inception** 

The idea for a Mill Operators’ Conference came from a proposal in 1977 put to the Committee of North West Queensland Branch of the Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (AusIMM) in Mount Isa. The Branch wanted an Australian equivalent of the successful _Canadian Mineral Processors Conference_ which had commenced its modern form in 1968. The emphasis was to be on mineral processing operations with the conference to be held at a regional mining centre rather than a capital city. Mount Isa Mines Limited enthusiastically endorsed the concept with senior management aggressively ‘pushing’ its execution through their positions on the North West Queensland Branch. 

Ideally the group in Mount Isa wanted to attract plant supervisors and operators in addition to professionals. This applied to maintenance people as well, recognising their vital role in production. Both large and small companies were at that time then enlightened enough to still believe in the benefits of a free exchange of ideas so cogently put by Dr James Douglas, President of the then American Institute Mining Engineers in 1900: 

_“The ridiculous secrecy maintained at so many of the metallurgical works, especially in Europe, benefits no one. It stands to reason that there must be in art as well as in science, a give and take rule, and those who contribute nothing t

o the information of the world or their co-workers are not those who are generally most progressive in their own practice. No misguided ‘claptrap’ about so-called ‘intellectual property!”_ While the initiative for the Mill Operators’ Conference came from a local branch, the event has always been firmly under the auspices of the AusIMM. This contrasts with the Canadian experience where the Canadian Mineral Processors which runs the Canadian Mineral Processors Conference, voted to become a ‘society’ within the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum (CIM) in 1981 and seemingly operates its events with limited interaction with the parent organisation. ###### **When and where** Table 1 – Mill Operators’ conferences: year, location and attendance. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 |**Year**|**Title**|**AusIMM –**

###### **MILL OPERATORS’ CONFERENCE AND METPLANT CONFERENCE** 

###### **Background** 

The first officially branded _Metallurgical Plant Design and Operating Strategies Conference_ ( _MetPlant_ ) was held in Sydney in 2002. This was the ‘… third in the series of 

conferences reporting state-of-the-art advances in metallurgical processing of ores covering plant design from test work and in plant expansions and retrofits, use of new technologies in processing ores, plant control and sampling, maintenance and water 

management, and the whole of life of operations through to site rehabilitation.’ (Dunlop and Pollard 2002). This followed two conferences, _Mineral Processing and Hydrometallurgy Plant Design - World’s Best Practice_ in 1998 and _Biomine ‘99/Water Management in Metallurgical Operations_ in 1999 organized by the Australian Mineral Foundation. 

Since Sydney in 2002 a further seven _MetPlant_ Conferences have been held in Perth, normally at intervals of two years and recently _de facto_ on alternate years with the _Mill Operators’ Conference_ . 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Simply the _MetPlant Conference_ emphasizes **design** whereas the _Mill Operators’ Conference_ theme is **operations** , and topics seen as such. 

Chemical transformation as opposed to physical mineral beneficiation by physical means is more appropriately dealt with in a _MetPlant Conference_ . 

###### **Co-existence and collaboration** 

The current _de facto_ position is that the _MetPlant Conference_ alternates with the _Mill Operators Conference_ . The AusIMM should formalise this arrangement into a _de jure_ position with the _MetPlant Conference_ also catering to the extractive metallurgy fraternity who haven’t had a venue since the 1994 _6_<sup>_th_</sup> _Extractive Metallurgy Conference_ in Brisbane. Australasia still has a large sector transforming minerals into finished products that seemingly been ignored over the last 20 years. There are 26 major plants in Australia smelting and refining aluminium, base metals, ferroalloys and precious metals. 

Formalising this _de facto_ position means that the AusIMM has only one specific mineral processing/metallurgical conference per year. This is realistic if we want to maintain the quality of submitted papers. Specific themes such as geometallurgy can be added as a one day special event before or after the main one rather than being the subject of a specific conference. 

Authors of potential

papers to either _MetPlant_ or _Mill Operators_ Conferences presumably slant their offerings to fit the theme of each. It is unlikely that they consciously classify the paper as specifically belonging to one or other of the conferences and delay publication for two years. 

###### **A VISION FOR THE FUTURE** 

Edward Gibbon in his 1788 classic _The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire_ observed that ‘all that is human must retrograde if it does not advance’; conferences being a gathering of people presumably follow the same law. 

The Mill Operators’ Conference has survived for 40 years and is now in its 14<sup>th</sup> episode. 

Our mining colleagues have emulated its success by having _Open Pit Operators’_ and _Underground Operators’ Conferences_ . 

Where should it go from here? 

###### **Regional versus national/international** 

It has been necessary to move away from the original concept of the _Mill Operators’ Conference_ being held in a regional centre in Australasia. Such a conference can have only a limited attendance because of the relative decline of the traditional regional mining centres due to FIFO and the lack of suitable accommodation and venues. The small number of attendees makes the event less attractive to sponsors and potential overseas delegates who will incur increased time and higher travel costs. 

The original concept of an operator-focussed gathering in regional centres has been admirably filled by the recent MetFest events. The Lachlan Branch of the AusIMM held one in Orange in 2016 and then in Parkes in 2017 to coincide with the annual Delprat Lecture. The Kalgoorlie Branch held its first MetFest in 2017. These less formal local events are an excellent way of gathering processing people. 

While the emphasis has been on informality, making any presentations available through the AusIMM’s web site communicates with an industry-wide audience. 

###### **Thoughts for the future** 

The following points are a personal view about the future of the _Mill Operators’ Conference_ : 

- The Conference should _de jure_ be in alternate years to the _MetPlant Conference_ with the venue switching between Brisbane and Perth. The _Canadian Mineral Processors Conference_ has always been held in Ottawa in January; certainty of timing and venue helps people’s planning. 

- It should aim to be the premier event of its type in the Asia-Pacific region attracting around 750 delegates. We need to reach out to our colleagues in Asia to achieve this. 

- Papers on processing of significant interest that have been presented at other venues such as an AusIMM conference for a specific commodity like iron ore, lithium, mineral sands or uranium should be considered for ‘recycling’ to the _Mill Operators’ Conference_ to reach a wider audience. Relying solely on AusIMM publications such as the laudable _We are Metallurgists, Not Magicians_ volume (Pollard, Dunlop and Herzig 2017) for such communication means that the immediate benefits of this

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

potential cross fertilisation of ideas could be lost. This multi-sector approach should extend to coal through interaction with the Australian Coal Preparation Society. 

- Recent changes to the structure of the Conference to provide a more meaningful experience for the delegates and increase their involvement should be vigorously pursued. These include: 

   - Maintain the single session structure; this maximises interaction and ‘rations’ papers by quality and relevance. 

   - Adopt the format of the 2016 Mill Operators’ Conference which grouped papers into themes for each session, limited authors’ presentation time to allow extended discussion moderated by a discipline expert on the podium in addition to the Session Chairperson. This created more interaction between the floor and the podium than I have ever experienced at an AusIMM Conference. 

   - Have a Conference App as was done at the Tenth International Mine Geology Conference 2017 in Hobart. This allowed delegates to be polled on questions submitted to panel discussions. 

   - Introduce a session along the lines of a “Five Minute Thesis” where the presenter has 5 minutes and three to five overhead slides to talk about a new product or technique. The topic must have genuine technical content and not be mere advertising by a Conference sponsor. 

Continue the AusIMM tradition of catering for meals and sponsored refreshment breaks which facilitates delegates mixing and networking. This contrasts with practices encountered at similar events in North America where there is a hurried exodus to nearby restaurants with selected colleagues.

###### Metallurgical test work – between a rock and a hard place 

###### _A. Newell_<sup>_1_</sup> _, P.D. Munro_<sup>_2_</sup> _and K. Fiedler_<sup>_3_</sup> 

1.MAusIMM, Executive Consultant - Processing, RPMGlobal Pty. Ltd., Brisbane, Queensland 4000. Email: anewell@rpmglobal.com 

2.FAusIMM, Principal Consultant, Mineralis Consultants Pty. Ltd., Taringa Queensland 4068. Email: pmunro@mineralis.com.au

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Test work is the foundation upon which the success of projects and subsequent operations is laid, reflected in Professor Arthur Taggart’s pithy observation: ‘Make your mistakes on the small scale and your profits on the larger scale’. Indeed, Professor AllanTrench has succinctly noted that ‘Get the metallurgical characteristics wrong and you don’t have a project’. 

With deposits becoming lower grade, more structurally and mineralogically complex, final products requiring lower levels of impurities and tailings management demanding more attention, test work now assumes even greater significance in the acceptance and successful execution of a project. 

This paper is the first in a series aiming to stimulate thought on the metallurgical test work process by getting back to the fundamental basics through exploring and providing some guidelines for the metallurgical testing world, noting preferred practices as well as precautions and mitigations. This covers the key characteristics of metallurgical test work programs, including what needs to be done, sample selection, quality control and associated drivers, and most importantly, selecting, assessing and managing test work facilities. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

###### **TEST WORK** 

This paper is the first of a planned series discussing the basis for metallurgical test work and the associated issues and requirements and issues encountered when doing it. 

The papers can simply be thought as fitting into the categories of ‘before’, ‘during’ and ‘after’ for a program of metallurgical test work with this first one examining the ‘before’ stage. 

We have been stimulated to write these papers both as originators of metallurgical test work and consumers of the product because of our growing dissatisfaction with the standard of much of the metallurgical work we encounter in our jobs. The papers do not aim to provide a completely detailed check list or ‘how to’ guide for metallurgical test work but rather discuss key issues that need to be understood and resolved. We believe that the industry must be more transparent and explicit reporting the results o

f metallurgical testing as a precursor to achieving better outcomes. 

Frankly, the “fuzzy” framework we currently have for metallurgical testing compares very poorly with the much more structured environment that geologists operate under when producing a mineral resource/reserve estimate. An excellent example of this is for the reader to compare the geology and processing sections of say 10 reports for projects and operating mines prepared under the Canadian National Instrument 43-101 Standards of Disclosure for Mineral Projects (Ontario Securities Commission 2016), hereafter referred to as ‘NI 43-101’. We have not singled out Canada for any reasons of poor practices but rather because Canadian companies are required to disclose more technical data than companies registered on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) or its counterparts in South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States of America. Also, the NI 43-101 reports follow a structured format for the technical data. 

Observations from comparing the quality of the technical data in geological sections with that in the metallurgical processing sections of NI 43-101 reports; for the former: 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

- Samples are firmly located in 3-D mineralised space; 

- Standards for quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) in sampling and assaying are firmly embedded in geological practice; 

- Laboratory doing the assays is identified; and 

- There is usually a statistical treatment of data. 

Whereas for metallurgical test work: 

- The concept of what the “sample” actually represents is poorly understood (this is discussed below); 

- Not usual to quote precisions and accuracies for test procedures; for example people would be more cautious using comminution test data if they understood the range of outcomes for a test at an assigned confidence level; and 

- Statistical treatment of data is rare; too many mineral processing engineers are prepared to draw unwarranted inferences from a set of metallurgical test data without considering the range of outcomes e.g. is a copper recovery difference of 1% absolute between different conditions really significant in the context of the errors inherent in metallurgical testing? 

An exemplar of QA/QC procedures used in metallurgical testing has been the work done on the geometallurgical program at Olympic Dam (Ehrig, Liebezeit and Macmillan 2017). 

The section ‘Essential Components of the Process Support in the Technical Report’ in the document _CIM Best Practice Guidelines for Mineral Processing_ (Sub-Committee on Best Practice Guidelines for Mineral Processing 2011) discusses **what** should be in the NI 43-101 but not **how** to produce the information of which metallurgical testing is the major determinant. 

While we are aware that some companies have guidelines for metallurgical test work as mentioned by Colbert (May 2018, personal communication) the industry does not.

A seemingly honourable exception is the uranium sector (International Atomic Energy Agency 1990). 

The Global Mining Guidelines Group has a Working Group on industrial comminution efficiency (2018) and in future might consider the topic of metallurgical test work. 

###### **WHY PROCESSING IS IMPORTANT** 

While it may seem obvious, the importance of processing, and thus the requirement for test work, needs to be clearly elucidated: 

- Many deposits require processing in order to produce a saleable product; 

   - Project economics are ‘sensitive’ to processing recoveries and product type, quantity and quality 

- Processing can be a significant, if not major, source of upfront project capital and ongoing operating costs and thus a ‘critical path to revenue’; 

   - Processing has a major impact on infrastructure requirements, principally power, water and in this paper taken to include tailings disposal. The total capital cost of these three items are becoming an increasingly proportion of the total. 

The project should be developed on a sound and competent basis because it can be time consuming and expensive to address and correct ‘fatal flaws’ encountered upon start-up. 

The first few years of operation are the ‘payback period’ when the revenues generated are principally redirected to repayment of debt capital. Project failure for the providers of equity capital is imminent when these loans are not repaid when the project has negative revenues. 

Capital spent on ‘correcting’ the technical problems, assuming that it can be raised worsens the problem. 

While Professor Allan Trench’s wry comment in the Mining News ‘Get the metallurgical characteristics wrong and you don’t have a project’ is correct, it is also how the metallurgical information is applied as well as executed. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### **WHY DO TEST WORK** 

Test work is conducted for a number of reasons: 

- Develop a solution to a processing problem (existing operation) 

   - Includes potentially ‘novel’ or unconventional processing options 

- Confirm, optimise or improve an existing flowsheet (existing project or operation) 

   - May include testing new equipment and process flowsheets, as well as new ore types 

- Provide geometallurgical performance predictions in operating mines (existing operation) 

   - Characterize the process behaviour of ore types for a selected process flowsheet 

- Develop a flowsheet and characterise metallurgical response (project evaluation) 

   - Supporting project studies such Scoping, Pre-Feasibility and Feasibility Studies; 

- Generate engineering data for process design and infrastructure requirements (e.g. tailings, acceptability of water source, power – project design); 

- Generating products (project evaluation) for other studies, such as marketing, environmental, downstream processing 

   - Extractive metallurgy studies; smelting or hydrometallurgy 

   - Tailings

studies; beach angles for wet tailings disposal, ‘dry stacking’ 

- Test new equipment (e.g. HPGRs, Up Current Classifiers, etc.) or process flowsheets/circuit configurations  (innovative). 

Tailings studies are important as mining projects are becoming increasingly driven by the ‘back end’. Geotechnical test work can require significant amounts of ‘sample’. 

Supporting proposed projects is the most common reason for test work and what the outcomes are used for provides a foundation for understanding the range and depth of test work requirements. 

Studies are used to assess the technical and economic feasibility in stage-gate driven process (Scoping/Preliminary Economic Assessment, Pre-Feasibility Study and Feasibility Study) of proposed projects, with the amount and type of test work conducted increasing with the study level, as outlined in the Appendix. 

One of the primary aims of study test work is to demonstrate a feasible and practical way of producing marketable mineral products in terms of a robust flowsheet that can handle all feed blends presented to the plant over the Life of Mine (LOM). 

Another important study test work outcome is the determination of likely mineral recoveries and product grades. 

Outcomes from metallurgical test work drives study development by providing key technical and engineering design input that allow: 

- Development of mass, water and energy balances (once the mining rate has been determined); 

- Determination of Process Design Criteria (PDC); 

- Establishment of metal recoveries based on feed grades as well as product grades; 

- Selection and sizing of equipment; 

- Development of process capital and operating costs 

   - Consumable requirements including power and water 

   - Labour schedule 

- Comparison of process flowsheets  and equipment options (cf. trade-off studies); 

- Infrastructure requirements (power, water, tailings storage requirements, etc.); and 

- Support marketing studies and logistical requirements. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Anyone who reviews the process flowsheets and operating conditions of porphyry copper deposits all over the world would realize that a generic treatment protocol would be: 

- Grinding to 80% passing 150µm; 

- Rougher/scavenger flotation time of 30 minutes; 

- Regrind rougher flotation concentrate to 80% passing 38µm; and 

- Multi-stage cleaning with the cleaner block tailing to final tailing; popular configuration is to use washed froth cleaning backed up with conventional cells treating the tailing. 

While this configuration might be applicable under most circumstances, consider the consequences for a project whose ore’s comminution behaviour conforms to the Bond Equation if (a) the flotation feed **could have been** 80% passing 212µm i.e. 21% of unnecessary primary grinding power installed, or; (b) the flotation feed **had to be** 80% passing 106um i.e. throughput reduced by 21%. ###### **SAMPLES FOR TESTING** 

###### **A Discourse** 

Unfortunately too many metallurgical test programs are fatally compromised in achieving their objective from poor sample selection. A necessary precursor for sample selection is a coherent narrative of the deposit’s geology that is intelligible to participants such as metallurgists, mineralogists and mining engineers. 

Two questions that always asked in any review of work are. 

- Where did the samples come from? 

- What do the samples represent? 

All samples taken for any metallurgical test work should be plotted on the ore body geological model to fix their spatial positions.  This helps determine whether sample coverage of the deposit has been adequate. Thinking in spatial terms about all samples helps answer these que

stions. 

###### **Ore Types** 

A prelude to selecting sample types is undertaking what ore types are present and their likely abundances or proportions. 

Two paradigms control processing outcomes: 

- Mineralogy controls metallurgy. 

- Rock type and associated alteration controls comminution performance i.e. throughput. 

An admonition is required about the loose use of terminology such as ‘rock type’, ‘lithology’ and ‘ore type’.  For example geological dictionaries define ‘lithology’ as: 

- ‘The character of a rock described in terms of its structure, colour, mineral composition, grain-size and arrangements of its component parts’ (Thrush 1968) 

- ‘All those visible features that in the aggregate impart individuality of the rock’ (ibid) 

- ‘Generally relates descriptions of rocks based upon hand-specimens and outcrops rather than microscopic or chemical features’ (Whitten and Brooks 1972). 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The metallurgist must not be unduly influenced by the terms ‘rock type’, ‘lithology’ or ‘ore type’ as described by geologists logging alterations and visible features in the drill core.  These may not coincide with a **‘metallurgical ore type’** . This will be more properly determined by a mineralogist or perhaps only after the results of chemical and/or metallurgical tests. 

A ‘rock type’, ‘lithology’ or ‘geological ore type’ could contain several different ‘metallurgical ore types’ or conversely a ‘metallurgical ore type’ can cover several different ‘rock types’. 

Examples are: 

- The flotation performance of a porphyry copper deposit with an epithermal overprint was driven by the iron sulphide:copper sulphide ratio which was normally ~2 to 3:1 but reached 10 to 20: 1. It was much more useful to think of the iron sulphide: copper sulphide ratio _within a rock type_ than to compare the metallurgical performance _between different rock types_ ; 

- In a copper deposit geologists defined ‘supergene ore’ as material ‘having visible chalcocite’. This ranged from (a) traces of chalcocite to (b) where chalcocite was the co-dominant copper mineral.  Subdividing ‘supergene ore’ into two separate zones according to the chalcocite content allowed accurate prediction of metallurgical performance; and 

- The flotation performance across three different rock types in the primary zone of a copper deposit where chalcopyrite was the only copper mineral was identical at the same rougher feed sizing. Material classified as ‘andesite’ also had chalcopyrite as the only economic sulphide with the same texture but recovery was lower due to the significantly lower head grade. 

Generally, at the Scoping study level, ore types with an abundance of less than 10% are not tested, unless they will be an early feed to the process plant and/or have a characteristic that would significantly impact the metallurgical response of blends incorporating them. This may be due the presence of clay, organi

c carbon, penalty elements (arsenic, fluorine, mercury etc.), highly reactive sulphides, oxidised minerals, etcetera. 

A good understanding of the deposit and the geological domains, namely the lithological units/rock types, faults, alteration zones and oxidation zones, is required as a ‘first pass’ classification of possible ore types. 

For separation test work samples in particular, the typical classification scheme is based on the following characteristics: 

- Degree of oxidation; hypogene (e.g. primary sulphides - chalcopyrite), supergene (e.g. secondary sulphides – chalcocite) and ‘oxide’ (e.g. malachite, native copper); 

   - Interestingly, some geologists believe that there is a difference between weathering and oxidation, so degree of weathering may be a more appropriate terminology 

- Presence of _in situ_ metal ions on mineral surfaces; 

- Degree of alteration; increasing water content : hematite – hydrated hematite – limonite – goethite; 

- Mineral:gangue ratios; e.g. copper sulphides:iron sulphides; 

- Mineral:mineral ratios; e.g. galena:chalcopyrite; 

- Impurity elements or gangue mineral; arsenic, antimony, mercury, clay, organic carbon, talc, etcetera; and 

- Combination of the above. 

The focus must be on rock types modified by alteration when selecting comminution samples. It is meaningless to have a comminution sample at 0.5% Cu described as ‘chalcopyrite ore type’ when it will be the other 98.5% of its constituents that will influence its breakage properties; calling it ‘andesite – medium alteration’ is much more informative. 

###### **Sample Selection** 

The objectives of the test work program must be clearly defined to determine the sample mass and particle size needed for each section of work. 

Once the test work program has been mapped out selecting samples is a critical stage underpinning the meaningfulness of the program outcomes.

###### **Composite Samples** 

The preferred methodology is to: 

- Test individually; and if needed, 

- Composite arithmetically or by ore type proportions based on the mine schedule. 

Once the metallurgical characteristics of individual zones have been established then our previous experience on a variety of ores suggests that plant performance should be the mean of the individual ore zones weighted according to their proportion in the feed. 

That is if there are two metallurgical ore types “A” and “B” then the metallurgical result from treating a mixture of the two will be the weighted mean of the individual results from “A” and “B”. 

The exception to this outcome is when there are deleterious chemical ef

fects in one metallurgical ore type which also affect the other one(s).  An example would be a high amount of soluble copper in one metallurgical ore type which degrades the flotation performance of any others mixed with it. 

Hence the preferred route on undertaking the metallurgical evaluation of a deposit is test entities rather than composites. 

We have two objections to the practice of testing composites. 

1. All compositing schemes assume a mine plan and associated production schedule thus introducing the dimension of “time” into what is a purely “spatial concept” if we consider the deposit solely in terms of its geometry. Since a credible mine plan and production schedule is supposed to be the outcome of the feasibility study then how can these be accurately known at the start of test work? 

2. Compositing invariably diminishes the investigators’ ability to determine the level of variability within the deposit. We have encountered the absurdity of samples called the ‘variability composite’! 

Lunt, Ritchie and Fleay (1997) discuss the use of composites and some finance providers specify using them to confirm metallurgical performance for the initial years of production. 

People preparing a composite must be fully cognisant of what they are doing; too often materials are mixed together to provide a sufficient mass for a particular test.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The industry needs better understanding and co-operation between its technical disciplines to improve test work outcomes and thus project decision making, 

For example, this means metallurgists working with geologists during the exploration stages to better understand the nature of the mineralisation and the likely deposit characteristics so that ore types can be 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

identified as well as the probable make-up of representative samples. This may result in the need for dedicated drilling programs to obtain suitable samples for test work as well as confirming the quality of geological logging and the need for any drill core sample measurements. 

With regard to mining engineers, metallurgists should be involved in the mining studies, providing estimates to assist in the mining rate (and subsequent plant throughput capacity) and mine scheduling studies. The mine scheduling needs to be critically reviewed in terms of ore type blends, feed grades and mining rates and revised to ensure that it can be accommodated by the proposed plant design. 

Metallurgists need to be more informative and transparent on what is being done in test work programs because our efforts do not compare favourably with the more rigorous regime that geologists adhere to in producing a mineral resource estimate.

###### Developing flotation circuit control and automation for the Phu Kham C Gold O opper- peration concentrator 

###### _D Baas_<sup>_1_</sup> _and L Mikhael Gurieff_<sup>_2_</sup>

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Phu Kham Copper-Gold Operation (Phu Kham Operation) is located in the Lao People's Democratic Republic and is owned and operated by the Lao-registered company, Phu Bia Mining Limited (PBM). Australian-headquartered copper and gold producer, PanAust Limited holds a 90 per cent interest in PBM; the Government of Laos owns the remaining 10 per cent. 

The Phu Kham Operation was commissioned in 2008 with an initial concentrator nameplate throughput of 12 million tonnes per annum (Mt/a). Subsequent improvement projects, including the Phu Kham Upgrade Project (PKU), completed in 2012, and the Phu Kham Increased Recovery Project (IRP), completed in 2013, increased the design throughput to 18 Mt/yr. In 2016, the actual mill throughput exceeded 19 Mt/a, this throughput is budgeted to be maintained until the end of 2020. 

The con

centrator flotation circuit upgrade, completed during the IRP, called for a non-selective bulk sulphide concentrate to be generated from the rougher circuit. This in turn caused the mechanical flotation cells in the cleaner circuit, particularly those in the second cleaner bank, to become volumetrically overload. The overload reduced the cleaner circuit performance to approximately 92 per cent copper recovery at a 23 per cent copper concentrate grade, below the expected 95 per cent recovery. This bottleneck restricted copper units entering the plant to approximately 14.5 tonnes per hour (t/h) due to uncontrolled recirculating load build-up in the mechanical cleaning circuit. 

Maintaining the operating methodologies would have led to a copper production shortfall beyond 2016, to address this shortfall the Phu Kham Operation looked to optimise the Jameson Cell and mechanical cleaner circuit performance. The work included fundamental application of flotation practice and modelling, mineralogical analysis, bubble size analysis, plant surveys and test work. The results were used to develop and implement an innovative automated control system strategy incorporating flotation theory and operating strategies. The automation has the ability to quickly adapt to disturbances in the circuit and maintain optimised performance with little or no intervention by flotation operators. 

Upon completion, cleaner recovery increased to 95 per cent at a final concentrate grade of 23 per cent copper, and copper units entering the plant increased to 17.5 t/h. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Phu Kham Copper-Gold Operation (Phu Kham Operation) is located in the Lao People's Democratic Republic and is owned and operated by the Lao-registered company Phu Bia Mining Limited (PBM). Australian-based copper and gold producer, PanAust Limited owns a 90 per cent interest in PBM; the Government of Laos owns the remaining 10 per cent. 

The Phu Kham Operation comprises a large open-pit mine feeding ore to a concentrator with recovery of copper and precious metals into a saleable concentrate using conventional flotation technology. The concentrator was initially designed to achieve a 12 Mt/yr throughput, treating high-pyrite copper-gold skarn ore with significant clay content (Meka & Lane 2010). The concentrator has subsequently been upgraded through a series of projects aimed at offsetting a scheduled decline in head grade and to improved recovery performances. 

The initial design for the Phu Kham concentrator was a compromise that balanced the need to achieve high copper recovery while maintaining the final concentrate grade. This high-recovery bulk rougher flotation design concept was developed during the pre-feasibility study. Very high pyrite content and complex intergrowth of secondary copper sulphides made it difficult to achieve a 24 per cent copper concentrate grade. A selective flotation was implemented which produced a lower final copper recovery but at a lower

usIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

capital cost due to the decreased cleaner capacity required. The risk of not achieving a saleable concentrate grade due to high pyrite in the early years’ feed blend was also reduced. 

Study work for the Phu Kham Upgrade (PKU) commenced in 2010 with the objective of maintaining copper production above 60,000 t/y and offset a scheduled decline in copper head grade from 2013. The PKU included increased grinding and flotation capacity which lifted throughput to a nominal 16 Mt/yr and addressed capacity constraints in grinding and flotation circuits Bennett, Crnkovic and Walker (2012). The PKU was commissioned in the third quarter (Q3) of 2012 and the design capacity was reached by the fourth quarter (Q4) of 2012. 

The Increased Recovery Project (IRP) study was initiated in 2009 in response to poor copper recovery performances and was completed in May 2013. The IRP reduced the selectivity of the rougher circuit, increasing the rougher mass recovery from 10-12 per cent to over 20 per cent of feed tonnes. Additional regrind and cleaning capacity was required to achieve the target recovery and concentrate grade. The process flow diagram after implementation of the IRP is shown in Figure 1. 

The IRP provided the expected benefit of increasing copper recovery by 2 per cent when treating less than 14 t/hr of copper in concentrate but at rates over 14 t/hr the cleaner circuit tended to build up large recirculating loads resulting in a significant drop in copper recovery. Limiting the copper feed to below 12 t/hr would significantly reduce the plant throughput. 

The project discussed in this paper to debottleneck the cleaners began 2014.  Using metallurgical test work and analysis to identify the optimal method of operating the cleaners, then automating this process, the project’s aim was to ensure the cleaners ran in the optimal zone for the ore type being processed. Effectively automating the Jameson Cell and mechanical cleaners as a whole unit locks in the value of the project’s metallurgical test work and analysis. Process automation must cope with all operating conditions, constraints and disturbances to become part of the normal operation of the plant. It allows operators to move from changing setpoints, to monitoring, and to ensure the process is achieving its objectives. 

This methodology has increased the recovery of the Phu Kham cleaning circuit by three per cent whilst the final concentrate grade has increased by 0.7 per cent.

###### **Jameson Cell optimisation** 

The function of the Jameson Cell is to scalp the cleaner feed by removing the liberated fast floating chalcopyrite and leaving the slower floating less liberated particles to be recovered in the mechanical cleaner circuit. During the first half of 2015, the Jameson Cell achieved 47.75 per cent recovery at a copper concentrate grade of 29.65 per cent. This was far below the optimised simulation prediction of 63.23 per cent recovery at 30.61 per cent copper concentrate grade. 

The targeted concentrate grade for the Jameson Cell followed the recommendation by Munro and Munro (2015) that industrial flotation processes should be able to make a concentrate with 85 per cent w/w valuable mineral content from a feed with >80 per cent mineral liberation. For the highly liberated, predominately chalcopyrite feed at Phu Kham, this equates to 29.4 per cent copper. The Jameson Cell was achieving this but at a much lower recovery rate than the simulations suggested. The 2015 Jameson Cell performance data confirmed the recovery varied from less than 20 per cent to greater than 80 per cent, while the copper concentrate grade remains in a tight band between 26 and 30 per cent copper. The focus therefore was placed on improving recovery while maintaining the c

oncentrate grade. 

Since the Jameson Cell was installed in 2012, 79 surveys have been undertaken to investigate the impact of level, air flow rate and wash water on grade and recovery. No definitive correlations between Jameson Cell performance and the three variables were determined from this test work leading to a consensus that the Jameson Cell’s performance was driven mainly from mineralogy and liberation and level, air flow rate and wash water had little influence on the final performance.

###### **Mechanical cleaner optimisation** 

The mechanical cleaners receive the Jameson Cell tailings. Their performance is therefore reliant on the Jameson Cell performance. Higher feed grade will generally result in a higher recovery. The higher recovery and concentrate grade of the mechanical cleaners versus the simulations was due to the underperformance of the Jameson Cell. Optimisation of the Jameson Cell will make the recovery in the mechanical cleaners more difficult to achieve. 

Post-commissioning of the IRP mineralogical data collected from the three open tailings streams indicated the majority of the liberated copper sulphide particle losses occurred in the <12 micron range as shown in Figure 5 taken from Chan and Mehrfert (2015). As with most copper circuits, less than 32 micron fully liberated chalcopyrite particles made up the majority of the mechanical cleaners losses, accounting for approximately 12 per cent of the total loss or 2.8 per cent of the total copper in the feed. The installation of Proflote units from Ausmetec reduced these losses by 9 per cent in the <12micron fraction as indicated by Zoetbrood _et al_ (2018).

It has been demonstrated by several studies that the correct selection of air profiles in the cleaning stage can generate significant performance gains. Cooper et al (2014) found that increasing the air profile gave the best performance at Xstrata’s Brunswick division in the final stages of its zinc cleaner bank Cooper et al (2014). Copper concluded that the improvement was due to the reduced entrainment of non-sulphide gangue in the first cells of the bank due to the low water recovery caused by low air flow rates. Combining the correct air flow profile and the flat recovery profile argued by Maldonado, Araya & Finch (2011) will yield the maximum separation between two floatable minerals for a target bank cumulative recovery. 

Three different profile arrangements were tested to try and achieve a balanced recovery profile. The target recovery for this stage of cleaning is 95 per cent as there should be very little unrecoverable copper in the feed after two stages of cleaning. Using the equation developed by (Maldonado, Araya & Finch 2011) the target recovery per cell is 53 per cent. Although none of the tests were able to achieve the target recovery in each cell, increasing the air profile produced the most consistent recovery and grade across both tests in terms of cell-by-cell recovery and grade recovery curve, as shown in Figure 8. This inability to reach the recovery target is due to insufficient total air flow to the circuit, when compared to the flat air profile. Increasing the total air flow but maintaining the profile will allow for the 95 per cent target to be achieved. The final profile was the increasing air profile and a slight (60mm) decrease in froth depth across the four cells to allow for more drainage in the first cell. As the Cleaner 2 and Cleaner 3 circuits are broadly similar, it was decided the same profile would be implemented for both.

This explains why the increasing velocity profile struggled to reduce the concentrate grade to the targeted 10 per cent. 

When applying the flat recovery profile theory to the Cleaner 1 circuit, which targets a 90 per cent recovery, each of the individual cells should be recovering 28 per cent. ###### **Removing Cleaner 2 constraints** 

The options considered in the simulations were: relocation of the Cleaner 1A and 1B banks first cell’s concentrate directly to Cleaner 3, rectification the feed box to limit surging, and installing an OK70 cell at the head of Cleaner 2. The simulations identified a possible increase in recovery of up to five per cent with a one per cent increase in concentrate grade when compared to the plant performance data. 

While optimising Cleaner 1, it was found the concentrate from the first cell of each Cleaner 1 bank could be maintained at the mechanical cleaners final concentrate grade. The concentrate from these cells was diverted to the head of the Cleaner 3 bank. To achieve this, a VF-150 pump was installed to transfer the concentrate from the first cell of Cleaner 1B, while the concentrate launder at th

e first cell of Cleaner 1A was redirected to the concentrate hopper in Cleaner 2 which feeds Cleaner 3. 

Due to limited space at the front of the Cleaner 2 bank and the relatively small anticipated improvement in recovery, the Cleaner 2 feed box could not be modified to eliminate short circuiting that caused surging in the first cell. 

Space constraints also prohibited the installation of the OK70 cell at the head of Cleaner 2, but rather an OK20 was installed which would provide similar benefits to the performance at a reduced cost. This new cell is located below Cleaner 2 and its concentrate is pumped to the Cleaner 2 concentrate hopper and tailings are pumped to the front of the original Cleaner 2. It was decided to feed the new OK20 cell with Cleaner 1B concentrate only, removing four metres of head from this line which was a known constraint. 

The redirection of the Cleaner 1B concentrate line combined with the dampening through the new cell reduced the amount of surging experienced by Cleaner 2. This resulted in better control of the first cell, eliminating the need to modify the Cleaner 2 feed box. 

###### **Cleaner circuit automation** 

Metallurgical test work and analysis identified how to operate the plant under steady state conditions. If an automated solution is to hold the plant at its identified optimal points, it must be able to deal with all normal disturbances from variations. This includes from feed types, to the failure of instrumentation and equipment used by the automation. If the automation is susceptible to disturbances, it will be disabled by the operator. 

###### **Dealing with noise** 

The on-stream analyser (OSA) sometimes provides a reading that deviates from expected readings caused by a short-term disturbance in the plant or sampling system. Under normal operating conditions, the OSA grade readings change slowly with changes in the feed to the plant. On the occasions the feed type to the plant changes quickly, there will be a jump in the OSA reading followed by a successive reading similar to the previous reading. A poor reading caused by a process disturbance or a sampling error will cause a spike in the OSA reading and then return to the norm. 

The first attempt to eliminate the effect of this ‘noise’ was to pause the control logic if the OSA reading deviation exceed a specific value. Determining the level of deviation that sets a good quality reading apart from a poor quality reading proved difficult. A first order difference equation to filter the discreet OSA removed the noise but tended to delay the signal using a large filter time constant. A shorter time constant did not delay the signal or remove the noise. 

The OSA copper grade measurement behaviour can be best described as a stochastic process. Individual readings are subject to random change while the overall long-term measurements are confined to specific boundaries determined by the mineralogy of the feed type and the performance of the cleaner

banks. As the process normally changes slowly, it is assumed that the smaller the change is between successive OSA readings, the greater the probability the measurement is true. The required filter should vary the filter time constant depending on the probability of a reading error. A true stochastic filter varies the filter constant depending on the difference between the new reading and the predicted new reading. The level of accuracy of a predicted reading in the cleaners is low due to the lack of measurements of the physicals that influence the flotation behaviours. The assumption is made the process is stable and the predicted OSA reading is equal to the last OSA reading. If there is no difference between two subsequent readings, the two reading can be considered to be accurate and no filtering is required. As the absolute difference between two subsequent readings increases, the probability there is an error in the new reading increases. ###### _Jameson Cell air flow and froth depth control_ 

As identified during the metallurgical analysis of the Jameson Cell, increasing the air to pulp ratio increases the Sb which in turn reduces the grade and recovery. The increased air flow increases the amount of froth generated which reduces the time for a bubble to reach the lip of the cell. In a similar way the froth depth effects the grade, increasing the froth depth increases the time to reach the lip. The combination of air flow and froth depth determines the mass recovery and concentrate grade of the cell, each with their own mechanisms. To effectively control the Jameson Cell the air flow and froth depth controllers are linked together.

The air to pulp ratio is controlled to maintain the concentrate grade above the setpoint of 28.5 per cent copper. If the concentrate grade increases beyond the setpoint, the air to pulp ratio is increased, increasing the mass recovered by the Jameson Cell. The Jameson Cell concentrate hopper level is maintained by controlling the discharge pump speed. If the concentrate hopper level exceeds the setpoint, the air to pulp ratio is reduced, reducing the mass recovered by the Jameson Cell. The two air to pulp ratio controllers are configured as a pair of constraint controllers where the non-controlling controller uses the actual applied ratio to calculate its output to ensure control is gracefully transferred between controllers. The air to pulp ratio is limited from 0.25 to 0.75 as identified during the test work. 

The froth depth also controls the Jameson Cell concentrate

grade and the concentrate hopper level as per the air to pulp ratio. There is a bias between the two controllers that will cause the froth depth to be the primary control if the concentrate grade increases slowly. Sudden changes in the Jameson Cell copper concentrate grade will allow both the air to pulp ratio and the froth depth controller to react simultaneously, making the overall control robust to disturbances and able to maintain tight steady state control. Figure 11 – Jameson Cell air and froth depth controller. ###### **Cleaner 1 automation** Both Cleaner 1 banks are fitted with froth analysers which measure the velocity of the froth going over the lip in centimetres per second (cm/sec). The control of the cleaner banks can be broken down into a number of steps. First, the froth velocity of each cell must be controlled to a setpoint by using the froth depth and the air flow rate. Then the concentrate grade is controlled by determining the appropriate froth velocity setpoints. ###### _Froth velocity control_ The froth velocity is proportional to the number of bubbles that leave the pulp phase within the cell, less the number of bubbles that collapse on the journey to the lip of the cell. The number of bubbles that collapse is proportional to the froth stability and the time taken to reach the lip. The time taken to reach the lip is proportional to the distance to travel over the velocity. Velocity is determined by the number of bubbles that survive the journey. From this it can be deduced that when treating stable froth, froth depth has little effect on froth velocity, the volume of air used to create the froth has the major impact. Similarly, the froth depth has a large influence on froth velocity when treating unstable froth. Stable froth is normally observer when the froth depth is deep while unstable froth is observed when the froth depth is shallow. The actual current froth depth is a proxy for the froth stability which determines the dynamics of the froth and should then also be used to determine the behaviour of the froth velocity controller. The air flow to froth velocity relationship is very direct and is therefore ideal to quickly change the froth velocity. The froth velocity controller implemented at Phu Kham makes uses two velocity controllers: one that controls the froth depth, and another that controls air flow. The froth depth

controls the froth velocity via ZIC1; the gain of this controller varies according to the froth depth. At a shallow froth depth, the process gain is high requiring a low controller gain, while at a deep froth depth, the controller gain is higher. The controller is configured as a PI sample and hold controller only acting when a new froth velocity measurement is received. The controller calculates the deviation from the current froth depth process variable providing control even if the froth depth controller has deviated from the setpoint. Metallurgical test work proved the ideal froth depth and air flow profiles across the banks in Cleaner 2 and 3. As the grades and flotation kinetics of the ore being treated changes, the air flow rates and froth depths will need to change. The copper tailings grade of both Cleaner 2 and 3 increases if the feed grade to the banks increases or if the flotation kinetics degrade. In both cases, the cleaners should recovery more mass to reduce the tailings grade. 

In the same way as the Jameson Cell had two interlinked concentrate controllers, Cleaner 2 and 3 make use of two tailings grade controllers, one for the air flow profile and one for the froth depth profile. The air flow controller responses quicker to deal with short-term disturbances, while the froth depth controller provides long-term guidance. The Cleaner 2 tailings grade controller changes the air flow and froth depth of the first cell of each bank. The subsequent cells air flow and froth depth are a ratio of the first cell as determined by the profile trials.

Figure 19 – Cleaner circuit performance histograms. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** In order to maximise the performance of a concentrator, a firm understanding of the metallurgical behaviours and the behaviours of the equipment must be developed. This information correctly identifies the bottlenecks, their solutions and the best operating strategies for the plant. Methods to ensure the plant is always running according to the strategies can then be implemented. In this case, an automated solution was adopted. At the Phu Kham Operation, a unique set of metallurgical tests were designed and conducted to accurately identify the behaviour of the equipment under different metallurgical conditions and a range of different setpoints. These tests were identified in papers published on the topic or were developed with the assistance of consultants. The data was analysed and correlated with historical test work and the results identified the bottlenecks and the best methods of operating the plant. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 PBM chose advanced automation solutions to ensure the Phu Kham plant is always running optimally as opposed to manually implementing operator guidelines. The automated control solution noticeably improved the stability of the plant, reduced the standard deviation in the recirculating loads, and increased recoveries and copper concentrate grades of the Jameson Cell and the mechanical cleaners. The cleaner circuits recovery increased by 3 per cent while the copper concentrate grade increased by 0.7 per cent. Successfully improving the performance of a mineral processing plant through automation must be approached as a project that identifies the behaviour of the equipment metallurgically and physically – both equally important. This information identifies the constraints of the plant and the best setpoints and profiles to operate the plant. An automated solution based on this information can then be developed and implemented. ###### **ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS** The writers of this paper acknowledge the metallurgists who conducted the trials required, metallurgical technicians who gathered the samples and the laboratory technicians who conducted all the tests at Phu Kham. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

SAG Mill process control classically maintains the SAG mill volumetric filling within a set operating range. Typically a SAG mill weight measurement, by either bearing pressure transducers or load cells, is used as an inferred measurement of volumetric filling. To maintain volumetric filling within a set operating range the SAG weight setpoint use for process control requires regular review due to changes in SAG mill charge density (rock:ball ratio) and the wearing of mill liners. At Lihir Gold Mine in Papua New Guinea, the use of SAG mill weight for process control is additionally complicated by compromised load cells and drifting bearing pressure measurements. The need for an improved method of measuring and controlling volumetric filling led to the recent installation of the Outotec MillSense, a SAG mill toe angle instrument. This paper presents the integration of the toe angle control in to the Lihir SAG mill process control philosophy as replacement for the traditional mill weight control.

and/or size|Hardness|Throughput constraint|Speed constraint| |High / Coarse|Hard or soft|High SAG mill load|Maximum SAG mill speed| |Low / Fine|Hard|High ball mill recirculating load|Low SAG mill load| |Low / Fine|Soft|Maximum throughput|Low SAG mill load| Table 1 – Process control constraints during normal operation. ###### **Background** Experienced SAG mill operators are familiar with the concept that an optimal volumetric mill filling exists which maximises the mill throughput rate of a set feed material. The grindcurve work of Powell and Mainza (2006) and Powell et al (2009) demonstrated that the optimal volumetric mill filling for maximum feedrate does not necessarily align with maximum power draw, especially for high aspect SAG mills. It follows that SAG mill process control systems that target maximum SAG motor power will not necessarily result in the maximum milling rate. Instead, SAG mill process control systems that aim to maximise SAG mill feedrate should target operation at the optimal volumetric mill filling for the prevailing feed. Despite the importance of volumetric mill filling, a measurement is not traditionally provided to the mill operator or metallurgist by instrumentation (Toor, 2015). However an inferred measurement can be made using a SAG mill weight measurement, using either bearing pressure transducers or load cells. Details of various SAG process control systems have been published extensively in literature (Karageorgos, 2006; Baas, 2014; Ruel, 2013; Smith et al, 2004). A common approach across these systems is to provide the mill operator with a SAG weight setpoint. Mill feedrate and mill speed (for VSD equipped mills) are manipulated by the control system to control mill weight to this setpoint. As mill feed competency and feed size changes, the optimal volumetric mill filling for maximum feedrate changes. The weight setpoint is adjusted by either an experienced operator or an advanced process control system in response to the feed changes. The SAG mill weight measurement combines mill shell mass, charge mass and liner mass. Powell (2006; 2009), via a series of mill charge inspections at various operating mill weights, confirmed that strong relationships can be developed between volumetric mill filling and mill weight. These relationships will only hold in the short term if ball charge is constant with time (changing charge density), and will not hold over the longer term due to wearing of mill liners (wearing liner mass) (Toor, 2015). Consequently to maintain volumetric filling within a set operating range, continual review of the weight setpoint is required due to changes in SAG mill charge density (rock:ball ratio) and the wearing of mill liners. ###### **EXISTING SAG MILL PROCESS CONTROL OF AT THE LIHIR PROCESS PLANT** 

###### **Description of constraint-based, advanced regulatory SAG mill control** 

A consistent process control philosophy is applied across the three Lihir SAG mills. An advanced regulatory control approach is deployed within the Lihir Process Plant’s Foxboro IA control system. As depicted in Figure 5 a series of advanced PID constraint controllers operate in parallel to manipulate SAG mill throughput and SAG mill speed until a circuit constraint is reached. 



Figure 5 – Simplified Process Control Diagram for SAG mills at Lihir - prior to Toe Angle Control. The approach increases SAG mill throughput until one of four throughput constraints is reached: 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

1. Maximum SAG throughput limit (SAG feed conveyor capacity); 

2. High SAG mill load (set by mill metallurgist or operator to desired volumetric filling); 

3. High SAG mill power (SAG mill motor rated capacity); and 

4. High ball mill recirculating load (cyclone feed pumping capacity). 

Once a throughput constraint is reached, the mill throughput is manipulated by the relevant adv

anced PID controller to consistently operate at that constraint. The prevailing throughput constraint is automatically selected by the Foxboro IA control system via automatic low signal selector. The throughput constraint controllers receive feed forward signal from pebble return rate and pebble crusher operating status (HGO1 and HGO2 only), and are configured with deadtime compensated control action. 

Simultaneously, the approaches increases SAG mill speed until one of following three speed constraints is reached: 

1. Maximum SAG speed (80 % critical speed); 

2. Low SAG mill load (fixed offset below high SAG mill load constraint); and 

3. High SAG mill noise (tolerable mill shell impact by steel limit as measured by an array of acoustic sensors mounted around the toe quarter of the SAG mill). 

Once a mill speed constraint is reached the mill speed is manipulated by the relevant advanced PID controller to consistently operate at that constraint. The prevailing mill speed constraint is automatically selected by the Foxboro IA control system via automatic low signal selector. The mill speed constraint controllers receive feed forward signal from the SAG mill throughput rate. 

Mill throughput rate is controlled to the constrained setpoint by a master PID controller which adjusts feeder speeds through a series of slave feeder ratio PID controllers. The ratio controllers allow the mill operator to set a specific drawn down ratio across the coarse ore stockpile and allow a near bumpless reallocation of feeder speeds in the event of a feeder trip or start-up. 

A density calculation ratios the SAG mill dilution water flowrate to the total SAG feedrate to achieve the mill operator-specified % solids setpoint, typically between 70-74 % solids. A density optimiser embedded in the Foxboro IA control system automatically applies a bias to the operator setpoint based on the SAG mill load deviation away from its high load setpoint. 

###### **Maximising SAG mill throughput when load constrained** 

Under normal operating conditions (eg correct SAG ball charge), the prevailing SAG mill process control constraints are determined by the characteristics of the ore being processed. In particular, feed size, ore competency and ore hardness lead to the Lihir Process Plant SAG mills operating under the process control constraints summarised in Table 1. 

When throughput is constrained by the high SAG mill load controller, it can be maximised by adjusting the high mill load setpoint to align with the optimal volumetric mill filling for the prevailing ore as outlined by Powel et al (2009). 

At the Lihir Process Plant, the task of adjusting the mill load setpoint is carried out by an experienced mill operator in conjunction with mill metallurgist (who also reviews ore source selection, primary crusher performance, COS stacking practices and pebble crusher performance). The task is complicated by suddenly drifting load cell and bearing pressure relationships with v

olumetric filling on the HGO1 and HGO2 SAG mills, as discussed below. This drifting behaviour means that an optimised mill load setpoint that delivered maximum throughput at the start of a shift, is likely not the optimal mill load setpoint later in that shift even though the same ore is being fed throughout. 

To assist selection of the high mill load setpoint, the Lihir metallurgy team explored a technique similar to that outlined by Toor (2015) to determine whether a SAG mill is operating at the desired volumetric mill filling, independently of mill weight and liner wear. 

The technique estimates the prevailing total filling by utilising the Morrell power model for tumbling mills; the actual mill speed and power draw as provided the by the plant control system; and also the current ball charge as estimated by a daily steel mass balance of the mill. This method requires accurate accounting by the plant operators of daily ball addition; and by the metallurgists of medium term steel media consumption rates. In addition, regular SAG ball charge inspections are required to baseline the steel media mass balance and zero accumulated errors. 

For Lihir, this technique was not successful due to an inaccurate daily estimate of the SAG ball charge. ###### **SAG MILL LOAD MEASUREMENT AT LIHIR GOLD MINE** 

Historically, the Lihir Process Plant has utilised the bearing pressure to calculate load measurement for the HGO1 SAG mill. This reading has historically been unreliable with regard to both accuracy and precision. 

The HGO1 SAG mill utilises hydrostatic slipper bearings at both the feed and discharge ends which have a forced lubrication spherical seat for self-alignment. Pressure transmitters are installed on each bearing, two at the feed end and two at the discharge end. The mill weight was calculated using an average of the feed end bearings. 

The precision and accuracy of the system was impacted by: 

- Changes in the temperature of the lubrication oil impact the pressure, which as a result, influence the weight calculation. The temperature control

for the bearing supply oil maintained the reservoir temperature despite the heat exchanger discharge being located between the reservoir and bearing; 

- Small changes in the bearing alignment caused by both planned and unplanned starting and stopping of the mill caused step changes of the bearing pressure. The front end bearings were more susceptible to alignment changes due to the axial load imparted by the mill drivetrain. Manual operation of the spherical seat alignment pump had some success in mitigating the step change of the bearing pressure; and 

- The bearing design uses a hydrodynamic bearing that has been modified to be hydrostatic. 

The Lihir Process Plant made efforts to address these issues by: 

- Mechanical locking the feed end bearing in an attempt to avoid changes in alignment; 

- Changing the load calculation to use the discharge end bearings rather than the feed end bearings. The discharge end bearings were not exposed to the same axial forces as the feed end bearings during starting and stopping the mills; 

- Tuning of the lube oil temperature process control; and 

- Relocation of the bearing lubrication oil control temperature sensor to a position in bearing supply piping (post heat exchanger) from the lube oil reservoir (pre-heat exchanger). 

These issues would result in events where there were changes in the mill load between stopping and restarting a mill. The majority of these events would increase the apparent load reading causing the control to decrease mill throughput to reduce the perceived high load. An example is shown in Figure 7. The standard operational responses to a mis-alignment event was to: bypass the constraint controllers and manually set the milling rate until the bearing alignment corrected; manually operate the spherical seat pump; and/or stop the mill to disengage the clutch and let the mill settle on the bearings. ###### **DESCRIPTION OF THE OUTOTEC MILLSENSE TOE ANGLE MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENTATION** 

In many cases, grinding mill power draw, bearing pressure and other typically available measurements are not ideal variables for optimal grinding process control. To address the need for a more reliable state indicator with robust control, Outotec has developed the MillSense system for analysing and controlling a grinding mill’s volumetric charge. MillSense works by identifying the position of the charge inside the mill, which is accomplished by continuously measuring the vibration and strain of a liner bolt. The following sections describe both the analysis equipment and the mathematical principle. 

###### **System components** 

The MillSense system consists of an on-bolt sensor unit, an on-shell transmitter, a radio receiver, a connection cabinet, an inductive charging station and an analysis computer. Figure 9 shows the equipment and their locations on the shell and near the mill. 



Figure 9 – MillSense field equipment. 

###### **On-shell transmitter** 

The on-shell transmitter gathers data from the on-bolt sensors (up to 3) through a digital bus and transmits this data to the analysis system. The transmitter is attached to the mill shell using a base plate that uses super strong neodymium magnets as a secure mounting mechanism, with a layer of double-sided tape on the bottom of each magnet to provide friction. The combination of magnets and tapes provides approximately 7,200 N of force in the normal direction and 4000 N in the tangential direction. The amount of force is huge in comparison to the transmitter weight, making it impossible for the transmitter to become detached from the mill. The magnet-based mounting mechanism is ideal, because it is suitable for all mills and doesn’t complicate the work of the relining crew. 

###### **On-bolt sensor** 

The on-bolt sensor features a circular strain gauge, designed to accurately measure the liner bolt’s tension. The sensor also has a three-dimensional accelerometer that serves two purposes: reliably determining the mill revolution’s start and end times and measuring the bolt’s vibration. This is the only component that needs to be handled during mill relining, and the analysis software has been designed such that it allows the sensor to be reattached in any orientation. These features ensure that the system stays functional after the relining process.

###### **Inductive charging station** 

The on-shell components need power to function, but it is not convenient to use potentially unreliable pendulums or batteries in an instrument that needs to remain reliable in all conditions. That is why Outotec chose to use an inductive charging station to power the on-shell electronics. This has the added benefit of providing a means of shutting down or resetting the on-shell system components, even when the mill is running. For quick testing purposes, the on-shell components can also use battery power. 

###### **Receiver** 

The radio receiver collects data packets from the transmitter and sends them to the analysis computer by hard-wired TCP/IP communications. The receiver is mounted in a fixed location adjacent to the on-shell transmitter, that provides the greatest possible amount of time with a line of site between the transmitter and receiver. For the HGO1 MillSense installation, the receiver was mounted the receiver approximately 10 metres away from the mill, providing line of sight to approximately ¼ of a shell revolution. 

###### **Analysis computer** 

The analysis computer gathers the data packets into continuous signals, determines where a revolution starts and ends and finally calculates the charge position from the revolution’s profiles. The computer can be – based on preference – an industrial PC that is placed directly in the cabinet, a separate server computer or a virtual computer. The HGO1 MillSense installation made use of an existing separate server (previously installed for Outotec FrothSense camera instrumentation), that communicated to the Foxboro IA via MODBUS communication protocol. 

###### **Charge volume measurement** 

MillSense can detect the mill toe angle either from the revolution’s bolt strain or bolt vibration profile. When considering the strain profile, the toe can be identified by finding the point where the signal changes most rapidly. When the vibration signal is used, the toe can be found at or near the maximum. Figure 10 illustrates the vibration and strain profiles for a single mill revolution.

In steel-lined mills, the vibration signal usually produces a more consistent toe angle measurement, while the strain signal tends to be extremely clear in rubber-lined mills.
