Even though MillSense was successfully installed on 5 SAG and AG mills around the world prior to this installation, the Lihir HGO1 SAG mill forced a review many of the design choices in MillSense. The following sections describe the biggest challenges and their respective resolutions. ###### **Preventing the mechanical failure of on-bolt sensors** After a successful initial installation and approximately two months of operation, intermittent losses were experienced in the acceleration signals measured by the on-bolt sensor. The sensor eventually failed altogether, and it turned out that the unusually powerful shell vibration of the SAG mill had caused the accelerometer chip to become detached from the sensor’s circuit board. It is worth mentioning that this happened despite the sensor’s electronics being moulded inside a protective epoxy casing. This issue was resolved by switching the accelerometer chip to a model that has better soldering properties and improving the soldering process and the associated quality assurance. When the sensor with the failed accelerometer chip was replaced, another problem presented itself; the replacement sensor was broken during bolt torqueing. Consequently, a special washer (refer to Figure 11) was designed that can be anchored into position during installation, thereby protecting the sensor from the torque. (b)

Figure 11 – (a) MillSense sensor with the protective washer (b) Installation with protective washer. ###### **Dealing with a limited wireless communication window** In MillSense installations, the radio receiver placement must be chosen such that the communication window, i.e. the amount of time during a mill revolution that the receiver and transmitter are visible to one another, is maximized. In indoors installation, this usually means placing the receiver in an elevated location in relation to the mill, but this is obvious

ly harder to achieve in outdoors processes, such as at the Lihir Process Plant. To make the system work with a shorter communication window, the radio communication packet structure was redesigned such that one radio packet can contain several signal samples. This is more efficient, because the radio packet header doesn’t need to be repeated for each sample, reducing the time required for the transmitter and receiver to be in line-of-sight for complete transfer of data.

###### **Achieving an accurate toe angle measurement from bolt vibration** 

After the installation, initial analysis of the process data indicated that the vibration-based toe angle measurement provided a quality measurement of the charge toe angle. However, the most obvious method of locating the vibration curve’s maximum value did not yield the most stable results, since the curve frequently experiences small changes in shape. This issue was addressed by defining a crossing value (e.g. 90 % of maximum vibration) and implementing an algorithm that locates the centroid of the curved area above said crossing value. The resulting toe angle signal has less noise, because the centroid is more constant than the maximum. 

###### **Coping with harsh environmental conditions** 

The combination of Lihir Process Plant’s tropical climate and the mill’s powerful vibration proved very effective at exposing components in the MillSense system that didn’t have a sufficient IP rating or operating temperature range. Each of these design oversights were corrected. 

###### **Implementing the improvements** 

Frequent communication between the development team in Finland and the Lihir Process Plant’s Technical Services metallurgists, combined with systematic follow-up via a secure remote access system, made it possible to overcome the technical challenges and keep the implementation of improvements on track. As a result, MillSense is now a significantly more robust instrument than before this project. 

###### **ASSESSMENT OF THE QUALITY OF THE TOE ANGLE MEASUREMENT** 

After the MillSense was commissioned and subsequent reliability improvements were completed, the Lihir Process Plant’s technical services group began a process of validating the MillSense toe angle signal as an improved measurement of the total volumetric mill filling over the existing HGO1 SAG mill bearing pressure based load measurement. 

Two approaches were employed to validate the toe angle signal. 

Firstly, the total volumetric mill filling during operation was estimated using the Morrell power model for tumbling mills; the actual mill speed and power draw as provided by the plant control system; and also the current ball charge. ###### **Instrument fault detection and response** 

Measurements from the MillSense instrument are received across a MODBUS communication link from the Outotec ACT server, rather than standard analogue 4-20mA signal from a hard-wired field instrument. Fault detection logic specific for the MillSense instrument signals was required due to this configuration. 

A heartbeat signal exists to allow the DCS to identify if a fault has occurred in the MODBUS communications link or if the ACT server has failed. 

If a MillSense sensor fails (e.g. loses field radio communications or loses field power) the DCS will still receive toe angle signals from the Outotec ACT server without indication of an instrument fault. Thus sensor validity status signals for MillSense sensors are provided from the Outotec ACT server to indicate if a field fault has occurred and the sensor is unhealthy. 

A DCS based MillSense watchdog monitors the sensor validity status signal and the MODBUS communications heartbeat. The watchdog generates a signal for alarming, bypassing and interlocking functions whenever a MillSense sensor is considered to be in an unhealthy state. 

If a MillSense sensor that is actively being used for process control is detected to have failed, a series of mill control protection actions occur. Initially, an operator alarm is generated and the toe angle controllers are placed in to a hold condition. If after a specified delay the sensor status has not returned to normal, the stockpile reclaim feeders will be stopped on a process interlock. After a further delay, the toe angle controllers will be bypassed until the MillSense fault clears. This allows the mill operator to restart the milling circuit whilst the MillSense failu

re is investigated. 

###### **Toe angle control integration** 

The integration of toe angle control in the existing HGO1 SAG mill process control philosophy was as a direct replacement of the existing high and low load controllers. The existing constraint based, advanced regulatory control structure was retained. The new process control configuration is presented in Figure 15. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 



Figure 15 – Simplified process control diagram for SAG mills at Lihir – after toe angle control. 

Two advanced PID controllers, high and low toe angle controllers, were used to achieve toe angle control. The setpoints of the two controllers were offset by a fixed bias. The high toe angle controller targeted a higher toe angle setpoint by manipulating SAG mill throughput rate. The low toe angle controller targeted a lower toe angle setpoint by manipulating SAG mill speed. The two controllers, together with the their biased setpoints, work to maximise SAG mill speed or to maximise SAG milling rate depending on whether the prevailing ore is competent, hard ore or is not competent, soft ore. 

Both controllers use feed forward action to reduce the disturbance caused by the operation of the pebble crushers (high toe angle controllers) and by the changes in milling rate (low toe angle controllers); and use dead time compensation to account for the delayed process response to controller output actions.

The MillSense toe angle control was implemented in March 2018. It was commissioned approximately 2 weeks prior to a planned mill reline. ###### **CONCLUSION** 

Controlling the volumetric filling in the mill is necessary to optimise the throughput rate.  Traditionally, volumetric filling has been inferred by controlling to a total mill weight either from bearing pressure or load cells. Mill weight is destabilised by two factors, decreasing liner mass and changing charge density. Lihir Process Plant had the additional difficultly that the bearing pressure and load cell derived measurements had historically been shown to be both inaccurate and unrepeatable. Recognising these issues, the Lihir Process Technical Services team, with the assistance of Outotec, installed a MillSense toe angle measurement instrument on the HGO1 SAG mill. Despite encountering initial technical challenges, utilising charge toe angle in a process control scheme has been demonstrated to be a viable alternative and better alternative to the use of mill weight at Lihir Process Plant. 

The toe angle was shown through a review of mill inspections and operational data to have a stronger correlation than the incumbent mill weight reading. This allowed the toe angle signal to be integrated within Lihir’s advanced regulatory control system for the HGO1 SAG mill as a direct replacement for the mill weight. 

Initial results indicate that toe angle control has delivered a b

enefit to Lihir process control by being repeatable measurement, consistent through process interruptions and independent of mill liner wear. Quantifiable production improvements were not available at the time of writing, but improved control of

volumetric filling was achieved and a reduced the risk of further mill overload events was realised by the implementation of toe angle control on the HGO1 SAG mill.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Nova Operation (Nova) is wholly owned by the Independence Group NL. The processing plant is in the Fraser Range of Western Australia, about 120km east of Norseman. It utilises differential flotation to produce separate Copper and Nickel concentrates (IGO 2017). Construction and commissioning of the processing plant was completed in late 2016. 

Since the early feasibility phases of the project, the importance of automation and control was recognised and planned for to ensure that the plant performance would achieve the design expectations. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

An advanced process control system has been implemented by Process IQ Pty Ltd on the complete milling and flotation circuits at Nova. This paper focusses on the implementation and benefits of the advanced control on the copper rougher-scavenger circuit. 

The control was implemented on the StarCS control platform, which was developed by Mintek (Mintek 2016). Mintek has a range of application specific modules that run on the StarCS platform, like the FloatStar Advanced Level Stabiliser which is used for stabilisation and disturbance rejection in flotation cell level control, and the FloatStar Optimisers that control the grade, recovery and concentrate pull rates on a bank of cells. 

The Nova circuit was designed with automated optimisation in mind and therefore included advanced instrumentation from the start, including the Blue Cube MQi and Blue Cube TempoTracks. The Blue Cube MQi (Mineral Quantifier Inline) Slurry Analyser gives fast, accurate and reliable in-line measurements of the elemental and mineral composition of plant feed, tailing and concentrate slurries. The Blue Cube TempoTrack is designed for use on flotation cells to measure the froth velocity and froth height above the cell lip. 

The objective of the control system on the copper rougher-scavenger circuit was to optimise the copper recovery while minimising the nickel recovery. It was done by implementing the following strategies: 

- Ensure the stability of the circuit by utilising the FloatStar Advanced Level Stabiliser. 

- Ensure a stable Mass Flow is recovered in the concentrate stream by adjusting the level and air setpoints of the cells. 

- Adjust the concentrate mass pull target based on the copper feed grade (from the online Blue Cube MQi) and feed rate to the circuit. 

- Balance the pull rate from individual cells in the bank to a pre-defined ratio as set by the plant metallurgists. The pull rates from the individual cells are determined from the TempoTrack measurements (installed on each flotation cell). 

- Maintain a steady pressure and d

ensity from the copper rougher concentrate hopper discharge. The concentrate line is equipped with a pressure gauge, flow meter and density meter (Mass flow is calculated based on the flow rate and density). 

The benefits of the system will be discussed in the final sections of this paper after the implementation and interfacing is explained. 

###### **PROCESS OVERVIEW** 

This section provides a general overview of the processing plant in order to explain where this project fits in. 

The concentrator crushing circuit comprises of a single stage, open circuit jaw crusher that reduces run of mine (ROM) ore to an 80 per cent passing size of 90 mm and conveyors that deliver the ore to a 375 t surge hopper. Coarse crushed ore is ground in a two-stage grinding circuit that comprises of an open loop semi-autogenous (SAG) mill and an overflow ball mill in closed circuit with hydrocyclones. The ore is reduced to an 80 per cent passing size of 75 μm. The cyclone overflow undergoes differential, sequential flotation to produce separate copper and nickel concentrates. Both flotation circuits are comprised of a rougher/scavenger flotation stage followed by two stages of cleaning. An on-stream analyser (OSA) and several Blue Cube MQi analysers are provided to assist in management of metallurgical performance. 

The copper and nickel concentrates produced in flotation are thickened in separate high rate thickeners. The thickened concentrates are pumped to dedicated concentrate storage tanks prior to filtration via separate chamber filter presses. Filtered concentrates are loaded into trucks for shipment off site. 

Two separate tailings streams are produced - a non-sulphide tailings from the nickel scavengers tails and a sulphide tailing from the nickel cleaner scavenger tails. Both tailings streams are thickened in dedicated thickeners. Non-sulphide tailings report either to the paste plant, where it is filtered by a belt filter, mixed with cement/binder and deposited as paste fill underground, or it bypasses the paste filter and mixer and is pumped to the tailings storage facility (TSF). Sulphide tailings are pumped direct to the TSF for storage. 

The reagent mixing system consists of manual solid mixing facilities for potassium amyl xanthate (PAX) and sodium sulphite and automated mixing systems for the quicklime (delivered in bulk) and flocculant. Other reagents consisting of tri-ethyl tetra amine (TETA) and frother Methyl Isobutyl Carbinol (MIBC) are delivered as solutions. PAX, sodium sulphite and TETA are delivered to the process via a system of constant head tanks

and dosing valves. Frother is dosed via dedicated variable speed dosing pumps. Lime is delivered to the process via dosing valves while flocculant is delivered by dedicated variable speed dosing pumps. 

###### **Copper rougher scavenger circuit layout** 

Figure 1 illustrates the physical circuit layout fo

r the Copper rougher scavenger Circuit at IGO’s Nova site. The circuit is fed from the Copper Rougher Feed Conditioning tank. There is a Blue Cube MQi on the discharge end of this conditioning tank. The measurement from the Blue Cube MQi is used to determine the  per cent copper in the feed. This copper measurement, along with the solids feed rate into the SAG Mill, is used in a calculation to determine the desired Mass Pull Target for the copper rougher-scavenger circuit. 

There is a single Rougher cell of which the level can be manipulated via a pinch valve. The air flow rate is controlled through a valve and it is the setpoints for these two variables that are used to control the mass pull from the Rougher cell. There are 4 Scavenger cells in the circuit. The levels of the first and second Scavenger cells are controlled using a single pinch valve, similarly the third and fourth Scavenger cell levels are controlled through a single pinch valve. All four cells can have their air addition flow rate individually manipulated. 

The concentrate from all the cells is combined into a single concentrate hopper. The discharge of the concentrated hopper can feed the regrind circuit or bypass the regrind circuit. The discharge line of the concentrate hopper has a pressure measurement as well as a flow and density measurement that is combined to calculate the total mass pull from the circuit.

The hopper’s pump may then be run to a pressure setpoint on the hopper discharge.

charge, the pressure setpoint is altered slowly, by increasing the pressure setpoint, more water needs to be added to the hopper to maintain the hopper level, this results in a decrease in the discharge density. The converse is also true for decreasing the pressure setpoint, less water is added to the hopper and the density increases. Since fluctuations in the pressure are undesirable the density control is a very slow acting loop on the pressure setpoint (i.e. the density setpoint will not be maintained very tightly). The operator has the option to enable different parts of the control strategy (for example the pressure setpoint may be run at a manually entered value). Separate control loops have also been implemented to aid in maintaining CRSC hopper’s Level between a minimum and maximum setpoint (user defined) during abnormal circumstances when the mass pull rate (see below) cannot be achieved. Should the hopper approach its minimum level setpoint the pump will slow down (the pressure setpoint will no longer be maintained) and the water addition setpoint to the hopper will increase more aggressively (the density setpoint will also not be maintained). Should the hopper approach its maximum level, the pump speed will increase (the pressure setpoint will no longer be maintained). The water addition setpoint will also decrease more aggressively and consequently the density setpoint will no longer be maintained. The FloatStar Level Stabiliser is designed to look at the interaction between different flotation cells and is able to compensate for interactions between cells quickly and effectively. Disturbances entering a train of cells will not propagate to downstream cells, since the controller will react t

o these disturbances in a timely manner and allows all the valves to move appropriately in response to a disturbance. The control system will therefore not wait until the disturbances reaches a cell before it reacts, as is the case with simpler control loops that only look at individual cell levels when moving the valves. 

In short, this means that the FloatStar Level Stabiliser will, in a particular flotation circuit, open downstream valves by the correct amount when a disturbance is detected in the preceding levels. 

To aid stability, the effect of the flow rate into the Copper rougher is also taken into account when controlling the banks (Feed Forward Control). The FloatStar Level Stabiliser is applied to the whole flotation plant, including the following three levels in the section under consideration:

###### **Mass pull target for the CRS concentrate stream** 

The target for the Mass pull rate for the controller is based on a formula that takes into account the copper units coming into the circuit and the desired recovery for the circuit. In order to aid in accounting for the time delay between the material entering the SAG Mill and the material entering the flotation circuit, a 30-minute moving average of the Solids feed rate is used in the mass pull target calculation. 

There are several functions available to the user to alter the manner in which the mass pull target is calculated. 

Shown on Figure 5 point 3: The option is available on the StarCS screen to enter a manual target in the cases when a copper grade measurement is unavailable. In order to tell the system to stop using the calculated target and utilise a manual target the checkbox on Figure 5 at point 1 should be unchecked. Should the Blue Cube Measurement fault, the controller will utilise the manual target. Since the manual target may become outdated when not in use, it will update once every 30 minutes to the calculated target (only when it is not in use). 

If the copper grade measurement has a known offset, this can be entered on the StarCS screen to correct the calculation. This offset is entered on Figure 5 at point 4, the offset is simply added to the measured copper grade. 

A build-up of an inventory in the flotation bank could result in the integrity of the froth being compromised and will influence the processes’ ability to produce a concentrate. For this reason, the error between the Mass Pull Target and the actual mass pull is integrated.  This integrated error is then used to increase the mass pull target (but never decrease) and thus the optimiser will be able to ‘catch up’ if the mass pull is below target for a period of time. The FloatStar Optimiser has been developed by Mintek to provide continuous, online optimisation of circuit operation throughout fluctuating plant conditions (Muller 2005). The FloatStar Optimiser is highly 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 configurable. The strategy was further expanded to incorporate froth velocity measurements to achieve the system targets. The behaviour of the circuit (ultimately the final grade and recovery) will be influenced by, amongst others, the level setpoints, aeration rates, the bank residence times and reagent addition. The FloatStar Optimiser uses multivariable control techniques to continually optimise air and level setpoints (shown in Figure 6) to achieve the desired mass pull, while reagent additions are ratioed to what’s coming into the circuit. The optimiser is enabled by placing any of the copper rougher Scavenger Level or Air controllers into SCS CAS mode. This can be done from the PID interface blocks on the SCADA or from the StarCS screen (see Figure 5 Point 7). On the StarCS Screen there is the option to enable all or disable all the SCS CAS modes with a single group button. If the controllers are put into SCS CAS mode from the StarCS screen, then the controller will automatically be placed into SCS mode as well (if not already enabled). When the controllers are taken out of SCS CAS mode from the StarCS screen, they will not automatically go out of SCS mode. Each of the flotation banks is equipped with a Blue Cube TempoTrack in the field. This instrument provides measurements of the froth velocity and froth height. These values give an indication of how much material is being pulled from each flotation bank. The measurements are modularly incorporated in the control to balance how the cells pull material (for example having the front of the train pull harder than the back end of the train). Internally the controller incorporates the use of these measurements to adjust the Base Values of each of the control variable setpoints. The Base Values define an offse

t from which the control variables should deviate in a configurable ratio with respect to other control variables. 

The use of the TempoTrack measurements directly impacts the Base Values for the air setpoints and indirectly impacts the Base Values for the level setpoints. This is because the Base Values for the level setpoints are based on a linear relationship with the Base Values of the air flow rate setpoints. When the TempoTrack measurements are enabled for a particular cell, the Base Value for the air setpoint for that particular cell will be adjusted. These can be switched on and off from the checkboxes shown in Figure 5 Point 8. One can choose to have the level Base Values adjusted as well by checking the box shown in Figure 5 Point 9 (however not required). 

The strategy was setup such that not every cell has to use the TempoTrack measurements in order for the strategy to function. If there is a problem on a particular cell the strategy can be disabled for that cell. The same is true for putting the air and level loops into SCS CAS; any cells that are experiencing problems can be left off and the controller will use the remaining cells to achieve the desired targets. 

Figure 8 shows the main inputs and outputs that are used for the StarCS Optimiser. One can see that a weighting is placed on each of the control variables (level and air setpoints), these weightings are used to determine how much each of the control variables move relative to the others. This enables the user to decide for example how much faster the air flow rate setpoints will change relative to a change in the level setpoints. At the time of writing this paper the air flow rate setpoints were set to move three times faster than the level setpoints.

###### **Fault detection and error handling within the StarCS Optim

iser** 

A great deal of effort was put into the control system to handle errors and faults that may arise with instrumentation and equipment in the field. Since the controller was built in a modular manner, parts of the system can be disabled while still allowing the system to achieve the required targets (up to a point). The following is a list of some of the faults that the system will check for: 

- Check that a froth velocity measurement does not remain unchanged for a long period of time. 

- Check that the froth velocity measurements are within a predefined range. 

   - If a froth velocity is below a threshold, then ensure that the level setpoint and air flow rate on that cell is not lowered further. 

- Check that the Copper Feed Grade measurements are within a predefined range. 

- Check that the percent solids in the copper feed is within a predefined range. 

- Check that the Copper Feed Grade measurements do not remain unchanged for a long period of time. 

- Check that there is feed to the SAG Mill. 

- Check that the actual levels and airs are within a band from their respective setpoints.

###### Optimising flotation plant operation by using a digital twin in the control room 

###### _S J Oliver_<sup>_1_</sup> _and R Tooher_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. Principal Technical Consultant, MathWorks, Sydney NSW 2067. Email: sam.oliver@mathworks.com.au 2. Superintendent Metallurgist, Newcrest, Perth WA 8000. Email: ryan.tooher@newcrest.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The operation of copper flotation circuit is a challenging task for the site metallurgists and plant operators. To optimise the performance requires meeting both grade and recovery objectives. These plants have numerous pieces of equipment that are monitored by hundreds of sensors. The challenge is to review these sensors and adjust the numerous control inputs to maintain peak operational efficiency for extended periods. There is also a need to respond to equipment failure. These challenges lead to in operational inefficiencies and can result in a reduction in revenue. 

This paper details an overview of an operational assistance tool implemented at Newcrest's Telfer plant’s copper flotation circuit. This tool is based on a digital twin of the plant. A digital twin is a model of the plant that is simulated in parallel to the normal plant operation. It is fed with the plant data in real time to provide a prediction of plant operation. The model outputs directly generate the metrics that are used to assess the plant performance, and these are compared with the metrics calculated from the actual plant’s operation. Deviations between the model estimate and the plant’s actual performance are used to gather insight into plant health and alert the operator to poor performance. The operators gather more information regarding the root cause by reviewing the model’s inputs that have deviated outside their normal operating range. An evaluation of the plant performance, following the commissioning of the digital twin, showed an overall reduction of acid soluble copper in the tails. 

This paper discusses the implementation of a digital twin of the plant to monitor plant performance during live operation. It will include details on data collection and cleansing, data reduction techniques, model development, and real-time implementation. The results of the case study of an implementation of a digital twin at Newcrest's Telfer copper flotation plant will be used throughout the paper. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Operation of a mineral processing plant, in particular a copper fl

otation circuit, is a challenging task for the site metallurgists and plant operators. It involves monitoring hundreds of sensors to determine the operational state or health of the plant. Often, the sensors don't directly measure plant health, and therefore, different operators can have varied interpretations. To maintain optimal operation efficiency, the plant requires periodic adjustment and changes to respond to events experienced by the plant. These events could include changes to the feed material, degradation of the plant equipment, or equipment failures. Even an expert operator finds this task challenging at the best of times, and they often perform this task in nonideal conditions such as at the end of a long shift and throughout the night. These challenges result in operational inefficiencies, and therefore, result in a reduction in revenue. 

The digital twin is the concept of combining models of the plant or process with operational data to provide ongoing insights (Pettey, 2017), (Parrott and Warshaw, 2017), (Forbes, 2017). These models are a composite of artefacts that characterise and predict behaviour of a specific real plant or process. The objective is to identify deviations from optimal operating conditions that are characterised by the models and use this to trigger an action. In some cases, this could be monitoring and evaluating wear and tear to identify maintenance events or provide guidance on potential operational efficiencies. This concept is over 30 years old, with early adoption in aerospace industries. It has become more widely applicable due to the availability of low-cost, scalable computing and storage resource options, particularly with modern cloud platforms. The modern framework of the ‘digital twin’ (Figure 1) requires system integration between the smart asserts, edge systems, operation technology (OT), and information technology (IT). Requirements such as response time, dependability, and data access determine where the smart algorithms are deployed across this framework. The term digital twin is widely used at the corporate IT level, but less adopted by people at the technical level. 

When considering the general concept of the digital twin in the context of metallurgy, there are numerous examples presented on modelling the flotation process. These leverage both classical first principles 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

mathematical (Jovanovic and Miljanovic, 2015b), and soft computing or machine learning techniques (Jovanovic, Miljanovic and Jovanovic, 2015). Applying models developed using these techniques to the direct and indirect control of a plant has yielded promising results, but there have been limited examples of implementing these techniques in production plant operations (Jovanovic and Miljanovic, 2015a). Successful trail applications of model predictive control (MPC), which uses model predictions to optimise plant performance as part of a direc

t control system, are discussed (Jovanovic and Miljanovic, 2015a). 

This paper, aims to highlight the process of developing a digital twin in a copper flotation plant operation, followed by the practical aspects of integrating this into a production environment. The model will take multiple sensor inputs and predict the production grade of the various parts of the floatation circuit. Once this model is embedded in the production operation system, it runs in real time alongside the physical plant. Deviations between the model and actual plant provide insight presented to the operators as circuit health scores. This along with additional sensor health checks directs the operators to the potential causes and potential remedies for the operational issues experienced through a response action plan. As a result, the operators are more efficiently able to respond to these issues throughout the shift, allowing increased production efficiencies. 



Figure 1 – Digital twin framework. 

###### **SYSTEM AND PROBLEM DESCRIPTION** 

The copper flotation circuits at the Newcrest Telfer site are organised into two trains. One takes feed from the open pit mine and the other is a combination of ore sources from open pit and underground cave mines. Essentially, the two trains are identical, so we focus on the flowchart (Figure 2) of the second train from this point on. 

The rougher circuit at the initial stage of the plant takes the feed material that is mixed with reagents. The rougher concentrate is then fed into a Jamerson Cell, which produces most of the final concentrate. The tails from the Jamerson Cell are fed into the cleaners and the cleaner scavengers. The concentrate from these cells is recirculated into the Jamerson Cell or the re-cleaners whilst the tails is recirculated back to the rougher feed. 

An initiative was created with the objective to reduce copper rejected to the tails whilst maintaining copper concentrate targets. The initiative focused on applying data science techniques, such as machine learning or soft computing, to leverage the existing physical plant assists to deliver on the objective. 

###### **DEVELOPING A PLANT MODEL OR DIGITAL TWIN** 

In this case, the digital twin or system to be modelled is the copper flotation circuit described in the previous section. 

Although there are numerous options for developing models, this modelling decision is based on the end application, configuration of the circuit, behaviour of the flotation cells, availability of sensors, and the quality of the data. For this study the end application of the model will be used to track deviations from normal behaviour to deliver insight to the operators. The available data is studied comprehensively to choose an appropriate modelling technique. 

The digital twin framework presented (Figure 1) is used discuss the key components and how they integrated into the production environment. In this case the operational technology (OT) is collocated with the flot

ation plant and is primarily made up of the distributed control system (DCS). Information technology (IT) components of the system exist both collocate with the plant (edge IT) and centrally on the cloud (central IT). The actual edge devices are typically smaller scale controller platforms attached to equipment within the plant are not relevant for this application.

MATLAB<sup>®</sup> and associated toolboxes were used to clean the data, implement the model, and deploy it into the production environment. 

###### **Data access and exploration** 

From the author’s experience, it is common for up to 80 per cent of the effort in data science and modelling projects to be spent during this phase of the project. 

In this case, the plant is monitored and controlled using the OT systems that include the distributed control system. This system provides hundreds of measurement channels known as tags, which are stored in a commercial grade historian. An application like this that involves logging streamed data is a big data application in disguise. Big data created a significant challenge during the data access and exploration phases of the project. 

To handle the big data challenge, a scalable cloud data storage architecture as part of the central IT infrastructure that was used to store the historical plant data. The data is routinely transferred from the historian to the cloud to ensure that the latest data is available. During the access and exploration phase of the project, the cloud provides a convenient way to access and slice the data from within or outside the organisation, which is important when collaborating with third-party organisations. 

It was critical during this phase to collaborate with a domain expert, in this case the plant metallurgist, to understand what data was available, how it mapped to the equipment within the plant, and how to differentiate phenomena created by sensor issues from plant performance issues. 

To speed up the data investigation and exploration, tooling that leveraged the map between the tags, equipment type, and location was created. This allowed tags to be filtered based on arbitrary characteristics, such as type and location, and then displayed the tags’ values over time. As it was visual, it allowed phenomena present in the data to be identified to determine the type of event and potential source of the issue. 

This case from the data exploration exposed the following: 

- Large variations in plant feed type and composition are present, 

- The plant periodically encountered periods of poor performance due to events that were triggered from various sources such as feed material changes and equipment failure, 

- Sensor reliability, spikes, and subsequently availability impacted the data quality, and 

- Online stream analysis sensors (MSA) that measured copper, iron, and percent solids were measured every 15 to 30 minutes, wh

ereas most other sensors were captured every 30 seconds. 

The MSA sensors provided the most tangible measurement of the plant’s end goal as they could be used to determine plant recovery and the target grade periodically during plant operation. Although more accurate spot grade measures were collected, the results from these were delayed by two days, and therefore, limited their useful application. Given this, the location of the MSA sensors limited the fidelity of the models. Their location provided guidance to the potential model boundaries. 

The sensor data was aggregated from 30-second to 15-minute intervals. This interval aligned with the typical process resonance times and measurement of MSA sensors. This aggregation allowed issues due to sensor noise and spikes to be filtered. It also had the added benefit of reducing issues when dealing with large amounts of data. 

###### **Model development** 

There are about 100 influential flotation variables required to characterise the flotation process including feed characteristics, physicochemical factors, and hydrodynamics (Jovanovic and Miljanovic, 2015b) (Jovanovic, Miljanovic, and Jovanovic, 2015). 

In this case, although machine learning techniques were adopted to model the flotation process, knowledge of the process principles was used throughout the modelling process. This was motivated by the project scope and timeframe, but also the need to develop a number models of various parts of the flotation circuit. 

It was quickly determined that a model of the entire flotation circuit was not viable. To better align with the operational goals of the various parts of the circuit and the availability of MSA sensors, it was separated into three models highlighted by the boxes in Figure 2. 

1. Rougher from the feed to the trail used to monitor the performance of the rougher which is focused on recovery. Green Box. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

2. Cleaner circuit from the rougher concentrate to the scavenger tails which is focused on recovery. Red Box. 

3. Cleaner circuit from the rougher concentrate to the final concentrate which is focused on producing the final concentrate grade. Red Box. 

This paper will focus on the model of the rougher highlighted by the green box in Figure 2. 

The model of the rougher included the entire bank of eight flotation cells as the MSA sensors are only available on the feed, tail, and concentrate streams. The model included reagent addition, feed material, cell froth level, dart valve position, air addition, pH, hopper levels, and pump speeds as predictors for the delta between the feed copper and tail copper concentrations. 

Knowledge of the process principles, and not statistical methods such as principle component analysis, was used to reduce the input data to from 60 down to 11 predictors. Primarily this was done by aggregating the same measured properties across all cells, for example cell air was det

ermined based on the sum of total air addition across the bank of eight cells. Therefore, the model inputs reflected physical measures of the plant which allowed them to be understood and interpreted from the domain experts and operators. This is important when shifting to the production implementation. 

When developing a machine learning model, it is important to ensure that the inputs have equal weighting. Normalisation using the z-score method, which is based on the mean and standard deviation, provided a more robust method than when compared to using the inputs min and max limits which are vulnerable to the data spikes. The z-score was calculated for each channel, or tag, by subtracting the mean (of the channel) from the raw value and then dividing by the standard deviation (of the channel). 

Models were developed using many machine learning techniques including linear model, support vector machines (SVM), various types of decision trees, and neural networks. It was found that best performing models were the linear model and the variant of the SVM that included a linear kernel. It was found that the more complex nonlinear models were fitting to sensor maintenance issues and various poor performance events, whereas the linear models rejected these events as outliers. It highlighted that more effort was required to train these complex models focusing on modelling the healthy plant performance. Also, leveraging a classification model used to help identify predictions that are outside the data range used to train the model would be required. 

Residence times and plant system dynamics had little impact on the model performance. In this case the resonance times of the plant were roughly equivalent to the MSA sample rate of 15 minutes. Therefore, aggregating the data into 15 minutes periods removed the impact of system dynamics and allowed more traditional machine learning technique to be leveraged. 

Considering the model’s final application to plant health monitoring in a production environment, this ability to systematically reject outliers in the training data was leveraged. The final machine learning model was trained using the data that represented good healthy plant performance and removed outliers that represented poor plant performance. In this case, the linear model provided adequate performance to predict normal healthy plant performance. Once the plant moved to suboptimal performance or it encountered a failure, the physical plant performance would deviate from the model performance. This was the foundation for the application of the model for plant health monitoring.

###### **Plant health monitoring** 

The application of the digital twin is used this gather ongoing insight into the plant’s operational health. This is achieved by running the model in parallel to the actual physical plan

t and feeding it in ‘real time’ with the operational senor data from the actual plant. Deviation between the actual physical plant and the model is then used to trigger actions. In this case, if the physical plant reports a copper grade delta that is less than the model predicted the operator, it provides indication of suboptimal plant performance. One of these events is shown in Figure 3 shortly after 12 mid-day on January 23. The actual plant performance undershoots the model predicted value. The root cause of the issue can be traced back using the model inputs. Just before the period of poor performance the dart valve position jumps from 0 to 3 standard deviations above the normal value, followed by a drop in cell air addition, and then a drop in pH. Once the dart value position is return to its normal level the plant eventually returns to a normal operating range after 48 hours. The goal is to reduce the impact and period of these issues by alerting the operators as soon as possible, and guiding them to a possible set of responses. It is essential to ensure the health of the sensor before these values can be used to infer the health of the plant. When considering a production system, it would be counterproductive if the operators responded to problems with the model prediction. To ensure robust performance of the model prediction, sensor health (used as part of the model inputs) needs to be monitored for correct operation. The z-score normalisation allows for easy limit check to ensure the sensor remains within normal bounds. An explicit check that ensured new MSA readings were gather was used to infer correct operation of the sensor. Checking that the system sensors reading are good offers significant value to the plant operation, and it is an area for potential further work. An important capability was to allow the model to continuously learn and update so that it could take advantage of the latest operational data. This would allow the model to adapt to potential operational changes in the plant. Integrating the models into a production environment and then communicating these to the plant operators in real-time is a key step to the successful implementation of the digital twin. 

###### **Model deployment** 

The publish literature highlights a gap when integrating advanced models into a production environment (Jovanovic, Miljanovic, and Jovanovic, 2015) (Jovanovic and Miljanovic, 2015a). A possible reason behind this is that it requires specialised production corporate IT knowledge and support to realise a robust and reliable implementation. Creating a workflow that supports integration of these models into the production environment is important to support ongoing innovation. This is achieved by allowing the existing models to be continually refined as knowledge of the process improves. In addition, this workflow can be used to support future initiatives. 

It was important to partner with corporate IT to ensure smooth integration into the production environment. The production system was integrated as part of the edge IT systems. This included server hardware colocated to the plant to minimise latencies and risk of downtime due to communication issues. Real-time plant data was accessed through a OBDC database, which acted as a bridge to the plant distributed control system. The model was compiled and deployed to MATLAB Production Server™, which provided a HTTP web served interface to the model. The model was called periodically by an SQL Server<sup>®</sup> task. 

The model is designed to be continuously rebuilt using the latest production data, so that it could adapt to the changing plant operations. To support this, the plant data was continuously uploaded to the cloud storage, which is part of the central IT system, to support the rebuild using the latest data. 

It is important to create an environment that allows new versions of the model to be deployed to MATLAB Production Server, so that the insights gained while running the model in production could be used to improve the model. This workflow supports innovation by allowing the domain expert to create and deploy updates to the model. 

###### **User interface development** 

Communicating the insights to the operators was important. The goal is to give them feedback in real time, so that they understand how the plant is operating, and if an issue is encountered, can provide targeted guidance to the possible source of the issue. The user interface was implemented using a web dashboard that could be accessed from a variety of devices and locations. This formed part of the edge IT systems. 

In this case, the comparison between the model predicted and the actual plant performance was transformed into a score along with a green, orange and red traffic light rating to indicate plant performance. If the plant was performing well, the operator would get a score of 100 per cent and green. If it was performing poorly, they could receive a score of 50 per cent and red. Individual score

s were used to indicate rougher recovery performance, the cleaner circuit recovery performance, and the cleaner circuit grade target performance. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

This simplified view allowed the operators to quickly gauge plant operation. The operators could drill down on one of the metrics to reveal more detail, including the plant’s performance over time and detailed warning messages. Based on the different warning messages, an action response plan was put in place to assist the operators to rectify identified issues. 

###### **RESULTS** 

Once the digital twin was commissioned as a tool for the flotation circuit operators an operational trial period was setup. It successfully passed the operational trial by reducing acid soluble copper found in the tails. 

It achieved this by providing real-time feedback to the operators with a goal to keep the plant health scores in the green or above 80 per cent. For instance, it prompted routine maintenance of the MSA sensors that were prone to blockage and highlighted periods of below average performance. 

During the operational trial, the user interface was refined to move the warning messages to the first level so that the operators didn’t need to drill down to understand the errors that were occurring. 

Once installed, the z-score normalisation for model inputs and model continuous learning allow the models to adapt to their installed configuration and haven’t required ongoing manual adjustment or intervention. This has reinforced the importance of robustness and adaptability requirements in the design of the models for a digital twin, which are installed as part of a production tool. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The paper aimed to highlight the process and benefits of leveraging a digital twin to optimise the operation of a copper flotation circuit. This first phase implementation has yielded positive results, and more importantly, created an environment that will support ongoing model refinement and further innovation. Some of these opportunities are discussed below. 

Although the linear models provided a robust foundation to establish a production system, better performance could be achieved by using more sophisticated machine learning techniques such as a neural network or decision trees. Additional effort is required in validating that the data used to train the model captures the required operating scenarios, as well as ensuring that the valid model predictions are limited to this range. 

The effects of system dynamics are accounted for by aggregating the data into 15 minutes periods. Model structures that include the dynamics have the potential to achieve better performance during transient periods. This type of model could be used to provide forward predictions of plant behaviour. 

Once modelling and forward prediction challenges have been solved, there is a potential to integrate model predictive control (MPC) techniques to

provide guidance to the input setpoints that would maximise plant yield. 

Clearly, these innovations and opportunities are dependent on further elaborating the model of the plant presented that captures the insights and knowledge gathered in the process of developing this digital twin.

###### Glencore Mount Isa lead zinc flotation circuit – experiences from the implementation of model predictive control 

###### _A Price_<sup>_1_</sup> _, D Okle_<sup>_2_</sup> _and K Brooks_<sup>_3_</sup> 

1. Superintendent – Concentrator Metallurgy, Mount Isa Mines, Mt Isa QLD 4825. Email: adam.price.2@glencore.com.au 

2. Metallurgist, Mount Isa Mines, Mt Isa QLD 4825. Email: darius.okle@glencore.com.au 3. Chief Engineer, BluESP, Johannesburg Gauteng South Africa, 2144. Email: kevin.brooks@bluesp.co.za 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The operation of flotation plants has been improved over the years by use of fundamentally based design techniques, a better understanding of reagent chemistry, online metal analysis and the use of digital control systems.  However, optimal operation of flotation banks is not consistently achieved using manual operation. The reason for this is that the system is a highly interacting one, with changes in air additi

on, cell interface level and reagent dosages all being available, without it necessarily being clear as to which change should be made for a particular situation. 

This situation is made more complex by the fact that the feed to a flotation bank can vary in flowrate, composition and density over a fairly short period of time.  It is not possible for a human operator to reject these disturbances, given the extent of the operation that is typically being monitored. 

Model predictive control (MPC) is a control and optimisation technique, developed in the oil refining industry, that aims to manage just such interacting multiple input multiple output (MIMO) systems.  This technology makes use of linear dynamic models of the plant, that are experimentally derived.  These models are then used in a receding horizon strategy to determine an optimal trajectory of the inputs to the system. 

MPC has been applied to four areas of the lead zinc flotation unit at Mount Isa mines.  A total of 31 cells are being controlled by the system, which varies air to the cells, levels and reagent addition on a minute-by minute basis.  The MPC controls concentrate and tail grades, reagent dosages, as well as recoveries to ranges set by the plant metallurgists. 

The development of the MPCs is discussed, together with the benefits realised.  The key factors in insuring an ongoing return on investment are described. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Glencore Mount Isa Lead Zinc Concentrator has operated for over 60 years and has made multiple additions and changes in order to process the variety of feed encountered.  In 2013 it was being fed from three different mines; the George Fisher mine, Black Star open cut mine and the Lady Loretta mine. Each mine presents challenges in processing their unique set of ore bodies. Optimal performance was difficult to achieve while processing the three different ore sources, with constant changes in blends, ore bodies and grades. 

A study undertaken in 2015 aimed to answer the following questions: 

1. What are the potential benefits from the application of improved control techniques throughout the plant? 

2. For the identified applications, what are the first pass returns on investment (ROI)? 

3. For applications with simple ROIs, what is an improved cost estimate? 

4. Are the based level control systems and measurements needed for MPC in place? 

This study is a techno-economic one, with an emphasis on establishing the most beneficial applications. Benefits are calculated from historical data by applying standard statistical methods as derived by Martin, Turpin and Kline (1991).  The essence of the method is to identify variables that would benefit from tighter control, estimate a reduction in standard deviation of the variable and the change in average, and relate this to an economic benefit. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The study identified eight applications with attractive ROIs.

The applications included the SAG and Ball Mills, the SAG and Ball Mill rougher flotation circuits, the zinc rougher scavenger, and the lead and zinc IsaMill circuits.  The existing base level control system implemented on the Yokogawa Centum Distributed Control System (DCS) has the capabilities necessary to interface to the MPC, while the extensive use of MSA and OSA analysers provided the opportunity to close the loop on the flotation control. 

While it would be possible to take a ‘big bang’ approach to the installation of MPC, Mount Isa and BluESP agreed on a phased approach.  This methodology is lower risk, puts less of a load on the plant resources and allows for benefit review between applications.  The study identified that the zinc rougher, scavenger and recleaner would benefit the most from a model predictive controller. This is due to the rougher and scavenger recovering all zinc that will eventually report as zinc final concentrate. The recleaner produces 6080 per cent of the zinc final concentrate for the plant. The zinc circuit feed has large fluctuations in feed based on the performance of the lead circuit and over half the reagent cost for the plant is dosed to zinc circuit feed. In February 2016 the zinc rougher, scavenger and recleaner units were commissioned. A post audit showed that the application had met its economic goals. 

The success of the zinc controllers is due to the increased stability achieved from predictive control allowing tighter reagent dosage control. This allows an increased frequency in the rate that dosage requirements are challenged and reviewed and results in lower overall reagent usage. In addition, the increased control has allowed quicker implementation of flotation strategy and greater flexibility in the way the flotation circuit is operated. 

There are opportunities for the improvement of the controller; including data validation, determining activator addition and tuning the controller to not only reduce cost during optimisation but balance recovery, grade and cost reduction. These require an increase in the amount of input data for their quality to be successful. 

In 2016, based on the success of the zinc circuit, one of the lead rougher circuits was also completed. As of January 2018, a controller for the second lead rougher is being developed, and will be finished in Q1, with an outlook to implement predictive control across the entire lead circuit. 

The remainder of this paper is arranged as follows: an overview of the Mount Isa Lead Zinc flotation circuit is presented, an outline of the MPC method is presented, the particular implementation on the zinc roughers, scavengers and recleaners is discussed, qualitative and quantitative results are given, and finally some conclusions stated. 

###### **PROCESS OVERVIEW** 

Glencore Mount Isa Lead Zinc Flotation Circuit can be seen in Figures 1 and 2. The lead mineral galena is floated off first with lead tails reporting to the zinc circuit feed.

Once in the zinc circuit, collector, activator and a depressant are added to recover the zinc mineral sphalerite. Rougher concentrate reports to a recleaner bank to produce final concentrate, while rougher tails report to a scavenger recovering material for the tertiary grinding IsaMilling and cleaner circuits. 

Glencore Mount Isa Lead Zinc Flotation Circuit begins with 3 separate grinding circuits: a 350tph semiautogenous grinding (SAG) milling circuit with ball mils in closed circuit, a 400tph Ball Mill in closed circuit and four separate Rod Mill circuits with ball mills in closed circuit, each processing 80tph. 

The lead mineral Galena is floated off first through a series of roughers, treating the SAG mill and ball mill flotation feeds separately. The rod mill flotation feed is treated with either of the larger grinding circuits. Frother is only added at the head of the roughers, while the collector is added through staged addition. Concentrate from the lead roughers is treated together in a three-stage cleaner with a tertiary grinding and cleaner scavenger circuit. 

The zinc circuit is fed by the tails of the lead circuit and is shown in Figure 2. An activator (copper sulphate), a collector (ethyl xanthate) and an iron depressant are added to the circuit feed to recover the zinc mineral sphalerite. In the rougher, performance is controlled through staged addition of collector and manipulation of air and levels. No additional activator or depressant is added. Concentrate from the rougher reports to the recleaner in which only airs and level are used to produce a zinc final concentrate. Tails from the rougher report to a scavenger in which more collector is added to recover a concentrate, which combines with the recleaner tail, for processing through the tertiary grinding and cleaning circuits. 

Scavenger concentrate, and recleaner tail are classified using cyclones, where ultra-fine particles report to the pre-IsaMill cleaner bank to produce final concentrate and tail. The underflow reports to a closed-circuit tertiary IsaMill circuit. Once classified out of the IsaMill circuit, additional activator and collector is added for flotation in the post-IsaMill cleaner to produce a final concentrate and tail. 

Performance of the grinding circuits is measured using two particle size analysers, a PSI200 and PSI500. The flotation performance is measured using 2 multi-stream analysers (MSA) and an online-stream analyser

This control layer is implemented on a Yokogawa Centum Distributed Control System (DCS). Table 1 summarises the key measurements, control loops and indicators used in the solution. The air and reagent flows are controlled to an operator setpoint by use of a proportional integral (PI) algorithm built into the DCS. The loops are tuned to give good setpoint tracking, without necessarily being very fast. The control of the levels is more complicated, since it is well known that level control in tanks in series can be challenging. Satisfactory operation has been achieved using a feedback-feedforward scheme developed in-house. This system has to achieve a balance between setpoint tracking and disturbance rejection. The required reagent dosages are set by the plant metallurgists and communicated to operations using the PI system. It is the responsibility of the control room operator to adjust one or more of the reagent flow setpoints to achieve the required dosage. It is also possible to split the flow of certain reagents in ratios; the ratios are seldom changed. |**Description**|**Measuring**
**Element**|**Units**|**Frequency**| |---|---|---|---| |Liquid Level in Cell 2 (PID loop)|Ultrasonic|mm|Sub second| |Air flowrate to Cell (PID loop)|Pitot|mn3/hour|Sub second| |Copper Sulphate Addition (PID loop)|Coriolis|m3/hour|Sub second| |Sodium ethyl xanthate flowrate to cell (PID loop)|Coriolis|m3/hour|Sub second| |naphthalene sulphate flowrate to cell (PID loop)|Magnetic|m3/hour|Sub second| |Feed volumetric flow (Indicator)|Magnetic|m3/hour|Sub second| |Feed online X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyser|XRF|% Zn, Pb, Fe|> 10 minutes| |Concentrate XRF analyser|XRF|% Zn, Pb, Fe|> 10 minutes| |Tails XRF analyser|XRF|% Zn, Pb, Fe|> 10 minutes| Table 1 – Process measurements and analysers. ###### **MODEL PREDICTIVE CONTROL** The use of MPC in the minerals processing industry has been relatively limited, with few publications on implementations on industrial scale plants. In a review of the progress in flotation control, Bergh and Yianatos (2011) state that “after more than one hundred years of history, there are few reports on applications of novel techniques in monitoring and control of flotation units, circuits and global plants”. Nevertheless, MPC is particularly suitable for the control and optimisation of the units found in a typical concentrator. As its name implies, MPC uses models of the plant to achieve multi-input multi-output (MIMO) control. The design process consists of identifying the outputs that need to be controlled in a range or at setpoints; these are known as the controlled variables (CVs). The inputs that can be changed to affect the CVs are the manipulated variables (MVs). The MVs

are in general the setpoints the operators already use to control the plant.  In addition, there may be variables that affect the CVs but cannot be manipulated; these are known as disturbance variables (DVs) or feed-forwards (FFs).  The control described is thus a multivariable cascade control. 

The model used in the majority of MPC implementations are linear dynamic models.  These are obtained experimentally, by performing step-tests on the plant.  A pre-step of approximately one week is performed to generate a seed model.  The seed model is then used to perform automated stepping (Kalafatis _et al_ , 2006). The step test period depends on the number of MVs and the settling time of the process.  In the case of the zinc flotation plant the automated step took twenty days in total. 

Step testing is definitely a tedious phase of the application design because it has to be performed in a way that does not cause large negative impacts on stability and performance but does yield the data required for an appropriate response to be detected. This is where it is vitally important that the BluESP engineers, metallurgists and operators work closely to determine the size of steps to be tested and what limitations are going to be placed on each controlled variable. The process needs to be closely monitored by all parties to ensure that the impacts to circuit performance don’t exceed limits. Hence, as an overall there will be disturbances to circuit stability but this is a necessary occurrence to ensure the models are developed with accuracy. It simply comes down to making sure these disturbances are within reason, can be controlled downstream/upstream as best as possible, and closely monitored. 

Re-stepping may be required if there are significant change to the process; these would include major changes to feed, circuitry changes and reagent changes.  The automated stepper makes this process considerably easier. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The step test data is used in a custom program that generates finite impulse response (FIR) and sub-space (SS) models of the process.  The most appropriate are used to generate a final model matrix, an example of which is shown in Figure 3.  The curves shown in each cell of this matrix are known as unit step responses; they are the response of a CV to a unit change in an MV or FF.  The time axis extends to the measured time to steady-state (TSS) of the system, in this case ninety minutes.  This matrix (which is for the zinc roughers) includes as MVs two level setpoints, four air setpoints, two ethyl xanthate (EX) additions and copper sulphate addition. The FFs are feed density, flow and zinc percentage, while the CVs are rougher concentrate zinc, rougher tail zinc, EX and copper sulphate dosages and the EX split between different cells. 

Armed with these models, together with some tuning parameters, the MPC application is able to answer the following questions: 

1

. What is the optimum steady-state operating point for the system? 

2. What is the optimum dynamic path of the CVs? 

3. What MV changes are needed to achieve these changes? 

Mathematically, the posed problem is a quadratic optimisation; the interested reader is referred to Brooks and Koorts (2017) for the mathematical details.  The MPC performs these calculations every minute (or faster if necessary). The calculation is performed for the control horizon of the controller, but only the first move is implemented.  The MPC is therefore from a class of control algorithms known as receding horizon control. 

Feedback is included in the control by comparing the predicted CV with that measured.  This ensures stability of the system, even in the presence of plant-model mismatch. 



Figure 3 – Subset of a model matrix. 

###### **MPC ON ZINC ROUGHERS, SCAVENGERS AND RECLEANERS** 

Brooks and Koorts (2017) have described the details of the implementation of MPC on the zinc rougher circuit.  The controller they describe is a subset of a larger controller that includes the roughers, scavengers and recleaners.  The resulting structure has twenty-three MVs, five FFs and thirty CVs.  It may seem that the control problem is not possible to solve, because there are more CVs than MVs, but it must be remembered that not all the CVs will be at constraints at all times.  In this particular application, fourteen of the CVs are concerned with maintaining air and level profiles and will in most circumstances not be at limits.  The result is that the MPC is able to optimise much of the time. 

The optimisation referred to above is implemented by defining direction for the MVs and solving the resulting linear program. In this case the optimisation is set up to minimise reagent dosing to lower limits, while maximise recovery by maximising air.  Although the models show that decreasing levels (i.e. increasing pulp height) will also increase recovery, this is not implemented in the controller as it is preferred to move the levels only slowly, due to the sensitivity of the base level control loop. 

The operators interact with the system using a browser-based interface.  This is used to change ranges on the variables and to switch variables on and off.  Switching is also available on the DCS; this serves as a backup should there be a communication issue to the browser.

###### **RESULTS** 

###### **Performance** 

From the time of commissioning the MPC has performed well, achieving its objectives of controlling tails and concentrate grades within ranges.  During the post commissioning period, the controller was online for ninety percent of the time, and of the time it was off nine percent was due to there being no feed to the circuit. To all intents and purposes the MPC was on all of the time that it could be on.  No re-tuning to improve performance was done during this time. 

In order to

calculate the benefits that accrued from the MPC, data over two three-month periods was compared.  These periods corresponded to the three months before and after commissioning. The trial period was immediately after commissioning, and only usual maintenance measures were in place for the MPC. It is acknowledged that on-off tests are a more accurate way of measuring the benefits, since it is more likely that like is compared to like.  The reality is that very few plants want to switch of the MPC shortly after it is installed, merely in order to prove it is working, since the economic impact of doing so is large. Comparison of two periods with similar feeds and in similar times of the year are commonly employed.  By taking enough data the results are statistically significant.  In this case the advantage is that the grade measurements are much more frequent than when laboratory values are used or the audit. 

In order to ensure that the pre and post audit periods are comparable, the head grades were compared.  As can be seen from Table 2, the head grades are similar, with the average head grade during the MPC audit period being slightly lower. It is acknowledged that mineralogy can also play a role in recovery; unfortunately, detailed mineralogical comparison is not available. As shown in Table 3, feed between the two comparison periods was very comparable in terms of an ore source related perspective.   The ratio of material from various sources Black Star Open Cut (BSOC) and George Fisher (GF) was almost identical and the dominant sources. The main difference is that in November 2015 Lady Loretta ore was still being fed and this made up 5 per cent of feed, while for the MPC on case there was no feed from this source. 

Despite the lower head grade, the recovery with MPC on is higher by some 0.3 per cent.  While this is a small number, a t-test on the data shows that the 95 per cent confidence range for the value is 0.22 per cent to 0.42 per cent.  It can be said with reasonable confidence that the recovery has improved, largely because of frequent online measurements. 

The results for the reagent dosages are shown in Tables 4 and 5, and in the form of frequency distributions in Figures 4a and 4b.  The benefits of using MPC are significant, with reductions in copper sulphate usage of more than twenty percent and Ethyl Xanthate of thirty eight percent.  These savings represent a considerable financial benefit to the operation. 

The reagent savings and control are without a doubt the overlying and clear benefit that has stemmed from introducing the MPC on the zinc rougher, scavenger and recleaner. Zinc flotation is more complex than some other minerals, for example lead, due the requirement of an activator reagent, which is typically copper sulphate. It is more difficult to sit in a position of minimum activator and collector for maximum/target recovery and grade as an increased amount of both won’t necessarily be evident in flotation performance

. If both reagents are in excess, they have the ability to react with one another, essentially cancelling out the increased addition. Obviously if either is well in excess, then it will be evident but this range is quite significant. The MPC has the ability to continually test these limits, which an Operator or even Metallurgist, dealing with a multitude of issues in a large complex plant, simply does not have time to do, particularly when zinc KPIs are being met and performance is as expected. Priority will always be given to the section of the plant not achieving targets. A large amount of the reagent savings noticed from the MPCs introduction was because of this reason. There is also an element of the MPC being able to utilise air and level more effectively and again, having the ability to continually push boundaries, such as minimum concentrate grades and maximum flows. Furthermore, the MPC removes a high amount of human error with regards to adding reagents and large periods of excessive additions because of this are minimised. Benefits on grade and recovery are harder to quantify, due to the changing nature of the process. Figure 5 – Distribution of zinc final concentrate with and without MPC. ###### **Change management** The introduction of model predictive control to the Mount Isa Lead Zinc Flotation circuit was not completed without resistance from both human and technical perspectives. There is a learning curve with operations that can be overcome quickly depending on the attitude of the c

rew and the tools with which they are provided to understand what the controller is doing. To ensure the adoption by operators, they were encouraged to make changes to the limits and targets themselves, thus showing that they were still in control of the circuit and the controller was making the specific moves while they dictated the overall strategy. This helped reinforce the view that the controller is a tool for the control room operator to improve the float performance allowing them to focus more closely on other areas of the plant. For this to occur successfully some operators required some upskilling in their understanding of the flotation circuit to ensure good decision making. The models and plots of the controller were simplified to show which manipulated variables the controller will move to change certain controlled variables. Troubleshooting skills were developed, including the use the controller’s in built historical and inspector tools to show how variables are being constrained at any point in time. 

The main goal of all these changes were to ensure that the operators are confident and capable in their operation of the controller which has allowed them to report back issues and help with troubleshooting. As the operators became more confident with the controller the number of times it was being turned off due to unexpected behaviour began to decrease.
