###### **ABSTRACT** 

Geometallurgy is a tool that, for more than a century, has been present in the implicit operations of mineral beneficiation. There’s a need to understand the characteristics of the material to be processed. This has led metallurgists to ask geologists what type of rock and mineralogy is entering the Beneficiation Plant and vice versa. The geologist needs to understand the beneficiation process in order to be able to carry out the production programming. The paradigm is whether geometallurgy can be applied to small-scale mining or if it is only aimed at large companies that invest millions of dollars to conduct studies. With this work, we provide an example of how geometallurgy can help improve the processes of a small mining company located in Ecuador (South America). 

We performed characterizations of geological and mineralogical and metallurgical tests in universities and the National Research Institute of Geological Metallurgical Mining. The origin of the theme is based on the fact that gold has been detected in the final tailings. The flotation concentrates meet the standards in terms of the content of economically profitable metals, but this isn’t the case with regards to the percentage of arsenic, which has hindered sales. The hypothesis is: conducting technical and scientific research will optimize the metallurgical process for the recovery of gold and concentrates. The referential framework is the mining geology of the Bella Rica District, current status of the Beneficiation Plant. In the theoretical framework there are parameters of the veins, comminution operations, gravimetric concentration, flotation, and cyanidation. The methodological framework contemplates the characterization of the gold ore, the chemical, mineralogical, textural, metallurgical analysis and the interpretation of the results. Thus, the design of a geometallurgy model of the deposit, with its main characteristics, is a conclusion that serves as a basis for the proposal of the optimization of the metallurgical process. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Geometallurgy is a tool that optimizes mining operations while relying on geological and mineralogical correlations based on metallurgical tests that aim to generate predictive models (Dominy _et a_ l, 2016). Mining operations require geometallurgical studies, such as quantitative analyses, validation of analytical techniques and the establishment of sampling protocols directed to predict the behaviour of the ore during ore processing. The results of the geometallurgical studies are later applied to optimize the design of the processing plants that are tailored to the ore geology (David, 2007). The case study we present focuses on the application of geometallurgy processes for a mining project that is in the production stage. Therefore, the application of geometallurgy is focused on reducing the correlation of geological and metallurgical turnaround processes (Dominy _et al_ , 2016). 

It

is important to note that geological and extractive metallurgy alone do not make up geometallurgy due to the paucity of predictive models that allow for process optimization (in general, it is used as a block model for the realisation of the prediction of variability at the time of processing). 

In our case study, we seek to optimise mining operations through the concept of geometallurgy, which is applied to small mining projects. Mining operations on a small scale do not have sampling protocols, lithology studies, mine geology, mine mapping, drillcore data, a predecessor design of the project or sampling protocols in the processing plant. This is a reality faced by the small-scale mining industry in our study region (Ecuador - South America). Although data is available, the data has not been validated due to the paucity of laboratories required to perform quality control tests. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

With the implementation of geometallurgy, the objective is to have a common language among geologists, mining engineers, metallurgists, project managers etc., resulting in cooperation that benefits the durability and profitability of the mining project (David, 2007). 

Our aim is to apply the concept of geometallurgy to optimize the mining operations and increase the recovery of the minerals of interest. We challenge the common misconception that only large companies can benefit from geometallurgy, because they have resources to implement what is needed. In this study, where the budget was almost $5000, the concept of geometallurgy was applied to help the company improve its recovery and identify points to be improved in comminution and gravimetric concentration operations. With regards to concentration, it is important to highlight the need to introduce more variables for the geometallurgical analysis, that is, the variables that help our model of the blocks, such as the geochemistry, biota, atmospheric, hydric characteristics, etc. with the purpose of helping us correlate geology, mining and processing to optimize mining operations. 

###### **CASE STUDY: MINEREICIS S.A** 

The mining company, MINEREICIS S.A., is dedicated to the exploration, production and beneficiation of gold and concentrates, complying with the mining and environmental laws of Ecuador. The concession has 1350 contiguous mining hectares, located in the Camilo Ponce Enrнquez parish, in the county with the same name, in the province of Azuay, which is located in south-eastern Ecuador in the low part of the Andes mountain range, at altitudes between 360 and 320 m.a.s.l., respectively and in the coastal zone of this region (Figure 1) of the sector the Lopez (Matamorros, 2014). The estimated reserves will allow for at least fifteen more years of production at the current levels. (CODIGEM, 1998). 



Figure 1 – Modelling the location of the deposit. 

###### **Regional geology** 

The Ponce Enrнquez mineral field, located w

ithin the Machala-Naranjal Subdistrict, in the western part of the Azuay District, is known for its Cu-Au-Mo deposits in porphyries and veins, breccias and epi-mesothermal stockworks developed within the volcanic box rocks that are spatially related to porphyries. Mineralization in ‘stockwork’ of quartz + pyrite +/- pyrrhotite +/- chalcopyrite also appears along the cornealized margins of Gaby's porphyry at the Oro mines and Liga de Oro mines, which cut the Bella Rica system Gold grades. They are generally low and subeconomic (<0.3 g/t), but locally they can yield up to 15 g/t. The "stockwork" is formed by multiple intersecting veinlets and fracture systems normally featured in narrow zones of silicification and propilitization of a structurally-controlled epidote. The mineralized veins with auriferous quartz, coupled with pirrotina, pyrite and chalcopyrite, constitute the production fronts in the entire district. In the upper part of Bella Rica, the reserves are practically being produced. 

###### **Geology of the deposit** 

The MINEREICIS. S.A Mining Company has defined gold veins and quartz veinlets with a NNW-SSE orientation. These veins have been affected by transverse faults, mostly normal, highlighting the reverse 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

transversal fault (overlaid). The main mineralized structures (veins) are essentially constituted by auriferous quartz together with pyrrhotine, pyrite and chalcopyrite, arsenopyrite, sphalerite, galena, and hematite. 

The geology evaluation under the microscope reveals the presence of magnetite and marcasite, as well as other secondary minerals, such as molybdenite associated with chalcopyrite inside veinlets of quartz. There is secondary enrichment chalcocite, coveline, cuprite, malachite, limonite and oxidation minerals as well as gangue minerals such as calcite, muscovite, chlorite and epidote. To maintain profitability, the minimum gold concentration should be 5-8 g of gold per ton of material processed. In the mine, mining works are planned based on the characteristics of ore reserves and the bedding rock. 

###### **Mining exploitation** 

The method of mining exploitation is room and pillar and consists of excavating the mineralized veins as much as possible, leaving mineral pillars that support the sterile roof. Therefore, the chambers are aligned in the direction of the ore deposit, leaving pillars between them. In addition to the pillars between the chambers, pillars are also left on the transport gallery. The height of the chambers reaches up to 20 m and the maximum length is 30 m, unless the ceiling rock is stable and continuous, which allows the chamber to be longer than 30 m. 

The width of the pillars under the same conditions varies between 3-4 m. Prior to the production of these blocks, certain preparatory phases are necessary, such as the delimitation of the block, exploratory wells, inclined recesses, horizontal galleries and

the placement of mine services. (Salazar, 2017). The ore from the mine contains precious metals finely disseminated in minerals such as metal sulfides. Pyrite and arsenopyrite are the most common minerals in which gold is immersed in its crystalline network. The presence of associations of galena, sphalerite and chalcopyrite has also been found. In Figure 2 we have the flow diagram of the mineral processing of the company (Salazar, 2017). 

###### **Beneficiation plant** 

The MINERACIS S.A. Mining Company's Beneficiation Plant processes around 50 t every 24 hours. The operations carried out are classification, crushing, grinding, gravimetric concentration, leaching, flotation, acid refining and smelting. 

###### **SAMPLING** 

The implementation of the work will directly affect the company in terms of proposing technical-operational facilities with the equipment that is currently available. The goal is to create a culture of proper sampletaking, based on the theory of Dr Pierre Gy's ‘Theory of Sampling’ and the calculation of the variance of the fundamental error in the sampling protocol (Pitard, 2009). We also apply a study carried out by PEng Vicente Balseca, environmental care in artisanal mining, providing guidelines for taking samples in Chilean-type mills that are widely used in Ecuador's small mining industry (Balseca, 2005). To cover all the material from the mine, strategic sampling points were established, including one in the storage hopper where materials that arrive directly from the mine were sampled, in addition to sampling on the conveyor belt that transports the material to the Chilean mills. Sampling was done in a type of network, taking samples from all sectors and sedimentation pools to obtain more precise values. Sampling was carried out for eight consecutive days and with frequencies of 1-2 hours. 

###### **Mine sampling** 

Applying the technique of channel-type sampling, 15 samples of the quality or average conditions of the mineralized bodies were collected for each study area along the enabled work fronts. An _in situ_ description of each one of the veins was also performed to understand the structural and mineralogical characteristics. With regards to the veins, sampling has been facilitated, as the galleries were crossed in the same direction and they are delimited veins. Manual sampling chutes were recorded by stitching the grain perpendicular to the direction. 

The samples corresponding to veins V1, V2, V3 and V4 obtained in the field were described petrographically prior to the selection and elaboration of 7 thin sheets and 3 polished sections (briquettes) in the petrography laboratory of the Faculty of Engineering of Geology Mines, Petroleum and Environmental (hereinafter FIGEMPA) of the Central University of Ecuador. as well as in the Petrography Laboratory of the Mining and Metallurgical Geological Research Institute. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The geometallurgical characterisation of the veins gathered chemical, mineralogical, physical and mineralogical analyses; the same that were performed on samples coming from the interior mine and the Beneficiation Plant, following the methodology of systematic sampling to obtain results with minimum probability of mistakes. 

Regarding the mineralized structures (veins), they are characterized by having a NW-S, N-S orientation, and a width ranging from 15-40 cm: The mineralogical associations determined were: gold, quartz, pyrite, chalcopyrite, arsenopyrite, pyrrhotine, blende, galena and tetraedrite. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The results provided by the mineralogical and granulometric tests indicate that the gold is occluded in the mineralogical network of the sulphides (arsenopyrite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, tetraedrite), and would have a release mesh of 163 μm. 

The company has been proposed making adjustments in the grinding, gravimetric concentration, flotation and cyanidation phases, as this analysis provides a current view of the methodology of work. 

There is the presence of molybdenite foot damage that must be paid in the concentrate by molybdenum as well as copper and gold. 

These conclusions are reached thanks to the application of the foundation of geometallurgy resulting in an improvement to the company almost immediately. Additionally, th

e guidelines are given so that all the processes, especially those related to comminution and recovery, can be improved, emphasizing the sampling and analysis to control the processes. 

With this work we demonstrate that an alliance between the private company, universities and government entities can be united for the innovation in the processes helping the sector in this mining case so that it can be maintained in the time generated work for the surrounding communities.

###### _S Palaniandy_<sup>_1_</sup> _, R Halomoan_<sup>_2_</sup> _and H Ishikawa_<sup>_3_</sup>

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Karara iron ore project is a magnetite operation consist of open pit mining and concentrator to produce high-grade magnetite concentrate. The concentrator has adopted three stages of comminution, ie fine crushing in the high pressure grinding rolls (HPGR), primary ball milling and fine grinding in the TowerMill plus magnetic separation in between these comminution devices. Since 2014, the concentrator has increased the plant feed rate by 18 per cent. Meanwhile, the ore hardness has increased by 13 per cent to a Bond work index value of 15 kWh/t that led to a coarser flotation feed. Karara Mine has decided to shift the comminution workload from the primary ball mill to the TowerMill circuit by bypassing the 100 µm fine screen in between the ball mill and TowerMill circuits. This action has increased the circuit feed particle size distribution with a top size close to 1 mm. The specific energy consumption of the TowerMill circuit was approximately 3.4 kWh/t, and the circuit product sizes (P 80) were ranged between 38 and 45 µm. 

A joint process improvement exercise was carried out to reduce the circuit product size closer to the magnetite liberation size, ie 35 µm. Among the activities were circuit audit, recommendation for improvement, modelling and simulation, multicomponent analysis, implementation of recommendations and quantification of the improvement. One of the key findings was the density effect of multicomponent minerals in the hydrocyclone. The analysis revealed that the low density coarser gangue minerals were bypassed to the hydrocyclone overflow stream that has resulted in a coarser particle size distribution. Meanwhile, more than 20 per cent of fine (-35 µm) high-density magnetite particles were recycled back to the mill through the hydrocyclone underflow stream and increased the circulating load. Based on these outcomes, several recommendations such as conversion to bottom feed configuration, use of smaller grinding media, high operating hydrocyclone pressure and additional grinding power to the TowerMill circuit were made to improve the overall circuit performances. Karara Mine has prioritised to implement those recommendations that have a minimal financial implication. Full-scale plant trials with bottom feed configuration and 17 mm grinding media were conducted to evaluate its performances. These trials have indicated that the grinding efficiency in the TowerMill was enhanced by 10 – 30 per cent. In May 2017, all the five TowerMills were converted to the bottom feed configuration. This paper discusses the impact of shifting the comminution work

load load from the primary ball mills to TowerMill circuit and the performances enhancement of the TowerMill circuit. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Grinding is an integral and important part of a mineral processing concentrator. The main objective of the grinding circuit is to prepare the feed to size with adequate mineral liberation for the subsequent separation process. Ball mills are commonly used for grinding, and it is well known for its high energy intensity where only a small fraction of the input energy was used for particle breakage. There is a strong movement in the industry seeking for new technologies that may enhance the comminution efficiency. 

The mining industry is also facing other challenges such as the decrease in the commodity price and ore grade, water scarcity, increase in energy price, increase in ore hardness as the mining progress deeper, ore variability plus other social and environmental issues that have direct and indirect implications towards grinding. Many concentrators have increased their plant throughput as a measure to overcome some of the challenges and to maintain the concentrate productivity. In some cases, the increase in the plant throughput was done with the existing equipment and pushing them to operate beyond its original design capacities. This action has led to situations where the equipment (such as mills, hydrocyclone and pumps) were reaching its operational capacity, water deficiency in the grinding circuit due to a limitation in pumping capacity, coarser grinding circuit product and a higher wear rate on the parts. The industry has started to adopt new technologies such as 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

HPGR, stirred milling, ore sorting to address and gangue mineral rejection to address some of the above mentioned technical challenges (Jankovic _et al_ , 1999, Shi _et al_ , 2009, Palaniandy _et al_ , 2013). 

Karara Mine (a magnetite mine and concentrator operation in Western Australia) has adopted HPGR and stirred mill (TowerMill) in their comminution circuit. Additionally, the gangue minerals rejection (via magnetic separation) was introduced between the comminution stages to reduce the subsequent comminution energy demand in the circuit and avoid energy wastage of grinding the gangue minerals. Karara Mine was also facing the similar challenges where the ore became more competent as the mining progress into a deeper pit plus the plant throughput was increased to enhance the concentrate production. These two phenomena have impacted the comminution circuit operation in general, and specifically the primary ball mill circuits operation. 

Karara mine carried out several modifications in the grinding circuit to improve the efficiency of ball mill circuit. One of the major modification was to shift the comminution workload from the primary ball mill to TowerMill circuit that reduces the circulating load in the ball mill circuit. This modification has

changed the grinding condition in the TowerMill circuit hence requires process optimisation. 

Nippon Eirich installed four units of TowerMill (ETM 1500) for fine grinding duty. Karara mine and Nippon Eirich have joined forces to improve performances of the fine grinding circuit.  This is an on-going effort exercise from both sides since 2016, and it is being carried out in stages. Among the key activities were circuit audit to evaluate the circuit performance and identifying the opportunity for improvement, recommendation for improvement, circuit simulation to quantify potential improvement for budget approval, implementation of recommendation and finally quantifying the improvement through circuit audit. This paper focuses on the impact of shifting the workload from the primary ball mill to TowerMill circuit and the joint efforts taken to improve the fine grinding circuit product. 

###### **GRINDING CIRCUIT, MODIFICATION AND ITS OPERATIONS** 

Figure 1 shows the comminution circuit at the Karara Mine concentrator. The ball mill circuit was receiving feed from the rougher magnetic separator. The ball mill circuit product was scalped through a 100 µm fine screen. The fine screen undersize was fed to the fine grinding circuit while the screen oversize was recycled back to the ball mill circuit. The increase in ore hardness and plant throughput has changed the plant operating condition. The HPGR circuit product size was increased from 1.8 mm to 2.2 mm. Meanwhile, the ball mill circuit product was coarsened from 55 to 70 µm that has resulted in a higher circulating load from the hydrocyclone underflow and fine screen oversize streams. 

The grinding circuit operational condition and design were modified to suit with the new grinding conditions. The fine screen was bypassed in November 2014 by removing its grid meshes. This action has reduced the circulating load in the primary ball mill circuit but coarsened the feed to the TowerMill circuit with a wider particle size distribution. Figure 2 shows the particle size distribution of the TowerMill circuit feed in three different periods. In December 2013, the circuit was operated with the 100 µm fine screens, and the feed top size was approximately 150 µm. In May 2016 and January 2017 the circuit audit data show that feed top size was close to 1 mm with a coarser particle size distribution. These phenomena have changed the grindability of the TowerMill grinding circuit. Figure 3 shows the hydrocyclones efficiency curves in the TowerMill circuits. The data from May 2016 and January 2017 show the deflection at the coarse end of the efficiency curve which was caused by the coarse and low-density gangue minerals bypassed to the hydrocyclone overflow stream. Minimal deflection was observed for data on the December 2013 indicating that scalped TowerMill circuit feed at 100 µm may reduce the bypass effect. 

Besides the fine screen, the coarse classifier at the TowerMill discharge launder was bypassed as well

. The main function of the coarse classifier was to recycle the coarse material back to the bottom of the mill. This action reduces the circulating load in the hydrocyclone streams. The coarse classifier was not required for this grinding application as the circuit feed was fine (F80 < 100 µm). The coarse classifier is useful when the feed contains a substantial amount of coarse particles that are larger than 1 mm and widely distributed. This modification was done simply by shutting off the coarse classifier recycle pump (that pumps the coarse classifier underflow stream to the bottom of the mill) and allow the solids sediments to fill the coarser classifier. This action allows the mill discharge stream to flow directly into the hydrocyclone feed sump. The recycle pump speed was an important operational variable that was associated with the coarse classifier operation. The pump speed had a direct impact on the particles residence time in the grinding zone. A high recycle pump speed had resulted in a shorter residence of the particles in the grinding zone as slurry flow rate was high. The particles residence time in the grinding zone affects the grindability. Shorter particles residence time in the grinding zone had resulted in a coarser mill discharge particle size, so it is important to control the recycle pump speed. Figure 4 shows the effect of particles size on rougher mass recovery and collector consumption over a period of six months. The Fe content in flotation concentrate was ranged between 64 - 68 per cent during this period. The data shows as the particle size increases; the rougher concentrate mass recovery reduces and the 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 collector consumption increases. These trends have a negative impact on the business as it reduces the final concentrate productivity and increases operating expenditure (OPEX). Based on these observations, it is necessary to optimise the TowerMill circuit to reduce the flotation feed particle size. Besides the effect on the grindability, the hydrocyclone operation has influenced the circuit product quality. For instance, the coarse end deflection in the hydrocyclone efficiency curves (as shown in Figure 3) has affected the overall particle size distribution of the circuit product. This phenomenon was a classic observation in a multicomponent system especially when the ore contains two distinct types of minerals with different densities. In this case, the ore contained magnetite (SG = 5.5) and gangue minerals (SG = 2.8). After the primary grinding stage, there were possibilities that some of the magnetite particles were liberated from the gangue minerals and resulted in dual densities minerals population, ie high-density magnetite and low-density gangue minerals. The particle size and density factors have influenced the classification in the hydrocyclone. There is literature reported that coarse end deflection in the efficiency curve resulted from the coarse, low-density minerals bypassed to the hydrocyclone overflow stream (Laplante and Finch, 1984). This phenomenon has resulted in a coarser particle size distribution of the hydrocyclone overflow stream. Physical observation during sieving of the hydrocyclone overflow stream sample in the laboratory had shown that the particles were retained in the coarser size sieves (between 600 – 1180 µm) have a lighter colour compared to the finer size sieves. The gangue minerals have lighter colour compared to magnetite which was typically black. Furthermore, the assay by size analysis had indicated that the magnetite content in the coarser size fraction (ie + 150 µm) was less than 40 per cent while the fine size fraction (ie, 38 µm) had more magnetite content (approximately 75 per cent). 

These observations demonstrated that the hydrocyclone had played a vital role in the circuit product quality. Conversely, a minimum deflection

was observed when the grinding circuit was operated with the fine screen as shown in Figure 3. The key question was whether the impact of bypassing the fine screen had intensified the coarse end deflection in the efficiency curve due to a wider particle size distribution. It requires a more detail understanding of the impact of multicomponent minerals on the hydrocyclone operations. Another question was the possibility to partially solve this issue by decreasing the cut size by increasing the hydrocyclone operating pressure. Rigorous laboratory or pilot hydrocyclone tests with multicomponent ores are necessary to answer the above-mentioned questions and to understand the insights of the hydrocyclone performances when treating the multicomponent ore.

###### **Multicomponent analysis of hydrocyclone** 

A multicomponent analysis was carried out to evaluate the performance of the hydrocyclone to understand the coarse end deflection in the hydrocyclone efficiency curve. 

Samples from TowerMill circuit surveys were sieved into a single size fraction, and each fraction was subjected to magnetite content analysis in Satmagan 135 magnetic analyser at the Karara site laboratory. This analysis determined the fraction of magnetite content in the sample. Figure 8 shows the particle size distributions and efficiency curves of the magnetite and gangue minerals. Magnetite and gangue minerals have different efficiency curves that have resulted in two particle size distributions. Magnetite’s particle size distribution was finer compared to the gangue minerals. For example, the P80 of the magnetite and gangue minerals in the hydrocyclone overflow stream were 32 and 57 µm respectively. The magnetite particles have reached the liberation size (< 35 µm) while the gangue minerals remained coarser. Equation 4 shows the Plitt’s hydrocyclone cut size model (Palaniandy _et al_ , 2017). The model shows that the solid density has an inverse effect towards the cut size. The high-density particles have a finer cut size while the low-density particles have exhibited a coarser cut size that coincided with these results. The combination of the fine magnetite and coarse gangue minerals particles have resulted in a coarser overall circuit product size distribution. The occurrence of fully liberated magnetite and gangue minerals could further augment the densities effect in the hydrocyclone. These results have exhibited potential opportunities for gangue minerals rejection by screening to improve the Fe content in the flotation feed. Furthermore, the screened product would exhibit a narrower particle size distribution that potentially enhances the flotation performances. 



An additional analysis was carried out to evaluate the bypass of fine magnetite (< 35 µm) that were recycled back to the hydrocyclone underflow stream due to the density effect.

The hydrocyclone underflow stream contained 20 – 28 per cent of the – 35 µm particles. These particles should have been classified out as the final product through the overflow stream. This phenomenon may result in potential overgrinding as the fine particles were re-entering the mill for further breakage. Figure 9 shows the fraction of – 35 µm magnetite particles in the hydrocyclone feed that reported to underflow stream as a function of hydrocyclone operating pressure. In this case, the amount of – 35 µm magnetite particles that bypassed to the underflow stream when the operating pressures were 150 - 155 kPa was approximately 35 per cent. There were no data available in between 155 kPa to 180 kPa, but it was reduced to 26 per cent when the operating pressure was 183 kPa. These results have indicated that at higher operating pressure, the bypass of – 35 µm magnetite particles were reduced. This aspect requires more detail studies to understand the multicomponent effect of the fine particles bypasses to the underflow stream plus more data collection is required in between 160 to 180 kPa. Conversely, the circulating load in the circuit could be reduced if these fine particles can be classified out from the grinding system which potentially improves the grindability in the 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 TowerMill. The objective of these recommendations was to achieve the circuit product size close to the design value, ie P80 = 35 µm despite changes in ore characteristics, operational condition and circuit design. The recommendations were; - Convert to bottom mill feed configuration The TowerMills at the Karara Mine was originally installed with top feed configuration. The top feed configuration was suitable for the initial design where the feed was scalped at 100 µm and low reduction ratio grinding duty, ie F80 = 55 µm to P80 = 35 µm. In the current operational conditions (with F80 reaches 75 µm and top size close to 1 mm), the mill requires bottom feed configuration to enhance the grinding efficiency. Nippon Eirich’s previous experiences in West Asia has demonstrated that bottom feed configuration improved the grinding efficiency. Based on this experience, Nippon Eirich has recommended converting the TowerMills to bottom mill feed configuration. - Smal

ler grinding media The TowerMill was using 20 mm grinding media. It is well known that smaller grinding media increases the grinding efficiency as it has more contact surface area compared to the larger media. In this case, 15 or 17 mm grinding media were recommended to enhance the grinding efficiency. - Higher hydrocyclone operating pressure Based on the survey data and hydrocyclone theories, the hydrocyclone could be operated at a higher pressure to improve the quality of the circuit product, ie finer hydrocyclone overflow. Conversely, the authors are aware that operating at higher pressure may induce higher parts wear rate. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 - Additional grinding power into the fine grinding circuit The regrind TowerMill could be converted into tertiary grind duty for additional grinding power in the circuit to cope with the increase in particle size and ore hardness and achieving finer circuit product size. Based on the abovementioned recommendations, activities such as grinding test to determine the required specific energy and TowerMill circuit simulations were carried out. These activities have quantified the potential improvement that can be gained if these recommendations were implemented. ###### **Grinding test to determine specific energy requirement** The TowerMill circuit feed samples were collected for grinding test to determine the specific energy requirement. The KM-5 TowerMill grinding test was carried out at the Nippon Eirich technical centre in Narita, Japan. The test was carried out by using the standard scale-up test methodology to determine the specific energy requirement. The test has indicated that specific energy of 3.6 kWh/t was required for the current feed characteristics to achieve the circuit product size of 35 µm (P80). Table 3 shows the grinding power requirement at different levels of plant throughput. If the plant throughput reached 3000 t/h, then an additional one unit of ETM 1500 was required to achieve the targeted grind size of 35 µm. The grinding test justified the conversion of the regrind duty TowerMill to fine grinding duty. An innovative short-term solution approach is to operate the existing regrind mill in dual mode, ie regrind and fine grinding duties. If the plant throughput is less than 3000 t/h, then the fifth TowerMill can be operated in the regrind duty, but if the plant throughput exceeded 3000 t/h, then it can be operated in the fine grinding duty. This approach offers the operational flexibility especially in adjusting the circuit operation based on ore variability and requires minimum capital expenditure as it only involves additional piping, valves and modification/replacement of the circuit feed distributor. Based on the simulation results, Karara Mine has carried out the economic analysis to evaluate the potential gain if the recommendations were implemented. Nippon Eirich has developed the TowerMill circuit simulator comprised of two main models, ie TowerMill comminution model combined Plitt’s hydrocyclone model. The simulator has model fitting and simulation capabilities. The TowerMill comminution model was a population balanced based model that was developed using the industrial scale TowerMill operational data from the circuit surveys. The comminution model consisted of two functions, ie selection function and breakage function. The selection function responded to the operating conditions of the TowerMill while the breakage function was based on the ore characteristics. The breakage function was determined using the Austin breakage function model (Austin _et al_ , 1984). The Plitt’s efficiency curve that response towards operating and design condition was used to model the hydrocyclone. The coarse end deflection was omitted in the hydrocyclone efficiency curve model for simplicity, and furthermore, till date, there was no available model to represent the coarse end deflection of the efficiency curve. The TowerMill circuit survey data (mass flow rate, circuit streams per cent solids and particle size distribution) were used to model fit the TowerMill circuit in the simulator - a site-specific TowerMill circuit model. Two simulation scenarios were simulated as per the recommendations. They were - Bottom mill feed configuration - Convert the regrind TowerMill to tertiary grind The simulations were carried out at two different level of feed rate (ie 2850 and 3137 t/h) and particle sizes (64 and 74 µm). The circuit feed rate of 2850 t/h was close to the design condition while the 3137 t/h was the condition when the plant was operated at a high throughput. These are the common operating conditions of 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 the plant and TowerMill circuit at Karara Mine. Table 4 shows the simulation conditions. Both base case conditions were obtained from the TowerMill circuit surveys. All scenarios were simulated for both conditions. The selection function for the bottom feed configuration was adjusted based on previous experiences from a magnetite application. The second scenario simulation was carried out by splitting the total throughput to the TowerMill circuit into five equal streams, and one circuit was simulated.

Table 5 shows the simulation results and the potential improvement that can be achieved through the implementation of the recommendations. The simulation results show that converting the mill feed configuration from top to bottom has improved the hydrocyclone P80 by 20 per cent. The simulated P80 of Condition 1 was close to the design condition, ie 35 µm. Secondly, the bottom feed configuration has exhibited a narrower top size distribution (P98/P80) as the long tail at the coarse end distribution was diminished. Moreover, the bottom feed configuration also exhibited a finer P80 and narrow particle size distribution that may enhance the flotation performance. Conversion to the bottom feed configuration had a minimal cost implication as the hydrocyclone underflow launder pipe could be re-routed to the existing recycle port at the bottom of the mill. The slurry could flow to the bottom of the mill by gravity as there was sufficient head in between the hydrocyclone underflow launder and the recycle port at the bottom of the mill. An additional grinding power in the TowerMill circuit by converting the regrind mill to the fine grind duty had improved the P80 by 30 per cent. In the design condition (ie Condition 1), the addition grinding power had resulted in P80 of 35 µm while at higher throughput the P80 was reduced to 41 µm from 55 µm. Potentially, the flotation concentrates mass recovery could be improved by 12 per cent while the collector consumption could be reduced by 13 per cent. In general, additional grinding power in the tertiary grinding circuit has a positive impact towards flotation performances, especially when the plant is operated at a higher plant throughput. In this case, converting the regrinding mill to the multi-task grinding duties, ie fine grinding and regrind might be a good short-term solution. The mill could operate in the regrind duty when the plant was operating at the design throughput. Meanwhile, it can operate in fine grinding duty when the plant was operated at a higher throughput (ie above 3000 t/h). Implementation of this recommendation involved the modification of circuit feed distributor tank and additional launder pipes. ###### **CONCLUSION** 

Since Karara Mine had started its operation in 2012, there have been changes in the ore characteristics, operational condition and circuit design. The plant throughput and ore hardness were increased by 21 per cent and 18 per cent respectively. These conditions had increased the circulating load in the ball mill circuit. Karara Mine has decided to shift the grinding workload from the primary ball mill to TowerMill circuit by bypassing the fine screen in between the primary ball mills a

nd TowerMill circuits. This action has reduced the circulating load in the ball mill circuit. The implication of the workload shift to the TowerMill circuit includes an increase in circuit feed size with wider distribution, top size close to 1 mm and circuit feed rate. These implications have increased the circuit product particle size. Karara Mine and Nippon Eirich have joined forces to improve the TowerMill circuit performance and reduce the circuit product size close to the design value, ie P80 = 35 µm. 

A comprehensive TowerMill circuit audit was carried out in May 2016 to seek for opportunities of improvement. The audit outcomes have revealed that the hydrocyclone operation has impacted the overall circuit product quality. The hydrocyclone efficiency curves have exhibited the coarse end deflection that indicated coarse material bypass through the hydrocyclone overflow stream. A detail multicomponent analysis was carried out around the hydrocyclone circuit by treating the ore into the individual component, ie magnetite and gangue minerals. The analysis has revealed that magnetite particles have a finer cut size compared to the gangue minerals. The multicomponent analysis has discovered that the low-density coarse gangue minerals bypassed through the hydrocyclone overflow stream. This phenomenon has impacted the overall particle size distribution of the hydrocyclone and shifted it to a coarser distribution. Furthermore, more than 20 per cent of the fine magnetite (< 35 µm) that had reached the product size was bypassed to the underflow stream. 

Based on the current feed characteristics and hydrocyclone operation, several recommendations were made to improve the performance of the TowerMill circuit. The recommendations include the conversion to the bottom feed configuration, use of smaller grinding media, high hydrocyclone operating pressure and additional grinding power in the tertiary grinding circuit. The laboratory TowerMill grinding test was carried to determine the specific energy. The specific energy requirement for the current ore was 3.6 kWh/t. The TowerMill circuit simulation of bottom feed configuration and additional grinding power in the fine grinding circuit have exhibited positive outcomes. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Karara Mine has focused on implementing the recommendations that had low financial implication due to the challenging business condition. Two recommendations were implemented, ie conversion to bottom feed configuration and the use of smaller grinding media. Both implementations have shown 10 – 30 per cent improvement in the grinding efficiency. This exercise had demonstrated the cooperation and knowledge sharing between Nippon Eirich and Karara Mine had improved the TowerMill circuit performances. This is a good example of cooperation between METS sector and mine operator for a profitable operation.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

This work goes beyond the general perception of how the well-known mine to mill process can be applied, by applying deeper knowledge along the mining chain. Grade deportment and dilution are considered at the mining stage, and modelled with the new SMI blast movement simulator, linking with the block model data. Assessing the shift to a considerably more competent section of the orebody is quantified via substantial milling trials at standard and higher-intensity blasts. These were stockpiled for batch processing through the mill to ensure feed integrity. The trial work included operating the mill at widely different fillings to develop Grindcurve milling responses. Additionally, model informed process control is initiated via a mill prediction tool. 

It has been found that accounting for blast movement for the higher intensity blasts could generate additional value of around $1.5M per blast. With the high-intensity blast and changing mill control, the plant was easily able to exceed projected mill throughputs with the far more competent Pipeline ore. Strategies to shift the workload and debottleneck the milling circuit were proposed and proven during the milling trials, demonstrating an increase in throughput of 7 per cent despite running at a lower SAG mill speed, and potential of 16 per cent for increasing the SAG mill to standard operating speed. A number of process improvement opportunities have been identified to enhance current productivity and ensure long term capability to process the considerably more competent future ores. All of this is being linked in with the major digitisation program at the Barrick Cortez site, with an objective of linking all the data into a mine-wide process optimisation system, that can embed the processes by providing process-wide data access and production support via the future dynamic models linking ore body knowledge to productivity along the full process chain. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The concept of mine-to-mill was established by the JKMRC over 20 years ago Kanchibotla et al. (1998) and is well known worldwide as a route to increasing mill throughput through more intensive blasting as the feed becomes more competent. However, there is far more to the concept than higher powder factors, the deeper concept is to match blast output with crushing and milling or alterna

tive comminution circuit requirements. In this paper we explore the potential of more holistically integrating the mine plan, blasting design, stockpile management, primary crusher operation, milling circuit set-up and control linked into recovery and thus production of product, or overall mine productivity. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The JKMRC was invited by the management of the Barrick-Cortez mine site in Nevada, USA to work closely with site as part of the Barrick initiative of implementing a mine-wide digitisation program aimed at process integration. The direct production driver was the upcoming shift from a soft easy-processing ore to the considerably more competent ore of the second pit and later to the equally competent Cross Roads future ore-body. Between the two drivers this represented a classic mine-to-mill need but also the opportunity to build a site-wide integrated process improvement program. 

Barrick and Cortez management were clear that the objective was to build a sustainable process improvement route embedded in the operating capability and philosophy of the mine. Process improvement is not a single point step-change but an ongoing journey of continuous improvement. This needs to be embedded in the tools and management processes, and most importantly in the operating philosophy – the people who run the mine. Barrick is developing a strong Digitisation program across all their mines, and this project presents an ideal opportunity to embed and enhance mine to mill practices via linking plant-wide data through a digitised platform, to feed production data along the process line to a sequence of advanced ‘live’ models and to then feed back measured performance to continuously test, tune and update the models. 

###### **Cortez mine** 

The Cortez mine is located 120 km from Elko in Nevada, part of the great gold belt that is tracked by the original California trail. It has three main deposits: Cortez Hills with open pit (CHOP) and underground workings; Pipeline open pit and the Crossroads ore body which will be the major ore source for the future. Cortez has been open longer than any gold mine in the state of Nevada and is Barrick's and Nevada's largest gold producer. 

The CHOP pit has a highly friable ore, with an Axb in the range of 70 to 100, presenting easy milling, but it is close to end of life. The high wall of the pit (shown in the top of Figure 1) cuts into a mountain of cultural significance and the wall is fractured, so there are strict controls on blast vibration and movement to prevent damage to the pit wall. This limits the intensity of blasting, but fortunately the ore requires only low powder factors due to its friable nature. The pit is 20 km from the processing plant, so is linked by an overland conveyor in three sections, the longest of which is 16 km – illustrated in Figure 1. The view is from the Gyratory crusher and associated RoM pad across to the pl

ant in the far distance. The Pipeline pit has distinct regions of different competence, and production enters the most competent zone this year, with an Axb of around 35. Fortunately, the pit does not have the same stability and blasting constraints as the CHOP pit. It is located adjacent to the Plant with a direct drive by Dump trucks from the pit to the RoM Pad and associated Jaw crusher located next to the coarse ore stockpile that feeds the mill. Low grade ore is fed direct from the pits to an extensive leach pad. The recovery plant is a conventional SAG and recycle crusher with a single ball mill feeding the leach plant. The SAG mill is 26 ft diameter by 12 ft long, the ball mill is 16 ft diameter by 29 ft long and both mills have 3.3 MW (4500 HP) motors. The SAG mill discharges onto one of two vibrating screens, each feeding separate sumps – providing standby facility. A cluster of eight Krebs gMAX-26 cyclones (4 operating) closes the ball mill. The mine plans indicate that mill feed from CHOP pit will reduce significantly and need to be substituted with feed from Cross roads pit, which is considerably more competent than the current CHOP ore. ###### **SITE CHALLENGES** 

As with all mine sites there are a wide range of operational challenges, ranging from daily to short-term planning to long-term mine planning. While addressing the big challenges, there are always a range of operating issues and bottlenecks that can be identified and immediately implemented to open up processing capacity, bringing quick wins to what is otherwise a long-term project. These early gains are seen by the JKMRC team as a major bonus to early and intense engagement with site. In addition, it is ne

cessary to identify these in order to unlock the longer-term potential and thus address the overall project goals. 

###### **Preliminary diagnosis** 

A series of process reviews provided insights into the constraints and opportunities on site that should be a prime focus of the development work. Fundamental to this process was that the JKMRC domain experts and relevant site personnel studied the full process chain together on site and then reviewed the observations, findings and deductions jointly in workshops. The detailed site knowledge held by operating personnel is essential to this process. Geology, geomet modelling, block modelling, mine planning, drill and blast, Haulage, run-of-mine (RoM) pad stockpiles, primary crusher operation, conveying, coarse ore stockpile (COS) ahead of the mill, milling plant, leach pad, leaching, data-management, control systems, laboratory grade and production control, and plant management were all included in the review. Some activities of this journey are illustrated in Figure 3. 

Observing the mining process chain showed a range of issues or constraints, each of which presents an opportunity to capture higher productivity. These are listed as issue and corresponding opportunity: 

- The future ores had limited characterisation of use in modelling processing potential (blast design, competence for coarse grinding and specific energy for fine grinding). Develop a plan for adequate characterisation, based on the existing data and cores, that will populate models developed of the blasting and milling circuit. 

- The Measure while drill (MWD) data logging was facing considerable technical challenges preventing useful implementation Support site in developing models to link MWD data to ore competence for use in blasting and milling modelling. The link will provide the financial value to drive investment in full uptake. 

- Blast design was primarily constrained by vibration limits for wall protection, limiting the possible powder factor. Opportunity to use higher powder factors in the neighbouring pits with the more competent ore. 

- No allowance is made for blast movement in demarcating the grades for mill, leach and waste. Test, calibrate and implement the new SMI blast movement model to predict 3-D digging zones. Implement advanced blast design (spacing, sequencing, timing, stemming, etc.) to control movement.

The Grindcurve methodology developed by Powell over a number of years on many sites (Powell et al, 2009, 2011) was used to seek the optimal operating regime as feedrate is steadily increased. It also provides many points to a performance curve that can be used to fit and tune models and responses to a wide range of conditions. This also applies to the mill response with a changing blend of two ores, where the filling is held constant and the feedrate changes as the blend is systematically varied. ###### **Link into the digitisation program** 

The specific value sought through the digitisation program is to develop the model relationships that can utilise mine-wide data to inform the operation of optimal operating setpoints. This is planned to be via the model-informed process control (MiPC) approach. 

For example, using measure while drill (MWD) data to predict SAG mill throughput. Black-box correlation approaches have been found lacking in validity (Eloranta, 2003) and have no possibility of being applied to future ores (Galvez, 2017). According to Paredes et al. (2018) Such correlation relationships cannot account for: 

- Changes in rock fragmentation – especially when changing the blast design in future advanced process control 

- Changes in load, haul and conveying dynamics that can impose external constraints on ore delivery 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

- Changes in SAG mill filling, SAG mill speed, ball mill overload, cyclone cut-size, pebble crusher utilisat

ion, etc, in the milling plant as the feed type changes – especially active control with improved process models 

Black-box correlations can only shift an operation to the best part of its historic operation, not guide improved operational practice. 

It is necessary to establish what the important data and responses are that dictate the total process response. If the key data are missing, no amount of data correlation will elucidate these. For example, if penetration rate has a 30 per cent influence on the drilling energy per meter but is not measured, then correlations of apparent rock hardness based on energy used per meter drilled will be useless in predicting 20 per cent variations in mill throughput. 

Calculating missing data that are the underlying controller of parts of the process is a further contribution. A key driver of mill performance is mill filling, when measured by bearing pressure alone two significant factors are ignored: temperature of the oil – which can vary with season and time of day – affecting viscosity and thus bearing pressure; and mass loss from liner wear – which can change apparent load mass by 50 per cent over the life of a liner (Powell et at, 2012). 

Thus, linking MiPC into the Digitisation program is a key contribution for the JKMRC team to make in working with the Barrick-Cortez Digitisation team. The project aims to develop key process models, upgrading to dynamic models in an extension of the work, calculate key operating data, guide and assist in building the business justification to gather missing data or add in the sensors to measure important missing data. This input is based on using knowledge of the process, an aspect that appears to be ignored in the rush to utilise big data and computing power.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A number of new initiatives have been brought to the well-established mine to mill procedure. This takes advantage of upgraded models (blast movement, blast fragmentation with fines prediction, multi-component SAG mill model, mill filling, dynamic mill models), improved measures and instrumentation (measure while drill (MWD) data, GPS shovel monitoring linked to digging software, GPS load tracking, size specific energy (SSE)) and coupled with massive increases in data logging and computation (big data capabilities, processwide digitisation initiatives, live calculation of model outputs). These are not all fully developed or implemented but are underway as the program of work progresses. The outcomes should provide sustained implementation of advanced mine to mill and modelling capabilities to boost mine production. 

The importance of being on site, as opposed to conducting desk-top studies cannot be over-stressed, there is no comparison in the derived value – as noted from the many practical observations and recommendations that would not have otherwise been made. Initial project outcomes have provided a number of avenues for immediate production increases in addition to input for dealing with the long-term production objectives. 

Black-box correlations can only shift an operation to the best part of its historic operation, not guide improved operational practice. Hence, process knowledge and our best models should be captured in digitisation and big data initiatives. This input is based on using knowledge of the process, an aspect that appears to be ignored in the rush to utilise big data and computing power.

###### An economic approach to optimising mill reline frequency – a case study of SAG mill relines at Rasp mine 

###### _C M Standen_<sup>_1_</sup> 

1.  AAusIMM, Plant Metallurgist, CBH Resources Limited, 130 Eyre Street, Broken Hill NSW 2880. Email: caitlynstanden@cbhresources.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The SAG mill at Rasp Mine has undergone a number of liner design modifications since commissioning in 2012, making liner wear and failure difficult to predict from historical data. During 2017, several instances of liner failure or near failure were experienced resulting in unplanned downtime for emergency relines or to patch liners in the lead up to a planned shutdown. 

The strategy for relining mills is often to minimise the frequency of relines (and subsequent shutdown costs) by extending liner life, achieved through design modifications. However, it was observed that as the Rasp SAG mill liners wear, mill performance declined with power draw increasing and throughput declining. Opportunity and inefficiency costs start to erode the revenue per additional tonne milled for a given set of liners, and in turn the benefit of delaying relines. As such, optimising the frequency of relines becomes a trade-off between reline costs and opportunity/inefficiency costs in delaying relines. 

The aim of this paper is to demonstrate a frame work for analysing costs using a marginal economic analysis with the assumption that the Law of Diminishing Returns can be applied to the life of mill liners. The SAG mill operating variables can be modelled to determine their impact on costs and an optimal reline point can be defined where the total costs are minimised. This prevents unexpected failures due to accelerated wear by providing justification to reline earlier and thereby allowing efforts to be focused on sustaining milling performance. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Rasp Mine, owned and operated by CBH Resources, is located in Broken Hill in western New South Wales, approximately 1100 km west of Sydney and 500 km north-east of Adelaide. The mine operates on the CML7 tenement in the central section of the historic Line of Lode, a lead, zinc and silver deposit discovered in 1883. Current mining operations focus on the extraction and treatment of the Western Mineralisation with lesser amounts of remnant areas of higher grade main lode and zinc lode ores. 

The mill was commissioned in April 2012 and produces lead and zinc concentrates. Design throughput is 750 000 tonnes per annum with a feed rate of 92 t/h. Ore from the ROM pad is blended as it is fed into a double toggle jaw crusher producing a product with a P80 of 110 mm. Crushed ore is conveyed to a coarse ore storage bin before it is reclaimed and fed to the semi-autogenous grinding (SAG) mill followed by a ball mill for secondary grinding (Figure 1). Target product size is a P80 of 200 µm for feed to a two stage, conventional sulphide flotation circuit. Concentrate slurry is thi

ckened and filtered before being containerised and railed from site. Lead concentrate is railed to Port Pirie, while zinc concentrate is railed to the CBH Resources export facility, ConPorts at Newcastle and shipped to international customers. The Rasp SAG mill is a fixed speed mill with an internal diameter of 4.8 m and an effective grinding length of 3.15 m. Mill liners are composite in design with steel capped rubber lifters in a high-high configuration. Currently the shell design is a 26 row configuration with 300 mm lifters and 30-35° face angles. Feed and discharge head lifters are 250 mm high with 15° face angle. Discharge grates apertures are 15 mm x 30 mm consistent with the original design aperture. Media charge is up to 15 per cent based on design, but typically operates around 10-11 per cent with 105 mm balls used. No pebble crusher is currently installed, although there is the capacity within the design for installation at a later date. Scats are reintroduced to the circuit via feed to the jaw crusher. A number of modifications to the liner design in the Rasp SAG mill have been made since commissioning which were focused on preventing localised wear in an attempt to extend liner life and minimise total liner costs. - The outer section of the discharge grates was blanked off and the size of lifters was increased to prevent localised washing on the discharge end of the shell. 

- Addition of steel wear bars on plates at the discharge end of shell and outer section of feed head. 

- Increase in steel components on the mid and feed end of the shell as a result of increased wear to the feed end of shell following design modifications to the discharge end of the shell. 

To date, steel liners have not been considered due to safety concerns surrounding manual handling of lifters during reline activities. 

Cost pressures, especially evident during the most recent low in zinc metal prices drove the site to maximise utilisation of the entire life of the SAG mill liners and minimise the annual cost of liners. As such, the reline strategy was to reline as close to end of liner life as possible. Up to this point, all design modifications have focused on extending liner life and reducing the cost of parts. However, accelerated wear towards the end of liner life proved difficult to predict the failure point, which increased the risk of unplanned downtime. Additionally, relines for different liner sections did not line up with feed head, shell and discharge head relines tending to occur separately, increasing shutdown time and labour costs. 

Apart from the increased risk of failure with the existing reline strategy, operational performance suffered as the SAG mill efficiency was observed to decline significantly towards the end of the shell liner life. Power draw was seen to increase throughout the SAG mill shell liner life resulting in operators reducing throughput to protect the mill motor and remain below the power draw upper limit. It was apparent from operation that internal volume of the mill was not the limiting factor for throughput. Decreased throughput was therefore surmised to be a result of increased slippage as the shell liners wear. This led to a crash stop of the SAG mill to check for lifter packing which revealed some minor evidence of packing on the feed end of the shell, but not severe enough to be a cause for concern. Given the constraint of a fixed speed mill, grinding media usage increased throughout the liner life as operators attempted to counteract inefficient grinding and minimise the impact on throughput. 

However, it is important to note that additional limitations exist as outlined below, which may impact throughput and overall mill operation: 

- Management of run-of-mine (ROM) stocks around ore shortages. 

- Different ore types and their inherent metallurgical characteristics impact throughput particularly at maximum flotation capacity. 

- Ore hardness affects grinding throughput due to hold up of ore in the SAG mill. This typically correlates to lower feed grades. 

- Coarse ore due to segregation in the coarse ore bin at low bin levels due to the site’s close proximity to the commu

nity and noise restrictions on night shift. 

- Financial considerations during the design phase and subsequent operational period also limit mill operation such as the purchasing of specialty reline handling systems, or the choice to install a fixed speed motor versus a variable speed drive. 

These limitations around the operation of the SAG mill are not deemed to be critical limitations as annual throughput is still achieved (as per design) whilst the mill is not the bottleneck for Rasp Mine. However, it became evident that despite these limitations there was still an opportunity to maximise throughput with more efficient management of reline schedules. Reline strategy therefore shifted from utilising the entire SAG mill shell liner system life to focusing on the most cost effective reline point and in turn reducing the risk of unexpected liner failures. 

###### **PLANT DATA AND ANALYSIS** 

Observations of plant data indicated that the SAG mill shell had the greatest influence on mill performance. Therefore, this was the focus for the analysis of SAG mill performance. This paper focuses on a set of shell liners installed in January 2017 and replaced in June 2017 with a life of 320 000 wet metric tonnes (wmt). 

The key performance indicators for SAG mill performance were power draw (kW), throughput (t/h) and a grinding efficiency parameter related to power draw (kWh/t). Obvious outliers that were indicative of plant start-ups, blocked SAG mill feed chutes/sensor events, or mill trips were removed manually. A linear regression was then applied with standard residuals (>|3|) removed to generate a statistically significant model. 

The filtered data and corresponding linear regression models (Figure 2) confirmed plant observations of power draw increasing throughout shell liner life. Throughput trends downwards as the shell liners wear. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Typically, there is a period directly following a SAG mill reline where throughput is limited (Toor _et al_ , 2012; Yahyaei _et al_ , 2015; Russell, 2007). Toor _et al_ (2012) outlines a number of possible causes for this. This period was not observed for the Rasp SAG mill. The author hypothesises that this is a result of liner weight being limited for safety considerations and might indicate that there is capacity to increase liner weight dependant on safety considerations. 

Grinding efficiency was also seen to deteriorate with the required power draw per tonne increasing over time. As it is calculated using average throughput over the life of the mill, the accuracy of this data is impacted by the throughput constraints previously mentioned. 

As a whole, these models indicate that as liner wear progresses, revenue decreases as fewer tonnes are milled and the cost to mill each tonne increases with declining efficiency. Since mill throughput is not constrained at the start of shell liner life, the period of concern is towards the

end of liner life where throughput declines. This highlights an opportunity to increase mill revenue with more frequent relines to reduce the throughput limitation at the end of liner life without increasing overall costs. 

###### **Economic analysis** 

###### _Defining costs_ 

In order to determine the optimum reline point a number of costs need to be considered. John Russell proposed in his paper (Russell, 2007) that there are two key performance indicators for liners: cost of liners and mill metallurgical performance. In essence, this means that there are two main opposing costs to consider: the cost of additional shutdowns and shell liner systems, and the cost of reduced mill performance due to additional power costs and lost throughput. The aim is to find a cost-effective point where the sum of the two opposing costs is minimised. 

The cost of additional relines can be broken into three categories – cost of liners parts, cost of lost revenue and cost of reline labour. In comparison, the cost of reduced mill performance is a result of two cost components – cost of additional power requirement due to decreased grinding efficiency and the opportunity cost of reduced throughput. The additional power requirement was calculated by determining the difference between the minimum power requirement (kWh/t) at maximum grinding efficiency (i.e. start of shell liner life) and the additional power requirement as the liners wear. Integration between the two curves was used to calculate the cumulative power requirement over the life of the shell liners at intervals of 50 000 tonnes. The opportunity cost can be defined as the loss of revenue for the additional tonnes that could have been milled if the SAG mill was operating at maximum efficiency. Integration between the curve for maximum throughput at the start of liner life and the curve for reduced throughput with liner wear can be used to determine lost throughput and in turn lost revenue. 

###### _Marginal analysis and the Law of Diminishing Returns_ 

A marginal economic analysis was applied to this case study with the assumption that the Law of Diminishing Returns can be applied to the life of SAG mill shell liners. Marginal economic analysis is used for extent decisions and looks at the marginal benefit of producing one extra unit. Marginal benefit is defined as the marginal (or incremental) revenue associated with producing one extra unit less the marginal (incremental) costs for this extra unit (Froeb _et al_ , 2014). In this case, it is one extra tonne for a given set of SAG mill shell liners that is being considered and the extent decision is to determine how many tonnes should be milled before the cost of delaying relines outweighs the reline cost itself. The marginal revenue is the revenue for each additional tonne processed and for the case at hand, this would be the net smelter return (NSR) for each tonne of ore milled. The marginal cost is the variable cost to process one extra tonne.

It is important at this stage to further examine how costs are defined. It was assumed for the purposes of calculating opportunity costs that the boundary for this analysis is between the ROM and the crusher. Therefore, it is assumed there are no ore shortages and ore is readily available on the ROM. As such, any business activity that occurred prior to milling is not relevant to the cost analysis. Sunk costs and fixed costs are not relevant to extent decisions as these costs do not vary with output (Froeb _et al_ , 2014). Hence, the following assumptions can be made. 

- Once the ore has been mined and is available on the ROM (run-of-mine) pad, all mining costs are considered sunk costs (i.e. mining costs cannot be recovered) and are not relevant for an extent decision. 

- Any costs associated with the running of the business, but not directly related to mill production (e.g. safety, administration, mine maintenance, etc. are considered fixed overhead costs. These costs are also irrelevant to extent decisions. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

- Variable mill maintenance costs were considered negligible relative to the throughput that comprises the opportunity cost (lost throughput to delay relines). In reality, an increase in throughput would result in increased wear and tear for equipment and therefore higher maintenance costs. However, the available costing data was not detailed enough to define these costs for increases in throughput accurately. Average mill maintenance costs were applied to the lost throughput for shutdown activities to avoid overestimating the impact of lost throughput on revenue. 

Variable costs for milling would be the additional cost to increase throughput by one tonne. As the opportunity costs relate only to the difference between throughput at maximum and reduced efficiency, it is assumed that the mill is running and costs such as labour are considered as overhead (fixed) costs. Therefore, variable costs in this situation relate to additional reagents, water consumption and electricity. Note that for lost revenue due to additional shutdowns (increased frequency of relines) the variable milling cost includes all milling costs as the variable cost now includes the cost to energise the mill. 

The premise of the Law of Diminishing Returns is that as output increases, the marginal productivity (or benefit) will eventually decline. Diminishing marginal productivity implies increasing marginal costs leading to increasing average costs (Froeb _et al_ , 2014). Typically average costs will decline with increased output as fixed costs are distributed over a greater number of units. For example, the liner cost per tonne decreases with each extra tonne milled. However, as inefficiencies increase, marginal milling costs increase, causing the average cost to eventually increase. This is why it can be misleading to only consider the totalised liner and shutdown costs. 

A graphical

representation of the Rasp SAG mill shell reline costs is shown in Figure 3 (assuming budget figures). The shutdown cost curve was generated by calculating the number of shutdowns given the number of milled tonnes between reline events. As the frequency of reline events are pushed out further (frequency of relines decrease), the shutdown cost decreases. Initially this decrease in cost is substantial, but lessens as milled tonnes increases. Electricity costs and opportunity costs were calculated as the cumulative difference between the maximum efficiency and reduced efficiency curves. The total cost is the sum of all cost curves. This initially follows a similar shape as the shutdown cost curve indicating shutdowns are the dominate cost in the short term. In the long term ie. as milled tonnes increases for a given set of liners), the total cost curve turns upwards as the opportunity cost (and to a lesser degree electricity costs) counteracts the savings of delaying reline activities, demonstrating the diminishing returns relationship. Therefore, the optimum reline point is the minimum of the total cost curve. Delaying relines past this point will increase costs as inefficiencies drive average costs higher, while relining too early will result in higher reline costs. This provides a justification to increase reline frequency based on costs and supports the theory presented by several authors such as Russell (2007) and Toor _et al_ (2012) to design mill liners for performance as opposed to life. ###### _Sensitivity analysis_ An inherent limitation of the economic analysis is the variability of the value of recoverable metal per tonne of ore.
