###### **Case studies** 

Figure 11 presents a case in which one screen was receiving evenly distributed feed while the other screen was receiving uneven feed due to blockage of top deck on one side of the screen. As can be seen in Figure 11, uneven distribution of feed resulted in over-loading of one side of the screen and under-loading of the other side. Another issue, which is evident in FIG 11 for both screens, was over-loading of screens. Further investigation indicated that over-loading of screens was due to pegging and blinding of screen panels due to a high moisture content of the feed. 

Figure 12 presents a screen used in closed-circuit with a crusher which suffers pegging and blinding issues. Sizing a sample from the screen over-size stream indicated that 23 per cent of under-size material was missreporting to the over-size stream. The high fraction of fine under-size reduced the crusher capacity, through increasing the volumetric feed, preventing operation in choke feed condition. The issue also resulted in high potential for mechanical damage as fine particles caused packing inside the crushing chamber which lead to pressure spikes and which can eventually break crusher components. Pressure spikes also lead to activation of the crusher’s tramp release which results in excessively coarse particles in the crusher discharge. 

Cleaning screen panels on a regular basis to prevent pegging and blinding issues will improve classification efficiency as presented in Figure 13, which shows the crusher feed before and after cleaning the screen.

It is common to observe cyclones in a cluster that are operating very differently, as presented in Figure 14. The most common underlying reason for the difference in operation of cyclones is different spigot sizes usually due to a lack of control over the utilisation of each cycloen in a cluster (the most common and easily addressed reason) and vortex finder sizes due to uneven wear. In addition, faults can exist in the operation of automatic valves which prevents them opening fully, there may be a problem with the design of the distributor or the design of the feed arrangements (eg, different lengths to separate cyclones or clusters, number of bends, pipe diameter, etc.) which will cause differential operation of individual cyclones. 

In parallel cyclone clusters (such as in parallel milling lines), differences in operating parameters will result in different classification efficiencies. result, line 2 cut size (d 50c) was 100 μm coarser. Figure 15 – Frequency analysis of operating pressure of secondary cyclones of line 1 and line 2. ###### **OPERATIONAL ISSUES IN GRINDING** Unlike ball mills, SAG mills are difficult units to operate because of their sensitivity to operational conditions and slow response to fluctuations in feed characteristics. Grinding rates in SAG mills change significantly by changing the size distribution of feed, in particular amount of +90 mm material and the ore hardness (NapierMunn _et al_ , 1996). Ball mills are more robust in operation compared with SAG mills in terms of power draw and throughput capacity – however, the product size varies with changes in feed size and grindability. Expansion of comminution circuits and adding a pre-crushing stage to SABC circuits has introduced significant challenges to operation of grinding units. Powell _et al_ , 2015, provided a more detailed analysis of operational issues related to pre-crushing. ###### **Common issues in grinding** ###### _Feed_ Common issues: inadequate +90

mm rocks in SAG mill feed, coarse particles in ball mill feed due to oversize apertures in SAG mill trommel or screen, uneven mass and size distribution in parallel units. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 Impact: reduced throughput, high ball consumption, excessive liner wear, high circulating load, low energy efficiency, pebble scatting from ball mill. ###### _Operation_ Common issues: very low or very high percent solids, low mill filling, low ball filling in ball mills, wrong liner design, wrong grate design, wrong control philosophy. Impact: low grinding efficiency, low throughput, excessive liner wear, high media consumption, slurry pooling. ###### **Case studies** Figure 16 shows peening and spalling of liners in a SAG mill because of a low rock to ball ratio and low total mill filling which increased the direct impact of balls on liners. Further investigation by the authors indicated that the addition of a pre-crushing stage resulted in a reduction in the amount of +90 mm feed to the SAG to below the critical fraction needed to maintain a proper rock load in the mill. Consequently the mill throughput was dropped and site personnel decided to add more balls to increase the mill throughput. This decision resulted in increased media consumption and higher liner wear which forced the operation to operate the mill at a lower mill speed which in turn resulted in lower power draw. In general, it has been found that 7-12 per cent of +90 mm material is required in the feed to maintain a proper rock load in a SAG mill. The percentage is a function of how competent the rock is, and less is required for a competent rock feed. Over-loading of solids in ball mills is a common issue in operations because inefficiency of upstream comminution units passes the workload to ball mills. Inefficiency in the operation of classification also plays a role in mill over-loading. Figure 17 shows a case in which a ball mill is overloaded because of poor performance of the crushing and classification stages and stones in a ball after a SAG mill with a coarse screen. Overloading of ball mills can be identified through excessive circulating load against the standard on that mill, by drop-off in power below the peak value as feed rate is increased, or an increase in mill power as feed rate is decreased. The definitive identification technique is to conduct a proper crash-stop (stopping the feed for primary ball mill, the cyclone pump and mill simultaneously) and inspecting the mill charge. Ideally, the solids should settle to the same level or within 10 cm of the surface of ball load. Higher solids loading indicates that the feed rate is too high, or the feed is too coarse or too competent. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

This paper presents operational issues which have been observed on a number of plants during the course of plant surveys or process reviews conducted by the authors. The operational issues discussed in this paper are common and, although they are sometimes simple to resolve, they usually have a significant and detrimental impact on overall performance of operations. 

Materials handling and storage are important processes in concentrators, which often do not receive proper attention at the design stage and during operation. Inappropriate feeding arrangement, under-sized or over-sized units, size segregation induced by transfer points and uneven mass or size split are some of the typical issues in materials handling and storage. 

Classification efficiency has a significant impact on the performance of comminution units as well as separation processes. Over-loading, inappropriate operation condition, wrong control philosophy, uneven wear in cyclone clusters and under-sized units result in poor classification efficiency. Consequently, the downstream comminution units or separation process will receive a feed with inappropriate size, which results in sub-optimal performance. 

Crushing and grinding units typically operate in a robust fashion. However, incorrect feeding arrangements, uneven mass or size distribution, wrong feed size and inappropriate operating conditions result in reduced size reduction performance. Inefficient size reduction process results in excessive energy consumption for producing a desired final product, high wear of grinding media and liners and excessive mechanical failure of units. The overall plant capacity may also be reduced. 

To identify operational issues and to resolve them, operators should regularly conduct visual observations, measurement of key operating parameters and analysis of key process data. Resolving the operational issues may be as simple as improving control of the upstream process, or it may require engineering solutions which involves some capital cost. However, the authors’ experience indicates that the benefits of resolving the operational issues easily exceeds the costs of resolving them.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Rotary kilns have been in service in the gold industry to regenerate carbon for 65 years. At the time oxide ores with gold head grades of 8 to 10 g/t were being treated. Carbon could be regenerated adequately at 650°C and solution losses were less than 1%.  Forty years ago, research indicated that heavily fouled carbon from flotation circuits had to be held at 750 to 850°C for ten to twenty minutes for full reactivation (Avraamides and La Brooy, 1987), gold head grades were typically 5 g/t and solution losses typically 0.02 ppm – still less than 1%. In 2017 it was determined (Claflin et al., 2017) that a residence time of less than 1 minute at 750°C can be adequate to reactivate carbon fouled with organics sufficiently to achieve 0.005 ppm solution losses in a flotation tailings leach plant. 

With the potential for discovery head grades to drop below 0.6 g/t, solution losses of 0.02 ppm represent over 3% loss. Tight operation of the whole carbon circuit is required to keep gold solution losses below 1% going forward. 

There are alternatives to a rotary carbon kiln, e.g. vertical kilns of which the Minfurn, Rintoul and Combustion Air kilns are examples. The alternative kilns can be heated using electrical heating elements, induction, and microwave. These kilns can operate successfully under the right conditions, however, they are almost exclusively for small carbon throughputs and are not suitable for the large carbon advance rates that are required to process low head grade ore deposits. Large throughput carbon kilns are are almost exclusively fossil fuel fired rotary kilns and the subject of this paper. In the view of the principal author, a fossil fuel fired vertical carbon kiln is preferred to a rotary kiln, however, it is not currently used in the industry. 

Thermal regeneration of activated carbon has a major impact on gold recovery in the carbon circuit. The carbon kiln and associated equipment constitute 3 to 5% of the capital cost for an oxide processing plant and up to 10% of the capital cost if flotation tails are leached. Despite the capital cost and impact on recovery, the carbon kiln is often poorly selected, operated and maintained. 

Six years ago Ausenco embarked on the Carbon Kiln Initiative to reduce solution gold losses. This body of knowledge has been published in a series of papers culminating in this paper on how to: 

1. Select a kiln appropriate for the flowsheet; 

2. Maintain the kiln to achieve design operation; and 

3. Operate the kiln to minimise costs and maximise reactivation.

Minimising solids tailings losses necessarily involves significant additional capital and operating expense to liberate and extract the gold. Solution tailings losses on the other hand represents the most readily recoverable gold; the gold is already liberated and extracted, it just needs to be recovered. Most carbon adsorption circuits can be operated with solution losses less than 0.005 g/t, which for a head grade of 0.6 g/t will represent <1% gold loss. 

The carbon in leach (CIP/CIL) circuit is the heart of most gold plants. There are many factors that affect adsorption, but the fundamental issue is the activity of the regenerated carbon that reports the last CIL tank. If the carbon activity is not high (at least 90% to 95% the activity of Fresh carbon) then no matter how well the CIL circuit is designed, operated and maintained, 0.005 g/t solution tailings is not possible (Claflin et al, 2017). 

The carbon kiln does not operate in isolation. Carbon regeneration is a combination of acid washing, elution and thermal regeneration. Thermal regeneration is conducted in a kiln that is primarily designed to process typically 1.2 to 3.35 mm activated carbon. Activated carbon is relatively easy to transport as slurry. As a moist, drained solid or a dry solid, activated carbon flows readily through chutes and across screens. Add inorganic material (sand and gravel) of a size larger than the inter-tank screens, or other trash, especially plastic, and the carbon becomes difficult to transport, settles out in vessels and lines and blocks chutes and pumps. The carbon kiln, indeed the whole carbon circuit, becomes very difficult to operate and maintain. The nature of the feed must be considered during selection for the kiln to be operable, maintainable and perform as designed. 

Selecting equipment based on the equipment’s ability to produce highly reactivated carbon, or modifying existing kilns to perform to the same level, has been the focus of the authors a since 2013 (La Brooy & Claflin, 2013, Claflin et al., 2013, Claflin et al., 2015a, Claflin et al., 2015b, Claflin et al., 2017, Claflin & La Brooy, 2017, and Claflin et al., 2018). 

This paper pro

vides carbon kiln selection criteria, guides maintainers as to what to inspect for and maintain to keep the equipment able to perform, and guides operators as to how to get the best process performance from the kiln. The carbon kiln is discussed first in terms of the process design criteria that are applied, then in terms of mechanical requirements.  The issues maintainers face are the same ones that should be criteria for selection, hence comments to maintainers are scattered within the mechanical selection requirements. Finally, if the equipment is selected and maintained well, the operation of the equipment is relatively straightforward and discussed at the end of the paper.

All the following issues will not apply to all carbon regeneration operations, but all have been observed industrially and operators, maintainers, metallurgists and process engineers should be aware of them. 

###### **Flowsheet considerations** 

The industry has long been putting capital cost before carbon kiln performance resulting in kilns that do not reactivate carbon particularly well. These inexpensive kilns may be fine for the early stages of a project when grades are higher and free milling oxide ores are being processed, but they are unable to perform well when head grades drop or the ore becomes harder to process, and they perform very poorly if they have to treat carbon from a flotation tailings CIL circuit. 

The most expensive kilns do not necessarily deliver the best carbon reactivation, they are, however, generally better made and more robust. 

Carbon kilns perform best when processing what they are designed to treat, namely activated carbon. Eventually all carbon circuits build up trash and sand which move with the carbon and can interfere with solids handling and carbon reactivation. Carbon reactivation generates carbon dust and fines. These should be removed before returning the granulated activated carbon to the CIL circuit. The carbon reactivation circuit should always allow for trash removal, sand removal, and fines removal in addition to reactivating the carbon. 

A carbon kiln processing carbon from a free milling oxide ore should be different to that used for a pregrobbing ore and significantly different to that used to treat carbon from a flotation tailings CIL circuit. An ore containing little fouling material such as calcium carbonate or flotation reagents may only have a limited need of a carbon kiln. Preg-robbing ore may only require a low temperature kiln with a high throughput if there are no flotation reagents. Carbon from flotation tailings CIL and preg-robbing ores with flotation will usually require both high throughput and the carbon must achieve a high temperature in a water vapour atmosphere. 

Gold leaching and adsorption test work may be undertaken to size the CIL circuit to determine the amount of carbon inventory and carbon advance required, howeve

r, traditionally there was no method to determine optimal conditions in the carbon kiln. With no means to select the process conditions for the kiln, kilns were selected for less important reasons, e.g. capital cost or mechanical robustness. 

The carbon kiln must be selected to suit the specific carbon chemistry required to satisfactorily activate carbon and deal with other conditions such as fouling arising from the process flowsheet before other selection criteria, such as cost, is considered. 

###### **Process requirements** 

To reliably achieve a low solution tail (i.e. 0.005 ppm Au) a carbon regeneration kiln needs to regenerate activated carbon to as close as possible to the fresh activated carbon received from the manufacturer. Many operations accept 70 to 80% reactivation as satisfactory when chasing modest solution tail targets, but 70% reactivated carbon cannot achieve solution tails below 0.005 ppm (Claflin et al., 2017). 

Activated carbon for gold recovery is made by carbonising organic material, e.g. coconut shell and peat, in an inert atmosphere to form randomly arranged graphitic crystallites separated by amorphous carbon, with the amorphous carbon activated at high temperature in a steam atmosphere. 

Mwapwele (2015) shows a scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of what fresh activated carbon looks like (refer to Figure 2). The activated carbon was reagent grade as supplied by Merck Millipore, but there was no reference to the product number and thus the source carbon. Figures 3a and b show SEM scans of fresh coconut shell activated carbon (Snyders, 2015). Figure 3b is very similar to Figure 2 and thus Figure 2 is quite likely coconut derived activated carbon. 

Figure 3a shows that the carbon particle is quite amorphous while Figures 2 and 3b are atypical of the bulk of the particle. Figures 2 and 3b only present the activated carbon’s macropores and only from one perspective. Macropores allow easy diffusion into and out of the activated carbon, however, adsorption and surface diffusion takes place mostly on micropore internal surfaces. Mwapwele (2015) reports that fifty per cent of the carbon volume in Figure 2 is micropore volume and the average micropore diameter is just 2.56 nm (1/1000 of the 3 µm reference bar). Hence SEM is not able to provide information of what is happening in the micropores and can only provide information on gross fouling of macropores.

Mambe (1988) describes carbon activation as the oxidation of the carbon’s surface with ‘loose’ and ‘firm’ chemisorbed oxygen complexes. ‘Loose’ refers to carboxyl ‘CO 2-’ complexs, which are loosely bound, produced at temperatures less than 450°C, renders the surface acidic and favours polar adsorption. ‘Firm’ refers to carbonyl 'CO-' complexes, which are tightly (firmly) bound and produced at temperatures greater than 500°C and renders the surface alkaline so that anions such as cyanide can only be adsorbed as neutral species, i.e. as ion pairs. Carbon activated at 800-900°C will have predominantly firmly bound oxygen groups and, at gold plant pH, i.e. alkaline conditions, only allow ion pair adsorption (Mambe 1988). 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Of particular note is Mambe’s testwork on cooling in air versus nitrogen. Carbon black was activated in air at 300 and 500°C and cooled in either air or in nitrogen. It was observed that cooling in air resulted in more ‘loose’ activated sites and activity is reduced relative to fresh carbon. If the carbon is cooled in a nitrogen atmosphere, the carbon surface retains ‘firm’ activated sites and carbon activity is increased relative to fresh carbon (Mambe 1988). Nitrogen quenching is not practical, however, quenching (cooling) in water vapour is and results in less thermal shock to the carbon than dropping a hot carbon particle directly into cold water. 

If the target of carbon regeneration kilns is to regenerate carbon to as close to fresh as possible, then activation of carbon over 800°C followed by cooling in water vapour is preferred to promote and retain the firm oxygen complexes that preferentially adsorb ion pairs. 

###### **_Carbon reactivation_** 

Before reactivation, inorganic contaminants and large trash should be removed. Precipitated calcium carbonate can be removed by acid washing prior to elution. Trash and sand should be removed before dewatered carbon is fed to the kiln. While this paper focuses on the carbon kiln, these issues are mentioned in the Mechanical Requirements section of this paper. 

During thermal reactivation organic contaminants are removed from the base carbon. In general, larger molecular weight organic material (whether natural or introduced as reagents) will adsorb strongly to activated carbon and can reduce both gold loading kinetics and capacity of the carbon (Mahapatra, 2009). On heating, low molecular weight material may volatilise off the carbon leaving no residue, however, high molecular weight material will tend to pyrolyse to tar, then to char, which needs to be removed by oxidation wi

thout damaging the activated carbon. 

Figures 5a and b demonstrate the blinding effect of MIBC (Methyl Isobutyl Carbinol) and PAX (Potassium Amyl Xanthate) on the activated carbon shown in Figure 2 (Mwapwele, 2015). Figure 5a and b are the same scale as Figure 2 and all are of the same activated carbon – the only difference is about 5% w/w adsorbed contaminant. These SEMs show macropores and fouling of the surface heavy enough to alter its topography. Increased contamination in the micropores lead to reduced volume and pore diameter, especially for PAX, and reduced activity. 





Figure 5 a and b – SEM Image of activated carbon fouled in 300 ppm MIBC and 300 ppm of PAX (Mwapwele, 2015). 

To remove the organic material, the contaminants must be volatilised off or, in the case of longer chain molecules like MIBC and PAX, thermally decomposed (inert and oxidative pyrolysis) and the residual char removed by oxidation (Claflin et al., 2017). Oxidation using oxygen (or air) can remove the contaminant char, but oxygen is very reactive and it reacts with any carbon it contacts. Consider Figure 4 where the contaminant material is sandwiched between graphitic layers of base carbon. The oxygen reacts with everything and consumes base carbon in addition to the contaminant char. The result is the pores widen, surface area is lost and the carbon particle structural strength is compromised.  The reaction is so fast that activated sites on the pore surface are burnt away as fast as they are made, thereby limiting the number of active sites per area as well as the surface area. 

The reaction with water vapour, on the other hand, is a relatively slow reaction that is more selective. Water vapour oxidises more reactive carbon (contaminant char) in preference to the more structured base carbon. Water vapour does not reduce the activated sites, but rather promotes their formation. Water vapour is used

to manufacture the activated carbon in the first place over many hours – the carbon residence time at temperature in the kiln (minutes) is negligible by comparison. 

###### **_Kiln sizing_** 

Conventionally, a carbon kiln has been sized to: receive drained wet carbon, dry the carbon, heat the carbon to a nominal temperature and hold it for a specific length of time at that temperature. In practice, the target temperature is 650 to 850°C and the target time at the reaction temperature is 10 to 30 minutes. More recently the required time at temperature to remove adsorbed organic reagents and reactivate heavily fouled activated carbon to over 90% was observed to be as little as one minute at 750°C (Claflin et al., 2017). A kiln to heat carbon to 850°C for 30 minutes is a very different size to one designed to heat the same amount of carbon to 750°C for 1 minute. 

Two methods are available to size carbon kilns as reported by Claflin et al. (2018). These are the Tube Furnace and a modif

ied thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) technique. 

###### **_Tube furnace_** 

This approach considers heating carbon in a tube furnace operated under a simulated kiln atmosphere. The carbon is rapidly heated to the reaction temperature and held for the requisite length of time. The activity of the carbon can be measured in the normal way using a gold adsorption test. The results of this method are conclusive and can be used to set the time/temperature/atmosphere conditions of an industrial carbon reactivation kiln. This is the method that was used to prove that heavily fouled carbon can be reactivated in 1 minute in steam (Claflin et al, 2017). 

Figure 6 presents the data of fresh carbon artificially fouled with plant organic reagents to an activity of 22%. Each line contains three different temperature data points at 650, 750 and 850°C and each line represents different residence times at the reaction temperature. As expected, as the temperature rises, the rate of reaction increases and with increased residence times, the mass loss increases. 

There are two atmospheres used in Figure 6: steam (blue) and a water vapour/nitrogen atmosphere with 15% oxygen to represent products of combustion (POCs – red). Longer residence times, especially at higher temperatures, caused significantly more mass loss. 

The steam atmosphere activates carbon significantly better and for less carbon loss under all conditions, than a simulated POC atmosphere.  A steam atmosphere need only remove about 8% of the sample mass to yield 100% reactivated carbon, which suggests that the contaminant mass is only about 8% and that once removed, the activity was restored. 

Importantly, treating the activated carbon in a POC atmosphere can produce the carbon loss, but does not reactivate the carbon to the same degree as the steam and never exceeds 80% reactivation. This indicates that the mass being removed is not char and/or that activated sites are either not being generated or are being burnt away as fast as they are made. The carbon losses observed in the POC atmosphere for extended residence times suggest a significant amount of base carbon is being consumed. 



Figure 6 – The effect of kiln operating conditions on mass loss and carbon activity.

###### **_Thermogravimetric analysis_** 

TGA coupled with mass spectrometry (TGA MS) can be used to estimate the mass loss required and the rate of mass loss in a mildly oxidising carbon dioxide atmosphere to estimate the residence time that carbon needs to be in a steam atmosphere at the reaction temperature. 

Fresh, loaded and Regenerated carbon samples are heated at 10 C/min under a nitrogen to 950°C to produce TGA mass loss traces. These traces indicate the temperature at which the fresh activated carbon was manufactured (not shown), the carbon temperature achieved in the existing kiln and provides an indication of the mass loss associated with the physical and chemical removal of contaminants in acid washing and elution. If carbonates or organic sulphur bearing contaminants are present, they will present themselves in the MS traces (not shown). 



Figure 9 – Rate of mass loss

under nitrogen. 

Figure 9 presents the rate of mass loss for a kiln that is not hot enough to regenerate the carbon at all. The Regenerated carbon trace and the Loaded carbon trace are very similar to each other except for a shift to higher temperatures for the Regenerated carbon trace.  This shift is due to removal of contaminant material during acid washing (calcium carbonate) and elution where some breakdown products are likely being formed that require higher temperatures for their removal. If the kiln were performing properly, then the Regenerated carbon trace would be almost identical to the Fresh carbon trace. 

The mass of char to be removed is determined by comparing the mass loss trace as a function of temperature of a sample of material to be regenerated to the fresh carbon (not shown). The slope of the traces will be identical at low temperatures and again at high temperatures as is indicated in Figure 9.  The difference in mass between the point of divergence and the point of convergence of the slopes is the mass of char to be removed (Claflin et al., 2018). If the Loaded carbon in Figure 9 were to be regenerated, then the mass loss of char to be removed would be measured between 670°C and 820°C. 

Water vapour can condense and cause damage in the TGA MS equipment. To simulate a water vapour oxidising atmosphere, carbon dioxide is used at a 30 to 65°C higher temperature to compensate for the lower rate of reaction. The sample is taken to the reaction temperature as quickly as the equipment will allow (>50°C/min). The char will begin to oxidise before it reaches the target reaction temperature. Indeed, the contaminant char can be largely consumed before the target temperature is reached as shown in Figure 10. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

An estimate of the required reaction residence time is derived by comparing the contaminated carbon rate of mass loss to that of fresh carbon between 700°C and when the contaminated carbon mass rate is less than that of fresh carbon. The reaction between carbon dioxide and carbon (the Boudouard reaction) becomes favourable at about 700°C (Claflin et al., 2017), hence when the sample temperature achieves 700°C contaminant char will begin to be consumed. When the char is substantially removed, the contaminated carbon will have a rate of mass loss less than fresh carbon due the history of the two samples. Loaded carbon will have experienced high temperatures previously as it has travelled through the carbon circuit and will have greater inorganic build-up.  Fresh carbon has experienced a high temperature once (when it was manufactured) and will have no inorganic build up, hence it will generally be slightly more reactive. 

For the example in Figure 10, the residence time above 700°C until the loaded carbon trace crosses the fresh carbon trace is 3.5 minutes. 



Figure 10 – Determining the residence time to remove contaminant char from TGA data (Cla

flin et al, 2018). 

An alternative to performing a carbon dioxide TGA test to estimate the rate of reaction is to use data by van Vliet (1991). The data is for the rate of reaction of dodecylbenzene sulphonate (DBS – a surfactant found in the waste water industry) charred onto activated carbon and reacted in a steam atmosphere at different temperatures. DBS is larger than most contaminants found on activated carbon in the gold industry and when charred, will be less reactive than more disorganised amorphous char found in the gold industry. Claflin et al. (2018) fitted the data with the following equation: 

Equation 1: Contaminant Char Reaction Rate, %/min = (7.90E-42) (Temp, °C)<sup>**14.40**</sup> 

Reaction rate results for activated carbon contaminated with flotation agents and reacted in a tube furnace are typical 50% higher than that predicted by equation 1, hence the equation is conservative with respect to sizing a kiln (Claflin et al., 2018). Use of equation 1 is recommended as it provides a conservative rate of reaction and is far less expensive than performing carbon dioxide TGA tests. 

If the mass of char to be removed is divided by the reaction rate, then the residence time of the activated carbon in the carbon regeneration kiln can be conservatively estimated. The residence time, reactivation time and steam atmosphere is provided to the vendor as a specification. 

###### **Mechanical Requirements** 

Most kilns are expected to have a 10 to 20 year working life. Some kilns are still working after 40 years and others only worked for a few years. In both cases, the operator probably overpaid for the equipment. 

Mechanically, a rotary carbon kiln is a simple device. Solids get dropped into one end of an inclined rotating drum and fall out the other end. The drum is inside a combustion chamber (an oven) and the drum is heated up. Water vapour and off-gasses are driven off the carbon while products of combustion exhaust the combustion chamber. It is very important that the kiln operate robustly and reliably, but the kiln should be fit 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

for purpose to suit the specified working life. The effect of temperature on expansion/contraction, corrosion, fatigue and friction are the principal criteria to bear in mind from a mechanical perspective. 

Carbon temperatures are generally ambient to 100°C in the front end and less than 850°C leaving the heated zone.  If the kiln is very large for its duty, the combustion chamber temperature need only be 50 to 100°C higher than the carbon temperature. To get the carbon up to that temperature quickly, however, the combustion temperature is taken as high as the materials of construction will safely allow. 

###### **_Drum_** 

Most drums are made from austenitic steel, which means they have a pacifying oxide layer on their surface that protects them. The most common is 253 MA, and it is suitable up to 1,100°C under neutral

or oxidising conditions and tolerates oxidised sulphur well. To promote heat transfer through the drum, a drum can be as thin as 4.76 mm (3/16”). The thinner a drum is, the more susceptible it is to abuse, nonetheless, the drum should last 2 to 5 years and is a fraction of the cost of a thick, robust drum. 

Nonetheless, no drum can handle extreme temperature and burner management systems are required to protect the equipment. High temperature differentials cause thermal expansion-contraction stresses as shown in Figure 11 where cold lifters inside are ripping the outer hot drum apart. 

If the gas inside the drum has high oxygen levels, then a fire can occur inside the drum (Figure 12).  The combustion chamber temperatures will not detect an internal fire. Oxygen levels should be kept low and fire detection built into the design to prevent overheating the drum internally or externally. 





Figure 11 – Lifters pulling drum. Figure 12 – Carbon fire damage (Staunton, 2015). 

From a maintenance perspective, it is difficult to inspect drums directly without pulling a hood off and looking in the end. However, if the drum is contacting the shell at only one point on each revolution or the floating end rotates elliptically around the axis of rotation, then the drum is out of round or has a banana shape. Look for drum distortion by regularly measuring run out. A drum can operate with significant distortion so long as the rotating drum does not interfere with stationary refractory or other parts of the equipment. Holes in the drum can be patched, but this often leads to corrosion and warping problems. Thin-walled drums are relatively inexpensive and replacing the drum is likely to be more successful and ultimately less expensive than patching - keep a spare drum in stock. 

Activated carbon at high temperature in steam produces carbon monoxide and hydrogen, i.e. a reducing atmosphere. If the pacifying layer is removed, then the drum and lifters can corrode and distort. Figure 13 shows heat transfer fins made of 253MA that have corroded and become paper thin at the discharge end of the heated zone of a carbon kiln. Slowly rotating carbon kilns with deeper carbon beds are more susceptible to the pacifying layer being removed due to drum surface being exposed to the reducing atmosphere for a longer time.. Cooler areas are unaffected.

Figure 13 – Corrosion damage to heat transfer fins. 

Most carbon kilns operate with a very low mass load and can even stop at temperature with no damage. However, if solids back up, the drum will get heavy, and then the kiln must be designed to cope with high loads at extreme temperature for perhaps hours; an uninterruptable power supply (UPS) should always be included to slowly turn the drum. 

From a maintenance perspective, periodic inspections are required, initially every 3 months and when the behaviour becomes regular the inspection p

eriod can be pushed out to perhaps a year. If serious corrosion is observed, then a replacement drum should be considered as a stock item, especially for thin-walled drums. 

To increase heat transfer from the combustion chamber to the drum, combustion chamber temperatures can be increased, but the material’s strength will reduce. To increase heat transfer from the drum to the carbon, the drum’s rotational speed can be increased. This reduces the time any given part of the drum is exposed to the reducing atmosphere, but increases the fatigue and creep in the drum, tyres and trunnions.  Ensure venders have considered fatigue and creep on the drum, tyres and trunnions. 

Fatigue is exacerbated by thermal contraction and expansion. Figures 14 and 15 show the effect of excessive stopping and starting of a very well-made kiln – all the spider supports between the drum and the girth gear and riding rings have fatigued as have the spider supports between the drum and an internal heat tube (Note: only indirect/direct kiln have heat tubes – they are supposed to direct products of combustion to the feed end of the kiln to dry the feed and improve thermal efficiency).  If not turned on/off excessively and maintained, this make of kiln can be in service for 40 years.

Regular inspections will have no difficulty in picking up such failures before they are catastrophic. 

###### **_Combustion chamber_** 

Burners are typically fired under the drum. Temperature measurement is typically on the opposite wall from the burners or above the burners. When on the opposite wall, care must be taken to measure the gas temperature without flame radiation effects, because a burner set up wrongly can have a flame long enough to impinge on the far wall and melt refractory fibre (refer to Figure 16). If the temperature is measured on the burner side, then heat has already been transferred out of the gas to the drum and it will be much cooler than on the far wall, then over firing can inadvertently occur. From a maintenance perspective, use an infrared gun periodically and do a temperature survey of all components, including areas that do not have discoloured paint. Refractory damage as in Figure 16 will get worse with time and it is best to have a lot of forewarning before embarking on a refractory reline of a kiln that can take the kiln off-line for up to two weeks. Heat is normally supplied by burning fossil fuel, but if electricity is inexpensive, electrical heating elements can be used. Burners are generally reliable, however, in the mineral industry the fuels are often heavy and dirty. ###### **_Gas seals_** 

Combustion chamber exhaust (POCs) should not be directed into the drum because of damage to the carbon, poor reactivation and the possibility of a carbon fire which can damage the drum. Nonetheless there are designs that do this for reasons of thermal efficiency (refer to Figure 14 discussion). If POCs are directed into the drum, then the oxygen content must be kept very low (<2.5%). This requires almost ideal combustion and good gas seals, such as Figure 23a, which must be installed to prevent air ingress into the combustion chamber. 

If POCs are not directed back to the drum, then seals are not particularly important on the combustion chamber except to prevent hot spots. To achieve thermal efficiency, allow for a preheater/partial dryer that 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

uses the POCs at lower, safer temperatures before the carbon enters the kiln. To minimise the heat lost from the combustion chamber to the surroundings, a type of lip seal (refer to Figure 23b or c) may be used where refractory material (fibre or board) is held in the seal and the drum allowed to expand (due to temperature) into the refractory seal. It is very simple and adequate, but ensure that it can be serviced without having to disassemble the whole kiln. 







Figure 23 a, b and c – Combustion chamber to drum seals (leaf spring, flanged & stuffed lip seals). 

All gas seals that could permit air in or off-gases out of the drum are important (drum to feed hood, drum to discharge hood, feed hood to kiln feeder and discharge hood to quench tank). One end of the drum

will be fixed and the other floating (to allow for drum expansion). All gas seals should be accessible from the outside so they can be inspected and serviced. 

Mechanical seals on rotary kilns are typically on the periphery of the drum, hence even a small gap in the seal results in a large cumulative opening that can let air in or toxic gases out. For instance, a kiln suitable for a 1 t/h of carbon regeneration might have a 1.8 m diameter drum. A gap just 0.1 mm wide between the drum and the seal face results in the equivalent area as a hole 27 mm in diameter. A hole of that size would be automatically plugged and in most cases the gaps are much larger. 

Many kilns are operated with an induced draft (ID) fan drawing process gases out of the kiln usually at minus 125 Pa (- ½ inch H2O). This amount of suction certainly removes the risk of off-gases leaking out, but also guarantees air leaking in. For a 27 mm hole the air ingress is 32 m<sup>3</sup> /h – enough to burn about 1.5 kg/h of carbon. Arguably the best advice is to operate the kiln with a very slight overpressure (5 to 10 Pa) to prevent air ingress, but this means some off-gases could leak out. If toxic off-gases are present, operate at a slight negative vacuum of minus 5 Pa and the air ingress would be reduced to 6.5 m<sup>3</sup> /h – tolerable given the amount of water vapour produced during carbon cooling. 

Figure 24a, b, and c show examples of good drum to discharge hood gas seals used on carbon kilns. Figures 24a and b show a seal produced by two parallel faces pulled together with springs. One uses a high temperature gasket rope (as used in pump gland packing) and the other is a metal-metal seal with phosphorous bronze on one side and austenitic steel on the other. The discharge hood floats with the expanding drum, which is fine as the discharge chute reports to a quench tank full of water. 

Leaf spring seals, as shown in Figure 24c, offer a good seal when they are maintained. They consist of a fabric that effects the gas seal sandwiched between two layers of spring metal. The metal sheets protect the fabric and permit the drum to rotate inside. The problem comes as the inner metal sheets wear exposing the fabric and the gas seal is lost. The outer springs are usually still in fair condition, so a casual inspection will not pick up the lost gas seal. It is very common to see this type of seal in a state of disrepair. Unfortunately, these kilns are typically operated under a vacuum of 120 to 150 Pa and a significant amount of air can be pulled through a small gap in the seal causing damage to the carbon.

###### **_Lubrication_** 

The kiln itself has very few points requiring lubrication – usually four trunnions, a couple of thrust bearings (to keep the drum from moving longitudinally) and a gear or chain drive. Lubrication of the gear or chain drive can be achieved using grease or graphite depending on the temperature. A simple graphite block lightly abrading on the surface being lubricated is more than adequate and inexpensive, though it can be messy. 

The bearings in the discharge trunnions are particularly susceptible to seizing. The drum is very hot in this location and the trunnions get hot enough to melt the grease. If there is no lubrication, then the bearings will freeze and the drum can stop rotating, such as in Figure 26, with potentially catastrophic consequences. The trunnions need to be greased regularly and the grease should be able to flow out, so there is no doubt that grease is getting into the bearing. Trunnions should be oversized for their duty in terms of load carrying capability am hardness and bearings well designed to prevent overheating.

###### **_Trunnion alignment_** 

For such a simple piece of equipment mechanically speaking, aligning the various aspects of the drum inside the combustion chamber and getting all the gas seals parallel can be a challenge. Work with the vendor, preferably have the vendor come to site, and ensure the kiln is assembled and aligned from the outset. Significant damage can be done if not aligned correctly. 

Maintenance personnel should be involved in the initial setting up of the kiln to ensure what is required is understood and incorporated into the maintenance activities. Once aligned, the most likely thing to go wrong is for a trunnion to have slipped, which will drop the drum and alter the alignments of all gas seals. The misalignment is obvious and will show up as uneven wear of the tyre on the (refer to Figure 27). 

###### **_Trash and sand_** 

Carbon kilns are designed to process granular activated carbon, but from a solids handling perspective they will convey almost anything that is fed into them. Kiln feeders and discharge pumps are not so forgiving. The carbon return pumps are typically small and can block with trash larg

er than 12.5 mm. If there is a high sand load, then the pumps will not have the head to pump to the carbon return screen and, if they do, the pump speed will be very high and will erode the activated carbon. Sand will also dampen kiln tube feeders (sand is heavy and will dampen the vibration) resulting in an accumulation of sand in the feeder and variable feeding rates. 

Almost all CIL circuits will have sand and trash circulating with the carbon. Sand is inorganic material larger than the safety screen aperture up to nominally 6 mm (refer to Figure 28). Trash is all material that is larger whether inorganic or organic, e.g. plastic film, cable ties, rocks, wood, wire, scale, rubber lining, et cetera (refer to Figure 29 and Figures 30a and b). Sand and trash can enter the carbon circuit because the CIL trash screen is not maintained or because personnel drop rubbish into the top of the tanks. 



Figure 28 – Sand. 



Figure 29 – Inorganic trash. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 





Figure 30a and b – Plastic cable ties melted and partially oxidised in a carbon kiln. 

Once in the CIL tanks, the trash travels with the carbon, through acid washing and elution to the carbon regeneration facility. Because carbon volumetric flows are generally small (30 L/min for a 1,000 kg/h carbon kiln), the pipelines, chutes and pumps are not large and trash can cause obstructions and blockages. 

Sand and trash removal is therefore normally done post elution where carbon losses do not carry gold loss penalties. Trash prevents sand removal working reliably due to small bore underflow lines and valves. For very large, on-going trash loads, a small screen may be required. If the on-going trash load is not high, then a simple trash basket should be satisfactory. If the CIL circuit has built up a large amount of trash, then start the trash basket with large, say, 20 mm apertures and slowly (over months) reduce the aperture to 12.5 mm. Then keep the basket empty. 

If the site has an on-going trash problem that cannot be resolved easily and readily, then a more substantial trash screen will be required. Non-vibrating screens with large apertures are sufficient for most trash removal. Vibration is required only if water washing of the trash is required to remove excess carbon from the trash. 

From a maintenance perspective, the trash basket will erode. To be handled by hand, the basket will necessarily be small and all the flow will pass through a small area. The instantaneous flow rate to transport a typical batch of carbon could easily be 65 m<sup>3</sup> /h and the velocity through the basket will be high, hence the erosion. Check the basket regularly for erosion and replace the basket if significant erosion is observed. Keep at least one spare basket in stock. 

If a continuous screen is used, look for fatigue cracking due to vibration or erosion caused by the carbon and any sand that may be present. 

Sand can be

removed by jigs, spirals, classifiers (refer to Figure 31) and elutriators. Not all the sand needs to be removed on each pass and generally it is best not to lose any carbon as there will be 20 to 50 ppm of gold associated with the carbon loss. 

If the sand is a similar size to the carbon, dense and with a low surface area, then all of these devices can work. However, if the sand is a light precipitate, then density separation may not work well. If the sand is flat and thin, e.g. pipe scale, then relative settling velocity or relative acceleration will be less effective. If the sand proportion is very small relative to the carbon, then density separation will not work well. 

Classifiers (refer to Figure 31 and 32) and elutriators require very small volume, but can experience blockages and erosion in the water distributors (refer to Figures 33 and 34). Jigs are larger in volume and require power. Spirals do not function well with variable flow, hence would need to be set up so the flow was equal to the peak transport flow and the flow made continuous.

###### **_Dewatering_** 

Primary dewatering is generally straight forward and typically performed in a vibrating screen, which will operate robustly except for the need to be cleaned regularly or if irreversibly pegged, the screen panels will have to be replaced. Because of potential pegging, oversize the screen by 50%. The use of static screens is not recommended due to carbon losses that result from erosion. To protect the downstream equipment, provide ample washing sprays to remove elution chemicals (if using Zadra elution). 

Secondary dewatering is often performed in the carbon bins and in the chutes and kiln feeder. Free water drains readily from granular activated carbon even while the bin is being fed. By the time the bin is full, most of the free water has already drained away. For a 3.5 m tall charge of carbon in a 3 m<sup>2</sup> bin, the initial drainage rate for water after filling ceased was greater than 0.3 m/min (refer to Figure 35). However, water will continue to drain for hours. The longer the carbon is allowed to drain, the lower the energy cost to remove the water in the pre-dryer or kiln. Ultimately the drained water content can reach about 0.7 kg water/kg carbon, but practically, allowing for the bin to drain for 15 minutes after completing a fill, is sufficient to get most of the free water out of most bins. Most kiln vendors assume 1 kg w

ater/kg carbon, however, some vendors will assume 0.7 kg/water/kg carbon. Ensure the higher water content is used as the heat input otherwise the kiln can be undersized by 25%, resulting in burners operating with more intense flames and potentially increased heat damage to the kiln. 

Candle or pipe screens inserted into bins or part of a pipe or feeder work well if maintained and kept clean. If they are not routinely inspected, they blind and dewatering is not effective. If the kiln has such screens, they should be withdrawn, inspected, and cleaned or replaced monthly. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 



Figure 35 – Carbon drain time. 

Alternatively, using a small vibrating screen under the carbon bins is very effective. When draining the bin, the screen is static and the carbon itself acts as a pre-filter. When carbon is called for, the screen is turned on and carbon delivered to the kiln or preheater/pre-dryer. The screen is very small and need be only 300 mm wide and the length is simply whatever is required to deliver the carbon to the next chute. 

Ideally two bins are used in parallel with one being filled while the other is draining and or feeding the kiln. Because one screen is always static, the feeder screens can be cleaned while in service (while the bin is being filled). To change a screen panel, a rare event, the screen will need to be taken out of service completely, but the alternate screen can be used, hence kiln utilisation is not affected. 

From a maintenance perspective internal screens require regular inspection and cleaning. For the vibrating feeder screens, look for fatigue cracking due to vibration. 

Dewatering should not be performed in the kiln feeder if it is a screw conveyor. The screen will permit dewatering, but at the expense of the carbon which is eroded as the auger drags carbon across the screen. 

###### **Preheater/pre-dryer** 

Carbon is typically introduced into the kiln wet. This provides water vapour to prevent air ingress and as a reactant for the water gas reaction. It also means that all the water must be evaporated in the kiln with a temperature of 100°C when evaporated. Since the activation reaction only takes place above 700°C, the 100°C water vapour in fact cools the carbon and quenches the reaction, thereby requiring a larger diameter and longer high temperature kiln, which is an expensive consequence. 

Less expensive and more efficient, is to recover heat from the POCs before introducing the solids to the kiln. The solids can be totally dried, but this typically requires a unit as large as the rotary kiln itself. A compromise is to utilise as much of the waste heat as possible from the POCs in a relatively small preheater, which also performs partial drying. The solids simply flow through the unit as if it is a chute. Products of combustion are drawn through using an induced draft (ID) fan. At least two vendors provide such preheaters. 

Alternat

ive preheaters are available including hollow flight heaters and rotary dryers, but these can be large pieces of equipment requiring power and significant floor area at the top of a building. The associated infrastructure requirements are significantly more expensive. Small flow-through preheaters are more than adequate. 

From a maintenance perspective, the simple flow-through preheater designs are essentially just a chute with almost nothing to go wrong except for instrument connections. Because of the warm very humid atmosphere and carbon, any place water can pool will result in a reducing environment and stainless steel will corrode. The corrosion of the paddle switch shaft in Figures 36 and 37 took just three weeks. Temperature probes or level switches entering from the walls must be angled downwards to permit free water to drain out of the socket.

###### **_Kiln feeder_** 

The kiln feeder needs to deliver a known mass rate of carbon to the kiln. The kiln can tolerate small changes in water content, so generally a constant volumetric rate is satisfactory. If the feed has the sand and trash removed, then a tube feeder can deliver a constant volumetric flow of material with no damage to the carbon. 

If there is significant sand or other material that might alter the density or solids flow characteristics, then a screw feeder may be required. The screw feeder will have a gap between the screw and the housing. It is very common for this gap to be the same order of magnitude as the carbon, which permits the carbon to get caught in the gap and ground up. The cost of the carbon may not be large, but the value of the gold that can adsorb onto that fine carbon and report to tails can be high. If a screw feeder is used, then a fine carbon circuit is even more important to remove the increased carbon fines generated by the screw feeder. 

Screw feeders should be avoided; it is far more beneficial to remove the sand and trash, than to use a screw feeder. Nonetheless, if a screw feeder is selected, then oversize the screw to reduce the velocity the screw needs to operate at. Lower speeds will generally cause less damage. **Do not** use screens in the screw feeder. These act as grinding surfaces and damage the carbon.  The cost of carbon is inconsequential, but if the fines generated report to the last tank, then gold losses will be high. Dewater properly upstream, do not rely on a screw feeder to dewater the carbon. 

With respect to maintenance, tube feeders can block if there are salts in the wet carbon. The salts crystallise on the inner surface of the discharge end and can retain carbon and block the feeder. Normally these will break off, but they may need to be reamed out. In addition, some tube feeders are not designed for excessive sand load and the metal making up the vibrating

motor harness can fatigue – look for cracks. 

With respect to screw feeders, pay particular attention to erosion of the auger flights and replace to prevent excessive carbon damage. If the metal is being eroded, think of the damage being done to the much softer carbon. 

###### **_Fine carbon circuit_** 

All carbon kilns produce carbon dust. Carbon dust adsorbs gold very fast and to a greater loading than granular activated carbon. If the carbon dust gets into the last tank, it will adsorb the gold very quickly and give a false (low) solution tails reading. Fine carbon  will report with the solution when filtering solids for solids tail analysis, however, the fine carbon will be filtered and/or adsorbed when a solution is filtered for solution tails analysis. Hence fine carbon losses can go completely unrecorded. Recently the effect of fine carbon at one plant was estimated at $2million/y of gold lost to the tailings (confidential report). 

To eliminate this potential threat, fine carbon must be removed from the carbon before being returned to the CIL circuit. Dry carbon screens can work very well, but if hot carbon is exposed to air, it can catch fire at temperatures as low as 350°C. The principal author has observed three such carbon fires. 

Wet screening is preferred to avoid even the possibility of a fire. Very simply the carbon is cooled in the quench tank and the quenched carbon slurry passed over a vibrating screen with an aperture close to the small dimension of the fresh carbon. This aperture not only makes this screen very small and easy to operate, but helps prevent pegging of all other CIL carbon screens that usually have apertures 50 to 75% that of the smallest carbon dimension. Importantly, any fine inorganic material that reports with the carbon from the classifier is captured in the fine carbon circuit. Because of the fine inorganic material, avoid letting the fines accumulate; they will bridge like clay and block the discharge of tanks.

###### **Operation** 

If the equipment is fully commissioned and maintained as above, then operation is generally very straightforward. With respect to the kiln itself, the drum rotates at a predetermined speed and the drum speed determines the residence time. The feed is generally constant at a predetermined rate and the burners operate to a set point. The feed rate and burner set points determine the temperature that the carbon gets to and the residence time at the reaction temperature. 

Kiln feeders can get blocked. Pay attention to the average feed rate through the kiln and motor amperage. A blockage in a tube feeder will usually be caused by an accumulation of sand in the tube feeder, which dampens vibrations and slows the feed rate. The tube feeder may need to be reamed out to clear the blockage. Screw feeders will tend to grind their way through blockages (and carbon), but can jam due to trash, which t

ube feeders do not do. 

Many problems can be picked up by just walking through the plant and looking for abnormalities.  The fuel pressures should not have changed, there should be no fuel leaks and there should be no carbon particles visible on the platforms or in the bund, et cetera. 

Walk around the kiln and check there are no hot spots (you can feel hot spots before you can see them). If you find a hot spot, get an infrared gun and measure the temperature. Use a paint pen and put the temperature on the casing. Monitor and if it gets worse, act. Renewing refractory is a big job and requires a significant shutdown (up to two weeks), so provide ample notice. Most surfaces are not structural and surface temperatures of 200 to 300°C can be tolerated for extended periods. Put up guards to prevent people being potentially injured. 

Very often, the burners are not firing to their set point (SP). If the burners are not in control, i.e. the manipulated variable (MV) is 0% or 100% and the process variable (PV) does not match the SP, then report the problem and have the burners tuned. If most of the burners are under-firing, then you will not be getting the carbon hot and it will not reactivate. Fuel is being effectively wasted with no benefit. 

Look inside the kiln if you can. The carbon should be a warm red to a bright orange (refer to Figure 38). If the carbon is black, even when the kiln is red or orange, the carbon is cold and not reactivating, as shown in Figure 39. To keep the sight glass clean, purge with a couple of litres per minute of heated instrument air (IA). The small amount of IA used should not affect the kiln atmosphere significantly, but will increase char removal by a small amount. If heated, then the window itself stays warm and no condensation will develop when the site glass door is opened. 





Figure 38 – Fast rotation kiln activating carbon. Figure 39 – An overloaded kiln – not reactivating. 

Check the screens to ensure water is not flowing off the end of any of them. Use a needle gun, high pressure water wash or even a rubber mallet to un-peg the screens. If they do not clean up, then get the screen panel changed out. 

Spray nozzles are there for a reason, keep them clear and working. Duck tail spray nozzles with large apertures work well and are easy to clean. 

Regularly check screen under-pans and pump discharges to ensure lines are not blocked. If a line around a pump is hot to touch, do not open nearby flush points as the water may be superheated and steam will erupt out of the valve. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

If the site uses an accessible trash basket, empty it as you walk through. Keep it as empty as possible. If classifier is in use, ensure that flows are steady and there are no blockages, especially in the sand discharge. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

1. This paper only considered fossil fuel fired rotary carbon kilns as these kilns currently dominate the go

ld industry.  Vertical kilns work and should be considered seriously when they can handle the required throughput. 

2. Kiln selection should first be based on the physical/chemical processes required to return the carbon to its ‘fresh’ ‘as manufactured’ state, in preference to capital cost or mechanical robustness. 

3. To optimally reactivate carbon to adsorb ion pairs i.e. gold cyanide complexes, the carbon is reactivated at over 800°C and quenched in a non-oxidising atmosphere; practically cool water vapour is used. 

4. The amount of contaminant to be removed is variable, but laboratory tests can determine exactly how much to remove using thermo-gravimetric testing and equation 1 is used to estimate the residence required at any selected reactivation temperature in a steam atmosphere. 

5. Alternatively, tube furnace testing can be conducted to quantitatively determine carbon reactivation and carbon degradation as a function of the reaction conditions. 

6. Oxygen is always detrimental with respect to damaging the base carbon, however up to 2.5% can be tolerated with respect to surface activation. 

7. The effect of temperature on expansion/contraction, corrosion, fatigue and friction (lubrication) are the principal criteria to bear in mind with respect to mechanical selection and maintenance for a rotary kiln. 

8. Maintaining a carbon kiln is straightforward, but requires regular preventive maintenance checks and early corrective action. 

9. A fines removal circuit should always be incorporated to remove fine carbon after re-activation that would result in solution gold reporting to tailings. 

10. Allow for trash and sand removal as it will eventually become a problem. 

11. To avoid thermal expansion/contraction fatigue, keep the kiln hot and operating. If the kiln is oversized for the plant, either slow the feed rate or put the kiln on standby (low heat with no solids feed) rather than turning off the kiln. 

12. If trash and sand is removed, and the kiln not purposefully shut down, then the carbon kiln will operate reliably with just the periodic cleaning of screens and trash baskets.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Filtered dry stack tailing storage facilities offer many advantages over thickened tailing storage facilities and yet, most of the mining companies still prefer the latter. 

Some of the advantages of filtered dry stack tailing storage facilities are: increased structural integrity of the tailing storage facility, which is even more critical in areas of high seism

icity, close to nearby communities or environmentally sensitive areas; maximised water recovery which is particularly important in arid environments where water is an extremely valuable resource and its supply is regulated; optimised recovery of valuable metals in the process water, avoiding high cyanide concentration going to detoxification (both aspects haven’t been emphasised enough in technical papers on this subject); optimised space to store the tailings in mountainous regions; minimised elevation of embankment height, providing a safe option to store the tailings in places where there is limited area available; simplified license approval to operate where the tailing facility is a big issue; and avoidance of potential problems with nearby communities. 

Filtered dry stack tailing storage facilities have some disadvantages such as: technology limitations in operations that process high throughputs (eg >50 000 tpd) as they require many filters resulting in high maintenance and operating costs; higher capital cost; low efficiency in the filtration process, particularly in ores with high clay content increasing operating problems and capital cost; the new technology risk with possible debottlenecking issues and a longer time to achieve the design throughput; and the need to treat larger water flow rates when the water balance is negative. 

This paper analyses: the operating practices of Mexican gold and silver operations using filtered dry stacking storage facilities; implementation issues, advantages and disadvantages; quantifiable reductions in gold and silver losses and actual lower detoxification cost; and current trends to use filtered dry stacking storage facilities in new projects. The data gathered raises questions about (a) the need to collect data on tailings filterability, and; (b) reducing the current high operating cost of tailings filtration. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Tailing filtration has become a very important topic for the mining industry worldwide due to recurrent disasters when using conventional wet tailing storage facilities (TSF). Recent high profile events such as Mount Polley in Canada in 2014 and the Samarco tragedy in Brazil in 2016 are especially chastening. A solution for this problem is filtering the tailings and then dry stacking which offers many advantages over conventional wet thickened tailing storage facilities especially increased structural integrity of the TSF. This is even more critical in areas of high seismicity, close to nearby communities or environmentally sensitive areas. Additionally, water recovery is maximised which is particularly important in arid environments where water is an extremely valuable resource with its supply heavily regulated. Other advantages are optimised space to store the tailings in mountainous regions, minimised elevation of embankment height (providing a safe option to store the tailings in places where there is limited area available), simplified license approval to op

erate where the tailing facility is a major issue, and reduced potential for problems with nearby communities. During the AusIMM MetPlant 2017 Conference, it was mentioned that Mexican precious metals mines using cyanidation employed tailings filtration to obtain additional advantages such as increased recovery of values coming from the additional process water extracted together with savings in the consumption of both cyanide and detoxification reagents. Another savings from tailings filtration and dry stacking is reduced fresh water consumption as more process water is recycled. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 This paper reviews tailing filtration practices in Mexican gold and silver mines to discern the key reasons for selecting tailings filtration, the most common issues during commissioning, the main advantages of the tailing filtration implementation, the quantifiable reductions in gold and silver losses and the actual lower detoxification cost. ###### **Key reasons for selecting tailings filtration** 

In the following section, a summary of the site topography, climatic condition and social milieu for each of the operations in Table 1 is provided. 

Pinos Altos - Agnico Eagle. The property is in the state of Chihuahua in northern Mexico, approximately 280 km west of the capital city, Chihuahua, in the Sierra Madre mountain range at approximately 2000 m elevation above sea-level. The Pinos Altos climate is temperate sub-humid with a rainy season from the end of June to the end of August, where precipitation can reach 30 to 50 mm/h and a dry season from December to May having less than 50 mm of precipitation per month (total 650 to 1000 mm per year). As a result, the operation has to manage water efficiently so a dry tailings stacking method was selected. This offers the advantage of recovering most of the water from the process at the end of the milling circuit. It is especially advantageous from the point of view of the geotechnical stability of the tailings impoundment during the rainy season (Duquette _et al_ , 2008). 

Minera Media Luna – Torex. It is in Guerrero State, approximately 200 km south south-west of Mexico City, and it is surrounded by local communities within and near the property. The area is well-watered with approximately 1000 mm of rain per year. The first question was: how to protect the Balsas River (one of Mexico’s largest) and reservoir from a potential tailings spill in a seismically active area? With tailings filtration there would be no tailings dam that could possibly breach. The terrain is mountainous and areas available for tailings disposal are steep. Conventional hydraulic tailings disposal would have required a fairly large dam for a relatively small impoundment volume. Piling filtered tailings uses less land. The tailings are then compacted to reduce the susceptibility to liquefaction from seismic events. The design of the tailings stack allows progressive reclamation making it easier to rehabilitate at the end of mine life. Convent

ional wet storage dams would have been costly and increased the risk to the waterways. While the tailings filters were expensive to purchase and operate, the commercial impact has been less than expected. The decision to filter and dry stack was ultimately made taking into account the reduction in potential social issues (Neff et al, 2015). It was a condition for the grant of the licence to operate (Arguijo-Lopez, 2018). 

San Jose - Fortuna Silver Mines. Mean annual precipitation ranges from 500 mm to 750 mm, with nearly all rain occurring from April to October. The operation is located 47 km by road south of the city of Oaxaca, capital of the state of Oaxaca. The village of San Jose del Progreso is located 2 km to the southeast of the mine site which is surrounded by many small communities. The project was divided into three areas; paste fill plant, tailing filtration plant and dry tailing deposit. Part of the slurry pumped to the pressure filter is diverted to the paste fill plant for backfill supplying 30 per cent of the mines backfilling requirements. The tailing filtration plant serves two purposes: (a) recover approximately 86 per cent of the water from the tailings to be re-used in the plant’s flotation section, and; (b) produce better quality ‘dry’ tailings which has a lesser impact on the environment. The tailings cake is discharged from the filters to a stockpile for truck transportation 1.5km to the dry stack disposal area. The dry tailings deposit consists of platforms at different levels for the stacking, laying and compaction of dry tailings. The existing conventional wet dam is used as a contingency for disposal of tailings if a mechanical failure occurs in the tailings filter plant (Chapman and Gutierrez, 2016). 

San Dimas (Tayoltita) - First Majestic. It is on the borders of the Durango and Sinaloa states approximately 125 km north-east of Mazatlбn, Sinaloa and 150 km west of the city of Durango, Durango. Tayoltita with a population of approximately 8000 is the most important urban centre in the region with a sparse population outside of it. The mean annual rainfall varies from about 660 mm to 1080 mm. The very rugged mountainous terrain and steep-walled canyons in the district have presented formidable challenges to tailings management as the scale of operations grew and potential storage areas were depleted. A technical solution was provided by tailings filtration. High capacity thickeners have been added to increase the tailings slurry density and reduce the solution containment, hydrostatic heads, and return capacity required at the tailings dam. In 2011 ten relay tailings pumping stations using centrifugal pumps were replaced with two Putzmeister positive displacement piston pumps The Putzmeister piston pump has the capacity to pump the tailings (53 per cent w/w solids) over a distance of 1847 m and total elevation of 125 m above the mill level. Two belt filters were installed in 2011 with another added in 2014 together wi

th a third Putzmeister piston pump. In the five months that the new filters were operating in 2011, the process recovered an average of 43 000 tonnes of solution each month to be recycled into the leaching process (Voicu, Shannon and Webster, 2014). 

Del Toro – First Majestic. It is in the municipality of Chalchihuites, in the north-western part of the state of Zacatecas. Chalchihuites is within walking distance to the mine and there are other surrounding towns. The mean precipitation for the year is between 556 and 571 mm. Because of the operation of tailings filtration 8085 per cent of the water is recycled in the process. Make up water comes from groundwater wells. Tailings Storage Facility #1-2 was designed to hold 1.77 million tonnes of paste-filtered tailings in three benches for a total height of 50 m. Tailings are transported from the filter plant to the storage facility using front end loaders and conventional haul trucks. The tailings are then spread, levelled and compacted using a track dozer. Tailings Storage Facility #3 (TSF3) is designed to hold 11. 9 million tonnes of paste-filtered tailings in 10
