La Encantada - First Majestic. It is in the north-western portion of the State of Coahuila, in northern Mйxico, approximately 120 km east from the city of Melchor Mъzquiz and approximately 120 km north from the town of Ocampo. La Encantada lies within a region of desert climate with only 10 mm to 20 mm of rain per year. Recycled water accounts for 90 per cent of the plant requirements, and only 10 per cent from make-up fresh water. All fresh water that feeds the plant comes from a series of wells located on the First Majestic property. Fresh water usage in the plant is estimated at 529 m<sup>3</sup> /d (6 L/s) (Mendoza-Reyes _et al_ , 2015). 

La Parrilla - First Majestic. The La Parrilla property is in the municipality of Nombre de Dios, in the southeastern part of the state of Durango. La Parrilla is accessible from various nearby towns and villages located 10 to 20 km away. The mean annual rainfall is about 441 mm with most occurring during the summer months and only occasional rain during winter. La Parrilla operates two parallel processing circuits that recover metals from sulphide and oxide ores. Both processing lines at La Parrilla use a conventional flowsheet. Tailing from both circuits are filtered separately before being dry-stacked in the tailings storage facility. Water for each circuit is managed independently. 

The processing plant produces a dry filter cake which is transported via conveyors to the dry stack tailings storage facility where a small bulldozer distributes and grades the tailings. An expansion to the existing facility has been designed and perm

itted, and will have sufficient capacity for 12.5 years of production at current production rates. The majority of the plant process water is recycled. Any water captured in the catchments around the tailings facility is also recycled. Process water underground is also largely recycled. The tailings area has a constructed runoff collection system of drains and ditches, and reports to the water reclaim station downstream of the tailings area where it is pumped back to the mill for re-use as process water. The tailings are placed in lifts that are subsequently covered with mine waste rock. The historic tailings area is currently being rehabilitated with a waste rock cover, and will eventually be revegetated (Mendoza-Reyes _et al_ , 2016a). 

San Martin Silver Mine - First Majestic. It is on the eastern side of the Bolaсos River, 10 km north-west from the town of San Martнn de Bolaсos in the state of Jalisco. Mean annual rainfall in San Martнn de Bolaсos is registered as 592 mm, most of which occurs from June to October. The water source for the processing plant is the Bolaсos River. Potable water comes from municipal wells. First Majestic has constructed a 13 km pipeline from the regional mountains as a back-up process water supply to mitigate the effects of future droughts. Processing water is recycled at a rate of approximately 18 per cent of the water requirements for the leaching process. After the tailings press filters commence operation in late 2017, the expected water recycling rate will be approximately 80 per cent. The installation of a tailings filtering plant producing “paste tailings” by the end of the fourth quarter of 2017 will allow dry stacking, thereby reducing the inherent geotechnical risk associated with wet tailings storage, increasing the amount of process water that can be recycled and reducing the impact on the environment. Filtered dry-stack tailings will be stored above the current TSF. The TSF is expected to reach maximum capacity by the end of 2022 after stacking filtered tailings. Filtered paste tailings will be mixed with waste rock and used initially to reinforce the outer walls of the TSF for the first 17 months, afterwards the paste tailings will be stored as a dry stack in an area close to the processing plant. The LOM plan considers that the paste tailings will be stored above the current TSF (Mendoza-Reyes _et al_ , 2016b). 

Anonymous Gold and Silver Mine – While it was requested that details are not to be disclosed, it is possible to indicate the high process water requirements for Counter Current Decantation (CCD) needed to reduce the gold and silver losses and reagent losses in the process water sent to the TSF. At this operation there is not enough space to build a new conventional TSF. 

Tailings filtration minimises water usage which is often extremely important in the particular circumstances pertaining to mines in Latin America. David Garofalo, the President and Chief Executive Officer of the large Cana

dian gold mining company Goldcorp has stated that ‘when it comes to Corporate Social Responsibility, it’s all about water’ (Anon 2016). Generally, the mining industry will not be allowed access to water until competing demands for human, agricultural and pastoral uses have been met. ###### **TAILINGS FILTRATION EQUIPMENT** Data from the four mines that replied to the questionnaire are shown in Table 2. Some ‘learnings’ from these replies are as follows: - Filtering tailings can be a more onerous duty than what it seems from simply comparing the relatively coarse tailings P 80 with the much finer particle sizing of a typical base metal sulphide concentrate 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 where the feed to the flotation cleaner block is commonly reground to a P80 of ~38 µm. A major cause of this is the presence of ‘clay’ or altered phyllosilicates in the tailings from three of the mines; clay is not normally a significant constituent of a sulphide flotation concentrate. Tailings filter capacities quoted in Table 2 are not significantly higher than the ‘rule of thumb’ of 0. 5 t/h/m2 used for base sulphide concentrates. - Common benchmark performance of ~90 per cent running time, filter cake moisture of ~14-18 per cent w/w and operating cost of ~US$3. 25/t. The operating cost of tailings filtration make it one of the most expensive unit operations in the concentrator; equivalent to grinding. This confirms earlier predictions about the future importance of tailings thickening and filtration ie the ‘back end’ of concentrator operations starting to drive mineral processing outcomes (Munro 2016). - Respondents reported some dissatisfaction in their dealings with the suppliers of filtration equipment. The key reasons for selecting tailings filtration are: - Reduced water usage 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 - Insufficient space to build a conventional TSF - Reduced social issues - Improved case for granting of operating license The ‘chemical case’ for going to tailings filtration for a cyanide leaching operation using the Merrill Crowe process as is the case for Mexican operations with high silver feed grades is the potential large reduction in solution losses. An ancillary benefit is removing as much water as possible before detoxification. Filtered dry stack tailing storage facilities has disadvantages: - Ostensible technology limitations in high throughput operations (eg >50 000 tpd) as they require many filters resulting in high maintenance and operating costs. - High capital cost. - Low filtration efficiency in ores with high clay content – clay and clay-like minerals are most likely to be encountered in the upper part of a mineral deposit ie the portion mined first. It is not normal practice in metallurgical test work to determine the filtration characteristics of _ore_ as opposed to a _concentrate._ - New technology risk with usual debottlenecking issues and a longer time to achieve the design throughput. - Need to treat larger water flow rates when the water balance is negative. Despite the difficulties listed, large scale filtration of tailings is close to being an accepted fact. The proposed 90 000 tpd Rosemont operation of Hudbay Minerals near Tucson, AZ, USA was permitted on the conditio

n that the tailings will filtered and dry stacked. 

Suggested ‘take aways’ from this paper are: 

- There can be a sound ‘process case’ for selecting a tailings disposal system using filtration plus dry stacking for leaching operations, especially for silver. This is based on potentially significant reductions in solution loss of values. 

- None of the authors have ever sighted specific material dewatering data in a geological block model though the Olympic Dam block model has the chlorite content which causes ‘gelling’ affecting solidliquid separation in the uranium recovery section (Ehrig and Pitard 2017). Considering the likely capital cost and operating cost of tailings filtration; the latter being nearly the same as the operating cost of grinding, then this is clearly an anomalous situation considering the industry’s zeal in collecting comminution data. It is difficult to imagine a ‘Plan B’ that would compensate for tailings filtration + dry stacking not achieving design capacity. 

- A focussing question is whether the operating cost of tailings filtration is subject to economies of scale. If the ‘outcome drivers’ are filter cake thickness and area then _prima facie_ answer appears to be negative. 

On a more philosophical note, the high cost of tailings filtration will provide incentives for coarse particle beneficiation and coarsening the ‘up front’ grinding product sizing.

###### Addressing challenging applications of intensive cyanidation in gravity gold recovery 

###### _A King_<sup>_1_</sup> _and J Carrillo_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. Principal Process Engineer, Consep Pty Ltd, Perth WA 6000. Email: aking@consep.com.au 

2. Process Engineer, Consep Pty Ltd, Perth WA 6000. Email: jcarrillo@consep.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Gravity recoverable gold (GRG) is largely distinguished from other gold by its non-mineralised, metallic form, its high degree of liberation from the ore and its appreciable particle size. The gold mining industry has so widely accepted the use of batch centrifugal concentrators (BCC) and intensive cyanidation (IC) systems for the recovery of GRG that these may well be considered requirements of any plant processing ore containing appreciable GRG. The recovery of gold by gravity is quick, easy and cheap by comparison to alternatives. However, there are cases where attributes of the ore make recovery of gold by gravity and IC unusually challenging. This paper describes three examples where such challenges have been encountered and met, including those where the ore contains cyanide soluble base metals and where fine GRG is to be recovered from flotation concentrate. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

While well over 90 per cent of current installations of intensive leaching technology are in simple primary gravity applications in typical gold ore processing plants, the challenge for providers of IC technology has been to extend its applic

ation to more challenging installations. The installations addressed in this paper provide insight into three long operating, successful installations that required subtle variation in equipment design, but ultimately provide confidence that IC technology can be successfully applied to gravity circuits in base metal flotation plants. 

###### **BACKGROUND** 

The exploitation of gravity to separate gold particles from gangue is almost certainly the oldest of all extractive metallurgical techniques. It is simple yet effective, due to the very high SG of gold. Unsophisticated techniques such as gold panning and sluicing are still commonly employed techniques with relatively low expectations for gold recovery and an unfortunate association with mercury pollution. 

Since the late 19th century, gold cyanidation techniques have been refined to achieve very high gold recovery and are widely adopted by large scale gold producers world-wide. Flotation is also widely employed for gold recovery. BCCs, most notably Knelson and Falcon concentrators, were developed in the 1980s. These are able to recover free gold more efficiently than earlier gravity techniques. 

The grinding of ores in closed circuit with cyclone classification in preparation for cyanidation or flotation leads to upgrading of liberated gold particles in the circulating load. Treating a portion of the circulating load with BCC’s improves overall gold recovery by reducing the loss of gold to cyanidation or flotation plant tailings. 

The gold grade of gravity concentrate produced by BCC’s is typically in the order of 1000 times the ore grade, but it is still not high enough for direct smelting. Upgrading of gravity concentrate by gravity methods such as tabling is effective for coarse gold, but achieves a lower gold recovery from finer size fractions. This led to the development of IC systems, notably the Consep Acacia and the Gekko Intensive Leach Reactor (ILR), for the treatment of gravity gold concentrate in the 1990s. Gold in the pregnant leach solution produced by IC systems is recovered by electrowinning. The very high gravity gold recovery and improved overall gold recovery, achieved with combined BCC-IC systems, has led to increased focus on gravity recovery as key to reducing production costs and reaching maximised gold recovery. 

While the majority of BCC-IC applications are simple to manage and predictable in their performance, there are applications in which the ore characteristics or the targeted stream for gravity recovery introduce significant challenges. Examples of such challenges and the methods used to overcome them are addressed in this paper. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### **The Knelson Concentrator and GRG** 

The Knelson Concentrator (Figure 1) is a BCC primarily used for the recovery of GRG. It is designed on a fluidised bed principle to enable the extraction of high density material from lower density, granu

lar feed solids carried in the feed slurry, with the aid of centrifugal force and fluidisation water. 

The Knelson is designed to run as a semi continuous operation with the unit concentrating for an extended period (typically 30-60 minutes) and then cycling off for a short period (typically 2-3 minutes) to facilitate the automatic removal of concentrate from the Concentrating Cone before resuming concentration. Concentrate mass yield relative to mill throughput is typically in the range of 0.01-0.05 per cent. 

The concentrate typically contains 1000 to 10 000 g/t Au. Steel particles originating from degraded grinding media, high SG minerals and some coarse gangue make up the remainder of the concentrate. 

Knelson Concentrators are used in gold plants to efficiently recover GRG. Modelling of a gravity circuit is built on the design plant throughput together with the ore characterisation, grinding and classification behaviour and the recovery unit performance. The aforementioned three factors are also used for optimisation projects in plants were gravity recovery performance is subject to analysis or is altogether absent (Laplante Staunton, 2005). 



Figure 1 – Knelson Concentrator cutaway view illustration. 

###### **The Consep Acacia and reagent dosage** 

The Consep Acacia processes gravity concentrate batch wise. Concentrate is collected in a Concentrate Cone and transferred to the Consep Acacia reactor vessel on a batch basis, typically once a day. 

Following this transfer of concentrate to the Consep Acacia reaction vessel, the ultra-fine solids (slimes) are removed by a process of elutriation referred to as Desliming. This is achieved by injecting water into the base of the vessel which passes upward through the diffusion cartridge on which the concentrate rests, thereby fluidising the bed of concentrate. The gentle upward flow of water results in ultra-fine solids being carried out of the reaction vessel. The discharged water containing slimes is typically pumped to a suitable section of the gold plant where the majority of gold in the slimes will be recovered by cyanidation or flotation processes. 

Once desliming is completed the batch of gravity concentrate held in the Acacia reaction vessel is fluidised by leach solution which is pumped from the solution tank. Leach solution reaching the overflow weir of the reactor vessel does not carry solids due to the solids settling rate exceeding the solution rise rate. It returns to the Solution Tank to be recirculated for the duration of the 12-18 hour leach. Reagent levels are not topped up during the leach process. 

The IC leach solution is made up in the solution tank, comprising measured quantities of water, sodium hydroxide, sodium cyanide and a chemical leach accelerant called LeachAid<sup>®</sup> . The concentrate solids to solution mass ratio is typically between 1:2 and 1:3. 

LeachAid<sup>®</sup> is used to facilitate IC (very high rates of gold leaching) in the absence of diss

olved oxygen. Consep endorse the use of LeachAid<sup>®</sup> over dissolved oxygen (DO) because the initial LeachAid<sup>®</sup> concentration in the leach solution will be in excess of requirement and achieve maximised leach kinetics. By contrast, the DO concentration that can be achieved in the IC leach solution rarely exceeds 20 ppm. Even at this level, assuming a typical gravity concentrate grade of 5000 g/t Au, the solution will initially contain only 20-30 per cent of the total oxygen required to satisfy the demand of gold dissolution alone. The very high DO 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

consumption rate early in the leach typically results in very low DO levels and reduced leach kinetics, which may contribute to lower than expected gold recovery (Konigsmann Pyecha Boudreau, 2007). 

###### **APPLICATIONS** 

###### **Application 1: Handling of native copper in gravity gold concentrates** 

In this application, the gravity gold concentrate mineralogy turned out to be considerably different to that predicted from metallurgical testing at the feasibility stage. A change in approach was required to overcome the issue. 

Three sulphide oxidation domains were recognised: oxide, transition, and primary. The primary zone was characterised with predominantly chalcopyrite and pyrite mineralisation. The oxide and transition mineralisation were characterised by a diverse presence of copper oxide minerals such as malachite, azurite, chrysocolla and cuprite which are soluble in both strong acid and cyanide. Primary and secondary sulphide minerals of copper and iron such as chalcocite, covellite and bornite were also present. These, along with native copper have very low solubility in strong acid, but are soluble in cyanide. The presence of native copper was estimated as negligible, so no further efforts were made to consider process design risks associated with native copper, even as a potential issue in IC. 

Note that in general, copper concentrations are scrutinised on a percentage basis, whereas gold is scrutinised on a grams per tonne basis. The presence of native copper in concentrations similar to that of gold is therefore unlikely to be considered significant to the plant design criteria unless the influence of native copper recovery by the BCC-IC system is a known concern. Native copper has similar properties to gold and is readily recovered in gravity concentration. 

Prior to plant construction, gravity recovery test work was conducted on oxide ore samples. This produced concentrate of approximately 4 per cent of the sample mass containing approximately 3 per cent copper and 40 g/t Au. IC of the concentrate resulted in exceedingly high reagent consumption and a pregnant solution deemed unsuitable for direct electrowinning of gold due to excessive copper concentration. Leaching the gravity concentrate in sulphuric acid was found to extract the majority of copper (> 75 per cent), such that su

bsequent IC of the acid leach residue resulted in more favourable reagent consumption and copper to gold ratio in pregnant solution. The double leach design was built on the solubility of oxide and sulphide copper minerals to sulfuric acid and sodium cyanide solutions (Parkinson and Bhappu, 1995). 

The plant was designed and constructed with a Consep Acacia with special features that allowed for sulphuric acid leaching for copper removal followed by IC leaching for gold recovery. The acid leach liquor was to be discharged to plant tailings and the pregnant cyanide leach solution was to be transferred to electrowinning. 

During commissioning it was found that copper extraction by acid leaching was much lower than expected and copper dissolution during IC leaching overwhelmed and inhibited gold leaching. The gravity concentrate was occasionally analysed and found to contain as much as 21 per cent copper (the majority of which was native) while gold concentration was 0.1-0.2 per cent, as expected. Native copper solubility in sulphuric acid is very low, while its solubility in cyanide leach solution is high. 

It was understood that the presence of native copper would diminish as the mine progressed through oxide and transitional ore over the coming year, however gravity gold recovery was essential for the project and a quick solution was required. Consideration was given to using nitric acid to dissolve the native copper. Laboratory tests confirmed that this approach had technical merit. The Consep Acacia IC system was deemed suitable for use with nitric acid, however the plant would require the addition of a gas scrubber to manage the toxic NOx gas produced in the reaction between concentrate and nitric acid. 

Primarily due to concerns with the hazard associated with NOx, the project installed a shaking table (Figure 2) to process the gravity concentrate. Table concentrate was direct smelted and the copper rich table middlings were stored for later sale. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 



Figure 2 – Shaking table processing gravity concentrate rich in native copper and gold. 

When oxide and transitional ore was depleted, the presence of native copper in the concentrate diminished as expected. Therefore the use of the shaking table was discontinued and instead the gravity concentrate was then leached under typical IC conditions, without acid leaching for copper removal and has since been operating very successfully. 

This experience highlights that possible disparities in the properties of gravity concentrate produced in a laboratory and that produced in the plant should be carefully considered in the process design. In the vast majority of cases, the processing of gravity gold concentrate in an IC system is a certain success, however this application is an exception. 

The most influential factor contributing to the difference in laboratory and plant gravity concentrate properties is the concen

trate mass yield. In the plant, gravity concentrate mass yield is approximately 0.08 per cent. In the lab, concentrate mass yield was approximately 50 times larger, at 4 per cent. Another influential factor is the action of classifying cyclones in the plant. High SG metallic particles including gold, native copper and steel (which originates largely from degraded grinding media) are slow to grind and report to cyclone underflow in very high proportion. Cyclones are effectively a gravity concentration device with a very high concentrate mass yield.  The influence of cyclones results in concentrate becoming highly enriched with metallic particles, but is highly beneficial to gravity gold recovery. 

###### **Application 2: Managing cyanide soluble copper and iron in intensive cyanidation** 

A copper-gold ore processing plant, typically producing approximately 200 000 oz of gold and 40 Mlbs of copper annually, treats ore containing a moderate level of gravity recoverable gold (Figure 3) and a variety of copper, copper-iron and iron sulphide minerals. The action of classifying cyclones in the milling circuits results in enrichment of the sulphide minerals in the circulating load. High concentrations of these minerals are present in the gravity gold concentrate produced by Knelson Concentrators. This concentrate is treated in a Consep Acacia IC system. 

The concentrate was found to consume dissolved oxygen at a very high rate during initial IC leaches conducted without LeachAid®, resulting in low gold extraction. Subsequently, initial leaches with LeachAid® achieved unsatisfactory gold recovery until through experimentation, the LeachAid® demand became understood. Leach solution samples were collected at timed intervals during a series of sequential batches, on a basis of a leach per day for a week. These were analysed for copper, iron, gold and silver. The initial high rates of metal dissolution declined steadily in the first few hours of leaching, as is typically expected. In two particular batches, the concentrations of gold and silver in solution gradually fell to near zero after initially reaching values ranging from 2880-5280 ppm, while similarly high levels of iron and copper in solution fell some hours later. It was noted that in these two leaches the ratio of LeachAid<sup>®</sup> dosed to total maximum mass of metal leached was significantly lower than in the successful gold leaches (Figure 4). It was postulated that as the four metals were extracted into solution, LeachAid<sup>®</sup> was consumed to the extent that the solution chemistry favoured reduction of these metals on the surface of the steel particles (largely originating from degraded grinding media) in the gravity concentrate. The plating of gold onto steel particles has been observed at a number of sites using IC systems and has coincided with unexpectedly high gravity concentrate gold grades with corresponding lower LeachAid<sup>®</sup> to gold ratio. During the process commis

sioning phase the daily performance of intensive cyanidation was erratic and unpredictable. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 



Figure 3 – Typical classification of gravity recoverable gold based on its particle size distribution. 



Figure 4 – Leaching curve with insufficient LeachAid<sup>®</sup> dosage. 

In a brief trial the site did investigate the use of hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant. This proved to be a failure due to downstream electrowinning issues. Although abandoned prior to conclusively identifying the issue, it was suspected that the issue was caused by the combination of dissolved oxygen (from peroxide) and hydroxide leading to arsenopyrite dissolution. Arsenic, even in low concentrations, impedes electrowinning. Hence the decision was made to return to using LeachAid<sup>®</sup> due to its inherent advantages in intensive leaching. 

The grade of gold and silver and the mineralogy of the gravity concentrate was known to change significantly primarily due to changes in ore blend. To estimate the minimum dosage of LeachAid<sup>®</sup> required to achieve and retain the maximum level of gold and silver in solution, a stoichiometric model was proposed. 

The stoichiometric model was based on the total number of Mols of each cyanide soluble metal species expected to be in the concentrate on the basis of the leach extraction profiles from previously processed concentrate. Empirical leach extraction data made available to Consep from other sites and testwork programs was collated and a suitable mass of LeachAid<sup>®</sup> per Mol of cyanide soluble metal content was established as a starting point for the minimum LeachAid<sup>®</sup> dosage. This was adjusted as batches were completed and leach performance results became available. 

This approach was found to be successful as leach extraction profiles for Au, Ag, Cu and Fe no longer displayed any fall in gold or silver solution concentration. The metal extraction into solution continued throughout the 14 hour leach period and extraction rates were similar for all four cyanide soluble metals examined, declining steadily as expected (Figure 5). Site staff subsequently refined the model to fit the findings of their growing collection of leach data.

Figure 5 – Leaching curve with sufficient LeachAid<sup>®</sup> dosage. 

###### **Application 3: Flotation concentrate as gravity feed** 

In this application, flotation concentrate containing gravity recoverable gold is treated by Knelson Concentrators. The atypical gravity concentrate produced was classified as very fine similar to its gravity recoverable gold (Figure 3). The gravity concentrate was transferred to a Consep Acacia for IC. 

Due to the unusually high proportion of ultra-fine solids in the concentrate, the removal of ultra-fine solids by Desliming was undesirable. High gold losses could be reaso

nably expected. Eliminating the Deslime stage would have resulted in a number of issues, including solids carry-over during leaching of the concentrate resulting in contamination of the electrowinning feed and also very low pregnant solution drainage rates resulting in low pregnant solution recovery from the leach residue. To address the issue, Consep developed a Slimes Recovery Module to recover the majority of slimes removed during the Desliming process. It was integrated with the Consep Acacia package supplied to this project. 

The Slimes Recovery Module includes a nest of 2 inch hydrocyclones mounted over a cylindrical agitated tank. During the Desliming stage of the process, the discharged water containing slimes is pumped to the cyclones. The cyclone feed pressure is automatically controlled by maintaining a suitable volumetric flow rate. The cyclone overflow is transferred to a nearby thickener feed well. The cyclone underflow represents approximately 10 per cent of the cyclone feed by volume while containing over 90 per cent of the solids in the cyclone feed. The design cyclone cutpoint is nominally 10μm for solids with SG of 3. 

The slimes gold recovery to cyclone underflow has not yet been quantitatively assessed, however an extremely high proportion of the very fine gravity gold contained in the slimes originating from the gravity concentrate is expected to report to cyclone underflow due to its very high SG. 

The slimes recovered in the cyclone underflow are collected in the agitated tank below. A small fraction (2 per cent) of the IC solution from the Consep Acacia is added to the slurry facilitating the dissolution of gold. The transferred solution is equivalent to 12 per cent of the collected slurry volume and sufficient to leach the very fine contained gold. Leaching of the concentrate retained in the Consep Acacia reaction vessel after Desliming continues as normal. 

On completion of the two concurrent leaching processes, the solids in the slime recovery module’s agitated tank are allowed to settle. The supernatant solution is decanted into the solution tank below leaving the level in the tank very near the solid/liquid interface. The remaining residue is transferred to the CIL circuit. Pregnant solution in the Consep Acacia reaction vessel is drained from the leach residue into the solution tank. 

The very fine nature of the concentrate also required that the typical flowrates for desliming and leaching were re-evaluated due to initial poor recoveries. At the start of commissioning, concentrate supply was limited, such that the daily batch was approximately 50 per cent of the Consep Acacia reaction vessel capacity. The commissioning phase schedule was tight and operation of the Consep Acacia was paramount. The Desliming flowrate was initially 50 per cent of the standard and continued for at least one hour. The design philosophy at that time was to Deslime at lower than usual fluidising flowrates to guarantee the collection

of the ultra-fine gold by the cyclones. Over the first two weeks of operation, as a better 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

understanding of the system performance was gained, Desliming flowrate was progressively increased. It was then found that aggressively desliming, with 120 per cent of the standard Desliming flowrate over shorter periods, achieved the same ultra-fine solids recovery while allowing for a higher leaching flowrate. The higher leaching flowrate enhanced fluidisation of the concentrate solids bed such that a higher gold recovery was achieved (Figure 6). 

The addition of the slimes recovery module in this application effectively addressed the issue with processing very fine gravity gold concentrate (Figure 7).

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The optimisation of gravity gold recovery has tangible and intangible advantages. The economic benefit of operating BCC-IC systems can be easily appreciated with the reduction of gold inventory and reduced time for production. Reagents dosage in CIL circuits, carbon addition and volatile peaks in tailings assays are reduced particularly in operations where coarse gravity gold is present in the ore. 

Three particular cases explored in this paper highlighted how issues were overcome in non-standard applications of IC to produce gold from gravity concentrate. Time will provide further opportunity to collect data from sites where the concentration of cyanide soluble base metals in the gravity concentrate is significant, developing understanding of the response of these minerals to LeachAid<sup>®</sup> dosage, aiming for the 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

best process conditions to maximise gold recovery at minimal cost. The use of IC in operations with flotation concentrate as gravity concentrator feed creates an opportunity to produce gold bullion at sites that produce copper or other concentrate with significant GRG content.

###### A reliable solution for pumping mineral froth with challenging froth volume 

###### _P Loderer_<sup>_1_</sup> _and A Roudnev_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. P Loderer, Principal Hydraulic Engineer, Weir Minerals Europe, Todmorden, UK, OL14 5RT. Email: pavol.loderer@mail.weir 

2. A Roudnev, Chief Engineer Hydraulic Design, Weir Minerals North America, Madison, USA, WI53716. Email: aleks.roudnev@mail.weir 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Mineral froth pumping utilising centrifugal slurry pumps is a major engineering challenge for both the end users and pump manufacturers. The traditional approach has been to oversize the pump for pumping mineral froth. New horizontal slurry froth pump designs offer opportunities to improve froth pumping capability of mineral froth with challenging (high) Froth Volume Factor while maintaining high efficiency, long wear life and stable pumping performance. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The following terms are used in this document: 

Slurry: two-phase solid-liquid mixture (De-aerated mixture) 

Mineral froth: three-phase solid-liquid-air mixture (Aerated mixture) 

Froth Volume Factor (FVF): the ratio of the aerated volume to the de-aerated volume, as shown in Figure 1. 𝐴 𝐴 𝐴 𝑉 Equation 1: 𝐹 𝐴 𝐴 𝑉 𝐴𝐴 𝑉 𝑉𝑉𝐴𝐴 Boyle’s Law: P*V = Constant, where P is air pressure and V is air volume 𝐹𝐹= 𝐷𝐷𝐴𝐴−𝐴 𝐴𝐴 𝑉 𝑉𝑉𝐴𝐴 

Net Positive Suction Head (NPSH): absolute inlet total head above the head equivalent to the vapour pressure relative to the datum plane - pump axis for horizontal centrifugal pump. 

Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHA): as determined by the conditions of installation for a specified flow rate 

<mark>Pump critical speed: t</mark> he theoretical angular velocity that excites the natural frequency of a rotating object, such as a shaft and impeller. 

Best Efficiency Point (BEP): point on Flow & Head pump curve with the highest efficiency 



Figure 1 – Froth volume factor. 

Extracting minerals from ore generally requires crushing and grinding of the ore. In order to maximize the recovery of minerals, the ore is ground into fine particles. The flotation process liberates the minerals from the non-valuable material. The fine particles, in the form of slurry, are introduced into agitated flotation cells. Air and flotation reagents are then added. In the forward flotation process, the fine mineral particles attach 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

themselves to the air bubbles and float to the surface as mineral froth. The mineral froth spills over the side of the flotation cells and is recirculated through other stages of the flotation process to achieve the maximum efficiency and mineral recovery. 

Mineral froth consists of fine particles with a fine dispersion of air bubbles. To move the mineral froth from one flotation cell to another, and th

en to the next process, pumping is required. The characteristics of the mineral froth depend on the type of mineral, the particle size distribution, the solids concentration, the amount of air in the froth, and the type of flotation reagent used. 

Mineral froths can range from brittle on one end of the spectrum, consisting of large bubbles that break easily, to tenacious on the other end of the spectrum, consisting of small bubbles that can remain in the liquid for many hours. The characteristics of the mineral froth can change frequently depending on the varying process parameters. Combinations of various flotation techniques push the limits of the flotation process in order to recover more of the valuable minerals and improve flotation process efficiency. This typically results in a mineral froth with a high FVF. The air contained in the mineral froth complicates pump suction conditions, often resulting in an air lock at the impeller eye. 

###### **VERTICAL FROTH PUMPS** 

Vertical slurry pumps have been used for pumping mineral froths in the past. Vertical pumps do not have submerged bearings or shaft seals. Semi-open impeller designs with vanes located on both sides of the shroud are suitable for pumping froth. With a vertical cantilevered pump, the shaft critical speed limits the head that the pump can produce to about 25 meters. In some cases, shaft critical speed issues can be resolved by implementing special volute design and/or shaft materials. 

As flotation technology evolves, the volume of product will increase. To meet the demand, there will be a need to pump higher flow rates at a higher head. The vertical pumps used previously may become undersized and unsuitable to handle these tougher duty requirements. 

###### **HORIZONTAL FROTH PUMP DESIGN** 

Horizontal slurry pumps are easier to maintain, and they are not as prone to bearing and shaft failures as their vertical counterparts. An enlarged intake diameter helps facilitate the froth flow into the pump. The inducer vanes of the impeller help draw the froth into the pump suction as well. This pump configuration is a non-vented horizontal froth pump design. A large population of successfully operating pumps support the non-vented design concept. However, in certain mineral froth conditions where the froth is particularly tenacious and/or has a high FVF, the non-vented froth pump can still become air locked, causing surging and unstable pump performance. Measures can be taken to try to reduce the FVF in the suction tank before the froth gets to the pump, but these measures are often cost prohibitive. 

###### **HORIZONTAL FROTH PUMPS OF VENTED DESIGN** 

The solution to pumping mineral froths with high FVFs is to implement the concept of using the pump itself to separate and remove the entrained air from the froth slurry. The technique of separation and venting has been used in paper stock pumps since the 1980’s. The initial concept consisted of a single stage pump equipped with a

semi-open impeller with back expelling vanes and venting holes in the back shroud, and a gas collection chamber behind the impeller. The primary means to assist gas evacuation found in these pumps was the use of an additional vacuum pump. The vacuum pump would be either mounted on the centrifugal pump shaft inside the gas collection chamber or connected to the venting pipe separately. However, typical vacuum pumps are not slurry pumps due to their reliance on tight running clearances. Once slurry is introduced, the tight clearances are either blocked or opened up via wear. In either case, the operational life of a vacuum pump is dramatically reduced. 

Figure 2 shows the new horizontal froth pump of Continuous Air Removal System (CARS) design. The impeller has back expelling vanes and back shroud vent holes. In addition to the impeller modifications, the venting system includes a gas collection chamber with a flow inducer behind the main impeller. The flow inducer facilitates the flow of separated air through the vent pipe and out of the pump. As the inducer vanes apply a swirl effect, the heavier (compressed) portion of the mixture centrifuges to the outer periphery of the suction piping which forces the free air towards the middle. The air passes through the vent holes in the back shroud of the impeller into the collection chamber where the flow inducer forces the air out through the vent pipe. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 



Figure 2 – Horizontal froth pumps vented design – CARS. Legend:  1- slurry impeller, 2- propeller, 3- collection chamber, 4- venting pipe. 

The CARS design has been developed and refined using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) analysis and a significant amount of supplemental testing to confirm the CFD results. Testing was conducted, on site called Yara Siilinjarvi, Finland in a phosphate flotation process where the high FVF (>1.4) mineral froth was causing major issues for the operator. 

Standard horizontal 6” discharge froth pump non vented design works well in stable condition of FVF < 1.4 However in unstable condition when FVF > 1.4, pump was not working as efficiently, pump flowrate would drop and suction sump overflows. Added chemicals were needed to reduce FVF to stop suction sump overflow. CARS design managed to stabilize pump performance for FVF >1.4 without overflow and added chemicals. 

The CARS design separates and removes gas from the froth in a two-stage process. In the first stage of the process, the flow inducer blades of the froth impeller help draw the froth slurry into the pump while, at the same time, inducing slurry pre-rotation in the suction piping. This is where the initial separation occurs. 

In the second stage of the process, the flow inducer, which is located behind the impeller in the gas collection chamber, facilitates the movement of the collected air out of the collection chamber through the vent pipe. The rotating action of the flow

inducer also centrifuges the mixture inside the chamber resulting in additional separation. Solids in the collection chamber are forced back into the process by the centrifugal action of back expelling vanes of the main impeller. Unlike the vacuum pump, this arrangement has no dependency on tight running clearances, and all wetted parts are made of wear resistant materials specifically designed for handling abrasive slurries. 

As FVF increases, air volume starts to build up in the impeller eye, and the pump performance suffers. This causes froth levels in the tank to rise which causes the control system to increase pump rpm which only serves to exacerbate the initial air locking problem. The CARS venting design effectively helps to relieve this air lock in the impeller eye. The CARS design starts to vent intermittently until it reaches a continuous air venting state. At this stage, the air is discharged through the venting pipe at almost fan like pressure levels. The air that would accumulate at the impeller eye is continuously released and the pump performance remains stable. 

Tests were conducted on pump overall efficiency of CARS design using various froth pump impeller configurations including semi-open and closed impellers, both equipped with flow inducer vanes. A semiopen impeller with inducer vanes showed better pump efficiency relative to other impeller designs. It allowed the end user to keep original motor size for unstable froth condition with high FVF. 

Yara Siilinjarvi Case Study statement: “Weir Minerals made a huge effort to solve our froth pumping problems. The new Warman froth pump CARS design has helped us to complete the technology project and achieve maximum benefit from flotation without any restriction due to froth pump performance.” 

CFD was used to estimate froth pump performance and to understand air distribution and movement inside the pump. Based on the CFD results, the air venting and slurry compression in the pump are significant and both need to be considered in order to estimate pump performance. The volumetric flow rate at the pump discharge is significantly less than the volumetric flow rate into the pump suction.

Pumping mineral froth in flotation processes and froth tailing duties still remains a major engineering challenge for pump manufacturers and end users. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Yara Siilinjдrvi Plant is owned by Yara International, a Norwegian fertiliser company. Yara Siilinjдrvi is Western Europe's only apatite mine, and it primarily produces apatite concentrate for its Siilinjдrvi phosphoric acid plant. A portion of the concentrate is also dried and shipped to other Yara fertiliser plants. The site annually produces 1 Mt of apatite concentrate, which creates approximately 10 Mt of tailings. 

Extending the lifespan of the 1150-hectare tailings storage facility has been studied in Siilinjдrvi for a long time. The aim has been to use the same tailings area footprint, without any new land purchases or major dam increases. An important part of the process has been to study the possibilities for using new technologies, especially thickened tailings technology (Ruhanen, 2014). 

To extend the lifetime of the existing tailings storage area, Yara replaced the conventional tailings storage facility with a new tailings treatment plant. The new high-density tailings disposal system with two paste thickeners increased the percentage of solids in the slurry from 45-48 per cent to 66-68 per cent, making it possible to deposit it as a paste. This extended the life-span of the current tailings storage facility by 15 years; from 2020 to 2035.

This paper presents the storyline of the Yara Paste Plant Project. The project began in 2006 with initial laboratory testing, which then gradually progressed into pilot trials. After the pilot trials, the work continued with the building of a large 100 t/h pilot plant, which was used to develop and demonstrate the final Paste Plant concept. ###### **YARA SIILINJДRVI PASTE PLANT** 

###### **Laboratory and pilot

testing** 

The options to increase the life-span of the tailings storage facility started being examined in 2006, when Outotec carried out the first laboratory scale test work. This work continued over the following years and the final test results showed that it is possible to consistently increase the solids content of the tailings slurry from 45-48 per cent to 70-72 per cent, thereby significantly increasing the slope angle of the tailings deposit. 

The laboratory test work was followed by an extensive 1-meter pilot test campaign in late September 2010. This campaign was completed towards the end of 2010 and it produced valuable data that served as a good foundation on which to build the full-scale design for the Yara thickeners. Large quantities of thickened tailings were produced during the tests, improving our understanding of the rheological behaviour of the heavily dewatered material (see Figure 1). 

The mineralogy in Siilinjдrvi is very challenging. In general, tailings sand is relatively coarse, but it varies on a daily basis. Particles coarser than 300µm are mostly flaky mica, with an average thickness of roughly 20µm. The high content of mica brings its own characteristics to the process and heavily influences both the thickening and the pumping performance.  An additional challenge is that the mineralogy (and hence the rheology of the tailings sand) varies significantly on a daily basis. ###### **Pilot plant trials** 

Even though the laboratory and pilot trials were promising, there were still many concerns related to the material raking and the long-distance pumping to the tailings disposal area. The biggest issue was how to ensure that the full-scale plant would operate trouble-free and continuously, regardless of the varying mineralogy of the tailings. To better understand the thickening, pumping and deposition characteristics of the slurry, Yara commissioned Outotec to build a large 100-tph pilot plant unit. 

The pilot plant was located in the tailings disposal area, 6 km away from the main concentrator plant. The pilot plant included a feed tank, a hydrocyclone, a 14m-diameter thickener, underflow pumping, process instrumentation and automation. The pilot plant was operated during the three operational trials over the course of 2013-2014 and it could treat approximately 10 per cent of the total tailings from Siilinjдrvi’s operations (see

Figure 3). 

The first trial was started in April 2013 and soon thereafter, we observed that the high settling rate of the coarse solids make the operation of the thickener and the underflow pumping of the heavily dewatered material challenging. Although the target density was occasionally achieved, the performance of the thickener varied significantly, and the doughnut effect and torque limitations restricted the thickening process from being continuous. As an end result, the thickener design was modified to a steeper floor slope to improve the transportation of the thickened material inside the thickener. The drive system was also upgraded to deal with the higher yield stress levels. 

The second test campaign was completed at the end of November 2013. It was evident that the modifications made after the first trial were helping to improve the transportation of the mud bed to the underflow pumps. Although it was not possible to demonstrate that the thickener operation was fully 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

continuous, it did appear that the thickener was operable over longer periods of time. The underflow densities of 65-67 per cent were achievable, but the material remained problematic when we attempted to use higher densities. 

A third trial campaign was planned, and valuable discussions were had with several experts within Outotec and Yara.  It was recommended that only a fine portion of the total feed to the thickener should be processed. The coarse fraction could be removed with a hydro-cyclone, with the cyclone overflow reporting to the thickener.  A piston-membrane pump was obtained from Weir GEHO to transfer the heavily-dewatered material to the disposal. In addition, Outotec’s static picket design was installed in the thickener to prevent bed rotation. 

The third trial was started at the end of May 2014. After a series of test runs, it became apparent that processing the cyclone overflow was very challenging, because the fine material was prone to generate high yield stresses at low densities. It was also noted that underflow viscosity was sensitive to small changes in flocculant dosage rates, which resulted in pumping problems. Instead, we obtained a more stable underflow density and improved overall thickener operation when the total tailings feed was tested. The third trial campaign demonstrated continuous operation with the underflow density being between 68-70 per cent, although it was evident that the system was sensitive to the varying minerology of the slurry. Therefore, special attention needed to be paid to the process instrumentation and process automation when designing the full-scale Paste Plant.

###### _Process layout_ 

The main components in the Paste Plant are the feed tank, two 30-metre paste thickeners, three positive displacement (PD) pumps, and three paste discharge lines routed to the tailings disposal area. The basic operating principle is that one thickener always feeds one PD pump, which in turn feeds one discharge line (see Figures 5 and 6). 

The system is built to be flexible, so that one PD pump and one discharge line are always on standby. This ensures high plant availability and uninterrupted operation, for example, in situations when one discharge line is under extension. 

###### _Need for advanced process control_ 

As discussed in previous sections, the varying mineralogy at Yara makes process control challenging. For example, when the ore is extracted from areas with high quantities of sheared ore, the particle size distribution is very fine. The material is then more difficult to compact, but relatively easy to pump to the disposal area. In such circumstances, the thickener operates with very high inventory levels – even at 95 per cent – to obtain the required density and beaching properties. On the other hand, when the material is coarser, it compacts easily, and the required density levels can be reached with the inventory levels of 55-60 per cent. In these situations, there are high pressure losses in pumping, and the thickener rake torque operates at higher levels, so that the available

operating window is limited (Ruhanen, 2014; Ruhanen _et al_ , 2018). 

Large disturbances to the Paste Plant feed are caused by the milling circuits at the main plant. Mills are operating with 24-hour homogenisation stockpiles and the biggest changes occur when the stockpile (and hence the incoming ore type) is changed. In addition, each milling section must be shut down for 1-2 hours each week to load new rods. This significantly reduces the Paste Plant’s input mass flow, causing a disturbance to the plant’s feed. Although both incidents can be forecasted with some accuracy, the actual influence and duration of the disturbance is difficult to estimate. Therefore, the plant’s control system needs to be able to smoothly cope with variations in both the ore type and in the incoming mass flow. 

The Paste Plant is located 6.6 km away from the main concentrator plant, and the operators in the main plant have no visual contact with it. From the very beginning of the Paste Plant project, Yara’s long-term goal has been for the staff from the main plant to be able to operate the plant remotely. This means that the plant is required to be fully controllable remotely, which emphasises the importance of automated process sequences and efficient process controls.

###### **Controller setup** 

The structure of the optimising controller is shown in Figure 9. The controlled variables in the system are (Kosonen _et al_ , 2017): 

- Underflow density [kg/m3] 

- Overflow solids content [%] 

- Bed mass [%] 

- Bed level [m] and 

- Rake torque [%] 

From these variables, the underflow density was selected to be a primary controlled variable, which has a precise target value and the highest priority during normal operation. This was a natural choice, because the primary goal for the whole Paste Plant is to produce stable and sufficiently high underflow solids content, thereby ensuring stable pumping and favourable tailings beaching properties. 

The second most important variable for describing the cleanliness of the recovered water is overflow solids. As such, it is not important to control the solids at a certain, precise target value, but to avoid having excessive amounts of solids in the overflow for longer periods of time. Simultaneously, the flocculant dosage should be limited to a certain operating range, ensuring trouble-free thickener operation. Overall, the system should run with minimal flocculant dosage to minimise the plant’s operating costs. 

Bed mass is a pressure measurement gauge mounted at the bottom of the thickener tank. The sensor detects pressure in kPa, but it can be transformed into “% bed mass” units to ease interpretation. Together with the electro-mechanical bed level sensor, it indicates the inventory level of the thickener and provides information about the current operating point (Parker _et al_ , 2016). Therefore, the controller should maintain these variables within a certain operating range, but not aim for a specific target value.  The same principle also applies to the rake torque, which indicates the forces directed to the raking mechanism. The torque is considered to be a constraint in the optimisation, so control actions which lead to critical rake loads are avoided when operating at high torque levels. 

Information from the thickener feed line, such as the input flow rate and the slurry density, are also used in the controller setup. Since the input mass flow to the tailings thickener can vary quite rapidly, depending on the operations in the main concentrator plant, it is important to react to sudden changes efficiently to maintain the highest quality underflow at all times. As of February 2018, the controls have been in use for ten months, during 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conf

which time the overall controls usage rate has been over 92 per cent. In practice, the controls are in use all the time, and only exceptional situations are handled with manual controls. 

As an example, Figure 10 presents the optimising control performance in Thickener 1 between June–August 2017. Over the course of the observed 50-day period, the plant has been in continuous operation without any shutdowns. The feed mass flow to Thickener 1 has varied between 450–650 tph, and in many situations, there have been sudden changes of over 100 tph to the feed flow. Some short control off-periods have been removed from the data. 

The plant’s main controlled variable is underflow density. The basic operating principle is to run the system with the highest possible density that still ensures the trouble-free pumping. In practice, this means that the operator adjusts the density target value in accordance with the observed pumping behaviour and the visual appearance of the discharged slurry. Because the Paste Plant operates very close to the corner point in the solids content vs. the yield stress curve (Paterson, 2004), even a very small (10-20kg/m<sup>3</sup> ) change in the density makes a significant difference to the pumping resistance. 

As seen from Figure 10, the density control is working very well. Most of the time, the instantaneous density value (1-minute sampling interval) is very close to the target value, and even after large, sudden changes to the feed, there is only a minor deviation from the setpoint. Statistically, the 2-sigma value for control error is 20kg/m<sup>3</sup> , meaning that for 95 per cent of the control operating time, the underflow density is within a window of ±20kg/m<sup>3</sup> from the setpoint. In solid content, this means an operating window of ±0.85%. 

Another main controlled variable is the overflow solids. The target is to attain a solids content of around 0.3 per cent. As seen from Figure 9, this goal has been achieved most of the time, but sometimes there are longer periods when the given target is exceeded. The reason for this is that sometimes an extremely fine material comes to the thickener. This material responds weakly to the flocculant and hence, settles poorly. Therefore, when there is a lot of very fine material in the process, the overflow solids tend to increase. 

The other controlled variables are the bed mass, the bed level and the rake torque. These variables are not strictly controlled, but there is a preferred operating window for each of them. Therefore, as seen from Figure 9, these variables can float quite freely, but if they stray outside their operating windows, the control drives them back to the desired level. 

In Section 2.3.2, we mentioned that, due to the changing ore type and the minerology, the target density level is obtained with very different thickener inventory levels. This can be seen very clearly from the density and bed mass

trends. At those times, when the ore type remains the same, the bed mass and the density correlate well. However, sometimes when the ore type changes, the trend lines differ from each other (e.g., time intervals of 40–45 days). This also means that a constant bed mass does not guarantee constant density.

###### **Operational results from the advanced control strategy** 

One of the key goals set for the Yara Paste Plant Project was for the plant to operate continuously with an underflow solids content of between 68-70 per cent. The solids content obtained in June to August 2017 are shown in Figure 11. As seen from the trend lines, both thickeners operate inside the 66–68 per cent operating window. The reason for why the operating values obtained are slightly lower than the original targets is that the targeted beach slopes had already been exceeded with this operating range and there is no need to pursue higher solids content. The biggest variation comes from the density setpoint changes that the operator made. 

Before the advanced controls were installed, the Yara Paste Plant used a single-loop bed mass controller as the main tool for controlling the underflow quality. As such, the controller was working well, but it was rather challenging for the operators to recognise situations when they needed to make a major change to the thickener inventory level. Therefore, the multivariable control is much easier to operate. The operator sets the density setpoint and the control automatically adjusts the inventory level accordingly.  Other situations where changes are needed and which are now much easier to handle, include the sudden, large changes to the feed mass flow. At present, the control normally handles these disturbances, which last a few hours, automatically, without the operators needing to intervene manually. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Discharge line pumping pressure losses vary between 2-8 kPa/m, depending on the feed characteristics. Sometimes the losses may also be higher for short periods of time. Overall, the pumping performance has not been a major issue during the past twelve months of operation, but in some situations, extra underflow dilution is used to alleviate the high peaks in pressure. The optimising controller also helps in this, as the control maintains the process strictly within its operating window. Hence, the system is easier to operate, and the operators are required to make fewer manual corrections. 

One of the features of the optimising controller is that it attempts to run the system with the lowest possible flocculant dosage. If the controlled variables do not require a high dosage to perform, the control gradually reduces the amount of floccul

ant. On the other hand, when more flocculant is needed, the dosage level is increased. Typically, this kind of control philosophy leads to lower levels of average chemical consumption. This has also observed in Yara, where the overall flocculant consumption was reduced by 10-20%, compared to a system where the flocculant is dosed in proportion to the incoming feed mass flow. Since the overall tonnage is high, this translates to significant savings in the plant’s operating costs. 

Twelve months after the start-up, the Paste Plant has now obtained a consistent performance level. The underflow solids content is continuously maintained within the required operating window, and the average beach slope angles obtained are over 3.5 degrees (6.1 per cent), see Figure 12. 

One of Yara’s major long-term goals was to be able to operate the Paste Plant remotely from the main concentrator plant. Currently, the plant still has its own staff working there during the daytime, but the Paste Plant is now already operated remotely during the night shifts. The long-term goal is to gradually move into operating the plant completely remotely.

###### **CONCLUSION** 

This paper presented the storyline of the Yara Paste Plant Project. The project began in 2006 with initial laboratory testing, which then gradually progressed into pilot trials. After the pilot trials, the work continued with the building of a large 100 tph pilot plant, which was used to develop and demonstrate the final Paste Plant concept. The full-scale Paste Plant was commissioned at the beginning of 2017. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Currently, the plant has been in operation for twelve months. Overall, the availability of the plant has been very good, at over 97 per cent, and the plant has consistently reached the required performance level. The long-term follow-up demonstrates that with the optimising control, the paste thickeners can consistently run with high and stable underflow solids content of 66-68 per cent, despite the challenging minerology and the variation in the tailings feed rate. This results in average beach slope angles of 3.5 degrees (6.1 per cent) in the tailings disposal area. 

One of Yara’s major long-term goals was to be able to operate the Paste Plant remotely from the main concentrator plant. Currently, the plant still has its own staff working there during the daytime, but it is working autonomously and operated remotely from the main plant during the night shifts. The next goal is to gradually move into fully-remote operation.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Comminution continues to be the most capital-intensive unit operation in mineral processing. The fundamental purpose of comminution is to liberate the valuable minerals so that they can be economically concentrated into saleable products. Declining ore quality characterised by lower grade and increased complexity requires significant energy consumption for comminution. Low-grade magnetite ores are typically fine-grained and require fine to ultra-fine grinding (P80 ~ 30 - 40 µm) to enhance its liberation from the typically siliceous gangue

matrix. Historically, this has been achieved using multi-stage crushing and grinding technologies, which require high energy consumption with low energy efficiency. This motivated innovations in energy efficient technologies for comminution. Such technology has been developed in the IMPTEC super-fine crusher. It is an innovative, dry (with the potential to be operated wet), media-free, energy efficient crusher that can to reduce 10 mm feed particles to 19 – 30 µm with very low recycle loads. In this study, the mineralogical and physicochemical characteristics of crushed magnetite ore using the IMPTEC super-fine crusher have been investigated in comparison with those of rod milling. The super-fine crusher generated higher liberated magnetite minerals in the – 300 + 212 µm and < 45 µm size fractions compared to rod mill. Both comminution devices generated large low-grade hematite and goethite middlings. However, the rod mill produced higher locked/unliberated hematite and goethite compared to that of the super-fine crusher. Quartz mineral had the highest liberation irrespective of the comminution device used. The super-fine crusher generated higher entrapment of other minerals within the silica matrix compared to the rod mill. The breakage mechanism of the super-fine crusher which is predominantly through high compression with shear, generated improved mineral liberation in the coarse size fractions compared to the predominant abrasion and attrition breakage mechanisms of rod milling. The higher mineral liberation generated by the rod mill is potentially due to the prolonged batch milling of the ore compared to the single-pass open circuit of the super-fine crusher. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Comminution is the process of progressively reducing coarse materials into finer particles by crushing and/or grinding (Lynch, 2015). In mineral processing, the fundamental objective of comminution is to liberate valuable minerals from the associated gangue for efficient and economic downstream concentration processes (Little _et al_ ., 2017). It is also the most capital- and energy-intensive unit operation in mineral processing accounting for 30 - 60% of the total mining expenditure (Karmazin, Bikbov and Bikbov, 2002, Yuexin _et al_ ., 2012, Yu _et al_ ., 2016, Bikbov, Karmazin and Bikbov, 2004, Aldrich, 2013, Herbst, Lo and Flintoff, 2003). In addition, the cost of grinding media can contribute about 25% of the overall cost of ultrafine grinding (Kelsey, Kelly and Skinner, 2017).  As a result of the capital-intensive nature of comminution, comprehensive knowledge on liberation is paramount to ensure optimum balance between comminution product size and energy input is achieved, so that gangue particles are not unnecessarily over ground. Typically, processing designs are targeted at rejecting gangue particles at size as coarse as possible to minimise the energy expended on gangue (Vizcarra _et al_ , 2010). Mineral liberation can be influenced by the breakage

mechanism of the comminution equipment because the breakage mechanism applied during size reduction influences the stress intensity that is imparted to the feed (Xiao _et al_ ., 2012). This also determines the product quality such as particle shape, sintering behaviour, magnetisability, etc., (Schonert, 1995, Lin and Somasundaran, 1972). 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

There are four basic breakage mechanisms that are applied for size reduction namely, impact, abrasion or shear, attrition and compression. A combination of these mechanisms is utilised by various comminution devices. Impact breakage results from kinetic energy of the grinding media acting on the particles from instantaneous collision. Breakage by compression takes place when a bed of particles is restricted between two surfaces with the work being done by one or both surfaces. Energy is imparted to particles by means of surrounding particles, resulting in inter-particle breakage. Abrasion or shear breakage occurs when particles rub against each other, producing finer particles. Grinding media also promote abrasion. Attrition breakage is similar to abrasion; however, attrition occurs when finer particles are trapped between larger ones. Attrition occurs as the particle edges are chipped off (Lynch, 2015). 

As stated earlier, the objective of comminution is mineral liberation, a phenomenon where a mineral composite disintegrates into progeny particles with a range of mineral compositions (Evans, 2015). There are several techniques that are used to measure mineral liberation. Where suitable, bulk laboratory techniques such as magnetic separation together with assays are used to quantify the liberation characteristics of an ore (Xiao _et al_ ., 2012, Evans, 2015). This approach has been especially used to assess liberation in iron ores. The bulk techniques have the advantage of better sample representivity compared with optical microscopy, since bulk techniques analyse larger numbers of particles in the bulk samples (Evans, 2015). Other techniques used for liberation studies are optical microscopy which takes quantitative measurements on polished sections of ore particles, and Quantitative Evaluation of Minerals by Scanning electron microscopy (QEMSCAN) (Evans, 2015, Fandrich _et al_ ., 2007). 

Australia is currently the largest exporter of iron ore, exporting 53% of the global iron ore (Department of Industry, 2017). The largest source of iron ore exported from Australia is from the Pilbara regions of Western Australia, accounting for nearly 97% of the total production (Yellishetty _et al._ , 2012, Holmes and Lu, 2015). About 90% of South Australia’s iron ore deposits estimated at 14 billion tonnes is magnetite iron ore (Department of State Development, 2017). Low-grade magnetite mineralisation is generally fine-grained requiring fine to ultra-fine grinding (P80 ~ 30 - 40 µm) (Clout and Manuel, 2015) to liberate it from the predomin

antly siliceous/silicate gangue matrix (Jeswiet and Szekeres, 2016, Wills, 1990, Jankovic, 2015) for effective magnetic beneficiation processes, to make saleable Fe grades (Carpentaria Resources, 2017). In addition, declining ore quality characterised by lower grade and increased complexity requires significant energy consumption for comminution. Historically, this has been achieved using multi-stage crushing and wet grinding technologies, which require high power consumption e.g., 28 000 kW for Semi-autogenous (SAG) mill (Lynch, 2015), with low energy efficiency of about 40% (Musa and Morrison, 2009). Most of the energies generated are expended on liners and grinding media wear (Napier-Munn, 2015) and lost as heat in the rocks (Jeswiet and Szekeres, 2016). This motivated innovations in energy efficient and low cost technologies for comminution. Such technology has been developed in the IMPTEC super-fine crusher. It is designed to provide dry or wet, media-free and energy efficient crushing that can reduce coarse (10 mm) and fine feed to fine and ultra-fine (19 - 30 µm) product with very low recycle loads. 

In this study, liberation studies of crushed magnetite ore using IMPTEC super-fine crusher - 130 have been performed and compared with the liberation data from a laboratory scale rod mill. The major elemental compositions of the ore were 29% iron (Fe), 20% Silicon (Si) and 1% Aluminium (Al). The dominant iron phases are magnetite (Fe3O 4), hematite (Fe2O 3) and goethite (FeO(OH)), with quartz (SiO 2) as the dominant gangue mineral. 

###### **IMPTEC super-fine crusher** 

The IMPTEC super-fine crusher is a novel crusher that consists of a vertically mounted compression chamber with an internal gyrating mandrel as shown in Figure 1. It is designed to provide wet or dry, mediafree crushing. The axis of rotation of the mandrel is displaced relative to the axis of the vertically mounted compression chamber. The inner surface of the compression chamber is tapered at an angle equal to the displacement angle of the mandrel. The compression chamber shell also carries a product discharge impeller (Kelsey, Kelly and Skinner, 2017, Kelsey and Kelly, 2014). 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 



FIG 1 - Cross section view of IMPTEC super-fine crusher -130 

###### **_Mode of operations_** 

Feed entering the crusher is accelerated into a compressed particle bed, which lines the inside of the compression chamber. The depth of the bed progressively increases until the mandrel is engaged and free to rotate with the compression chamber. The particle bed is initially compressed under the influence of the centrifugal force generated by the rotating compression chamber. Additional pressure on the bed triggers the mandrel’s gyratory motion, directed counter to the direction of rotation. Once engaged by the particle bed, the freely rotating mandrel adopts a gyratory motion and delivers multiple compressive pulses at h

igh pressure in a direction opposite to the rotating particle bed. Product is transported to a collection facility or classification circuit. The closed side set of the crusher is adjusted hydraulically (Kelsey and Kelly, 2014, Batterham, Kelsey and Kelly, 2015, Kelsey and Kelly, 2016). 

Unlike conventional crushing and grinding devices the super-fine crusher is designed to confine the feed mass within the zone of maximum applied stress, resulting in the transfer of an extraordinarily high-level of productive strain energy to the particle mass. 

###### **_Operational benefits_** 

The super-fine crusher has demonstrated exceptional efficiency with high particle size reduction ratios and low levels of heat generation (Kelsey and Kelly, 2014). The super-fine crusher provides media-free superfine crushing which obviates media costs (Morley, 2006, Kelsey, Kelly and Skinner, 2017).  A typical ultrafine grinding circuit incorporates primary/secondary crushing followed by primary milling, e.g. Semiautogenous (SAG) mill (product size ~ 150 µm), secondary milling, e.g. ball mill (product size ~ 100 µm), and ultra-fine milling, e.g. IsaMill (product size 20 - 45 µm) (Jankovic, 2015). The super-fine crusher can receive secondary crushing product, e.g. cone crusher product (size ~ 10 - 30 mm) and crush to the required liberation size from a single stage open circuit operation, eliminating some comminution steps and reducing the overall capital expenditure of comminution plants (Kelsey _et al._ , 2017). Kelsey and Kelly (2016), compared the performance of the IMPTEC super-fine crusher (SFC-100) and Bradley BM3 roller mill for ultra-fine grinding of granulated blast furnace slag. The super-fine crusher and roller mill generated product sizes D50 of 12 µm and 46 µm with specific energy of 53.8 kWh/t and 55 kWh/t respectively. A recent pilot test crushing (single pass) on a magnetite ore with top feed size 10 mm, generated product size P80 18 µm and D50 11 µm with net specific power consumption of 2.25kWh/t. 

###### **_Wear factor_** 

During its operation, the consolidated particle bed lines the compression chamber thereby protecting it from wear. The gyrating mandrel on the other hand is prone to wear, however, its low impact velocities minimise the wear and heat generation during operation. In addition, the mandrel assembly is equipped with reversible tungsten carbide to enhance its durability and consistent operation (Kelsey and Kelly, 2014) and lowers the maintenance cost.
