###### **Quantitative X-ray diffraction (QXRD) analysis** 

QXRD is a qualitative and quantitative tool that is used for identification of crystalline phases within a sample (Loubser and Verryn, 2008, Wang and Vipulanandan, 2000). Two samples were collected for the analyses. Each of the samples was measured twice. The first measurement was done on the as-received samples whilst the second measurement was done on ~ 10 wt. % zinc oxide (ZnO) spiked samples. The first measurement was used primarily for phase identification, thereafter coupled with the second measurement 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

for quantification, with the ZnO spike phase acting as a reference to allow calculation of the amorphous phases. The reference selected for the amorphous calculation was defined by the primary phases identified upon measuring the as-received samples. 

The as-received and spiked samples were measured using a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer with Cu K-α radiation of wavelength 1.54 Е. Scans were conducted from 5 - 80 ⁰ 2θ at 0.02 ⁰ 2-θ intervals. The X-ray conditions were set to 40 kV and 40 mA. 

Mineral phase identification was conducted using the ‘X’Pert Highscore Plus software package linked with the ICSD FIZ Karlsruhe diffraction file. Quantification was conducted by the ‘Rietveld’ refinement method. 

###### **Sieve analyses and mineral deportment using X-ray fluorescence** 

Representative samples of known mass from the super-fine crusher and the rod mill products were subjected to sieve analyses. Each size fraction was weighed and the mass recorded. The size fractions from the sieve analyses of the two comminuted products were assayed to determine Fe and Si content. Mineral assaying was conducted using a field portable Olympus Delta XRF analyser (Kalnicky and Singhvi, 2001). 

###### **QEMSCAN analyses** 

QEMSCAN is a modern SEM-based mineral liberation tool use for detailed characterisation of ore (Ayling _et al_ ., 2012, Boni _et al_ ., 2013, Celep _et al_ ., 2009). The ore was analysed by QEMSCAN to confirm the mineral phases identified by QXRD and identify other elemental composition whose concentrations were below the detection limit of the QXRD. Unlike the traditional optical microscope and/or semi-automated SEM tools that were time consuming, costly and mostly generated semi-quantitative results from data sets that are too scanty to be statistically viable, QEMSCAN generates textural parameters such as mineral liberation and mineral association and modal mineralogy data of samples even at submicron levels in less than one hour. With its sophisticated image analyses software, more accurate characterisation data is provided for mineral processing (Fandrich _et al_ ., 2007, Knappett _et al_ ., 2011, Andersen _et al_ ., 2009). Super-fine crusher and rod mill product of various size fractions (- 300 + 212 µm, - 212 + 150 µm, - 150 + 106 µm, - 106 + 75 µ

m, - 75 + 45 µm, and – 45 µm) were analysed using QEMSCAN. A representative sample for each size fraction was obtained using a micro-rotary splitter. The sub-samples of required mass were mounted in 30 mm diameter sample blocks using Epofix resin, polished to a mirror smooth finish and carbon coated to about 20 nm thickness. The Particle Mineral Analysis (PMA) method of QEMSCAN measurement was used to provide quantitative mineralogy (mineral abundance, %) of the sized fractions, mineral liberation and locking statistics. Manual investigation (with 1 000 000 counts) allowed for developing Species Identification Protocol (SIP) to specify the elemental composition of unclassified phases which were present in the sample. Specific attention was paid to the discrimination of magnetite and hematite, and other similar mineral phases which show very little differences in energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) chemistry and backscattered intensity. 

###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS** 

###### **Chemical composition** 

The chemical composition of the ore is given in Table 2 for five important elements. From Table 2, it can be seen that the ore is very rich in silica. Silica is a non-magnetic mineral and can be rejected easily in magnetic separation. Silica content is significant in determining the quality of iron concentrate because high silica content (SiO 2 > 5%) in the concentrate increases slag production during blast furnace operations, thereby increasing limestone consumption to maintain the fixed CaO/SiO 2 ratio required for their effective operations. The presence of aluminium in the ore can also affect the concentrate quality because high aluminium content (Al2O 3 > 2.8%) in the concentrate increases melt viscosity in sintering and blast furnace operations, thereby increasing their fuel consumption rates (Clout and Manuel, 2015). The presence of these impurities above their allowable thresholds significantly increases the overall operational cost of sintering and blast furnace.

Other iron phases identified were hematite (Fe2O 3), goethite (FeO(OH)) and amakinite ((Fe, Mg)OH). Hematite was mainly in maghemite mineral associations and goethite with limonite. As shown in Figure 4, both comminution devices generated fully liberated magnetite mineral. The highest liberated magnetite mineral was produced by the rod mill in the - 106 + 75 µm size fraction. In general, the rod mill generated more liberated magnetite mineral in all the size fractions except the finer where only 20 % was generated compared to more than 40% of that of the super-fine crusher and the coarser size range where the rod mill produced 13% compared to 18% of the super-fine crusher. Conversely, the super-fine crusher generated more secondary middlings in all the size fractions, except the < 45 µm and > 212 µm size fractions. The primary middlings were consistent for both comminution devices in all the size fractions. As expected, the coarse size fractions generated the highest locked magnetite mineral and they decreased with decreasing size fractions. Mineral liberation can be characterised in different terms depending on its predominant property that is exploited for concentration (Tonžetić, 2015). For example, in leaching process, liberation characterisation is based on the % free surface exposure of the mineral of interest that allows access to the bulk mineral. Magnetic concentration exploits the difference in the magnetic susceptibility between the magnetic mineral and the associated non-magnetic gangue and hence it is possible to achieve high recoveries in magnetite concentration even though the magnetic mineral may be completely locked, i.e., zero degree of liberation (Wills and Napier-Munn, 2006, Wills and Finch, 2015). 

Hematite mineral liberation was predominantly low-grade middlings for both devices. The super-fine crusher product generated higher low-grade middlings in all the size fractions except for the - 45 µm and +212 µm size fractions as shown in Figure 5. The highest low-grade middling hemati

te mineral was observed in the - 106 + 75 µm size fraction of the super-fine crusher. This was more than 80%. All the size fractions of both the super-fine crusher and rod mill generated less than 10 % high-grade middling hematite mineral except the - 45 µm size fraction of the super-fine crusher. Only 1% of the hematite mineral in the - 45 µm size fraction of both comminution devices was liberated. Significant portions of the hematite mineral are locked, even in the - 45 µm size fraction and thus, require further size reduction to ensure their liberation for effective downstream beneficiation. 

The liberation classes of goethite are similar to that of hematite. Significant portions of the goethite are lowgrade middling with the super-fine crusher generating slightly higher mass % goethite liberation in the - 150 + 106 µm and the - 106 + 75 µm size fractions than the rod mill as shown in Figure 6. Both the super-fine crusher and rod mill generated similar low-grade goethite middlings in the - 75 + 45 µm and < 45 µm size fractions. The super-fine crusher produced slightly higher high-grade goethite middlings in all the size fractions than the rod mill, with almost close to 30% high-grade goethite middlings in the < 45 µm size fractions compared to 20 % from the rod mill. However, the rod mill generated the highest high-grade goethite middlings in the + 212 µm size fraction but none liberated goethite in this size fraction. The highest liberated goethite mineral is in the - 45 µm size fraction of the rod mill. Significant portions of the goethite mineral are still locked and require further comminution to liberate them. 

Mineralogical studies on the ore show that quartz is the major gangue mineral, therefore, its rejection at a coarser size is necessary in a concentration operation. It is observed from Figure 7 that significant portions of the quartz mineral in all the size fractions from both comminution devices are liberated with the rod mill generating the highest except for the > 212 µm size fraction. The super-fine crusher generated higher quartz 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

liberation in the > 212 µm size fraction compared to the rod mill. Both devices generated significant high- and low-grade quartz middlings which show the possible entrapment of valuable minerals within its matrix. 

There is evidence in literature that particle breakage by compression generates much higher mineral liberation through preferential breakage along grain boundaries (Aydoğan, Ergьn and Benzer, 2006, Fuerstenau, Lutch and De, 1999, Celik and Oner, 2006, Daniel, 2007, Fandrich _et al_ ., 1997). However, Vizcarra _et al._ (2010) studied the liberation effects of compression and impact breakage on sulphide ores and concluded that liberation of valuable and gangue minerals was independent of the breakage mechanism. Vizcarra _et al_ . (2010) considered the observed increase in degree of liberation by the compress

ive breakage mechanism relative to conventional methods (impact and abrasion) in previous studies as potential errors associated with liberation measurements. Hence, there are conflicting observations regarding mineral liberation with respect to the breakage mechanism applied and this topic requires further studies using carefully designed experiments. 

###### **CONCLUSION** 

Liberation data on three iron (magnetite, hematite and goethite) minerals and quartz mineral on various size fractions of magnetite ore crushed and milled using IMPTEC super-fine crusher - 130 and laboratory scale rod mill, respectively were compared. The total magnetite mineral liberated was higher in the rod mill product compared to that of the super-fine crusher. The super-fine crusher only recorded higher magnetite mineral liberation in the - 300 + 212 µm and < 45 µm size fractions. Majority of the hematite mineral generated by both comminution devices were low-grade middlings with significant amount of unliberated hematite. The rod mill generated higher locked hematite mineral compared to the super-fine crusher. Furthermore the rod mill generated higher goethite liberation in the < 45 µm size fraction compared to the super-fine crusher. Only the super-fine crusher produced goethite liberation (about 10 %) in the - 300 + 212 µm size fraction. The rod mill generated higher quartz liberation in all the size fractions except for the - 300 + 212 µm. The IMPTEC superfine crusher generated liberated minerals with less over ground particles compared to the laboratory scale rod mill. The authors ascribe the higher mineral liberation generated by the rod mill to the prolonged batch milling of the feed compared with a single-pass open circuit of the super-fine crusher. Future works may include comparing the super-fine crusher’s product with that of a comminution device of similar operational mechanism, e.g. high pressure grinding rolls (HPGR) as well as comparing Bond Work Index and energy consumption of the IMPTEC super-fine crusher with existing comminution devices.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

High Voltage Pulse (HVP) technology is a novel process that could potentially be the step-change needed in ore processability in the mining industry. The propensity of high voltage pulses towards mineral-enriched ore particles during treatment makes this technology selective and has the potential to enable ore preconcentration by size separation. In this study, the potential for pre-concentration of a low grade copper-gold ore sample subjected to HVP pretreatment is investigated and compared to that achievable after mechanical breakage in JKMRC’s rotary breakage tester (JKRBT). The data show that a better pre-concentration result can be achieved after HVP processing than conventional breakage. The gold pre-concentration potential is much better than that observed for copper. 4D HVP pre-concentration characteristic curves were produced to assess the metallurgical performance possible as a function of energy input. The case study shows that when targeting a nominal metal recovery of 90 per cent for gold, the HVP pre-concentration technique can split the low grade ore (0.9 ppm gold and 0.28 per cent copper in the feed size 26.5-37.5 mm) into two components – a low grade oversize material (0.3 ppm gold and 0.15 per cent copper) and a high grade undersize material (1.0 ppm gold and 0.3 per cent copper). The mass split to the low grade is 23 per cent. Under this mass split scenario, gold recovery to screen

undersize is 90 per cent and copper recovery is 85 per cent. The HVP treatment of this feed size requires a specific energy (spark) of 2.8 kWh/t. 

There is further research that would be required before industrial uptake of the HVP pre-concentration technology would be possible. This paper also outlines the research challenges that need to be overcome. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Ore pre-concentration exploits the inherent grade heterogeneity within ores to allow early rejection of particles that are of no economic value and can result in a significant performance boost in terms of metal recovery and grade during the consequent processing stages (Bearman, 2013; Bowman and Bearman, 2014; Carrasco, Keeney and Walters, 2015; Lessard, de Bakker and McHugh, 2014; Pease _et al_ , 2015; Shi, Zuo and Manlapig, 2015, Walters, 2016). Ore pre-concentration is undertaken by exploiting a difference in the properties of the mineral in an ore to achieve a separation. 

In recent times, a significant amount of work has been undertaken by the CRC for Optimising Resource Extraction (CRCORE) to develop a coherent system-based industry approach (Grade Engineering®) for assessing specific pre-concentration technologies or equipment and the optimal configurations that deliver maximum operational value (CRCORE, 2017). Technologies investigated include sized based sorting which takes advantage of the preferential grade deportment by size after crushing or differential blasting, sensorbased bulk/stream sorting and coarse gravity separation (Keeney, 2017; Revell, 2017; Walters, 2016). An overview of the site implementation of the Grade Engineering approach was given at their 2017 Annual Assembly where key production trials were presented to demonstrate the overall economic advantages of achieving early waste rock rejection (Keeney, 2017). Worth noting is that the production trials primarily involved ore pre-concentration using size separation, taking advantage of preferential deportment of mineralisation into the finer sizes after crushing or differential blasting. While it is understandable that some ores, such as an intrusive vein-like deposit may exhibit preferential deportment of the valuable phases into the finer fractions after breakage, for many other ore bodies, waste rejection on a size only basis after conventional breakage may not be feasible. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Lately, there has also been a surge of interest in sensor-based ore sorting methods. The technology employs a sensor for particle detection and evaluation. An array of different sensors are available to detect different ore characteristics (optical, conductivity, magnetic, dual X-Rays, Laser Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy LIBS, etc). Typically, once identified, the particles of interest are rejected customarily through mechanical force to achieve separation (de Jong, 2005, Lessard, de Bakker and McHugh, 2014, Salter and Wyatt, 1991, Walker

, 2014). There have been a number of successful case studies which have been reported from an array of ore-sorting vendors (RADO, 2017; Redwave, 2017; Steinert, 2017; Tomra, 2017). Sensor based particle ore sorters are relatively low throughput devices (achieving approximately 30-100 t/h per metre belt width). For large tonnage, low grade, operations there is a need for high throughput bulk preconcentration techniques to reduce capital cost and footprint. 

In contrast to the above pre-concentration techniques, ore pre-concentration using high voltage pulses (HVP) is a new concept. When a high voltage pulse is applied to an ore it results in particle breakage as the voltage discharge passes through the rock. The HVP comminution team at the Julius Kruttschnitt Mineral Research Centre (JKMRC) have recently reported that during this process, particles with metalliferous grains are selectively broken as the charge is attracted to the high conductivity/permittivity minerals within the rock, while barren rocks remain intact. Application of relatively low levels of HVP energy to break mineral particles from barren rocks selectively, followed by size-based screening separation has been shown to enable the feed ore to be split into high grade (screen undersize) and low grade products (screen oversize) (Shi, Zuo and Manlapig, 2015; Zuo, Shi and Manlapig, 2015). The HVP treatment has also been shown to generate cracks/micro-cracks in the disintegrated particles, reducing the energy required for subsequent breakage (Wang, Shi and Manlapig, 2011; Shi, Manlapig and Zuo, 2014). The HVP treatment followed by conventional grinding can also result in improved liberation of the valuable minerals and better recovery in downstream flotation (Parker _et al_ , 2015). Thus the application of HVP treatment prior to conventional processing has the potential to facilitate rejection of low grade ore prior to processing, increase production rates, reduce the energy required for comminution and improve flotation separation recoveries. 

In this paper, the potential application of HVP for pre-concentration of a low grade copper-gold ore from a Newcrest mining operation is presented. This work involves comparing the potential upgrade possible by separation after HVP to that which would be possible using the ‘as received ore’ and after conventional breakage. 

###### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

###### **Materials** 

A low grade copper-gold ore sample from an Australian Newcrest mine was used in the study. The ore sample originates from a volcanic sequence of rocks hosting a porphyry gold-copper deposit. Gold, copper and molybdenum are associated with quartz veining, as fine disseminations and rarely present as massive sulphide. Mineral liberation analysis of the as received ore sample conducted by the SMI-JKMRC indicates that the main copper bearing minerals in order of abundance are chalcopyrite and bornite with trace amounts occurring as digenite and tennantite. The predominant gangue

minerals in this ore are anorthoclase, plagioclase, illite, quartz, orthoclase and biotite, and the predominant sulphide gangue mineral in the sample is pyrite. 

The sample was sourced from the SAG mill feed conveyor and supplied to the JKMRC in drums. The received sample was sized using a set of large diameter screens (Gilson screen) to acquire the desired size fractions for testing (13.2-19 mm, 19-26.5 mm and 26.5-37.5 mm). An 8-segment rotary splitter was then used to achieve sample homogenisation and divide each size fraction into representative subsamples for HVP testing. A total of 33 kg of ore (approximately 2100 particles, excluding those used in the repeat tests for other investigations) in the three size fractions were tested by HVP. 

Screening was also performed to establish the size distribution of the as received ore. Each of the size fractions was then assayed for copper and gold to establish the degree of preferential deportment of mineral naturally occurring in the process feed after mining and crushing. 

###### **HVP pre-concentration tests** 

The pre-concentration tests were undertaken using a commercial HVP equipment unit (selFrag Lab) installed at the JKMRC. The major components of this unit include a high voltage (HV) power supply, HV pulse generator, discharge electrode and a removable processing vessel (Figure 1). 

For the HVP pre-concentration tests, three subsamples from each size fraction were chosen and subjected to HVP selective fragmentation using three different spark energy inputs. The HVP specific energy input

levels were controlled by adjusting the number of cycles and the number of pulses per cycle applied to each ore sample. The applied voltage and electrode gap were not varied in the experiments.

Each HVP test involved testing multiple batches of the same feed size under the same HVP conditions to provide sufficient material for subsequent treatment, and to provide more statistically valid pre-concentration data. For each batch of sample a single layer of particles was placed on the ground electrode and subjected to a defined number of high voltage pulses. The product from each batch was sieved with a closing screen and only the oversize particles returned for the next cycle of HVP treatment. The closing screens used were 11.2 mm for the 13.2-19 mm feed, 16 mm for the 19-26.5 mm feed and 22.4 mm for the 26.5-37.5 mm feed. After all the feed material had been subjected to the first cycle of HVP treatment, the accumulated oversize was returned to selFrag in batches and subjected to another cycle of HVP treatment. This process was repeated until the appropriate number of electrical pulses had been applied. The undersize material from every cycle was collected and combined. After breakage, the product was collected from a container underneath the rotor, then sized and assayed for copper and gold. ###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** ###### **Natural mineral deportment in the as received ore** The assay and sizing data of the as received ore was analysed to determine the degree of preferential copper and gold deportments present in the as received ore. The aim was to determine the potential to apply conventional grade engineering size separation using this particular ore as a comparison to the HVP testing results. Figure 2 shows the cumulative mass versus cumulative copper recovery (Figure 2a) and gold recovery (Figure 2b) measured in the as received ore. These graphs show very little preferential copper or gold deportment with the size distribution of the overall mass being very similar to that of the copper and gold distributions. It was therefore conclud

ed that this ore in its current state would not be a suitable candidate for applying ore pre-concentration by size separation.

###### **Metal recovery in relation to mass recovery achieved during HVP testing** 

In contrast to the as received ore, the assay by size data after HVP treatment does display a preferential deportment of the copper and gold minerals into the finer size fractions. Table 2 presents an example of the product size distribution and the assay of these size fractions for the 13.2-19 mm feed after treatment by HVP. The results show a significant proportion of the copper and gold in the finer size fractions compared to the coarse size fractions after HVP treatment. This indicates that the mineralised particles have been broken by HVP preferentially, and are concentrated in the finer size fractions. Results of treating the other feed size fractions by HVP show a similar trend. This result has been obtained despite the copper and gold grades in the sample tested being relatively low (0.33 per cent copper and 1.1 ppm gold). 

The data (an example of which is presented in Table 2) were processed to establish the relationships between metal recovery and mass recovery. Figures 3a and 3b present the cumulative copper and gold recoveries versus cumulative mass recovery observed as a function of size in the product of the HVP tests, respectively. The red diagonal lines on these plots equate to no preferential deportment of copper or gold by size, eg 90 per cent copper or gold being recovered when treating 90 per cent of the feed. The further the test results deviate from this line, the greater the potential for pre-concentration. The black line on these plots was obtained by fitting a linear regression to the average result of all nine HVP tests.

###### **Metal recovery in relation to mass recovery after JKRBT Testing** 

Breakage in the JKRBT is achieved as the particles impact the stationary stator within the machine. Impact breakage is one of the predominant mechanisms by which size reduction occurs in most conventional crushers and tumbling mills and as such the degree of preferential breakage observed in the products of JKRBT should be similar to that which will be achieved after conventional comminution. Figure 5a and 5b show the copper and gold recovery as a function of mass recovery observed in the sized JKRBT products after breakage at different energy levels. 

As the energy used for breakage is increased, there is a degree of preferential breakage observed in the finer sizes (0-0.3 mm) of the JKRBT product. The degree of preferential breakage increases as the energy imparted to the ore is increased. The preferential deportment of the copper and gold observed in the <0.3 mm size fractions in the JKRBT products accounts for less than 20 per cent mass recovery (Figure 5).

However, for the purpose of pre-concentration characterisation, establishing the relationships between the test output, in terms of metal-mass-size distributions, and the test input, in terms of specific energy provided by the HVP facility, is required. This is particularly important in HVP electrical comminution, as different ore properties and factors affect pulse fragmentation. A new 4D graph to describe HVP pre-concentration characterisation has been proposed (Shi, Zuo and Manlapig, 2015), and is similar to the coal washability curves that are widely used in the coal industry. As an example, Figures 6 and 7 present the 4D pre-concentration characterisation graphs for gold and copper respectively for the 26.5-37.5 mm feed size fraction. There are four curves in each of the 4D graphs: Curve 1 presents the screen undersize grade (high grade) in relation to metal recovery to screen undersize; Curve 2 shows the screen oversize grade (low grade) in relation to metal recovery to screen undersize; Curve 3 displays mass recovery to screen undersize (100 mass recovery being the reject rate) in relation to metal recovery, and Curve 4 describes the specific energy (spark) input in relation to mass recovery to screen undersize. This data presentation has the advantage of plotting the four curves in the one graph. Given one point on

the graph, the corresponding values for the other three variables can be found from the characteristic curves. For example, if the pre-concentration operation is required to recover 90 per cent of gold to a high grade circuit, the gold grade of screen undersize, screen oversize, the mass recovery to screen undersize and the specific energy requirement from HVP can be determined according to the following procedures: Draw a vertical line upwards from the gold recovery to the screen undersize axis corresponding to 90 per cent gold recovery. Where this line intersects Curve 1 and 2, draw horizontal lines to the gold grade axis. Inspection of Figure 6 (26.5-37.5 mm feed, head grade 0.86 ppm gold) shows that the gold grades for screen undersize and screen oversize are 1.0 ppm and 0.3 ppm respectively. Similarly, extend the vertical line to intersect Curve 3, from here draw a horizontal line to the mass recovery to the screen undersize axis to find the value of 77%, from which the mass rejected to screen oversize can be calculated as 23%. Finally, extend the horizontal line corresponding to 77% mass recovery to intersect Curve 4, reading off the corresponding coordinate on the specific energy axis to give the required specific energy 2.8 kWh/t. Similar results are observed with the other feed sizes (19-26.5 mm and 13.2-19 mm), with a higher specific energy being required as the feed size decreased. Since gold and copper are associated in the same feed, the corresponding results for the copper preconcentration can be obtained by using the HVP 4D copper pre-concentration characterisation curves (Figure 7). Subjected to 2.8 kWh/t HVP specific energy, 77 per cent of the 26.5-37.5 mm feed would report to screen undersize and 23 per cent to screen oversize as determined from the HVP 4D gold pre-concentration characterisation curves (Figure 6). ###### **PLANNED FUTURE WORK TO FACILITATE INDUSTRIAL UPTAKE OF HVP TECHNOLOGY** 

The mining industry in Australia has contributed substantially to the nation’s growth in recent decades by producing minerals and metals to meet the needs of global society. However it is currently facing difficulties because of increased demands for metals, declining ore grades, increasingly complex ore mineralogy (harder, finer grained, disseminated) and stricter environmental requirements for mining operations. The mining industry is presented with the serious challenge of how to produce metals to meet the needs of society in an economical and environmentally sustainable way. The industry needs disruptive technologies to tackle these challenges. In the past 10 years, the HVP comminution team at the JKMRC have reinvigorated research on a novel application of HVP. Traditionally HVP investigations have involved breaking rocks down to the appropriate size for separation and this proved uneconomic because of the large amounts of energy required. Instead the JKMRC team have developed a novel method of applying HVP technology at much lower energy levels to improve ore processability prior to conventional processing. It has been demonstrated that HVP applied at relatively low energy levels can be used to enhance pre-concentration methods, reduce downstream grinding requirements by pre-weakening the ore and improve downstream mineral liberation. 

The work presented in this paper has further demonstrated the potential of HVP pre-treatment to deliver significant benefits to the mining industry. The pre-concentration result that would be achieved by size separation has been improved significantly for the ore tested after the application of a relatively low level of HVP energy (2 to 5 kWh/t), especially with respect to the gold mineralogy. This is in contrast to conventional breakage which resulted in only marginal preferential mineralised breakage into the finer sizes. 

The financial benefits possible by applying HVP enhanced pre-concentration to an ore prior to conventional processing is significant. I

t has been estimated that for a 20 million tonne per annum operation, rejecting 30 per cent of barren rocks at the mine face would result in a $14 million per annum saving in haulage costs, and also bring significant benefits associated with reduced water use and tailing treatment. Powell and Bye (2009) estimated that the viable size of an orebody can be increased by 50 per cent if the ore cut-off grade can be dropped from 1.2 per cent to one per cent using ore pre-concentration techniques. When using HVP to enhance pre-concentration there would also be additional benefits as the broken particles would also be pre-weakened leading to substantial energy saving in the downstream grinding processes. In a different case study presented by Shi _et a_ . (2014), it was calculated that this would result in a $19 million per annum saving in the 20 Mtpa operation studied. 

Nonetheless, barriers remain for the industrial uptake of HVP technology, not least of which is the need to scale up the process and equipment and demonstrate safe and effective performance in a continuous operation. In addition, fundamental knowledge gaps, around ore composition and amenability to HVP, or more precisely which HVP operational mode is most applicable for each particular ore. 

To close these gaps and sufficiently de-risk HVP in a pilot scale continuous operation, further research is required. Options for “at scale” HVP pre-concentration application that enable continuous operation at high capacity rates need to be designed and tested. The HVP generator systems need to be improved so that they are more robust and energy efficient at large scale. Fundamental understanding needs to be developed with the objective of optimising the HVP process for each ore type presented. Investigations need to be undertaken to determine how best to incorporate HVP into a process circuit and integrate HVP with other technologies to optimise value from the entire processing chain. 

This will be the focus of the future research on the HVP technology at the SMI-JKMRC. The aim is to work with industry to address the challenges surrounding HVP comminution and deliver the next generation comminution technology to the mining industry. A collaboratively sponsored research project is planned in which multiple higher degree students will be supported. A flexible HVP testing facility sponsored by Newcrest and the SMI-JKMRC is also being developed at the SMI-JKMRC to enable alternative methods of applying HVP to be built, tested and optimised in the laboratory prior to implementation at pilot or full scale.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The amenability of a low grade copper-gold ore to HVP pre-concentration was investigated by performing HVP breakage tests on three different size fractions, utilising three different energy levels. Breakage during HVP processing was found to be selective with the grades in the finer sizes afte

r HVP breakage being higher than in the coarser sizes. The potential upgrade of copper in the ore was found to be modest after HVP treatment whereas there would be the potential to upgrade the gold assay and discard large quantity of barren rocks in the feed prior to processing without losing significant amounts of gold recovery. Preconcentration potential after HVP breakage was significantly better than that observed in the ‘as received’ ore collected from the feed conveyor at the mine site. It was also better than that observed after impact breakage in JKRBT when compared at similar energy input levels. 

The HVP 4D pre-concentration characteristic curves were produced using the data presented in this study. These describe the relationships between metal recovery, screen undersize grade, screen oversize grade, mass split and specific energy requirements, providing a convenient tool for mining companies to assess HVP feasibility by inter-relating the metallurgical performance to the energy required in the process for economic assessments. This case study shows that the HVP pre-concentration technique can split the low grade ore (0.9 ppm gold and 0.28 per cent copper in the feed size 26.5-37.5 mm) into two components – a low grade oversize material (0.3 ppm gold and 0.15 per cent copper) and a high grade undersize material (1.0 ppm gold and 0.3 per cent copper).. The mass recovery to screen undersize is 77 per cent, which requires a specific energy (spark) of 2.8 kWh/t. Under this mass split scenario, gold recovery to screen undersize is 90 per cent and copper recovery is 85 per cent.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The GPM Gold Operation has been employing an Albion Process™ plant at its Sotk (Zod) gold mine in Armenia since 2014.  Long term data from the operation is now being published for the first time.  The data presented includes concentrate throughput, as feed to the Albion Process™ plant (tonnes per day), sulphur grade in concentrate (% S), total sulphide sulphur oxidation in the Albion Process™ plant (% SOx) and gold recovery from Albion Process™ plant residues (%).  The data provides a basis for evaluation of the effectiveness of the commissioning, ramp up and operation of the Albion Process™ plant.  Notwithstanding the impact of a slower concentrator commissioning than expected, the plant demonstrates Series 1 behaviour on McNulty ramp up curves, indicating successful commissioning and fast ramp up.  Interrogation of the data and operational experience indicates that this successful operation is a result of a process that is flexible, robust and stable, one that was designed well based on solid testwork results and pilot plant trials during the study phase undertaken by Glencore Technology and Core Resources, and where the local operators were provided with appropriate training in operation of the plant. 

###### **BACKGROUND** 

###### **The GPM Gold Project** 

GeoProMining Gold LLC (GPM) owns and operates the Sotk (Zod) gold mine and Ararat processing facility in Armenia (“GPM Gold”). The open cut mine is located near the border with Azerbaijan, and gold bearing ore is transported via a state-owned rail link to the process plant at Ararat, near the Turkish border. 

Reserves at the Sotk mine (as at an August 2011 estimate) were 14.2 Mt at 4.3 g/t Au.  Indicated resources were estimated to contain 28 Mt of ore at 4.2 g/t Au, and inferred resources were estimated to contain 16 Mt at 4.2 g/t Au.  The gold-bearing mineralogy is dominated by arsenopyrite and pyrite. Gold is preferentially associated with arsenopyrite and to a lesser extent pyrite. Gold occurs as free milling and finely dispersed through arsenical sulphides and tellurides. The geology of the deposit has been discussed separately (Voigt, Hourn, Mallah and Turner 2014). 

The project has been in operation for several decades, originally mining weathered oxide ores overlaying sulphides.  GPM acquired the project in 2007 and began initially treating gabbro and low sulphide ores. Testwork performed on samples obtained from exploration drilling into the underlying sulphide zones showed gold recoveries of around 20-30 per cent when treated through the conventional carbon in leach (CIL) pro

cess. Further testwork was performed to evaluate oxidation of the sulphide material prior to cyanidation. Oxidation of arsenopyrite and pyrite before cyanidation of the resulting residue was successful, with gold recoveries lifting from 20-30 per cent to over 90 per cent. 

GPM evaluated four oxidation technologies, namely roasting, pressure oxidation (POX), biological oxidation (BiOX) and the Albion Process™, an atmospheric oxidative leaching process. An environmental-technicaleconomic evaluation was performed, with the Albion Process™ prevailing as the most suitable technology. The main driver was a lower capital cost and reduced implementation time. 

Development testwork for the project began in 2009. Four sulphide ore samples (600 kg each) from across the ore body were tested, culminating in a continuous pilot plant oxidative leaching program.  The final flowsheet consisted of milling and sulphide flotation to generate a sulphide concentrate, which was then

treated through an Albion Process™ oxidative leach plant.  Residue from the Albion Process™ plant is combined with flotation tails and fed to the existing CIL circuit. 

Nameplate design for the plant is 100,000 tpa concentrate, generating on average ~100,000 ozpa gold as dorй. The Albion Process™ plant was delivered to GPM as a lump sum technology package linked to performance guarantees by Glencore Technology.  Mechanical design was completed in December 2012. Construction of the operation was completed in April 2014, and commissioning completed in July 2014. 

###### **The Albion Process™** 

The Albion Process™ is an established atmospheric oxidation technology for treatment of refractory sulphide concentrates.  It is currently installed in six operations globally, with two Albion Process™ plants applied to the leaching of gold hosted with refractory sulphides. The chemistry of the Albion Process™ has been widely reported (Voigt, Mallah and Hourn, 2017). 

In applications for gold, the Albion Process™ consists of fine grinding of the sulphide concentrate, followed by oxidation in tanks operating at atmospheric pressure with gaseous oxygen injected at supersonic velocities to maximise oxygen mass transfer and facilitate the oxidation reactions.  Oxidised residue from the Albion Process™ is then treated with a standard cyanide leach circuit for gold recovery. 

The oxidation reaction is carried out under a mildly acidic pH (5.5), and is maintained by the addition of limestone. The reactors are auto-thermal and typically operate in the range 85-98°C. Oxygen utilisations of 80-90 per cent are typical. The Albion Process™ for gold does not solubilise any base metals and does not produce any elemental sulphur or jarosites, meaning discharge slurry does not require washing and cyanide consumption remains low in the leaching circuit. Residues typically have good filtration characteristics, and materials of cons

truction requirements are typically lower than for acidic POX or BiOX circuits.

###### **FLEXIBLE, ROBUST AND STABLE** 

A key feature of the data is the stable performance of the Albion Process™ when treating a range of throughput rates and a range of quality of feed in terms of sulphur grade and gold grade. Gold recoveries have remained consistent since commissioning and have predominantly been ab

ove design levels. 

Consistent gold recoveries above design have been maintained in spite of unexpected variability in the throughput rate to the Albion Process™ plant, and significant variability in the sulphur grade being fed to the plant.  The figures below represent graphically the consistency of the Albion Process™ plant gold recoveries against the variability of these parameters: 

Throughput variability has reduced over time as the operation matures.  Nevertheless gold recoveries were consistent early in the life of the operation, a significant advantage for the operator of the plant as it works from that early base towards better process control. 

The ability of the Albion Process™ to process variable sulphur grades at GPM is due to the auto-thermal nature of the Albion reactors. Once a minimum sulphide-sulphur throughput is met, the reactors operate in 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

the range 85-98°C.  If the plant encounters lower sulphide levels it can usually operate for several hours due to the large thermal inertia in the process and has no material impact. 

By that time, the issues causing the low sulphur grade in the concentrator have usually been resolved. If the low sulphur condition persists and temperature drops in the first few reactors, the first reactor can be partially scuttled with slurry draining to the bunded area below the thickener and recycled to the process via spillage pumps. This allows the reactors to be re-filled with higher grade material with the temperature increasing again for regular operation. The reactors at GPM are open to atmosphere, so when the sulphide feed rate increases the additional exothermic heat released by oxidation of these units immediately raises the vapour pressure of the slurry, which in turn drives a greater evaporation rate that removes the additional heat. The reactors at GPM operate near the boiling point of water. 

This contrasts with Pressure Oxidation circuits which are typically sensitive to variations in sulphur grade due to the requirement to manage heat of reaction in an autoclave. During an environmental-technical-economic evaluation phase of the project, a more stable throughput and sulphur grade was assumed as a basis for comparison of the POX and Albion Process™ options.  The Albion Process™ was selected in part for its ability to handle any unexpected variability in feed arising from the ore body or from operation of the concentrator; selection of an autoclave circuit may have resulted in significant reduction in throughput in order to manage the ore variability seen as the project has operated. 

Additionally, during project development, different ore bodies required different levels of sulphide sulphur oxidation. Selection of VPSA type oxygen plant allows turn-down of oxygen generation to match the required oxidation level and subsequent oxygen requirements for the system. Due to the lower oxidation level requiremen

t than design, the leach reactions are normally completed in Albion Leach Reactor 6, and the full 9 reactors are not required. 

###### **Oxidation capacity** 

It is also noted that to achieve and exceed the design recovery, the extent of sulphide sulphur oxidation required has varied and typically is around 55 per cent, well below the design value of 76 per cent.  The Albion Process™ plant generally allows more control of oxidation levels than in an autoclave circuit. There is a reduction in oxygen operating costs associated with lower oxygen requirements. 

The principal duty of the Albion Process™ plant is the oxidation of sulphur, to release gold finely disseminated in the sulphide matrix for recovery in the downstream cyanide leach circuit.  The oxidation capacity of the Albion Process™ plant is constrained either by the residence time in the circuit, or by the available oxygen, and was a major consideration in the design and engineering of the plant during the design phase. The nominal and design oxidising capacities are 1.56 and 1.80 tonnes sulphide sulphur per hour respectively assuming an 80 per cent oxygen utilisation. 

The design for the GPM Albion Process™ plant is to achieve 76 per cent sulphide sulphur oxidation, with a nominal and design sulphur oxidation of 37.6 and 43.2 tonnes oxidised per day. The design oxygen consumption was 336 kg / t concentrate assuming 80 per cent utilisation.  Actual consumptions are around 215 kg / t concentrate based on plant experience due to higher than design oxygen utilisation and lower oxidation rates (Voigt, Hourn, Mallah and Turner, 2015). The reported plant data indicates the oxidation extent has been controlled and adjusted in order to maintain gold recoveries, demonstrating the flexibility of the process. 

Periods of oxidation that exceeded the design maximum were demonstrated in 2016 and 2017.  The spare oxidation capacity evident in the Albion Process™ plant is demonstration of the contingency applied in design, and is to the superior performance of the HyperSparge<sup>TM</sup> supersonic gas injection lance. Supersonic gas injection maximises the shear imparted to the slurry resulting in the resistance to gas to liquid oxygen mass transfer being reduced and in turn maximising oxygen mass transfer rate. The actual plant oxygen utilisation was found to be around 90 per cent or higher based on plant surveys and has been reported by Voigt, Mallah and Hourn (2017). 

###### **DESIGNED RIGHT – THE FIRST TIME** 

A pillar of fast ramp up and achievement of design throughput and recovery is a successful design process from the laboratory to the full-scale production plant. The GPM plant was designed and supplied by Glencore Technology based on results from batch and continuous testwork campaigns conducted as part of the BFS managed by Core Resources during 2011 and 2012. The purpose of the testwork was to obtain the following key design parameters which culminated in the mass and energy balance

and process design criteria: 

- optimise the grind size to minimise the IsaMill™ energy input,

- IsaMill™ Signature Plot to determine the grind energy required to achieve a certain particle size in order to size the IsaMill™ (The design specific energy to achieve 80 per cent passing 10µm was 59.0 kWh/t and recent plant data shows 59.7 kWh/t although not always required to run at 10µm), 

- sulfide oxidation against gold recovery to optimise gold recovery and minimise oxidation requirements, 

- measurement of slurry oxygen up-take rate under various conditions for designing the oxygen mass transfer system, 

- rheological measurements for sizing of the pumps, 

- determine the sensitivity of sulphide leach kinetics to key parameters such as operating temperature and slurry density, 

- dettling data for sizing of the thickener, and 

- test the process performance against samples that represent potential variance in the feed material during the life of the plant. 

Testwork was structured around defining metallurgical performance of ore types and composites based on the life of mine schedule. During the testwork it was found that different ore types gave a different flotation response and required different levels of oxidation to achieve greater than 90 per cent gold recovery in cyanidation. 

The design approach was to select a conservative sulphide sulphur oxidation target of 76 per cent to ensure that different combinations of ore types could be treated and still achieve the design target of greater than 90 per cent gold recovery in the CIL. The oxidation target largely drove the tank volume required and the oxygen plant size. Since oxygen is recognised as a large portion of the operating costs, two Vacuum Pressure Swing Adsorption (VPSA) type oxygen plants were selected for oxygen generating duty to allow oxygen output to be turned down when not required for the process and save on operating costs (as illustrated in Figure 6). VPSA technology was selected over PSA due to the lower power cost per unit of oxygen produced. The oxygen purity generated is 93 v/v %. 

The important part of oxidation design is oxygen mass transfer to the slurry system. The scale up of oxygen mass transfer process is critical to the process success and is well understood and proven through the use of the HyperSparge™ supersonic gas injection technology (Voigt, 2017). A conservative oxygen utilisation was assumed at 80 per cent although plant measurements have shown this to be closer to 90 per cent (Voigt, 2015). 

It can be observed from Figures 2 to 6 that there are no large drops in production rate over a monthly period. This stability of the production is a result of a well-designed plant.  Specific factors which have contributed to high-availability of the plant include: 

1. No major works or process modifications were required following commissioning, with most activity focussed

on bringing the grinding and flotation concentrator up to full production; 

2. The concentrator has two lines of operation and one line can be kept going while a mill re-line occurs; The Albion Process™ has been designed to avoid major downtime, through: 

   - the surge capacity around the IsaMill,™ 

   - the ability to remove, inspect and insert HyperSparge™ without stopping the process or emptying a leaching tank, 

   - the capability to by-pass the leaching section, and 

   - the process comprises well known and understood equipment (tanks, pumps, thickeners, agitators). 

As a result of this design, the process operates with very high availability (more than 95 per cent) and stable throughputs. 

###### **TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER** 

The Albion Process™ is an established technology but had not been previously deployed into Armenia or the wider CIS. This meant that training of operations and maintenance personnel was required to ensure safe and timely ramp up of the process. Training was performed in a class room environment during the final stages of construction and then on the plant during pre-commissioning checks and commissioning. Training was performed by Glencore Technology experts as well as representatives from sub-suppliers. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The training performed prior to commissioning meant that Glencore Technology (GT) was positioned to take the role as commissioning manager with minimal site presence (three personnel) while GPM personnel operated the plant. This ensured that a high level of ownership of the plant process management was taken on by the project owner at the very beginning of the project. 

Following commissioning and ramp up, bi-annual visits from Core Resources and Glencore Technology personnel ensured that regular communication on technical issues occurred. 

As a testament to the technology transfer process and ownership of the process, GPM have arrived at a number of process modifications and improvements: 

###### 1. By-passing the thickener 

The Albion Process™ leach residue is directed to a thickener to increase the solids content from 30-42 per cent suitable for feeding to the CIL process. Since the Albion Process™ residue is mixed with flotation tailings and sent to CIL, the Albion Process™ thickener has been by-passed and CIL feed density specification met by slightly increasing the flotation tailings thickener underflow density. 

###### 2. Reduced reagents and Closed overflow lines on tanks 

The Albion Process™ leach reactor design comprises inter-connecting launders for slurry transfer and each tank is fitted with an overflow arrangement that works with a weir to keep the head space sealed so only gases exit the ventilation stack. In the event of high carbonates in the feed or excessive flotation reagent accumulation in the process water, the tanks can overflow due to excessive foam production which is designed to be transported betwe

en tanks through the launders but often finds the path of least resistance through the reactor overflow pipes. Although this material is recovered back to the process with the bund and spillage system, it sometimes results in the oxygen flowrate to be reduced in the offending reactor and then increased in another causing gas surging and further foaming issues. The recycle of the spillage material also causes process surges. 

Site personnel undertook an improvement project to gradually reduce flotation chemicals (mainly frother) and to close up the overflow weirs. Froth generation has been significantly reduced through reduced reagent additions in the concentrator. The overflow weirs were also welded shut which directs all foam through the interconnecting tank launders. These two measures have eliminated froth overflow. 

###### 3. Control system 

The Albion Process™ was supplied with a distributed control system (DCS) with the plant operated from a centralised control room. The existing milling and CIL plant was controlled with minimal instrumentation and field control panels so transition to a centralised control system was a new concept. During the implementation of the Albion Process™ the milling and flotation plants were integrated into the DCS for fully centralised control from ore feeding to Albion Process™ discharge. 

###### 4. Tellurides 

The presence of gold hosted in tellurides was identified during the initial testwork phases and based on drilling would be encountered after a few years of mining primary sulphides. As such, GT designed the Albion Process™ plant to be able to raise the pH to around 9.0 in the last leach reactor allowing oxidation to occur at elevated pH with the aim of oxidising and liberating gold hosted in tellurides. This had the added benefit of conditioning before the CIL which is operated around 10.5. Since the Albion Process™ runs around pH 5.5 this is a simple process transition to make. The lime ring main from the CIL was extended to Albion Process™ leach reactor 9 allowing elevated pH operation and recovery of gold and silver from tellurides. Tellurides have been observed in the feed concentrate ranging from 80 ppm to 1200 ppm. Initially the plant suffered notable reductions in gold recoveries (around 2 to 3 per cent) and was mitigated through the implementation of the elevated pH in the last leach reactor.

###### _R G Coleman_<sup>_1_</sup> _and B Wong_<sup>_2_</sup>

###### **ABSTRACT** 

In flotation, the selection of the size, number and type of cell for a particular duty depends on two important factors. Firstly, the required flotation residence time and secondly, the physical constraints of how much concentrate can be recovered for a given froth surface area and concentrate lip length. 

The residence time is influenced by ore type and characteristics such as liberation, kinetics and reagent dosage. The amount of concentrate that can be recovered for a given froth surface area and lip length depends on ore type and other characteristics such as particle size, specific gravity and mineral grade. 

Residence time is determined through a combination of laboratory-scale test work and design scale-up factors. However the critical froth transport parameters such as froth carry rate and froth lip loading cannot be determined in a laboratory. This is because the froth is scraped during a laboratory flotation test and thus does not exhibit natural

behaviour, and it is not possible to scale-up froth transport distance or air rate. These values are generally compared via calculation to rule-of-thumb maximum values to establish if these values will be exceeded by the flotation cell selection. 

This paper first reviews these critical froth transport parameters and then discusses actual parameter values across diverse operating sites, with varying cell duties, cell sizes and types, orebodies and particle sizes. These values are compared against the industry rule-of-thumb to test the applicability of the rule-of-thumb to actual performance. Options are also presented for adjusting these parameters in operating flotation cells. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The selection of the size, number and type of flotation cell for a particular duty depends on two important factors. Firstly, the required flotation residence time and secondly, the physical constraints of how much concentrate can be recovered for a given froth surface area and concentrate lip length. The residence time is influenced by ore type and characteristics such as liberation, kinetics and reagent dosage. Looking at the amount of concentrate that can be recovered for a given froth surface area and lip length, it also depends on ore type and other characteristics such as particle size, specific gravity and mineral grade. 

Residence time is determined through a combination of laboratory-scale test work and design scale-up factors. However the amount of concentrate that can be recovered for a given froth surface area and concentrate lip length cannot be determined in a laboratory. This is because the froth is scraped during a laboratory flotation test and thus does not exhibit natural behaviour, and it is not possible to scale-up froth transport distance. These values are generally compared via calculation to rule-of-thumb maximum values to establish if these values will be exceeded by the flotation cell selection. 

So which of these parameters is most important for cell selection? If the required residence time is achieved with a certain cell selection but the froth transport parameters are exceeded, what are the options? One option would be to increase the number of flotation cells to increase the froth surface area or concentrate lip length. This, however, requires not only significant additional capital outlay, but also increased footprint and operating costs. The other option would be to customise the launder configuration to provide a larger froth surface area or lip length, without increasing the number of cells. 

This paper discusses actual parameter values across a range of operating sites. These values are compared against industry rule-of-thumb to test the applicability of the rule-of-thumb to actual performance. The options for adjusting these parameters in operating flotation cells are also discussed in more detail.

###### **FROTH ZONE** 

#

##### **Froth transport parameters** 

There are two main parameters that are currently used to describe the transport of the froth to the concentrate launder: froth carry rate and lip loading. 

The froth carry rate is defined as the amount of concentrate (tonne) transported by the froth over a specific surface area (m<sup>2</sup> ) in a given time frame (hours), providing units of t/m<sup>2</sup> h. Design rules-of-thumb for froth carry rates for different froth flotation duties were developed over fifteen years ago based on experience together with metallurgical surveying of flotation operations (Okely, 2004). These ‘rules-of-thumb,’ as shown in Table 1 (Murphy and Heath, 2013), are still being used today for the design and selection of flotation cells. 

The values given in Table 1 refer to whole banks of flotation cells. Individual cells in the bank may have higher or lower values. Particle size and mineral type will also affect these design values. Heath and Runge (in press) provide an extensive review of the froth phase and state that the values given in Table 1 are representative of typical base metal sulfide operations with a feed particle size P80 greater than 80 microns. For non-sulfide minerals much higher froth carry rates have been reported, for example in an iron ore reverse flotation application, the froth carry rate varied from 10 – 40 t/m<sup>2</sup> h (Miettinen _et al_ , 2013). The froth carry rate limits, both high and low, for a given duty, are likely a function of particle concentration, particle size distribution and particle specific gravity. Although some researchers have attempted to develop a first principal prediction of these limits, accurately predicting this parameter is still not possible. 

The second froth transport parameter is lip loading. This is defined as the mass of solids passing over the launder lip per hour per unit length, and is expressed in units of t/mh. When considering if a given flotation cell froth surface area is suitable, it is useful to think in terms of the overall “froth handling strategy”. After the froth carry rate has been confirmed in the correct range, the lip loading should be calculated and the rule-of-thumb is to keep this at less than 1.5 t/mh (Murphy and Heath, 2013). 

Froth carry rate and lip loading are important parameters to ensure there are not too much or too little solids in the froth phase. According to Morar, Bradshaw and Harris (2014), both of these conditions have a negative effect on either the froth stability or mobility and hence flotation cell performance. With insufficient solid particles in the froth phase the froth stability is significantly reduced and the froth is brittle and breaks down readily. This is often seen in the scavenger cells where very little mass is floating. Heath and Runge (in press) note that when there are too many solids in the froth, the froth becomes immobile, and the weight of the solids can overcome the carrying capacity of the froth lea

ding to froth collapse. This can sometimes be seen at the beginning of a rougher bank if the flotation kinetics are fast and there are a high number of particles trying to float, or also in cleaner and recleaner duties. Both of these situations results in a significant increase in particle drop back to the slurry phase, and poor transport of the mineral particles to the launder lip. This reduces the overall froth recovery and ultimately the overall flotation cell performance. 

Due to the distributions of floatability rates in the ore it is common for the fast-floating particles, which are typically the majority of the floatable mineral, to be recovered in the first few cells. In a bank of six cells the first two cells may recover 60-80 per cent of the valuable mineral from the entire bank, whereas the last four cells would recover the final 10-20 per cent. The implications of this recovery distribution can often lead to problems with the froth carry rate and lip loading in a full-scale plant. If a flotation circuit was designed with all six cells having the same froth surface area and lip length, by calculating the average froth transport parameters over all cells, using the example above the first two cells could be overloaded and the last few cells under loaded. Both scenarios would result in lower than expected flotation cell performance. The best solution is to tailor the design of the froth zone for each cell based on the expected mass recovery using detailed and robust laboratory or pilot test data. 

In cases where the feed grade has changed significantly since the original process design was performed, having the froth transport parameters outside of the ideal range will also cause lower performance. For example if the feed grade is 50 per cent lower than when the flotation circuit was designed, it can be expected that the mass recovery would also decrease by a similar amount. This would result in lower froth transport rates which could negatively affect froth stability and recovery.

Froth carry rates and lip loadings from actual flotation circuits are now evaluated using measured data provided by JKTech. JKTech is the technology transfer entity of The University of Queensland’s Sustainable Minerals Institute (SMI) and has been at the forefront of delivering research based technology to the global mining industry for over 25 years. ers drill and blasting, comminution and flotation data. The data is sourced from JKTech’s own global client base, from previous involvement in plant surveys, test work, consulting, simulation and process modelling.

###### **Comparison to industry rules-of-thumb** 

A comparison to the industry rules-of-thumb for froth carry rate can be made from Figure 1. The median froth carry rate for the roughers was 0.4 t/m<sup>2</sup> h and ranged between 0.01 and 4.1 t/m<sup>2</sup> h with the majority of the data less than 0.5 t/m<sup>2</sup> h. This is lower than the typical design range of 0.8 to 1.5 t/m<sup>2</sup> h. This indicates that either the rules-of-thumb are too conservative now for the lower grade ores currently being processed around the world and should be revised, or that the froth surface areas of currently installed flotation cells are too large in relation to the mass of concentrate being recovered. As a number of the froth carry rates are greater than 1.5 t/m<sup>2</sup> h, 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

which are likely to be the first cells in the bank, this suggests that operating at these higher rates is physically achievable and are not mechanically design limited. As the

majority of the data is lower than the typical design range it is therefore proposed that current rougher flotation cells have too much froth surface area for the mass of concentrate being recovered. 

The median froth carry rate for the scavengers was 0.2 t/m<sup>2</sup> h and ranged between 0.01 and 2.0 t/m<sup>2</sup> h with the majority of the data less than 0.4 t/m<sup>2</sup> h. This is below or on the low level of the typical design range of 0.3 to 0.8 t/m<sup>2</sup> h. As with the roughers it is proposed that current scavenger flotation cells have too much froth surface area for the mass of concentrate being recovered. 

The median froth carry rate for the cleaners was 0.5 t/m<sup>2</sup> h and ranged between 0.01 and 4.3 t/m<sup>2</sup> h with the majority of the data less than 1.0 t/m<sup>2</sup> h. This is lower than the typical design range of 1.0 to 2.0 t/m<sup>2</sup> h. The recleaner median froth carry rate was 0.9 t/m<sup>2</sup> h and ranged between 0.1 and 3.8 t/m<sup>2</sup> h, with more data points within the typical design range. The lower froth carry rates in the cleaners again suggests that the froth surface area in the majority of these cells is too large for the mass of concentrate being recovered. 

A comparison to the industry rule-of-thumb for lip loading can be made from Figures 2, 4, 6 and 8. The median of all lip loading measurements was 0.2 t/mh with none of the median values across cell duty, cell size, commodity or particle size greater than 1.0 t/mh. Lip loadings greater than 1.5 t/mh have been measured indicating that operating at these higher rates is physically achievable, and similar to the froth surface area, it is proposed that current flotation cells have too much lip length for the mass of concentrate being recovered. 

###### **OPTIMISATION OF FROTH PARAMETERS** 

###### **Greenfield projects** 

During the design phase of a project the flotation cell launder type and/or cell froth crowding configuration can be adjusted to achieve the best design for the process conditions. Figure 10 shows the different launder design options for Outotec TankCells (Heath and Runge, in press). 

The flotation cells shown in Figure 10 all have the same tank and central froth crowder diameter. The different launder configurations do not significantly affect the tank volume or flotation residence time. The launder designs depicted represent some of the most commonly available launder configurations used in flotation cells, and from left to right the froth area decreases significantly due to the launder(s) placement and also the tank shape providing froth crowding. 

Therefore, the different designs for froth surface area and lip length can be used as a way to optimise the flotation cell design for particular duties in a plant based on the expected froth carry rates and lip loadings (eg, roughing, scavenging and cleaning). From the down-the-bank results it is also clear that designing the froth launders using average froth

parameters across a bank (equivalent to the same froth launder design for all cells in a bank) will not result in optimal performance. In the past this uniformity of design has been chosen by project owners and engineering companies to reduce capital costs, however design engineers should now instead tailor the launder design to suit the different cells in a bank. A better understanding of the flotation kinetics and expected mass pulls down a bank will be required in order to do this and laboratory and pilot scale test work should focus on understanding this aspect better. 

Figure 10 – Outotec flotation cell launder configurations (L to R: External Launder, Internal Launder, Double Internal Launder, Donut Launder). 

###### **Brownfield projects** 

For brownfield projects it is possible to retrofit additional launders and froth crowding to the flotation cells in order to reduce the froth surface area and increase the froth carry rate. In most cases it is possible to double the froth carry rate and significantly increase the grade, especially in scavenger duties. Another positive aspect when retrofitting froth crowding or additional froth launders is this usually results in a reduced average froth transport distance. Froth transport distance is the distance that a particle may have to travel from the froth surface to the closest launder lip, and is heavily influenced by the selected launder configuration. This means that the average residence time of a particle in the froth and the probability of particle detachment and drop- 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

back to the slurry phase will likely be reduced. This can be especially important in improving the recovery of poorly liberated coarse particles in a scavenger circuit. 

Another option to control the froth carry rate is to use an increasing superficial gas velocity profile down the bank, with lower air rates in the cells at the head of a bank. Selectivity and recovery have both been observed to increase in a flotation bank with an increasing gas rate profile to that achieved when the same gas rate was used in all cells (Cooper _et al_ , 2004). Down-the-bank staged addition of reagents can also be used to manage the distribution concentrate mass pull. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

This paper has reviewed the standard design range and actual operating values for the critical froth transport parameters currently used in industry. The operating values were measured across different cell duties, cell sizes and types, orebodies and particle sizes, with data taken from the JKTech database of flotation cells. The majority of the froth carry rates and lip loadings were found to be lower than the typical design rules-of-thumb, which indicates that either the rules-of-thumb are too conservative now for the lower grade ores currently being processed around the world and should be revised, or that the froth surface areas and lip lengths of currently install

ed flotation cells are too large in relation to the mass of concentrate being recovered. Based on the actual measurement of these parameters at levels higher than the rules-of-thumb, it was proposed that it is physically possible to achieve these higher values and that the froth surface areas and lip lengths are too large for the given concentrate mass flows. By reducing the froth surface and lip length it may then be possible to reduce the residence time scale-up factor between laboratory and full-scale as higher concentrate flows could be achieved using fewer flotation cells. 

This is further highlighted by the sharp decrease in froth carry rates down various banks of measured flotation cells, with the first two cells typically having more than double the froth carry rate compared to the subsequent cells. All of the cells are either higher or lower than the average froth carry rate for each bank, which is a number commonly used during the design process. The shows that designing the froth launders using average froth parameters across a bank, which is equivalent to the same froth launder design for all cells in a bank, will not result in optimal performance and instead the launder design should be tailored to suit the different cells down a bank, with the last cells in the bank having a smaller froth surface area and shorter lip length. For brownfield projects launders and froth crowding can be retrofitted to the flotation cells in order to reduce the froth surface area and increase the froth carry rate.
