###### **ABSTRACT** 

A recent survey of mineral processors undertaken as part of the International Mineral Processing Council (IMPC) Education Commission identified mineralogy as one of the key skills required for mineral processors (the other key areas being comminution, flotation, physical separation, sampling and extractive metallurgy). Past experience in a number of operations has shown what can be achieved when the data outputs from mineralogical tools are coupled with people with the right skills who can transform the data into actionable information.  This paper reviews what has been done successfully in plant operations over a period of more than four decades and gives examples of a range of applications with both long and short-term objectives. The examples demonstrate the usefulness of mineralogical data – both basic and complex – in optimising mineral processing operations, whether the data are applied in a simple analysis or in more complex modelling. Similarly, the examples show the range of options available for operations to access the mineralogy information they need – through in-house experts and equipment based in centralised technology centres, through on-site equipment and experts or through external laboratories and consultants. 

The examples from industry highlight the huge potential benefit of including mineralogy as an integral part of operational best practice and raise the question of why more operations do not utilise what should be readily available data. Successful application of mineralogical data requires skilled people to generate relevant data of the required quality, together with skilled people to interpret the data (this may be the same person). And, as in any project, corporate recognition of the value of this approach to best practice is required to ensure continuing support. With fewer university courses providing courses in process mineralogy to undergraduate mineral processing engineers and chemical engineers, there is an increasing lack of knowledge about what mineralogical information is needed, how to get the required data and, equally importantly, how to turn the data into useful information. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

As eloquently stated by Schouwstra and Smit (2011 _) “Mineralogy in the mining industry is not just about identifying minerals – it is the application of the knowledge of the behaviour of minerals and mineral phases during processing.”_

The collection of mineralogical data, whilst critical, is not enough. For best practice to be realised the data must be interpreted by those with the requisite skills and knowledge to transform the data into useful information.  The IMPC Education Commission recently released a roadmap for mineral processing education (Drinkwater, 2017).  Mineralogy and liberation are included as priority content in mineral processing education to ensure that graduates receive good quality education.  Acquiring the basic knowledge is only the first step, with real expertise being developed through the application of the knowledge i.e. putting theory into practice. 

There are numerous examples and a long history of what constitutes good practice.  The tools to collect data have been available for many years, indeed the examination of rocks and minerals using a microscope was pioneered in the 1850s (Sorby, 1858).  The development and maturation of automated mineralogical analysis systems has made this type of data collection faster and allowed for better statistics.  The collection of long term trending data on the liberation characteristics of minerals in the Mt Isa Pb-Zn circuit started in 1982, before automated systems were available and continued through the transition to data collection from automated systems.  The liberation data was used in conjunction with other available data to analyse mineral recovery on a size by liberation basis which was used to both monitor plant performance and enable decision making on plant modification (Johnson, 2016). 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

In the Mt Isa example, automated mineralogical data was provided by an external supplier and in recent years there have been published accounts of the successes that can be achieved by having the collection of automated mineralogical data close to (as in the case of Kennecott, McDonald et al, 2011) or physically onsite (as with the Kansanshi (Kalichini et al, 2017) and Northparkes (Jones and Morgan, 2016) examples). The key feature of these examples is that the availability of the data in close to real time provided quantitative evidence for understanding the mineralogical contribution to plant performance. 

At Kennecott this enabled the debunking of previously held beliefs based on anecdotal evidence and quantified the copper loss and loss distribution enabling development of best operating practice philosophies for particular feed types.  At Kansanshi, the extent of ore variability and its implications for recovery were revealed.  Northparkes found numerous advantages to having access to a site-based system to provide information for: 

- determining the nature of recoverable and non-recoverable copper, 

- the nature of impurities in the concentrate, mining and grade control, and 

- plant changes and upgrades and life of mine and exploration projects. 

A key feature of the success of all these examples is the presence of exper

ts (either in-house or external) who understood which samples to collect, what data to collect, how to collect it and perhaps most importantly, report it in a meaningful way to fully realise the benefits.  The value of these benefits and the contribution from automated mineralogy can be difficult to quantify (Gu, Schouwstra and Rule, 2014) and the tangible costs associated with data collection are often used as a justification not to collect the data.  The most significant benefit of having access to this information is in the minimisation of risk through better decision making 

In this paper tangible examples are provided to demonstrate the usefulness of mineralogical data in basic and more challenging contexts and include some of the basic data checks and typical data outputs that can be used to drive operational best practice. 

###### **USING MINERAL DATA IN MINERAL PROCESSING – THE BASICS** 

One of the well-known uses of mineralogical data comes from the lead-zinc concentrator at Mt Isa (Johnson 2016). The graph of sphalerite liberation and zinc recovery versus time shown in Figure 1 is one of the many standard plots the metallurgists on site produced to track the process efficiency over an extended period of time. 

In this case monthly composites of daily shift samples were analysed to assess their mineralogy and liberation and to track the process performance over time. The monthly metal balance formed the basis for the analysis, with mineral data overlaying the elemental balance for lead and zinc. The data shown in Figure 1 illustrate several things about this type of data. 

Note that the data collected each month provide a baseline of the mineralogy and liberation characteristics of the feed to the plant and how the liberated and locked minerals are recovered to the final product streams. As Young _et al_ (1997) showed, these data were valuable to the business in identifying the gradual decrease in sphalerite liberation and providing the evidence needed to install more grinding capacity to cope with the change in ore over time.

Figure 1 – Mineralogical data showing trends in sphalerite liberation over time at Mt Isa Mines Lead/Zinc Concentrator (from Johnson, 2016). 

The value of having baseline data to quantify what is “normal” operation in a concentrator is often only realised when problems occur – concentrate grade target cannot be achieved or recovery drops below accepted values. 

Figure 2 illustrates how recovery in a concentrator can decrease significantly with no reason apparent in the standard control data collected by the metallurgists. In this example the head grade is unchanged, the feed rate has not increased, and the concentrate grade is not significantly lower, but recovery has changed significantly. To develop a strategy to get recovery back to an acceptable level, metallurgists need to understand the cause of the problem. In this ca

se routine mineralogical analysis had been done on monthly composite samples and comparison with the baseline data showed that the mineralogy of the ore had changed. 

The lower recovery was caused by more of the copper being present as oxide minerals rather than the sulphide minerals which the flotation circuit was set up to recover. This knowledge allows metallurgists to develop a strategy to deal with the problem, depending on the likely duration of the change in mineralogy. If this material is only infrequently campaigned through the circuit, this data can be used to set the expectation for metallurgical performance by defining new operating targets based on how much copper is recoverable in the existing circuit. An alternative approach might be to change the flotation reagents to target oxide minerals.  Without the baseline data the cause of the problem may not have been identified so easily.

###### **What data are useful in understanding and optimising concentrator performance?** 

Two of the key questions for metallurgists when examining process performance in the concentrator are: 

- What causes losses to the tail? 

- What causes low grade in the concentrate? 

The information which underpins the analysis to answer these questions comes from periodic plant data, which are typically monthly composites of daily shift data but could also be weekly or daily data. The concentrator metal balance for the month provides mass flow data of key elements in the feed, final concentrate(s) and tailings. 

Composite samples of the feed and product streams are sized and the size fractions assayed to give a detailed picture of how the circuit is performing on a size by assay basis, for example elemental recovery by size data. 

While the detailed size and assay data are useful in assessing to some degree what is causing losses in the tailings and dilution in the concentrate there are some key pieces of information that cannot be obtained from the size by assay data in their raw form. Examples of these include calculating how much of the dilution of concentrate grade is due to pyrite (since the Fe assay should not be converted directly to pyrite) and whether the copper losses in the coarser size fractions in the tailings are due to poor liberation or poor recovery of low grade composite particles. Information about pyrite obviously requires mineral data, obtained either by estimating mineralogy from elemental composition or by measuring the mineralogy directly, while information about the liberation state of the target mineral requires micro-scale measurement of the composition of the particles in the tailings stream. If the circuit being analysed does not include any size reduction (secondary grinding or regrinding) then it would be possible to apply a data smoothing method (Lamberg and Vianna, 2007) to the mineral by size data or alternatively to sum the data for the product streams to create a recalculated feed stream which can be used to calculate recoveries. Note that if, as is the case in many operations, the circuit includes a regrind section then the sum of the product streams will not equal the feed stream in terms of size distribution or mineral distribution by size and in this instance summing the data for the product streams to create a recalculated feed stream is the solution to allow recoveries to be calculated. The differences between the mass and mineral distributions by size in the measured feed and the recalculated feed represent the effect on these distributions of the grinding stages within the circuit. The data required to answer key questions are typically obtained through a combination of in-house analyses and specialised analyses from external providers of mineralogy services, and these are discussed in the following sections. ###### **What data are readily available on site?** ###### _Elemental assay data and element-to-mineral conversion_ In most

mineral processing operations the processes are described in terms of the elements that are the target metal produced at the end of the process chain. For example, operations are described as coppergold or zinc-lead. One of the reasons for this is that elemental assays are the most readily available data measured in day-to-day operations of concentrators, with assays being used to track process performance in both recovery and grade. However, assays do not provide the whole picture about how an ore will behave in a separation process. Anyone who has pyrite or pyrrhotite in their ore will understand the importance of information about how much of the iron in the plant feed is present in these iron sulphide minerals which may end up diluting their concentrate. At the most basic level this type of information can be obtained by converting the elemental proportions to mineral proportions – a technique called element to mineral conversion. 

Metallurgists have used the element to mineral conversion methods described by Johnson (2016) and Whiten (2007) for many years. It is important to note that in this method the estimates of mineral proportions from elemental assays are based on prior knowledge of the mineralogy of the ore. Geologists also use

elemental data to estimate mineralogy but usually their interest is in the overall mineralogy of the rock while metallurgists are typically focussed only on the minerals of economic interest and minerals which affect their processing, with all other minerals being lumped into the catch-all term of ‘non-sulphide gangue.’ 

Where the mineral composition of an ore is relatively simple and not subject to variation in how the elements of interest are deported, the elemental data can provide useful estimates of the mineralogy. Where the target element is present in a number of minerals it may be possible to use specialised assay techniques to assist in differentiation. For example sequential copper assays used in a diagnostic leach are often used to identify copper deportment in copper porphyry ores, although research has shown the importance of using measured mineralogy to verify the estimates obtained from diagnostic leach methods (Benvie, Chapman, Robinson and Kuhar, 2013).

Taggart’s Handbook of Mineral Dressing (1927), the mineral processor’s handbook of the early 20th century, has a section on microscopy which includes the statement “ _utility of the microscope in an ore dressing laboratory is tremendous: no laboratory that makes any pretence to thorough ore testing or process research can get along without three or four types._ ” 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 A great deal of process mineralogy work has been done by highly skilled mineralogists using optical microscopes including among others (in Australia) Henley (1983), Knights (1983) and McArthur (1996). The optical microscope can be used to provide qualitative data such as descriptions of texture and quantitative data such as point counting to obtain modal mineralogy and estimates of how minerals are liberated or locked (Jones 1987). An example of the industrial application of the point count data can be seen in Figure 1 where the liberation data prior to approximately 1990 were measured by point counting using an optical microscope. Today, the number of skilled optical mineralogists working in or for the minerals industry is much lower than in the past and data from automated SEM-based systems, which can work 24 hours/day, 7 days/week are becoming more common. ###### _Automated mineralogy systems_

After the initial development of automated mineralogy systems in the 1970s, it took many years for these systems to achieve wide usage in the mining industry. However, since the 1990s the number of systems installed by commercial providers and mining companies has risen steadily, including the location of systems on or near operating sites as at Kennecott (McDonald _et al_ , 2011) or Kansanshi (Kalichini _et al_ , 2017) and Northparkes (Jones and Morgan, 2016). The automated operation of these systems allows large numbers of particles to be measured, providing more accurate descriptions of the particle characteristics than can be achieved by optical microscopy. The automation of mineralogical analyses is particularly useful for precious metals such as platinum group minerals and native gold ores where the ability to search many thousands of particles to find the small number of precious metal grains in a sample with grain sizes of 1 µm and grades as low as 0.1 ppm makes these systems useful tools. Figure 4 – Examples of images from automated systems which highlight different mineral textures. ###### **BEYOND THE BASICS – SPECIAL TECHNIQUES FOR SPECIAL PROBLEMS** As the mining industry develops the more complex mineral deposits around the world, metallurgists have needed to develop novel solutions to solve the technical challenges that these complex ores throw up. Since mineralogical analysis is applied at various stages during the development phase the specialists working in this field have also had to deploy novel tools and techniques to characterise these complex ores. In each case the mineralogy team will draw on the tools required to solve the specific problem(s) encountered in the ore being investigated so there is no single protocol to follow for more complex analyses. This section provides two examples of specialised techniques developed to measure the characteristics of precious metal ores that are needed for process development and optimisation. ###### **Quantifying gold deportment in complex gold ores** With mining companies increasingly processing complex gold deposits there has been a clear need for metallurgists to be able to quantify how the gold is carried in the ore in order to be able to design an appropriate process flow sheet to recover the gold economically. The quantification of gold

deportment is challenging due to the low Au grade in gold ores but this problem becomes even greater in double refractory ores such as those from the Carlin Trend in Nevada, USA where the gold is present as “invisible” gold in arsenian pyrite and in iron oxides and carbonaceous matter in the ore. No single mineralogical tool or technique can provide all of the data needed to understand gold deportment in these ores and so a range of tools must be deployed in a systematic way to provide the information that metallurgists need to design and operate circuits to treat these ores.  Barrick Gold Corporation has worked with mineralogy service providers 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

to develop such a systematic approach (Chattopadhyay and Gorain 2014) which is considerably more complex than the liberation analysis required in base metal concentrators.  Other providers have also presented similar structured approaches to quantifying gold deportment (Chryssoulis and Cabri 1990; Zhou and Cabri, 2004). 

The multi-step nature of the approach can be seen in Figure 5 which shows the flow sheet for the analytical approach used by Barrick. The techniques used to quantify the gold deportment include common techniques such as size analysis, density separation, fire assay, optical mineralogy and MLA/QemScan analyses. The more specialised techniques include dynamic secondary ion mass spectrometry (Dynamic-SIMS), Raman spectroscopy and time of flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS). Some examples of the data outputs from the various analyses are shown in Figure 6 and the suite of quantitative data which is delivered to metallurgists on completion of the analyses is summarised in Table 4. 

Barrick has applied this method to mass balance gold across flotation and leaching circuits which include some very low grade streams (down to 0,04 g/t Au) and to use this information to analyse process performance. One application identified the main source of gold losses in flotation tailings (grade 0.19 g/t Au) to be Fe oxides which accounted for 22 per cent of total gold lost in the rougher tails, an unusual source of loss in flotation stream samples (Chattopadhyay _et al_ 2016). In CIL residue (grade 1.9 g/t Au) carbonaceous matter, fine inclusions of pyrite and arsenian pyrite and preg-robbed surface gold accounted for unusually high gold losses, which is not typical for many gold leaching operations. The information obtained has helped Barrick to identify metallurgical strategies to improve recovery to an acceptable level and the value of this information to the company in terms of production of gold is obviously much greater than the cost of the multiple analyses used to obtain it.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The examples described in this paper have been used to highlight the operational advantages of having access to mineralogical data.  They demonstrate the advantages of long-term trending data for tracking performance and justifying improvements and the benefits that can be realised from being able to access this data in a useful time-frame.  Hand in hand with data generation are the people with the knowledge and skills to transform the data into information.  At a basic level this information can be applied to benchmark typical operation and provide a baseline for diagnosis when things go wrong.  Other commonly used indicators of flotation performance such as the nature of losses to tails and what is diluting the concentrate can be interpreted much more richly in a mineral and liberation-based context.  Applications in precious metals clearly demonstrate the effort that is required to properly characterise the deportment of key elements and the application of these techniques to solve processing problems indicates the value of the quantitative information they provide. Although a number of major mining companies routinely use mineralogical data, very few have published information about how they use the data or the value (in dollar terms) of the data to their business. Unfortunately, this lack of information can make it difficult for companies to weigh the visible cost of mineralogical analysis against the value of understanding the minerals in their ore and process streams.

###### How to find the optimum air rate for flotation cells 

###### _K Hadler_<sup>_1_</sup> _and J J Cilliers_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. Lecturer, Imperial College London SW7 2AZ, UK. Email: k.hadler@imperial.ac.uk 2. Professor, Imperial College London SW7 2AZ, UK. Email: j.j.cilliers@imperial.ac.uk 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Air is fundamental to flotation; not only is it required to collect the valuable particles, but it also controls the froth stability and consequently the separation performance for a given feed.  Froth stability can be described and quantified in numerous ways, which are subtly different.  Air recovery is one such measure of froth stability which accounts for both the stability of the bubbles and the mobility of the froth.  The benefit of using air recovery as a measure of froth stability is that it exhibits a peak as air flow rate is increased, and this corresponds to the air rate at which the optimal separation performance is obtained.  As such, it provides a single target value for optimising air flowrate for a given set of feed con

ditions. 

Use of air recovery, however, has one potential drawback:  accurate measurement of the inlet air flow rate to a flotation cell is required.  This can be problematic for operations, particularly where calibration of air flow rate is carried out infrequently or where there is no air flow rate measurement, such as for many self-aerated flotation cells.  To this end, we present an alternative method for determining the peak in air recovery (PAR) air rate. 

We introduce a simplified method for determining the PAR air rate using trends in froth velocity and overflowing froth height, both of which are readily measured using existing froth image analysis systems. We will show, using industrial data, the application of this simple technique to find the optimal air flowrate for flotation cells.  We will also discuss other alternative techniques for air rate optimisation that have the potential to improve separation performance using existing technology. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The stability of the froth phase in flotation is of critical importance to the final separation performance.  This has been demonstrated industrially using a number of different ways to quantify froth stability, such as bubble burst rate (Morar, Bradshaw and Harris, 2012), the froth stability column (Barbian, Hadler and Cilliers, 2006) and air recovery (Hadler and Cilliers, 2009; Qu, Wang and Nguyen, 2013).  Air recovery has grown in significance, both with the development and implementation of machine vision technology on plant (Aldrich _et al_ , 2010), but also as it embodies both the bubble stability and mobility aspects of froth behaviour.  Both of these play a key role in determining concentrate grade and mineral recovery. 

Air recovery is determined using the following relationship (Equation 1):

This assumes that all 𝑓𝑓 𝑓𝑓 froth overflowing the cell lip is predominantly air, which has been shown to be valid under conditions when 𝛼𝛼 𝑣𝑣 𝑎𝑎 the cell is operating well and is not sliming (i.e. there is loss of the interface and pulp reports to the 𝐿𝐿 𝑄𝑄 concentrate). 

The most significant development in the research linking froth stability to flotation performance is the finding that air recovery passes through a peak as cell air rate is increased.  This means there is an optimal air rate to produce the most stable overflowing froth.  Furthermore, it has been demonstrated through numerous industrial trials that when operating a flotation cell (or bank of cells) at the air rate at which the Peak Air Recovery (PAR) is measured, the ‘optimal’ flotation performance is also obtained, as shown in Figure 1 (Hadler and Cilliers, 2009; Smith, Hadler and Cilliers, 2010; Hadler, Smith and Cilliers, 2010; Hadler _et al_ , 2012).  The majority of

the flotation cells tested as part of these studies have been over-aerated, in which case reducing the air rate to find the PAR air rate results in an increase in concentrate grade and in mineral recovery (Hadler, Smith and Cilliers, 2010).

Consequently, the PAR concept has been shown to be an important tool for flotation cell optimisation and control, providing a single target that must be maximised.  There are, however, two fundamental challenges. The first is that the magnitude of the air recovery and the position of the peak in air recovery with respect to air rate varies with changing particle size, froth depth, and many other variables.  Since predictive modelling of PAR, either empirically or fundamentally, is not yet possible, this can be addressed through the development of a control system that seeks to continually check that a cell is operating at the PAR air rate, in an iterative approach (Shean, Hadler and Cilliers, 2017). 

The second challenge is that while froth velocity and overflowing froth height are readily measured by existing technology such as image analysis (using froth cameras) and laser distance measures respectively, cell air rate is also required in order to calculate air recovery.  In many plants, this is problematic due to poorly calibrated instrumentation.  While experimental techniques exist for measurement of cell air rate (eg Gomez and Finch, 2007), for online PAR optimisation, it is clear that to remove the need for inlet air rate altogether would improve the reach and applicability of the PAR concept for flotation optimisation, in addition to the speed of convergence to the optimal air rate region. 

In this paper, a simplified method of determining the PAR air rate is proposed; this is then tested using data from different concentrators.

Note the difference in the position of the PAR air rate. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** In recent years it has been shown that air recovery, the fraction of air entering a flotation cell that overflows the cell lip as unburst bubbles, exhibits a peak as cell air rate is increased. When a cell is operated at the air rate that yields this Peak Air Recovery (PAR), an improvement in flotation performance can be obtained through higher mineral recovery, often at a higher concentrate grade. Air recovery is determined using froth velocity and overflowing froth height at the cell lip, both of which can be measured readily using existing technology. Air recovery also requires knowledge of the inlet air flowrate; this can prove challenging where instrumentation is poorly calibrated. While air rate can be measured in-situ using techniques such as the Anglo Platinum Bubble Sizer, this is labour-intensive and inhibits the development of PAR optimisationbased flotation control. In this paper, it is shown that, for several plants, froth velocity exhibits a linear increase as air rate is increased, while overflowing froth height exhibits a linear decrease. In these cases, to find the PAR air rate requires only knowledge of the gradient and the intercept of the froth velocity and overflowing froth height as a function of air rate. This allows rapid determination of the region of the PAR air rate. This simple method for optimisation of flotation cell air flowrate is shown to be accurate both in the case where air is well calibrated, and in the case where the relationship between the nominal air rate and actual air rate is unknown. This provides a streamlined technique for optimising flotation cell air rate for improved separation performance. ###### Pyrite depression at Boliden Tara using F-250 – a biopolymer 

###### _R A Lauten_<sup>_1_</sup> _, C Burns_<sup>_2_</sup> _, Y Mu_<sup>_3_</sup> _and Y Peng_<sup>_4_</sup> 

1. Senior Scientist, Pionera, Sarpsborg, Norway. Email: rolf.andreas.lauten@pionera.com, MAUSIMM 

2. Process Engineer, Boliden Tara, Navan, Ireland. Email: colum.burns@boliden.com 

3. Research Fellow, School of Chemical Engineering, The University of Queensland, St Lucia, Brisbane, Australia, Email: yufan.mu@uq.edu.au 

4. Professor, School of Chemical Engineering, The University of Queensland, St Lucia, Brisbane, Australia, Email: yongjun.peng@uq.edu.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

In both laboratory flotation experiments and from analysing the composition of the lead concentrate at the Boliden Tara lead-zinc mine in Ireland, it has been found that F-250 may replace cyanide as a pyrite depressant. Replacement or reduction of the cyanide consumption is highly desirable from a safety perspective given the toxicity of cyanide. Scrutiny of results from the plant trial indicate that F-250 is less efficient as a cyanide depressant when the flotation feed contains high levels of pyrite. Statistical analysis of the results does not capture this trend, illustrating a need to collect more data at higher pyrite ore levels. 

A recent model proposed for biopolymer-induced pyrite depression is reviewed and discussed next to the suggeste

d mechanism for pyrite depression via cyanide. Review of the interactions causing pyrite depression point to different manners in achieving depression. In light of the less efficient F-250 pyrite depression at high pyrite levels, it is speculated if the two depressants may act synergistically at high levels of pyrite in the feed. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Boliden Tara is an operation that produces lead and zinc from an ore body that otherwise mainly consists of pyrite, quartz and clay minerals. Cyanide is used to depress pyrite and there is a desire to reduce or replace the cyanide usage. The motivation for reduction or elimination of cyanide is obvious, the toxicity imposes need for precautions on the handling of cyanide itself but also detoxification of all streams treated with cyanide. On the other side, cyanide performs as an excellent pyrite depressant and several different pyrite depressants have been evaluated at the Tara mine over the years. None with the same efficiency as cyanide. Below, results from a plant trial designed to evaluate F-250, a non-toxic pyrite depressant are presented. 

It is of interest to review hypothesises on how cyanide and F-250 depress pyrite in relation to other chemicals used in pyrite depression. Several explanations as to how cyanide may depress pyrite are described in the literature (Mu et al., 2016a), among them are preferential cyanide adsorption in place of xanthate, precipitation of hydrophilic insoluble iron cyanide compounds on the pyrite surface, formation of thiocyanate complexes with regions of sulfide on the pyrite surface and modification of the open current potential (E h), which may inhibit oxidation of xanthate. According to Guo et al. (Guo et al., 2016, 2014) cyanide depresses pyrite via the formation of iron cyanide compounds that precipitate on the mineral surface. These compounds prevent chemical adsorption of xanthate. Thus, even if addition of cyanide lowers the open current potential, and the reduction is not sufficient to prevent xanthate oxidation, xanthate adsorption is inhibited. The same authors mention that cyanide acts as an activator in the flotation of galena at some open current potentials while in general there is no competitive adsorption between cyanide and xanthate on the galena surface (Guo et al., 2014). Cyanide has also been reported beneficial in the separation of galena and sphalerite (Prestidge et al., 1993). 

Pionera F-250 is a pyrite depressant of natural origin. It is a water-soluble polymer and classified as a nondangerous material. While it has been used as a pyrite depressant around the world, a better understanding of the mechanism by which it depresses pyrite has recently been obtained. According to Mu et al. (Mu et al., 2016b), F-250 preferentially adsorbs onto copper-activated pyrite in place of xanthate. Preferential adsorption prevents chemical adsorption of xanthate and the following oxidation required to render pyrite hydrophobic and float. Copper is

not present in appreciable amounts as an ion for pyrite activation in the lead flotation circuit at Boliden Tara. Lead ions are known to activate pyrite flotation (Peng et al., 2003) and it 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

is assumed that lead-activated pyrite facilitates adsorption of F-250. Thus, it appears that both F-250 and cyanide obstruct adsorption of xanthate on the pyrite surface, although by different mechanisms. 

Polysaccharides like dextrin and guar are also used to depress pyrite. They also allow differential flotation of galena and sphalerite (Rath and Subramanian, 1999). Generally, they are assumed to adsorb onto pyrite via adsorption onto iron hydroxide complexes (Liu and Laskowski, 1989a, 1989b; Lуpez Valdivieso et al., 2004; Rath et al., 2000). The iron hydroxides are, depending upon the pH in the flotation pulp, electrostatically charged or neutral. They may precipitate on the pyrite surface or there may be an electrostatic attraction between the surface and the iron hydroxide. Hydroxides other than iron may form depending upon the composition of the process water and these may also act as binding sites for dextrin. A potentially important difference between polysaccharides like dextrin and F-250 is the difference in the mode of interaction. Dextrin binds via iron hydroxides which are pyrite oxidation products. F-250 binds via adsorbed metal ions, here originating from galena oxidation, that normally activate pyrite. 

Below, results from the experimental work is described and interpreted in light of relevant depression mechanisms proposed for cyanide and F-250. 

###### **BOLIDEN TARA** 

Boliden Tara is located near Navan, around 60 km from Dublin in Ireland. It is the largest zinc mine in Europe and they process a lead-zinc ore. Around 2600 ktons (metric) of ore was processed in 2016 and refined into lead, zinc and silver concentrates. The gangue minerals are mostly quartz and calcite while galena and sphalerite are the main sulfide minerals in addition to pyrite. Ore is broken underground, crushed and hoisted into a stockpile on the surface. Crushed ore is transported into the grinding circuit where cyanide or F-250 is added during comminution. The (non-standard) target grind size is P88 less than 75 microns, the corresponding P80 is less than 53 microns. Zinc sulfate is added together with sodium isopropyl xanthate in the lead flotation circuit. In the following zinc circuit, copper sulfate is used together with potassium amyl xanthate. In general, the zinc circuit is well-behaved and acceptable levels of pyrite depression are obtained. The lead concentrate is sensitive to pyrite and the degree of pyrite depression suffers when ore with a high pyrite content is processed. As the lead flotation circuit is the part of the plant that is sensitive to pyrite, its performance was monitored during the plant trial. The performance of the plant is monitored with an automatic onli

ne assaying system. The elemental composition of the different streams is measured every 20 minutes. To complement the online sampling, composite samples are collected over 24 or 48 hours and their composition determined using a calibrated and accurate XRF apparatus. 

###### **Laboratory floats** 

Flotation experiments were conducted by Pionera to evaluate F-250 as a pyrite depressant relative to cyanide, using an ore sample provided by Boliden Tara in a Denver flotation cell. The purpose of these experiments was to evaluate how use of F-250 compares to cyanide at conditions similar to the flotation circuit at Boliden Tara. Briefly, the ore sample from Boliden Tara was cone crushed to a size less than 2 mm and split into 1 kg samples. Prior to flotation, a sample was rod milled at 65% solids until 88% of the sample is smaller than 75 microns. Cyanide or F-250 was added during milling together with zinc sulfate. Floats conducted with F-250 was compared to the normal operation conditions at Boliden Tara where 15 gpt sodium cyanide typically are used. The Boliden Tara flotation procedure specifies the collection of five lead concentrates, with addition of sodium isopropyl xanthate in each step. After collection of the lead concentrates, the tails are floated and in total four zinc concentrates are collected. During zinc flotation, copper sulfate is used to activate sphalerite and potassium amyl xanthate is added as a collector in the three last concentrates. In the laboratory floats, the individual concentrates from the lead and zinc rougher floats where combined and assayed for lead, iron and zinc using digestion and ICP. 

Results from the lead rougher floats are presented in Figure 1, with % recovery along the abscissa and % grade along the ordinate. Largely, the laboratory floats indicate that replacement of cyanide with F-250 gives comparable lead recoveries and grades. The lead head grade was 0.76% lead, after flotation the lead grade increased to around 2-3% at around 85% recovery. The iron grade (head grade 5.5%) in the lead concentrates is around 14% at approximately 55% recovery. Finally, the zinc recoveries (head grade 4.8%) are at around 25% with a grade around 5%. Relative to the head grade, zinc is not concentrated in the lead rougher float while both the iron and lead grade increases. Three F-250 dosages were evaluated and it appears to be a tendency that the highest dosage, 50 gpt, increases both the zinc and iron recovery relative to cyanide. This indicates that the F-250 selectivity may be reduced at higher dosages.

Only data collected when the mill was operating at normal load, i.e. larger than 275 metric tons/hour, were used in the analysis. Data from plant trials can be analysed at several different levels with strengths and weaknesses associated with them.

###### **Mechanism** 

In the lead flotation circuit, the challenge is to achieve separation of galena and pyrite and maximise the recovery of galena. Separation of galena and pyrite, as well as the separation of other sulfides is a challenge because galvanic interactions take place between the two metals. Pyrite, having the higher rest potential will act as a cathode in a galvanic element with galena (or sphalerite). Oxygen reduction will take place at the pyrite surface and hydroxyl ions formed will bind to iron ions released from pyrite. Lead ions are released from the galena surface during oxidation. Adsorption of lead ions on the pyrite surface facilitates adsorption of extra collector and increases the flotation recovery of pyrite. Adsorption or precipitation of iron hydroxides 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

on the surface of galena will increase the hydrophilic character of the surface and reduce its flotation recovery. As the amount of pyrite in the flotation feed increases, it is likely that the extent of galvanic interactions increases. Peng et al. (Peng et al., 2003) conducted a thorough study on how conditions during grinding leveraged the flotation recovery of galena and pyrite. It was concluded that lead oxidation products enhanced the flotation recovery of pyrite (lead activation), while pyrite oxidation products reduced the flotation recovery of both sulfides. Conditions that maximised separation of the two sulfides where identified. Similar influence on the separation of galena and pyrite were observed by Pecina-Treviсo et al. (PecinaTreviсo et al., 2003). Greet (Greet, 2005) also looked at how oxidation of a galena-pyrite ore influenced its flotation recovery. Pertaining to the processing of the lead concentrate at Tara, these findings indicate that the magnitude of the galvanic interactions occurring between pyrite and galena may change in response to a varying iron/lead ratio in the feed. 

As a depressant, cyanide is known to improve the separation of polymetallic sulfides. Different mechanisms have been put forward in order to explain how it depresses pyrite and improves separation of sulfides. Guo et al. (Guo et al., 2016, 2014) indicated that cyanide will bind to iron and form iron cyanide complexes on the pyrite surface. These complexes prevent activation by lead ions and chemisorption of collector. The same authors also found that c

yanide had no adverse effects on flotation of galena. This scenario suggests that pyrite depression can be controlled by the cyanide dosage, as it has to expected that the hydrophilicity of pyrite will increase with higher amounts of iron cyanide complexes on the surface. 

F-250 is a biopolymer. The manner by which similar biopolymers depress pyrite in mixed mineral flotation of chalcopyrite and pyrite has been investigated by Mu et al. (Mu et al., 2016b). It was demonstrated that biopolymers preferentially adsorb onto copper-activated pyrite rather than chalcopyrite. At too high dosages, depression of both pyrite and chalcopyrite was seen, highlighting the need for a correct dosage matched to the composition of the ore. Once adsorbed, presence of biopolymer inhibits xanthate adsorption and reduces the magnitude of the galvanic interactions between the sulfide minerals. This work does not disclose if a similar preferential adsorption takes place on pyrite activated by lead ions, but it is not unreasonable. Potentially, preferential adsorption of F-250 on lead-activated pyrite will favour selective depression of pyrite as an adsorbed layer of F-250 will increase the hydrophilic character of the pyrite surface. 

Formation of a hydrophilic coating via adsorption of dextrin or other polysaccharides is the proposed mechanism for the depressing action on pyrite (Liu and Laskowski, 1989a; Lуpez Valdivieso et al., 2004). Dextrin does not prevent adsorption of xanthate, but it adsorbs on sites that are converted to iron cyanide complexes in the presence of cyanide. Hence, from a mechanistic point of view, dextrin and cyanide compete for similar sites on the pyrite surface. In contrast, F-250 is surmised to bind via metal ions that otherwise activate pyrite and facilitate interaction with xanthate. Conceptually, F-250 combined with cyanide or dextrin may act as an enhanced depressant system since they operate on different parts of the pyrite surface. From the data from the plant trial it is unclear if combined addition of cyanide and F-250 will be beneficial for depression of pyrite at high iron/lead ratios. Further studies are required to investigate this aspect of pyrite depression. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Initial laboratory flotation experiments and a full-scale plant trial has revealed that F-250, a biopolymer, may replace cyanide as a pyrite depressant at the Tara mine in Ireland. Use of F-250 gives similar flotation recoveries as when using cyanide as a pyrite depressant. However, for flotation feed with higher than normal content of pyrite, use of F-250 leads to poorer lead grades and recovery. Further trials are required to establish if acceptable pyrite depression can be obtained for these higher pyrite-bearing ores using F-250 as a depressant. 

For the mine, replacement of cyanide as pyrite depressant represents a significant change. It has been a long-term goal to reduce cyanide consumption and the results from the herein described plant t

rial may be the first step. 

Depression of pyrite is attained with both cyanide and F-250. Judging from mechanisms put forward to explain the way these depressants act indicate that they interact differently with pyrite, while for instance dextrin and cyanide interact with the similar pyrite surface sites.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Mount Isa Mines (MIM) Copper Concentrator currently utilises Agitair 120 banks for its roughing flotation circuit. Apart from a rotor change, the only other significant work completed to the Agitair banks since their installation and commissioning over 40 years ago has been a like for like refurbishment in 2016. The Agitair banks at the MIM Copper Concentrator currently utilise the Pipsa rotor design which progressively replaced the original Chile X rotor design in the 1980’s and 90’s in the copper concentrator. Since the development of the Pipsa rotors, modern rotors such as the Dorr-Oliver (DO) high shear rotors have been released to the market with proven recovery and concentrate grade improvements over previous rotor designs. This paper aims to detail the installation, testing and comparison of Pipsa versus Dorr-Oliver rotors in two different flotation sections of the MIM Copper Concentrator. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Historically, MIM Copper Concentrator has utilised Agitair rotors and stators for its flotation banks. Agitair banks were originally patented in 1932.  Agitair rotors were the industry standard until the 1980’s/90’s when modern high shear rotors were developed (Krishnaswam and Hoyack, 1989).  Experience shows that upgrading to this design significantly improves flotation kinetics and hydrodynamic performance resulting in short payb

ack periods (Bilney, MacKinnon and Kok 2006).  It was decided in mid-2012 that an upgrade project would be initiated at MIM Copper Concentrator to improve the performance of the Agitair flotation banks and the overall concentrator flotation performance.  FLSmidth Dorr-Oliver flotation technology was selected and retrofitted into a number of flotation banks to be evaluated from a mechanical and metallurgical basis. 

###### **PROCESS DESCRIPTION** 

Copper is mined and processed in the North West Queensland town of Mount Isa with operations owned and operated by MIM, a Glencore Company. The predominant feed source for the MIM Copper Concentrator comes from two underground copper systems (Figure 1): Enterprise, a high copper bearing chalcopyrite ore body and X41, a lower copper bearing chalcopyrite ore body. The MIM underground mine produces a total of 6.7 Mt of chalcopyrite ore per annum. Copper smelter slag from the MIM Copper Smelter is also processed at the concentrator on a campaign basis. 

The copper concentrator, formally known as ‘No. 4’, was commissioned in 1973 and replaced the original MIM ‘No. 1’ concentrator. No. 4 was commissioned with a primary and secondary crushing circuit, grinding and regrinding circuits and a rougher/scavenger/cleaner flotation circuit. Since 1973 however, a number of major equipment changes have been implemented. These include but are not limited to the replacement of surface crushers with SAG mills and the conversion of rod mills to ball mills (Leung _et al_ 1992), upgrade of the flotation circuit to include FLSmidth WEMCO tank cells and Jameson cells (Lawson and Carr, 2003), the replacement of the retreat and cleaning circuit with three stage Jameson cell cleaning (Lawson _et al_ 2017) and recommissioning of a third pre-float/rougher flotation line.

Current concentrator operation includes grinding, flotation, concentrate handling (thickening and filtration) and tailings disposal (fill plants, tailings thickeners and site process water systems). Two types of copper slag are processed: rotary holding furnace (RHF) slag and magnetic fines from crushed converter slag. RHF slag is processed through Line 2 of the concentrator grinding and flotation circuit. 

###### **PROJECT BACKGROUND** 

Converting Pipsa mechanisms to high shear Dorr-Oliver rotors has been performed at several concentrators (Traczyk, F, 2012).  The benefits of putting more power into the slurry with the use of high shear rotors are well documented (Kelley, K R, 2011).  Standard rotors are almost non-existent in new concentrators designed today.  Some of the expected benefits of high shear over standard rotors that would improve metallurgical performance include: 

- decrease in bubble size 

- increased bubble surface area flux 

- smaller variance of bubble size. 

Based on the change out of standard rotors to high s

hear rotors in the cleaner and recleaner banks at the Kanowna Belle Gold Mine, Bilney, MacKinnon and Kok (2006) documented a 50% reduction in bubble size and a 1.9% gold and 5.4% sulphur recovery improvement in the cleaners and a 1.1% improvement in overall plant gold recovery. Historically, copper recovery in the MIM Copper Concentrator runs at around 91-92%. Liberated chalcopyrite losses account for 20-40% of total copper losses as shown by Figure 2. Metallurgically, the rotors also present numerous benefits in their ability to improve concentrate grade and recovery at the MIM Copper Concentrator through improvements in grade and recovery in the 10-53 um size fractions where the majority of copper reports. Two different sets of data analysis on two di

fferent bank conversions prove with a degree of confidence that the rotors improve both bank and plant performance. Using the initial retreat full plant recovery result resulted in a positive payback period of less than 1 month.  A full plant conversion was recommended and is being implemented as each Pipsa mechanism wears out they are replaced with Dorr-Oliver mechanisms.

The processing plant is designed to process 2 Mt/y and has the capability to treat both refractory and free milling ore from the Kanowna Belle and Kundana mining operations. 

The Kanowna Belle ore is refractory with the gold mineralisation occurring mostly as fine-grained inclusions in pyrite or as very fine-grained gold located in pyritic arsenic rich growth zones. The Kanowna Belle refractory process includes flotation, roasting of the flotation concentrate, and calcine leaching to extract the gold from the ore. 

Mineralogical analysis of feed and tailings streams from the flotation circuit have shown that the gold bearing minerals are well liberated and confirmed they are mainly associated with pyrite. Nearly 40% of the flotation circuit losses are in the -38 µm size fraction. To improve the flotation circuit recovery, the fine particle gold recovery was targeted. Figure 2 – Monthly scavenger tail gold distribution. ###### **THEORY OF CAVITATION TUBE SPARGING SYSTEM** Hydrodynamic cavitation is a process of creation and growth of gas and/or small vapor filled bubbles (referred to as pico bubbles) in a liquid due to the rupture of a liquid–liquid or a liquid–solid interface under the influence of external forces. Based on the research results of Maoming, Daniel _et al_ , the work of adhesion (W a) between a solid particle and water is always smaller than the work of cohesion of water (W c), pico bubbles preferentially nucleate on the surface of particles and can eliminate the rate-determining steps for fine particle flotation - collision and attachment. In addition, Maoming, Daniel _et al_ , found out that particles are less likely to detach from smaller bubbles due to their lower upward velocity and centrifugal force associated with the detachment process, thereby reducing the probability of detachment. Luttrell _et al_ , suggest that pico bubbles substantially improve flotation recovery and capacity of poorly floating fine particles. These particles are of insufficient size or density and cannot penetrate the streamlines and collide with the bubble. Furthermore Maoming _et al_ , studies showed that W a decreases with the contact angle or solid surface hydrophobicity, as such pico bubbles are more readily formed on the surface of hydrophobic particles than that of hydrophilic particles, and thus increase the flotation selectivity, which is very important for fine or ultra-fine particles separation. Pico bubbles generated on a particle surface also serve as a secondary collector and reduce reagent c

ost, which contributes significantly to mineral processing plant operating cost. 

The Eriez Flotation Division cavitation tube sparger was designed to generate large amounts of pico bubbles. This device and its operation are illustrated in Figure 3. Air and slurry are passed through a specially designed bubble generator just prior to injection into a flotation cell or column. Slurry enters the sparger and passes through an area containing an abrupt reduction in diameter while maintaining a high inlet pressure. Following the small diameter orifice is a cylindrical throat and an area of gradual expansion. This configuration results in a release of pressure as the slurry passes through the sparger. The liquid in the cylindrical throat is higher in velocity and lower in pressure than the liquid at the sparger entrance and results in cavitation. As would be expected, the addition of chemicals such as frothers allow for the generation of additional pico bubbles which improve overall stability while preventing bubble coalescence. 

Improved attachment efficiency and flotation rates have been observed when tiny bubbles co-exist with the larger air bubbles commonly generated in flotation cells. Klassen and Mokrousov (1963) illustrated this synergistic effect when combining pico bubble flotation with typical mechanically generated bubbles. 

This method produces a higher flotation recovery than either approach applied independently. The pico bubbles on a particle surface improve flotation by promoting the attachment of the larger bubbles since attachment between the pico bubbles and the larger conventionally generated bubbles is more favourable than bubble–solid attachment. In other words, pico bubbles can act as a secondary collector for particles which results in reduced collector dosage, enhanced particle attachment, and reduced particle detachment. This is illustrated in the papers by Fan _et al_ (2010a, 2010b). Furthermore, the bubbles generated on the particle surface by cavitation naturally attach to the particle (ie, nucleation), eliminating the collision and attachment process, which is often the rate-determining step for flotation. This leads to substantially improved flotation recovery of poorly floating fine and coarse particles.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Pilot scale test work was completed at Kanowna Belle gold mine concentrator to quantify the benefit of the cavitation tube sparging technology in a rougher and final scavenger duty. A wide variety of operating points were tested providing information on the optimum operating conditions, and sensitivity to each parameter. 

A single stage cavitation tube column unit achieved up to 80 per cent gold recovery when acting in a rougher scavenger duty at grades consistent with existing operation. The existing Slam Jet flotation column cell achieved 70 per cent gold recovery at a similar concentrate grade. The single stage recoveries are impressive given that they were achieved with a contact time of 10-13 minutes. Laboratory scale tests conducted 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

concurrently with these tests indicated that the cavitation tube rougher column retrofit project could achieve up to 1 per cent overall circuit gold recovery improvement on the existing circuit with minimal capital requirement. 

When operating in a final scavenger duty, the cavitation tube column achieved a maximum gold recovery of 40 per cent by producing 4 g/t of gold in the concentrate. Further downstream cleaner laboratory test results confirmed that concentrate from the scavenger cavitation tube column can be upgraded in a cleaner cell to enable blending with the plant final concentrate stream. The net effect of utilising a cavitation tube column in the final scavenger duty indicated an overall net benefit of 2 per cent gold recovery for the flotation circuit. This represents an economically significant gold metal yield, and therefore an industrial scale installation is being considered. 

This test work provided good initial pilot scale data to support the use of this technology in gold sulphide flotation.

###### Selectively targeting hydrophobic gangue minerals at the Mount Isa Mines Copper Concentrator 

###### _A R O’Donnell_<sup>_1_</sup> _and M L Muller_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. Plant Metallurgist, Mount Isa Mines Copper Concentrator, Mount Isa QLD 4825. Email: roxanne.odonnell@glencore.com.au 

2. Operations and Technical Superintendent, Mount Isa Mines Copper Concentrator, Mount Isa QLD 4825. Email: marvin.muller@glencore.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Mount Isa Mines (MIM) Copper Concentrator has an extensive history of reagent trials, with different reagents coming in and out of favour over the years. The research and use of carbon depressants is particularly prevalent, as carbonaceous pyrite is a major source of concentrate dilution. Years of research led to the use of naphthalene sulphonate due to its excellent carbon depression properties. However, due to rising reagent costs carbon depression ceased in the late 1990s. This led to the loss of knowledge about the use and value of naphthalene sulphonate. 

Cyanide is used at the Copper Concentrator for the sole purpose of pyrite depression and over the years multiple projects have been devoted to finding alternatives to it. In 2012 the neighbouring MIM Lead-Zinc Concentrator replaced cyanide with naphthalene sulphonate which resulted in cost savings and the elimination of a hazardous reagent. In 2013, plant trials were conducted at the Copper Concentrator in hopes to replicate the outcomes obtained at the Lead-Zinc Concentrator. The results of the trials conducted at the Copper Concentrator showed that naphthalene sulphonate could not replace cyanide and this work was set aside to pursue more promising projects. 

Further research conducted in 2014 found that mineralogy and a better understanding of the depressing mechanism of naphthalene sulphonate held the key to improved pyrite depression at the Copper Concentrator. The findings showed that Mount Isa copper ore contains two

forms of pyrite; euhedral pyrite (cubic pyrite) and framboidal pyrite (carbon rimmed spheres of pyrite), both of which require different reagents to sufficiently depress them. Naphthalene sulphonate was found to be an excellent carbon depressant, suitable for depressing graphite and framboidal pyrite, whilst cyanide specifically targets euhedral pyrite. 

In 2015 laboratory test work was conducted to examine the use of naphthalene sulphonate in conjunction with cyanide to selectively target both forms of pyrite.  This work led to a full plant trial, the results of which showed a significant increase in plant performance, with higher copper concentrate grades and recoveries being achieved. This paper aims to focus on the benefits and importance of understanding past work and linking a detailed knowledge of feed mineralogy to reagent selection for improved plant outcomes. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper concentrate has been continuously produced by Mount Isa Mines (MIM) since 1952 (Schache, Pritchard and Canning, 1987). Although the original No. 1 Concentrator which treated the copper ore has long since been decommissioned, much of the research and subsequent findings are still applicable to the current No. 4 Concentrator which was commissioned in 1973. Extensive research and test work was completed during the operation of the No. 1 Concentrator due to the various ore bodies processed during its life. Each ore body presented a new challenge, as different minerals were contained in the feed (Lyon and Fewings, 1970). Chalcopyrite is the only mineral of economic importance contained in the current MIM copper ore. Gangue minerals such as pyrite, carbonaceous material and talc have always been present as the major diluents in the concentrate and this is still the case (Schache, Pritchard, and Canning, 1987). 

At the No. 4 Concentrator, ore is currently ground in two parallel semi-autogenous grinding (SAG) mills before being further ground in two parallel ball mills. Each ball mill feeds separate lines of Agitair pre-flotation banks, followed by four Agitair copper roughing banks. The tails from the roughers are further treated in a series of four Wemco scavenger tank cells, whilst the rougher concentrate is cleaned by three Jameson cells in series. A regrind mill is used to further increase the liberation of coarse composites from the concentrate collected from the scavenger cells. The reagents that are in use at the Copper Concentrator have not changed dramatically over the years since the foundation research that was completed during the operation of the No. 1 Concentrator. Sodium Isobutyl

Xanthate (SIBX) has been the sole copper collector in use since it replaced ethyl xanthate in 1967 (Lyon and Fewings, 1970). Cyanide additions began in the 1950s during the development of the py

rite rich 500 ore body as it is very effective at depressing coarse grained euhedral pyrite (Lyon and Fewings, 1970). Dextrin is used to depress talc and silica and was combined in a blend with carbon depressants from the late 1960s through to the 1990s (Bowen, 2007).  Naphthalene sulphonate was found to be the active ingredient in the carbon depressant blend, however in 1997 the addition of a carbon depressant ceased altogether.

###### **BACKGROUND** 

The MIM Copper Concentrators have a long history of varied depressant usage, however much of this has been lost over time due to staff turnover and has only been recently re-discovered. Extensive research was conducted on site from the 1960s through to the 1990s due to the development of new ore bodies. In 1967 mining and processing of the 1100 ore body saw a corresponding increase in carbonaceous material in the concentrate and test work began to investigate methods of carbon removal (Lyon and Fewings, 1970). Preconcentration of the carbonaceous gangue material prior to rougher flotation was trialled, however due to unacceptable copper losses to the pre-flotation concentrate, alternative methods involving reagents were investigated (Lyon and Fewings, 1970). In 1969 a 60:40 blend of nigrosine dye and dextrin was adopted as a permanent reagent at the Copper Concentrator following test work which showed the blend to be highly effective at depressing carbonaceous material (Johnson, 1988). 

Due to the success experienced with the nigrosine/dextrin blend, further research was undertaken to determine if other reagents would yield better results (O'Meara, 1968). In the 1970’s further test work was carried out on various dyes which were reported to have better carbon depression properties than nigrosine (Saxby, 1975). In 1971, Bayer’s Agent G (an azo dye/dextrin blend) replaced the nigrosine/dextrin blend and in 1979 MIM commenced the mixing of their own blend using an Australian supplied dextrin and an azo dye intermediate ‘G’ from Bayer which were mixed at a 60:40 ratio (Johnson, 1988). 

Whilst MIM utilised dyes for over 20 years to depress carbonaceous minerals it was only discovered after a significant amount of work that the dyes themselves weren’t effective carbon depressants. Rather, the viscosity modifier present in the dyes was depressing the carbonaceous minerals. It is now known that the intermediate ‘G,’ the viscosity modifier in the original dye blend, was naphthalene sulphonate and this was the active ingredient in all the dyes that were tested (Bowen, 2007). 

In 1997 the Copper Concentrator dropped naphthalene sulphonate from the blend altogether due to the rising cost of the reagent (Bowen, 2007). It is thought that this adjustment was not followed by a change in plant performance because the feed to the Copper Concentrator at the time may have been relatively low in carbon and the addition of a carbon depres

sant would have had negligible benefits (Lawson, February 2018, personal 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

communication). The reagent usage history detailed above was largely unknown to the current Copper Concentrator technical team due to staffing changes over the years. This has resulted in much of the original test work around the use of carbon depressants in a dextrin blend having to be repeated. 

The resurgence of the use of naphthalene sulphonate occurred in late 2012 when the neighbouring Lead-Zinc Concentrator completely replaced cyanide with it. This change resulted in significant cost savings in terms of reagent use as well as the removal of a hazardous reagent. This sparked renewed interest in the use of naphthalene sulphonate at the Copper Concentrator, prompting the beginning of laboratory and plant scale test work. 

###### **INITIAL LABORATORY AND PLANT TRIAL TEST WORK** 

In early 2013, it was decided that naphthalene sulphonate test work should be carried out at the Copper Concentrator to replicate the work carried out at the Lead-Zinc Concentrator and determine if cyanide could be replaced. No research was completed prior to the commencement of the test work to determine what the depressing mechanism of the naphthalene sulphonate was, what minerals naphthalene sulphonate targets or what the desired outcome of the test work should be. Naphthalene sulphonate was tested in various combinations that included the full replacement of both dextrin and cyanide 

The best performing combination from the laboratory tests was when naphthalene sulphonate was used as the sole depressant (no cyanide or dextrin additions) as this resulted in the largest copper grade and recovery improvement. However, there was no corresponding decrease in talc or iron sulphide recovery which would normally explain the performance improvement, and the repeatability of the test work data was poor. A major flaw in the initial laboratory test work was that non-repeatable data sets were averaged which resulted in misleading outcomes. 

Despite the results from the laboratory test work being inconclusive, a plant trial was commenced to determine if performance benefits could be obtained on a full plant scale. In May 2013, naphthalene sulphonate was used as a partial replacement for dextrin in a 75:25 dextrin/naphthalene sulphonate blend. Initial trial results were promising with performance improvements reported from using this blend. The ratio was gradually stepped up until dextrin was fully replaced with naphthalene sulphonate. After several weeks of trialling naphthalene sulphonate as a dextrin replacement, cyanide additions were reduced and eventually ceased to determine if it could be replaced as well. 

The findings from the full plant trial concluded that dextrin could potentially be replaced by naphthalene sulphonate due to the reduction of talc in the concentrate. However, the trial also coincided with a dr

op in the MgO feed grade which would explain the perceived improvement in talc depression. From the full plant trial it was determined that cyanide could not be replaced as low final concentrate grades and below model copper recovery were experienced for most of the cyanide replacement trial period. These results halted further test work with naphthalene sulphonate as it was thought that it would provide no benefit to the Copper Concentrator. 

If the history of naphthalene sulphonate use at the Copper Concentrator had been known prior to the commencement of the 2013 trial, the aim of the trial and the results would have been very different. A literature review and a mineralogical analysis would have shown that naphthalene sulphonate cannot be used as a like for like replacement for cyanide as they do not target the same minerals (Lyon and Fewings, 1970). It is thought the neighbouring MIM Lead-Zinc Concentrator had success replacing cyanide with naphthalene sulphonate as there is more carbonaceous material in their feed than euhedral pyrite. Consequently the replacement of cyanide with naphthalene sulphonate would have a bigger impact on the carbon depression, with little effect on euhedral pyrite depression. Dextrin cannot be fully replaced by naphthalene sulphonate at the Copper Concentrator either as it is required for talc depression. This test work and the setbacks it caused are important lessons in knowing the history of the plant as well as the value of mineralogy data and understanding what reagents actually do. 

###### **FURTHER WORK** 

In late 2014 the effectiveness of naphthalene sulphonate as a carbon depressant was discussed in communications with a reagent supplier. At the time no recent work had been carried out to investigate the impact of carbonaceous minerals present in the concentrator feed. This information led to basic total organic and elemental carbon (TOEC) test work being completed on a set of plant feed and concentrate samples for a two month period. The presence of elemental or organic carbon was confirmed with assays showing that carbon accounted for up to 0.5 per cent of the total feed and up to 1 per cent of the final concentrate. Grab samples of the Copper Concentrator feed around this time also showed strongly graphitic mineralisation in some samples. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

A mineralogical assessment was then completed to find the carbon species present in the plant feed on monthly plant composite samples, using backscatter electron images in a scanning electron microscope (SEM). Carbon is difficult to detect from QEMSCAN measurements and thus the work had to be carried out manually via point counting. The analysis indicated that pyrite in the Copper Concentrator feed occurs as a continuum between strongly developed carbonaceous pyrite through to euhedral pyrite. These results indicate that significantly carbon altered pyrite constitutes approximately 5

0 per cent of the total pyrite in the feed and the concentrate, and unaltered euhedral pyrite accounts for the other 50 per cent for the same samples. 

Strongly carbonaceous pyrite (framboidal pyrite) is characterised by its spherical shape, relatively small particle size (typically less than 10µm) and a carbon rimmed surface, compared to euhedral pyrite which has a cubic structure and large grain size, often greater than 50um (see Figure 2). Apart from the significant size and shape difference of framboidal and euhedral pyrite, the surface chemistry of the two pyrite forms are also different. The carbon coated framboidal pyrite is naturally hydrophobic and is not significantly affected by cyanide which would account for its presence in the final concentrate. Given the even distribution of carbonaceous and euhedral pyrite, it would stand to reason that both a carbon depressant and cyanide (a euhedral pyrite depressant) are required to depress the two forms of pyrite present in the Copper Concentrator feed.

###### **Laboratory test work** 

Based on the findings of the mineralogical investigation and a comprehensive literature review, during which the detailed carbon depression history at MIM was uncovered, the naphthalene sulphonate project was revived. Further laboratory scale test work was completed using several different brands of naphthalene sulphonate which were blended with dextrin. Four different blend ratios of naphthalene sulphonate to dextrin were tested from 25 per cent naphthalene sulphonate to full replacement of dextrin, increasing in 25 per cent increments. Increments of 25 per cent were trialled in the laboratory as this is a practical ratio for use in the plant as four bags of dextrin are used per mix. It is important to note that the current plant infrastructure does not support the addition of a new reagent without significant capital expenditure and for this reason naphthalene sulphonate and dextrin are blended at the on-site reagent mixing facility, as per its historical usage. During the laboratory test work program cyanide additions were held constant as there is no literature to support naphthalene sulphonate having any depressive effects on euhedral pyrite. 

The test work results (see Figure 3) showed that the addition of naphthalene sulphonate at all ratios apart from 100 per cent (complete dextrin replacement and therefore no talc depression) showed some improvement in copper grade and recovery compared to the baseline tests (100 per cent dextrin). Analysis was undertaken to determine the amount of organic carbon present in the samples and the impact of the naphthalene sulphonate on carbon depression. Figure 4 shows that as the ratio of naphthalene sulphonate to dextrin increases, the amount of carbon recovered reduces. The results of the laboratory test work program gave indications that naphthalene

sulphonate is an effective carbon depressant. 

Further analysis of mineral selectivity at varying naphthalene sulphonate doses determined that there was a trade-off between carbonaceous pyrite and talc depression. Lower dextrin additions resulted in reduced talc depression but better pyrite depression due to the increase of naphthalene sulphonate in the blend. The ultimate balance was struck at 25 per cent dextrin replacement in which both talc and pyrite depression were

improved over the baseline test, despite the lower amount of dextrin being used. This appears to be due to the dispersant qualities of naphthalene sulphonate which would help to depress otherwise entrained or naturally floating particles such as silica and dolomite. Because of this it was decided that a blend of 25 per cent naphthalene sulphonate and 75 per cent dextrin would be tested on a full plant scale in 2015.

###### **Full plant trial** 

Dextrin is dosed to numerous sections of the Copper Concentrator flotation circuit using a gravity fed reagent delivery system. Dextrin powder is dissolved in water at the on-site reagent mixing facility before being pumped to a stock tank where it is then fed into the plant. To keep the cost of the trial as low as possible, it was decided that naphthalene sulphonate would be blended directly with dextrin at the mixing facility and then the combined reagent blend would be pumped up to the plant. This method was standard practice in the 1990s when the dextrin/naphthalene sulphonate blend was still in use. Prior to commencing the full plant trial, the dextrin stock tank was run low so that when the new blend was pumped up it would take less time to see if there were any significant impacts on plant performance. 

###### _Results_ 

The 2015 naphthalene sulphonate trial ran for four months before the decision was made to keep naphthalene sulphonate in the blend permanently. Operator accounts state that almost as soon as the naphthalene sulphonate started being dosed into the plant the concentrate produced from the rougher banks was visibly cleaner and the plant was easier to control when naphthalene sulphonate was present in the blend. The concentrate grade target was also more achievable without sacrificing recovery. Data comparisons from before and during the trial show that before naphthalene sulphonate was used, the copper concentrate grade target of 25 percent copper was met approximately 40 per cent of the time. However, once the naphthalene sulphonate was being dosed into the plant it was much easier to achieve the copper concentrate grade target, which was reached more than 60 per cent of the ti

me. 

Statistical analysis of the trial data shows that the addition of naphthalene sulphonate to the process gave a copper recovery improvement of between 0.3 to 1.0 percent at the 90 per cent confidence level. Figure 5 shows that the variance to model recovery was significantly higher during the trial period compared to plant performance before the trial started which may indicate a step change in plant performance. 

It must be noted that the plant recovery improvement from the addition of naphthalene sulphonate will be in proportion to the amount of carbonaceous material in the feed for any given period, as higher carbonaceous material in feed will generally mean a more significant improvement in plant performance. However, during periods of low carbonaceous material in the feed the benefit of naphthalene sulphonate will be marginal. Due to this, fully proving the recovery and concentrate grade benefits with a high degree of confidence is difficult. The amount of carbon in feed appears to be proportional to the copper head grade which can vary considerably. 

Two underground mines supply the Copper Concentrator, X41 and Enterprise. The former typically yields a lower copper feed grade whilst the latter has a higher grade. The lower grade X41 material appears to be richer in graphite and carbonaceous pyrite whereas Enterprise is abundant in talc. Figure 6 shows that naphthalene sulphonate has a large impact on plant copper recovery at lower copper head grades due to the increase in carbonaceous material from the X41 ore. However, its impact on copper recovery from the higher grade talcose Enterprise ore is potentially minimal. 

Comparison of mineralogical data from both before and during the trial period shows that the amount of carbon in the concentrate has reduced since naphthalene sulphonate has been in use. As the amount of carbonaceous pyrite in the feed was similar during both periods, the data shows that this change is real and not simply related to decreased carbon in feed.  Figure 7 shows the ratio of carbonaceous pyrite and total pyrite in the fine fractions has reduced compared to before the trial. A reduction of gangue material in the concentrate has enabled a cleaner product to be produced.
