###### **FUTURE WORK** 

Since the 2015 trial, naphthalene sulphonate has become a permanent part of the Copper Concentrator’s reagent regime. Further test work has been completed to determine if the 25:75 ratio of naphthalene sulphonate to dextrin is the optimal rat

io. Test work has found that the ideal ratio is ore dependant and relies heavily on the amount of talc and carbon present in the concentrator feed. The current infrastructure in place for reagent delivery into the plant makes it difficult and time consuming to frequently change the ratio of naphthalene sulphonate in the blend. Ore changes can happen very quickly due to the nature of the mining process and changes to the naphthalene sulphonate/dextrin ratio can take several days to take effect depending on stock levels. Because of this, it has been decided that the naphthalene sulphonate/dextrin ratio will be fixed at 25:75 as this gives more flexibility in terms of talc and carbon depression as there is little risk of overdosing the flotation circuit with naphthalene sulphonate. 

Apart from testing various ratios of dextrin and naphthalene sulphonate, multiple naphthalene sulphonates have been trialled on a laboratory scale to determine if different manufacturers’ products produce different results. From this work a higher quality and cost effective product was trialled in the plant which has resulted in significant cost savings and further plant performance improvements compared to the initial brand which was trialled previously. The key quality specification for naphthalene sulphonate is having a sodium sulphate content of less than 5 per cent. The main difference between varying qualities of naphthalene sulphonates is that low quality naphthalene sulphonate is made with lime resulting in a sodium sulphate content greater than 5 per cent, whereas higher quality naphthalene sulphonate is made with caustic soda. Plant data shows that high quality naphthalene sulphonate is more effective as lower doses are required for improved plant performance. 

Consultation with reagent suppliers has led to investigations on the dosing method of naphthalene sulphonate in to the circuit. Historically, naphthalene sulphonate and dextrin have always been used in a blend as it was originally supplied this way. Work is currently being undertaken to determine if dosing naphthalene sulphonate separately during the primary grinding stage will yield further performance improvements by better coating the carbon surfaces and depressing the carbon minerals prior to flotation. The targeted depression of carbonaceous pyrite has led to test work targeting the depression of other gangue minerals reporting to the final concentrate. Through mineralogical investigation pyrrhotite has been found to be another mineral which is upgraded in the plant, from approximately 1.5 per cent in feed up to 6 per cent in the final concentrate, making it a significant concentrate diluent. 

Laboratory test work was carried out in 2015 to determine if there were any reagents capable of depressing pyrrhotite in the Copper Concentrator circuit. Reagents such as sodium metabisulphite (SMBS), DETA and specialty products as well as air sparging and the addition of lime were all tested on a laborator

y scale. The Laboratory test work and subsequent plant trial results concluded that there was no significant change in the final concentrate grade with the use of specialised pyrrhotite depressants. Although lime additions are affective for iron sulphide depression, the cost is prohibitive due to the required capital expenditure. At the time of writing there have been no successful trials for pyrrhotite depression, however the search continues for alternative methods. Further decreasing the amount of fully liberated gangue minerals in the Copper Concentrator’s final product represents one of the biggest potential copper grade and recovery improvements for the concentrator. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Naphthalene sulphonate has been in and out of use at the Mount Isa Mines No. 4 Copper Concentrator since it was first commissioned in 1973.  However, since its removal from the standard reagent dosing regime in the late 1990s, its value was not recognised by the current concentrator technical team until recently. A failure to pursue past research led to major drawbacks in project success as the 2013 plant trial results were misleading, resulting in an unsuccessful trial of naphthalene sulphonate in the Copper Concentrator. This investigation highlights that mineralogy holds the key for selecting reagents for improved plant performance outcomes. The more that is known about the mineral species present in the feed and concentrate, the more targeted test work can be, resulting in a more efficient and cost effective process. The use of naphthalene sulphonate at Mount Isa began some 50 years ago and findings from the early stages of this project are still relevant today.

###### Effects of pulp chemistry on plant and laboratory flotation modelling 

###### _A L Randriamanjatosoa_<sup>_1_</sup> _, C Greet_<sup>_2_</sup> _and G Small_<sup>_3_</sup> 

1. Senior Project Metallurgist, Magotteaux Australia Pty Ltd, Australia. Email: andry.lazamanana@magotteaux.com 

2. FAusIMM, Manager Minerals Processing Research, Magotteaux Australia Pty Ltd, Australia. Email: Christopher.greet@magotteaux.com 

3. MAusIMM, Manager Metallurgy - Development, Magotteaux Australia Pty Ltd, Australia. Email:grant.small@magotteaux.com 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

In flotation simulation models, the effects of pulp chemistry other than pH are often ignored and reduced to particles hydrophobicity or contact angle, neither of which can be measured readily in real time in an operating plant. The flotation response of a given sulphide mineral is known to be influenced and can be improved by changing the chemical characteristics of the pulp during grinding and flotation. The on-line measurement of pulp pH, potential, dissolved oxygen, temperature and oxygen demand of a process stream was completed with the PCM<sup>®</sup> (Pulp Chemistry Monitor) developed by Magotteaux in this study. The data generated together with relevant plant operating parameters were used to construct an empirical model and simulate the metallurgical performance of the ore. The same approach was also applied to laboratory flotation tests data using various grinding media types. The flotation models better fit the actual data when the chemistry of the pulp is taken into account. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Flotation is a complex physico-chemical process that is not yet fully understood. Prior to flotation, the ore is ground in order to liberate the valuable minerals from the gangue. Reagents are added to make the valuable minerals hydrophobic so that they can be separated from the gangue. Among many other parameters, the degree of hydrophobicity of the valuable minerals’ surface determines if they can attach to bubbles and report to the concentrate. Modelling the flotation process has been done with empirical to semi-empirical models for industrial applications (e.g. Coleman et al., 2007), with the intention of using these models to simulate plant performance so that better decisions can be made to potentially reduce costs as well as improve concentrate grades and recoveries. 

It is known that the flotation response of a given sulphide mineral is influenced and can be improved by changing the chemical characteristics of the pulp during grinding and flotation (e.g., Berglund, 1991; Trahar, 1984; Wei and Sandenbergh, 2010). Nevertheless, the effects of pulp chemistry other than pH are often ignored or reduced to particles hydrophobicity or contact angle in the existing models. Monitoring the sulphide minerals’ contact angle is difficult, however, and time consuming especially if the model is to be us

ed for process control purposes, where the feed grade, particles size distribution and mineralogy constantly vary with time. In contrast, it is possible with PCM<sup>®</sup> to monitor the pulp chemistry and relate the collected information to the metallurgy (Greet and Selga, 2016). The present study assesses the accuracy of empirical models with and without inclusion of some pulp chemical characteristics as input. Of particular interest are the effects of pH, pulp potential (Eh), dissolved oxygen concentration (DO), temperature and oxygen demand (OD). 

###### **Effects of pH** 

The effects of pH on sulphide minerals flotation have been extensively studied in the literature. It is commonly used to selectively separate sulphide minerals. For instance, high pH is often the preferred method to depress iron sulphides. On the other hand, the species present in a system depend on the Eh-pH relationship or Pourbaix diagram, which in turn influence the flotation response of sulphide minerals (Trahar 1984). pH, for example, affects the efficacy of activation and the activator consumption in the recovery of sphalerite as well as the stability of collectors such as xanthates. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### **Effects of pulp potential** 

The floatability of sulphide minerals is controlled by the redox potential (Guo and Yen, 2002; Healy, 1984). Trahar (1984) shows that sulphide minerals generally respond well to flotation under oxidising conditions. Collector induced flotation is often absent or poor in strongly reducing conditions (Trahar, 1984). Other works demonstrate that it is possible to improve the flotation response of some sulphide minerals by appropriately controlling the pulp potential (Qing et al., 2008; Uribe-Salas et al., 2000; Yuan et al., 1996). 

###### **Effects of dissolved oxygen content** 

Other studies also confirm that the flotation response of sulphide minerals usually improves with an increase in dissolved oxygen concentration of the pulp (Berglund, 1991; Graham and Heathcote, 1982; Ross and Van Deventer, 1985). Xanthate adsorption onto sulphide minerals surface increases with an increase in oxygen content (Leja, 1982; Plaskin and Bessonov, 1957). In some cases, aeration is used to increase the DO concentration to enhance the depression of pyrite. In addition, DO concentration enhances galvanic coupling in pyritic mineral systems leading to poorer metallurgical separations. 

###### **Effects of temperature** 

Although temperature is not a chemical measurement, it has its own influence on the thermodynamics of reactions that take place during flotation as well as the other chemical parameters (e.g. DO concentration). Therefore, it is worth investigating its impact on sulphide minerals flotation modelling. 

###### **Effects of oxygen demand** 

In an aerated system, the DO concentration of the pulp is a proxy for the oxygen demand (OD). A pulp with high oxygen demand has

near zero part per million dissolved oxygen concentration. Indeed, a very reactive system is expected to quickly consume a lot of oxygen, leaving insufficient dissolved oxygen concentration for collector adsorption. Carlson and Muir (1976) found the monitoring of oxygen demand useful when diagnosing metallurgical problems. 

###### **Effects of EDTA extractable iron** 

It is known that the precipitation of oxidation products or hydroxide species at the surface of sulphide minerals reduces their floatability (Senior and Trahar, 1991). Peng et al. (2003) found that iron oxidation species, mostly from the oxidation of grinding media, depress chalcopyrite particles. Ethylene diamine tetra acetic acid disodium salt (EDTA) extraction was used to quantify the extent of iron oxidation and model the laboratory flotation results in this study. An online measurement of EDTA extractable metal ions is expected to be incorporated with the PCM<sup>®</sup> in the near future for plant monitoring purposes. 

###### **DATA COLLECTION AND MODELLING** 

###### **Data** 

Three data sets will be examined. From our copper mine data base the laboratory data were taken from laboratory copper rougher flotation tests completed on different ores sourced from mines worldwide. Forged steel and different high chrome grinding media types are used to grind each ore to the same particles size distribution but with changes in chemistry of the pulp as the media type changes. The plant data, collected from copper rougher and cleaner flotation circuits from two copper mines, one in Australia and the other in Asia. 

The first plant treats an iron oxide hosted copper/gold ore containing a mixture of chalcopyrite and secondary copper sulphides with very low levels of pyrite. The rougher circuit is composed of six rougher and scavenger cells whose concentrates are combined and sent to the regrind and cleaner circuits for further processing. The copper rougher feed grade varies from 0.9 to 2.5 per cent with a P80 of 120 microns on average; and a copper rougher concentrate assaying nominally 19 per cent copper at around 88 per cent recovery is produced. 

The feed to the second plant is a porphyry copper ore. The copper mineralisation is mostly chalcopyrite. The ore also contains up to about 10 per cent pyrite. The cleaner circuit consists of seven cells and is fed by a Jameson and the recleaner tailing streams. On average, the copper cleaner feed grade is around 2 per cent but the cleaner concentrate grade can be as low as 3 per cent and as high as 16 per cent. As a result, the copper cleaner recovery varies between 88 and 97 per cent.

###### **Data collection** 

In all instances the pH, Eh, dissolved oxygen and temperature data were collected directly from the pulp. In the laboratory the pulp chemistry can be measured using a FLMV90 model TPS meter. And, in the two plants PCM<sup>®</sup> was used to c

ollect the pulp chemistry, whereby the process stream of interest is sampled continuously and pumped to PCM<sup>®</sup> . A subsample of this slurry is directed to the sample chamber, which is filled, the measurements (pH, Eh, dissolved oxygen and temperature) taken before the sample chamber is emptied and the probes cleaned with water and made ready to receive the next sample. The excess slurry and wash water are returned to the process. The raw data collected is sent to PCM<sup>®</sup> ’s on-board PLC where it is processed, stored and dispatched to the plant DCS (Greet and Selga, 2016). To ensure good quality and reliable data, PCM<sup>®</sup> requires one operator to calibrate the probes at least on a weekly basis.

###### **Data cleaning** 

Prior to modelling, the data was checked and cleansed. For the laboratory tests, the data cleaning consists of removing data sets with exceptionally high feed grades and very poor metallurgical performances. 

The PCM<sup>®</sup> and plant data cleansing was a little more complicated. Data were retrieved every minute from the historian to ensure that changes to the plant are captured when they occur. As the frequency of the actual measurement for PCM<sup>®</sup> is normally longer than one minute, the historian repeats the previously measured data until the next measurement cycle. The resulting duplicates and/or interpolated values between two cycles of measurement are removed from the data set. That is, only the data corresponding to the actual sampling cycles are used. Furthermore, obvious outliers such as unexpectedly high or low feed grade, low to no throughput surrounding shutdown times are removed from the data to be analysed. An in-house software application is used to clean the data.

Moreover, the model fit for Plant 1 recovery was poorer than its concentrate grade model due to scatters in tailing assays data that were used to calculate the copper recovery. Indeed, the tailing assays for Plant 1 varies between 0.05 to 0.44 per cent. 

The improvement in goodness of fit when using pulp chemistry is in agreement with the experimental results in the literature. The hydrophobicity of copper sulphide minerals decreases as a result of oxidation reactions during grinding and affects their flotation performance (Peres et al., 2005). Since the floatability of copper sulphide minerals is determined by the oxidation-reduction state of the pulp (Peres et al., 2005; Trahar, 1984; Yuan et al., 1996); the dependence of copper metallurgy on pulp potential Eh is expected to be seen in the data set. The better model is due to the correlation of the flotation results with the oxygen content and redox potential (Berglund, 1991). The galvanic interaction between the grinding media and/or grinding media debris and sulphide mineral species depletes the DO in the slurry and increases the OD. A simplified graphical representation of the relationship between concentrate grade, feed grade and OD for Plant 1 is shown in Figure 1 as an example. The lowest concentrate grades below 15 per cent copper correspond to the highest OD regardless of the changing feed grade from 0.9 to 2 per cent (zones 9, 8 and 7). In contrast and for similar copper feed grade, the concentrate grade increased from below 15 percent to above 25 percent when the OD decreased from zone 7 to zones 4 and 2, for example (Figure 1). It is likely that the highest concentrate grade in zones 5 and 6 with a feed grade above 1.5 per cent in Figure 1 is not attributed to the oxygen demand but other operating parameters.

###### **COLLECTOR OPTIMISATION** 

Prior to conducting collector optimisation studies, sensitivity analyses were completed on Model 2 to confirm the effects of pulp chemistry on metallurgy. Taking the data from Plant 2, the better model using pulp chemistry (Model 2) was used to optimise the collector dosage rates. That is, the collector dosage at the first and fifth cleaner cells that gives at least one percent improvement in modelled cleaner concentrate grade without deteriorating the cleaner recovery. To achieve at least a one percent increase in copper concentrate grade the model suggested that the collector addition to the first cleaner cell could be reduced 43 percent of the time, increased 21 per cent of the time and left unchanged for the remaining 36 per cen

t of the time (Figure 4). On the other hand, collector addition to the fifth cleaner cell could be reduced 32 per cent of the time, increased 30 per cent of the time and left as is for the remaining 38 per cent of the time (Figure 5). These results show some potential not only in cost reduction but also in metallurgical improvements, especially that collector addition rates for Plant 2 were decided at the discretion of the plant operator based on the operator’s observation and assessment of the plant’s performance. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Independence Group’s Jaguar Mine treats a polymetallic ore producing a copper concentrate and zinc concentrate. Effective separation of the sulfides requires relatively fine grinding with flotation feed P80 of about 75µm. Zn losses to final tails are greater than 60 per cent and <32 µm. 

When magnetic conditioning was first installed in 2010 it showed about an 8 per cent reduction of zinc in final tail and on some ores a similar benefit for silver as well. 

Current testwork is showing about a 12 per cent reduction in zinc and silver in final tail, consistent with the original testwork. Sizing of the final tail during the tests showed that the reduction of zinc and silver losses were only in the <32 µm fraction, as would be expected from an aggregation process. However, the most surprising result was about a 4 per cent reduction in zinc and silver in the plant feed with a >99 per cent statistical certainty. The reduction in zinc and silver in the feed is also only in the <32 µm fraction. Therefore, because the magnetic conditioning of Zn flotation feed cannot impact plant ore feed grade the hypothesis is that the magnetic conditioning is reducing the fi

ne mineral from downstream processes, like filtering and thickening, returning to the plant feed in the recycled process water. This hypothesis is consistent with plant observation of dirty concentrate thickener overflow and measurements of solids in the overflow, as well as the average % Zn grade in cyclone overflow that correlates with the magnetic conditioning ON and OFF days. This paper presents these plant test results. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Independence Group (IGO) operates the Jaguar Base Metals Project (Jaguar Operation), located approximately 60 km north of Leonora, in the north-east Goldfields. 

The project comprises several deposits which have been mined historically including the Teutonic Bore deposit in the 1980s; the Jaguar deposit 2007-2014; and the Bentley deposit, which is now the main source of ore to the Jaguar Base Metals Concentrator. 

The Bentley zinc-copper-silver-gold massive sulfide deposit was discovered in 2008 and brought into production as an underground mine in 2011. The Bentley mine ore’s value resides in the sphalerite, chalcopyrite and silver minerals. The ore is processed through the concentrator at approximately 500 000 t/a, yielding a copper concentrate with payable silver and gold and a separate zinc concentrate with payable silver. 

The processing plant comminution train consists of a single stage crushing circuit utilising a jaw crusher, followed by a SAG and Ball Mill each in closed circuit with classifying hydrocyclones. The product is a flotation feed slurry with a target P80 of 75 µm. 

Sequential flotation separates the copper concentrate first, followed by the zinc concentrate. Two stirred media detritors operate in closed circuit with classifying hydrocyclones, preceding each flotation circuit’s cleaning cells. The product is a copper cleaner feed and a zinc cleaner feed each with a P80 of approximately 10-20 µm.  The concentrates are dewatered using thickening and filtration, with the final copper concentrate containing between 23-25 per cent Cu and the final zinc concentrate containing 47-50 per cent Zn. Figure 1 shows a simplified process flow diagram for the Jaguar concentrator. 

A review of the cyclosized historical monthly composite samples of the final plant tails, as shown in Figure 2, indicated that approximately 70-80 per cent of the zinc metal losses to the tails stream are consistently in the -33 µm fraction, with approximately 60 per cent in the -11 µm size fraction. Ausmetec’s Proflote unit uses magnetic aggregation to increase recovery of fine paramagnetic minerals, such as the chalcopyrite and sphalerite ores processed at Jaguar. Figure 2 – Zinc distribution in historical cyclosized final tails samples. ###### **HISTORICAL TESTING** Magnetic conditioning has been shown at many plants and on a range of sulphide minerals, to increase the flotation recovery of <38 µm paramagnetic minerals. These have been published and include studies by: Englehardt, Ellis and Lumsden, 2005; Rivett, Wood and Lumsden 2007; Wilding and Lumsden 2010; Zoetbrood, Vass and Lumsden 2011; Lacouture _et al_ 2016. Less than 38 µm, liberated, paramagnetic, minerals will selectively aggregate if magnetised by a high gradient magnetic field. Aggregated particles will have greater momentum, therefore, increasing their collision efficiency with the bubble and increasing the flotation recovery and the flotation kinetics of these aggregated fine paramagnetic minerals. Generally, in sulphide flotation the diluent minerals in the ore, pyrite and gangue, are not strongly paramagnetic and are therefore, unaffected by the magnetic field. In 2010 the Jaguar plant was treating Jaguar ore and magnetic conditioning was evaluated in both the copper and zinc circuits (Wilding and Lumsden, 2010). This plant evaluation, using a paired “t” test, showed that magnetic conditioning substantially reduced the losses of paramagnetic chalcopyrite and sphalerite to tails. It also improved the chalcopyrite selectivity in the Cu circuit, reducing sphalerite reporti

ng to copper concentrate (probably through reduced entrainment of aggregated fine sphalerite). A further stage of plant testing, installing the magnetic conditioning on the zinc regrind cyclone overflow in the zinc cleaner circuit showed a further 1 per cent increase in zinc recovery. Interestingly this cleaner testwork showed that the silver recovery could also be increased to zinc concentrate on some of the ore types treated at Jaguar. This 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

could be because some silver sulphide minerals, like freibergite or tennatite-tetrahedrite are also paramagnetic, (Holloway, Clarke and Lumsden 2008) or it could be silver associated with the paramagnetic sphalerite. 

It was at Jaguar that magnetic conditioning clearly demonstrated that not only was it selective against nonparamagnetic minerals, as would be expected, but that it was selective between paramagnetic minerals. Results were consistent with homogeneous aggregation, rather than heterogeneous aggregation of paramagnetic minerals. Therefore, the magnetic conditioning in the Cu circuit not only reduced the Cu losses to the Cu tail, but also reduced the zinc in copper concentrate and increased the zinc recovery in the zinc concentrate. This has now been demonstrated at a number of other sites where separation of two paramagnetic minerals occurs (Musuku, Muzinda and Lumsden, 2015; Lacouture _et al_ 2016). 

From the publication by Wilding and Lumsden (2010) the key metallurgical improvements achieved with magnetic conditioning were in the copper circuit were: a 10 per cent reduction in average copper in final tail to 99 per cent level of confidence; a 7 per cent reduction in zinc grade in copper concentrate to 93 per cent level of confidence; a 1.8 per cent increase in zinc recovery to zinc concentrate to 99 per cent level of confidence; and a 10 per cent reduction in zinc in final tail to 97 per cent level of confidence. 

Subsequently, the magnetic conditioning remained ON continuously in the copper circuit and a second installation was carried out in the zinc circuit. The results in the zinc circuit were: a further 8 per cent reduction in zinc in final tail to 97 per cent level of confidence and a 1 per cent increase in zinc recovery to zinc concentrate to 98 per cent level of confidence. The 2016/17 trial on the Bentley ore reflects similar results. 

###### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

The magnetic conditioning in the zinc circuit is currently installed on both the zinc rougher feed and the zinc cleaner feed (zinc regrind cyclone overflow). The test on Bentley ore was initiated in late 2016 as a 2 day ON, 2 day OFF test with consecutive ON/OFF and OFF/ON days paired. The magnetic conditioning was turned ON or OFF automatically every 48 hours at the same time the shift composite samples were retrieved from the plant multi stream analyser (MSA) for analysis. 

The shift samples for the copper tail and final tail for the two con

ossible feedback mechanism is via the concentrate filtrate that reports to the process water via the zinc concentrate thickener overflow. The zinc thickener overflow can be directed to the process water tank, or to the tails hopper which reports to the tailings dam. Water is returned to the process water tanks via a decant pump. At 65 t/h plant feed, there is about 80 m<sup>3</sup> /h of process water, therefore, the calculated process water content is about 2.5 g/L of zinc, or about 4.2 g/L of sphalerite to give 200 kg/h of extra zinc. The losses to the Jaguar zinc thickener overflow have been documented for a number of years and instigated the replacement of the zinc thickener feed well (Thompson 2016). On days when the concentrate filter and thickener are not operating effectively the concentrate thickener overflow has been measured to contain about 4.0 g/L of solids and it is proposed that these solids are overwhelmingly sphalerite and are fine in order to appear in the thickener overflow. On other days the solids content of the zinc concentrate thickener overflow is lower. Nevertheless, the quantities are consistent with the observed difference in plant feed. 

Suspicion fell on the zinc concentrate filter and the filtrate because the final zinc concentrate has a P80 of 30-40 µm. The filter cloth supplier suggested that losses through the filter of 5 µm -7.5 µm mineral could be 4 per cent, with losses below this size even greater. Moreover, the 200 kg/h of extra zinc is about 4 per cent of the approximately 4-6 t/h of zinc filtered at Jaguar. Again, the data is consistent with what is observed in the plant. This seems a logical and plausible hypothesis and there are periods at Jaguar where the process water is particularly dirty that would support this hypothesis. On dirty water days the zinc thickener overflow was found to contain significant zinc. This load can build as the fine sphalerite recirculates in the plant. 

This hypothesis also has implications on the metallurgical accounting at Jaguar. The plant feed grade sample is measuring the recirculating zinc as fresh zinc. The feed grade when the magnetic conditioning was OFF was about 5 per cent higher than when ON. It also means that the concentrate assay is not accurate because it is measuring as recovered zinc, zinc that is actually being lost back to the plant feed. This zinc is actually being measured as reporting to concentrate but is just recirculating in the plant and a proportion would eventually recirculate out to tailings. This is most important when it comes to silver assays where the silver recovery calculation is very dependent on the zinc feed and tail assay to determine the weight of concentrate recovered. The use of these three sample assays introduce inaccuracies in metallurgical accounting due to the recirculating zinc unless allowance is made for the amount of metal recirculating. 

Another possible route for the return of some fine zinc in the process water could be

via the tailings. At Jaguar there is no tailings thickener and the tailings discharge is close to where the process water is extracted from the dam. When the magnetic conditioning is OFF there is more fine zinc in the tail and if settling in the tailings is insufficient then this can also recirculate back to plant feed. This recirculating zinc adds to the zinc assay in the feed. However, if it is recovered to zinc concentrate at a similar rate as in the first pass then for the metallurgical balance this increases the apparent zinc recovery, increases the apparent zinc feed grade and to a lesser extent increases the zinc in tail. Although the mechanism is different, this idea is not dissimilar to gold operations where gold in solution returning from the TSF to the plant in the process water needs to be measured and included in the metallurgical accounting.

###### _C Smith_<sup>_1_</sup> _, K Hadler_<sup>_2_</sup> _and J Cilliers_<sup>_3_</sup>

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Unstable flotation froths, that burst before they overflow, produce no concentrate. Increasing the froth stability to improve recovery is therefore an obvious control strategy. Froth stability can be measured readily as the fraction of air entering the flotation cell that overflows as froth, rather than bursting on the surface; the ‘air recovery.’ Air rate is one of the most significant variables affecting froth stability. 

It is interesting that froth stability (air recovery) is maximised at a specific air rate, above or below which it decreases. It is important for metallurgists to realise that this maximum froth stability also produces the maximum mineral recovery, without compromising concentrate grade. Flotation cells must be operated at the air rate that produces the highest air recovery. 

The peak air recovery (PAR) to maximum mineral recovery relationship was first demonstrated by Hadler and Cilliers in 2009.  Since then, the relationship between PAR and flotation performance has been widely explored; varying air rate, froth depth and particle size. Industrially, reducing the flotation bank air rate to achieve PAR yielded better mineral recoveries than other down-the-bank air rate profiles. 

In this paper, we present an overview of these key developments and findings in flotation optimisation based on PAR. Furthermore, using new industrial data, we show that PAR is not just applicable to rougherscavenger cells, but also to flotation columns. Finally, we consider the future application of such an optimising control concept. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

In this paper we discuss the Peak in Air Recovery (PAR), review its applicability as a measure of flotation froth stability and examine its potential for use as a control concept in flotation. 

Following a background, detailing the PAR concept, and some of the early findings a series of case studies will be presented broadening the range of application of the PAR concept upon industrial systems. 

###### **THE PAST: BACKGROUND** 

###### **PAR and froth stability** 

Air recovery is the fraction of air added to a flotation cell that overflows that cells lip as unburst bubbles. Air recovery has been shown to go through a peak as the air rate is increased, at constant froth depth (Barbian _et al_ (2006) and Hadler and Cilliers (2009)) and also to go through a peak as the froth depth is increased at constant air rate (Hadler _et al_ 2012). 

The concept of a fractional air recovery was first introduced by Moys (1984) where the horizontal velocity of the froth could be related to the froth stability, which was also defined as the air recovered into the launder in the form of unbroken bubbles. Woodburn _et al_ (1994) used the concept of a fractional air recovery in a semiempirical froth-based flotation model. Air recoveries were first measured industrially by Ventura-Medina and Cilliers (2002

). To determine air recoveries requires a measurement of the volume of air added to the cell, _Qair, in_ , and a measurement of the volume of air overflowing the cell lip, _Q air, over_ . The air added is often measured by in-situ instrumentation, but can be measured or corroborated by external measurements such as the Anglo Platinum bubble sizer. The volume of air overflowing can be determined by measuring the height the overflowing froth achieves above the cell lip, _hf_ , and the velocity of the froth across the lip, _v f_ , combined with the length of the cell lip, _L_ , and also the air content of the overflowing froth, _ξ_ , Equation 1. =<sup>ℎ𝑓</sup> Equation 1 𝑎<sup>𝑎𝑎,𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑎𝑎</sup> 𝑎<sup>𝑣𝑣𝑓𝐿</sup> 𝛼𝛼=<sup>𝑄𝑄𝑎</sup> 𝑎𝑎,𝑎𝑎𝑖𝑖 𝑎𝑎,𝑎𝑎𝑖𝑖 𝑄𝑄 𝑄𝑄 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The height of the froth above the cell lip and be determined by placing a laser distance meter a known height above the lip and subtracting the measured height of the froth surface from this value. The froth velocity can be measured using a machine vision system, of which there are many commercially available, Aldrich _et al_ (2010) provide a review of such systems. The lip length can be determined from either plant drawings or onsite measurements. It is important to use the overflowing lip length, that is to say, the lip length across which froth actually overflows. The air content of the froth is more challenging to measure accurately, but in most cases of standard operation tends to be very low (<5 per cent) for much of the froth height (Neethling _et al_ 2003). 

Barbian _et al_ (2005) correlated air recovery measurements with dynamic froth stability measurements, produced via a modified Bikerman test, in both laboratory and industrial tests. This data showed that the higher the air recovery, or the fewer bubbles which burst on the froth surface, then the higher the froth stability. In other words, the Peak Air Recovery corresponds to the peak froth stability. 

Hadler and Cilliers (2009) showed that operating a row of cells at the air rates yielding PAR, as opposed to higher or lower air rates, yielded the highest recovery of valuable minerals from the row. Smith _et al_ (2010) further showed that operating a row of cells at the air rates yielding PAR, as opposed to operating at different distributions of the same total air volume to the row yielded the highest recovery. PAR was thus proposed as a control concept via which to optimise both the total amount of air added to a row of cells and the distribution of that air between the cells in the row. 

It was postulated that PAR occurred due to the effect of increasing air rate on the bubble loading and the bubble motion. At low air rates, the bubbles are heavily laden with solid particles, which armour them against rupture, but the bubbles are also slow moving and so many still burst before they can overflow. At high air rates, conversely, the bubbles are now fast moving

, but have a low solids loading and so many still burst before they can overflow. Intermediate air rates balance these two effects of bubble loading and bubble motion and allow a maximum to overflow, yielding a peak in air recovery. 

Hadler _et al_ (2012) performed a study examining air recovery with both air rate and froth depth variation. It was found that there was a PAR with air rate at each froth depth, and the air rate yielding PAR tended to increase as the froth depth was increased. In addition, they found that it was possible to achieve a PAR by varying froth depth only, at a constant air rate. The hypothesis for this follows that for PAR with air rate, and the impact increasing froth depth has on bubble loading and bubble motion. 

At shallow froth depths, the bubbles are highly mobile, but only lightly loaded, and so burst before they can overflow. This is akin to the high air rate. For a deep froth, on the other hand, the bubbles are now heavily loaded, and thus resistant to bursting, but move very slowly, and so burst before overflowing. The intermediate froth depth balances these two effects. 

###### **Flotation Control** 

Sheen and Cilliers (2011) reviewed flotation control options, and came to the conclusion that, despite the large body of literature devoted to it, there have been very few successful implementations of Advanced Flotation Control or Optimising Flotation Control techniques into industrial applications. The majority of the successful implementations reported have been around so called mass-pull control systems, such as that reported by Supomo _et al_ (2008). In these systems the velocity of the overflowing froth is measured by machine vision and then the control system adjusts either the air rate or froth depth to achieve the desired mass pull. The basis of the concept being that recovery, mass pull and velocity are linked, such that higher velocities tend to yield higher mass pulls which yield higher recoveries. The relationships between these parameters will be unique to a plant and are empirical in nature. 

Hadler _et al_ (2010) presented data from two case studies examining this concept. The first study, in which the air rate was increased from the “As-Found” condition to yield the PAR condition, agreed with the mass pull control philosophy, in that as the air rate was increased, the froth velocity increased and this led to an increased mass pull and increased recovery from the cells being examined. In the second case study, however, to achieve PAR the air rates were required to be reduced from the “As-Found” condition. This resulted in an increased recovery (the basis behind the PAR concept), but for generally lower froth velocities in each cell and significantly lower mass pulls; especially in the cells towards the end of the row. 

This suggests that the PAR concept might be a useful one towards Optimising Flotation Control. One additional advantage of using PAR as the basis of a control concept is the clea

r set point to control to; the Peak. This removes any need for an operator to manually set a target value to be achieved, such as a mass pull or velocity, and any biasing this might introduce into the plants operation between different operators. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 ###### **THE PRESENT: CASE STUDIES** ###### **Case Study 1: Cu cleaner columns** In the studies reported to date (Barbian _et al_ , 2006; Hadler _et al_ , 2006; Hadler and Cilliers, 2010; Smith _et al_ , 2010; Hadler _et al_ , 2012) the PAR concept has been applied exclusively to mechanical, forced air flotation cells operating in a rougher or scavenger role. It was therefore decided to focus the majority of effort into ensuring these cells were maintained at the air rate yielding PAR, by performing multiple optimisations upon them over the duration of the trial.

The circuit included, and utilised, a number of automated courier systems to provide online, almost real time, analysis of the grades of key streams. The data for the Zn feed stream and Zn tails stream across the testwork period is shown on Figure 7 and Figure 8 respectively, while Figure 9 shows the circuit recovery determined from these two measurements. The time scale on all three charts is identical. The three charts have also been annotated with notes showing the data covered by the pre-optimisation and post-optimisation periods (the data used in the before and after analysis) and the PAR optimisation period. The data on the charts is the as measured data, the daily average and the average across the entire assessment period. What can be seen with the feed grade, Figure 7, is that the pre-optimisation period had a feed grade on average that was above the entire period average, while the optimisation and post-optimisation periods had feed grades on average below the period average. The tails grade, Fi

The low tails grade in the post-optimisation period is certain, in-part, to be related to the low feed grade, but as there was a low feed grade in the optimisation period and a high tails grade this suggests there was another contributor to the low tails grade: the recovery. The recovery trend, Figure 9, shows high Zn recovery in the pre- and post- optimisation periods. 

Two methods to assess the data and attempt to yield the performance benefit of the operation at PAR were utilised: 

1. A linear regression model with the before and after (ie not-PAR and PAR) conditions accounted for as a dummy variable; given a value of 0 and 1 respectively 

2. A comparison of regression lines between the feed Zn grade and the Zn recovery in the two periods (before and after) 

The first analysis yielded a highly statistically significant regression model, with a significance parameter > 99.99 per cent, in which both the feed Zn grade and the operating condition (PAR and not-PAR) were significant parameters. The coefficient associated with the operating condition can be taken as the change to Zn recovery obtained by operating at PAR. The value of this coefficient was 0.28 per cent, with a significance of greater than 90 per cent. In other words, this analysis suggests PAR yielded a Zn recovery increase of 0.28 per cent at a confidence level of 90 per cent (at equivalent feed grades). 

The second analysis, Figure 10, showed that the two regression lines have, statistically, the same slope, but statistically different y-axis intercepts, at a confidence of greater than 95 per cent. In addition, the mean separation between the lines was statistically different, at a confidence level of 98 per cent. The magnitude of this separation, projected on the y-axis, is 0.35 per cent with the after optimisation being higher than the before optimisation (called ‘on’ and ‘off’ respectively Figure 10). In other words, for the same Zn feed grade, operating the circuit at the PAR condition yielded a 0.35 per cent improvement in Zn recovery, with a 98 per cent confidence level that this improvement is not zero.

###### **Case Study 3: Self-Aerated cells** 

In the final study considered in this paper, PAR was applied to a self-aerated style of flotation cell. In this type of cell, the action of the impeller produces a vacuum, by dispersing air into the cell, and this vac

uum draws further air in to the cell to be dispersed and so on. The degree of aeration can be manipulated by adjusting either the rotational speed of the impeller or the submersion depth of the impeller. When in operation it is not standard to adjust the impeller speed, or indeed its height on the shaft, and thus the control variable adjusted is the froth depth, which varies the head above the impeller and thereby affects the aeration achieved. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

A preliminary study on this type of cell, measuring air recovery while varying the froth depth, showed that the air recovery could be varied by doing this, Figure 11a, but it was complex to decouple the effects of froth depth and air rate on the recovery,  Figure 11b. To this end a means to decouple the effects of the two variables was examined. 

There have been several studies (Gomez _et al_ , 2007) describing the retrofitting of self-aerated flotation cells as forced air flotation cells, via the addition of air compressors and suitable means of transferring the air to the cell. This was not feasible in this case, due to the need to minimise cost. As such, for this trial, as a means to decouple the aeration from the froth depth and allow the two to be varied somewhat independently, a collar was fitted around the air intake ports of a cell, with a chimney fitted to it (Harding _et al_ , 2012). The chimney contained a butterfly valve as a means of manipulating the air rate to the cell. The air rate was measured via an anemometer a suitable straight line distance below the intake port to the chimney, and the corresponding superficial gas velocities showed strong agreement with those measured in the cell pulp using a bubble sizer device (e.g. Gomez and Finch, 2007), Figure 12. 

The maximum achievable aeration was therefore still dependent upon the height of the froth in the cell, air rates lower than the maximum could be set, and maintained, despite froth depth variations to the cell, by adjusting the valve position, as can be seen in Figure 13. The data to the top of this figure shows what happens to the air rate when froth depth is varied on an unmodified self-aerated cell, as the froth depth is increased the aeration increases and vice versa for decreasing the froth depth. The bottom shows installing the equipment detailed above provides the ability to maintain an air rate independently of froth depth variations. This system was used to vary the air rate, at a constant froth depth, and the air recovery, along with the copper recovery and concentrate grade were measured. Figure 14 shows that it was possible to obtain a slight Peak in Air Recovery by shutting the valve to limit the aeration to the cell. Figure 15 shows that operating at the air rate giving PAR yielded the highest cu recovery of all the air rates tested, and also the optimum operating point in terms of concentrate Cu grade. The data shows the same trend as th

Figure 15 – Cu recovery and concentrate grade variation with air rate. ###### **THE FUTURE: FUTURE DIRECTION** In the case studies presented herein, and also to date in the literature, PAR was set in each cell by manual means. The next logical advance is to utilise an automated control system, based on froth measurements, to set and maintain cells at PAR. Such a system has been proposed; Wellwood _et al_ (2009) based on feedback control and Harding and Smith (2013) with feed forward control components to the control loop. Shean _et al_ (2017) published a study exploring the development and usage of such a system on a large scale (70 l) laboratory flotation cell. No studies have been published to date examining industrial application. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 Direct comparisons of a Peak Air Recovery control system with other control systems, such as mass pullbased control, would also be advantageous. Given the postulated reason for PAR occurring with froth depth and air rate, it seems reasonable that it might be able to achieve a PAR by varying other parameters, such as reagent dosage or even particle size, along with others which impact the structure of the froth. These areas have yet to be fully explored. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** The case studies shown in this paper highlight that air recovery optimisation can be applied across a range of cell types, operating in a range of duties to optimise metallurgical performance. In addition, the concept can be applied to all cells in a circuit to optimise its metallurgical performance. PAR was set on column cells operating as cleaners and also on self-aspirated mechanical cells, modified to decouple froth depth and aeration. In both cases the air rate yielding PAR also provided the optimum metallurgical performance, with the highest recovery and concentrate grade. Air rates

lower than that giving PAR typically gave similar concentrate grades as the PAR condition, but for lower recoveries, while air rates higher than that giving PAR tended to much lower concentrate grades, but similar recoveries as the PAR condition. 

The air recovery optimisation concept was also applied to a circuit consisting of forced air mechanical cells and column cells in a range of duties, roughers, scavengers, cleaners and cleaner-scavengers. The results showed that the total aeration to the circuit was reduced, while the cumulative air recovery was increased. This led to a 0.3 per cent recovery improvement across the circuit, significant at 90 per cent. 

The future direction for air recovery optimisation includes the development and testing of an automated optimisation control system, providing the air rate set point to yield optimum metallurgical performance based on air recovery measurements. Such a control system would be strengthened by knowledge of how the air rate yielding PAR varied with other changes to the circuit, for example feed grade, feed rate or particle size. This could then be followed by direct comparisons of the air recovery optimisation concept with other flotation control strategies, such as mass pull control. Inclusion of operating parameters other than air rate, such as froth depth or reagent addition, would also be a logical advancement of the concept.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Cadia Hill concentrator at Newcrest’s Cadia Operations has undergone several modifications and upgrades to treat an increased throughput rate of harder ore from the Ca

dia East block cave mine. Subsequent to the commissioning of the expanded circuit, the flotation cleaner block has undergone a systematic optimisation programme tackling all facets of circuit operation. This included debottlenecking circuit constraints and installation of Jameson cell technology to enhance copper and gold recovery while rejecting fluorine and gangue from the concentrate. This paper outlines the improvements over the course of the project and results obtained from the implemented actions. ###### **INTRODUCTION** The Ore Treatment department at Cadia mine operate two separate concentrators. Concentrator 1 (formerly the Cadia Hill Concentrator) and Concentrator 2 (formerly known as the Ridgeway Concentrator). The combined design throughput rate is 26 Mtpa, however debottlenecking completed since construction will see the throughput increase to 30Mtpa by June 2018. A simplified flowsheet of the Cadia concentrators is shown in Figure 1. Ore is crushed underground and conveyed to the surface stockpile where it is fed to the two concentrators. Concentrator 1 consists of a secondary crushed HPGR fed 40’ SAG mill, which feeds three parallel ball mill lines. The nominal target grind size is a P80 of 150μm. Two 10MW ball mills feed what is known as the T1T2 flotation circuit while the 3rd ball mill (16MW) feeds a separate flotation circuit (T3) that will be discussed later. Each grinding line has gravity gold recovery and flash flotation on the cyclone underflow. The Concentrator 2 32’ SAG mill (7MW) is fed from a newly constructed tertiary crushing circuit, with a ball mill (7MW) and secondary / tertiary grinding Vertimills. The primary grind size in this plant is lower than that achieved in Concentrator 1, typically around a P 80 of 120μm. The gravity effort in Concentrator 2 is higher than Concentrator 1, with a higher proportion of the cyclone underflow sent to gravity concentration and the flash flotation units. The flotation concentrates from each plant are thickened separately before being combined in thickened concentrate stock tanks. Positive displacement pumps transfer this slurry via buried pipeline to the Cadia Dewatering Facility located in the town of Blayney. The concentrate is dewatered to 9 per cent moisture and railed to Port Kembla for storage and shipping. The upper, copper-rich portion of the deposit is stratigraphically controlled within the upper volcaniclastic unit. Sulphide mineralisation is predominantly chalcopyrite, with lesser quantities of bornite and pyrite. Gold grade increases with depth as disseminated chalcopyrite levels decrease and disseminated and vein bornite levels increase. The deeper gold-rich zone is centred on a core of steeply dipping sheeted quartz-calcitebornite-chalcopyrite veins. The highest gold grades are associated with bornite-rich veins. Molybdenite forms a mineralised blanket above and to the east of the higher grade gold envelope. Figure 12 – Stage recovery for Concentrator 1 cleaner/cleaner scavenger circuit. ###### **Cleaner circuit hygiene** In 2014, the throughput rate and copper feed grade often exceeded the design capacity of the Concentrator 1 flotation circuit. This exposed several bottlenecks in the concentrate handling system such as overflowing launders, overflowing distribution boxes and overloading trash screens (refer to Figure 13). As a result the flotation circuit suffered from lower copper and gold recovery and unnecessary circulation of concentrate through the circuit sump pumps creating process instability and generally poor plant hygiene. Ultimately these events reduced operator confidence in the process and distracted them from optimising the circuit. Several modifications were made to improve concentrate handling in these areas of the circuits including increased launder depths, modified screen designs and modified pipework. None of which eliminated the requirement for additional cleaner capacity. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 Figure 13 – Left, overflowing cleaner concentrate launder, top right, overflowing concentrate box, bottom right, overloaded trash screen. ###### **Circuit modification and modelling** An immediate response to relieving the cleaner circuit bottleneck was to open the circuit up and reduce recirculating loads. This was achieved by redirecting the cleaner scavenger concentrate directly to the recleaner circuit, rather than to cleaner feed, to give the material the shortest path to final concentrate and to double the residence time in the cleaner stage. In order to predict the response of this change, a basic floatability component flotation model was built of the Concentrator 1 cleaning circuit using a block survey conducted by site on the 17th September 2013. The model was based on the AMIRA P9 flotation modelling methodology (Harris et al, 2002) where the feed is split into a number of floatability fractions to describe the observed distributed flotation rate. Only the cleaner block was considered in the model and resulting simulations. The recovery of a single floatability fraction across a single perfectly mixed cell is described by: Where: _R_ is the recovery of fraction, _P_ – the floatability of the frac

tion, _Sb_ – the bubble surface area flux of the cell, _Rf_ – the froth recovery of the floatability fraction in the cell, _ENT_ – entrainment parameter (size dependent) and _Rw_ – the water recovery across the cell. 

A total of three components were used to describe the flotation of each mineral species – fast floating, slow floating and non-floating. _ENT_ was estimated based on the particle size distribution using values reported by Johnson et al, 1974, and a simple water recovery was employed. 

In order to simplify the model, the term _Sb_ * _Rf_ was combined into a single cell scale up number, C for each bank of flotation cells. The C parameter is a measure of how hard the cell is pulled, which would be adjusted in practise by changing froth depth and/or air addition rate. Monte-Carlo style simulations were completed with the resulting model by varying the C parameter to develop grade-recovery curves for comparing different circuit configurations. 

The survey and modelling process were initiated to address two key issues: 

1. The cleaner circuit in C1 was underperforming, cleaner block recoveries were only ~80 per cent gold and copper versus well over 90 per cent as an industry benchmark; and 

2. With the ramp-up of Cadia East, higher copper feed grades resulted in a bottleneck around the cleaners. The Cadia East feasibility study identified that the cleaning circuit would require expansion in future years, however no commitment to an implementation timeline or process design was made.

###### **CLEANER CIRCUIT UPGRADES** 

###### **Concentrator 1 cleaner upgrade - stage 1** 

From the cleaner flotation modelling it was identified that future copper and gold recovery would be significantly impacted if the capacity of the cleaning circuit was not increased. A project was instigated to expand the flotation capacity in the Concentrator 1 circuit. The intent of the expansion covered two main criteria: 

1. Ensuring sufficient cleaner capacity for the next two years of operation until further cleaner expansion could be justified based on increasing mill throughput and copper feed grades; and 

2. Effective rejection of liberated fluorite to ensure a more saleable flotation concentrate and reduction or elimination of penalties. 

Based on this criteria, James

on cell technology was considered to be the best option for expanded cleaning circuit capacity. This was principally due to the documented benefits of the unit in the cleaner flowsheet as well as the ability to reject entrained non-sulphide gangue, in this case fluorite, by a combination of deeper froth and wash water. While there was limited information on the performance of the technology when specifically applied to fine free gold flotation, Newcrest was able to leverage from previous experience of debottlenecking the Telfer cleaning circuit by installation of two (E3432/8) Jameson cells (Seaman et al., 2012). 

To confirm the ability of the Jameson cell to deliver on these criteria, a pilot cell was installed within the Concentrator 1 flotation circuit. Results from the pilot installation found a fluorine upgrade ratio between 0.2 – 0.35, compared to a 1:1 ratio in the existing circuit, and a copper stage recovery of up to 70 per cent. Confirmation of the technology led to the installation of a 24 downcomer Jameson cell (B6500/24) primarily in a cleaner scalper duty (refer to Figure 15). 

Several options were considered in the design phase including the addition of two smaller Jameson cells; one as a cleaner scalper and the other as a recleaner. Ultimately the decision was made to add the Jameson cell in the cleaner scalper duty to maximise cleaner recovery in the first instance and defer capital for a final recleaner cell to improve grade when higher copper feed grades/tonnage necessitated. As an interim compromise, an option was built into the design to allow the conventional recleaner concentrate to report to the single Jameson cell rather than to final concentrate. The benefits of the Jameson cell in a cleaner scalper 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

duty have been well documented (Bennett et al, 2012; Seaman et al, 2012; and Huynh et al, 2014). Principally, the short residence time and high flotation rates of the Jameson cell capitalise on the fast floating particles with cleaned surfaces immediately exiting the regrind stage. The application of froth washing in the Jameson cell significantly improves the rejection of fine gangue otherwise recovered by entrainment, particularly fluorite in this application. Piloting and analysis was completed in February 2014, with commissioning of the new circuit taking place in November the same year. 



Figure 15 – Concentrator 1 cleaner circuit upgrade – stage 1, installation of cleaner scalper Jameson cell. 

Commissioning of the new Jameson cell highlighted several challenges that were not anticipated in the original design. Pumping of concentrate posed the most significant issue as the froth produced by the Jameson cell concentrate was far more tenacious than expected. Significant upgrades to the concentrate pump and feed hopper were instigated post commissioning to accommodate the high froth factor. The froth also significantly impacted the fina

l concentrate thickener, with surface froth that was difficult to disperse. The installation of a de-aeration unit to the feed-well was finalised in 2015, successfully breaking down the froth and reducing occurrences of dirty thickener overflow. 

It was also found that the Jameson cell was highly sensitive to the copper metal units in the concentrator feed. When the feed units to Concentrator 1 dropped below the design (9 tph of copper in the flotation feed) the cell would struggle to form a consistent froth. A short term solution for operators was to increase the units internal recycle load and allow mineral to build up in the froth. This was not sustainable as it lead to cycles of high copper and gold reporting to CST. A longer term solution was devised which involved the installation of moulded rubber sections that slide over the concentrate lip, to reduce lip length and improve froth mobility. In contrast, when high copper units were fed to the Jameson cell, for example when the conventional recleaner concentrate was fed to the unit with the rougher concentrate, it was difficult to effectively ‘unload’ the Jameson cell leading to large recirculating loads and a drop in overall circuit recovery. 

In spite of the post commissioning issues, the value of the project was immediate. A multivariable regression analysis of the pre and post installation, using the Jameson cell operation as the dummy variable, showed a significant copper and gold recovery increase of 2.85 per cent+0.82 per cent and 2.23 per cent+1.15 per cent respectively at a 95 per cent confidence interval. To validate the statistical analysis, these results were compared to other statistical methods including t-test and comparison regression which produced similar results.  Final flotation concentrate grade for the same dataset showed a significant increase in copper grade of 1.05+0.55 per cent at a 95 per cent confidence interval. Similarly this analysis was repeated using alternate statistical approaches giving the same result. It is important to note that some of the final concentrate produced within this period came from the conventional recleaner circuit (~20 per cent by mass) and therefore the actual upgrade of copper on the Jameson unit in isolation was even higher. 

A full plant flotation survey was conducted in June 2015 post the stage 1 cleaner upgrade to confirm the improvement in fine free gold and liberated copper recovery by installation of the Jameson cell unit. Figures 16 and 17 show a significant reduction in the fully liberated gold and copper particles respectively reporting to the cleaner scavenger tail. Tables 3 and 4 summarise the mineral calculated cleaner block recovery increase for each carrier of gold and copper, respectively. The balanced plant survey data from which the deportment samples were derived shows gold recovery in the cleaners increased across all size fractions with the installation of the Jameson cell (refer to Figure 18).

Since the commissioning of the first Jameson cell in Concentrator 1 in November 2014, the preferred cleaner flowsheet for Cadia used both conventional tank cell flotation technology to produce the bulk cleaner concentrate and Jameson cell technology to produce a final flotation concentrate. Using data from the previous installations, along with key learnings from operating the stage 1 upgrade, the concepts were combined to produce the final Concentrator 1 flowsheet, shown in Figure 21. The objective of the second Concentrator 1 cleaner upgrade was to effectively handle feed metal unit rates at the maximum of the expected life of mine schedule including expected variation in milling rates and feed grades. Circuit capacity post the first cleaner upgrade was 9 tph of copper in feed. To justify the expansion, the existing Concentrator 1 flotation model was updated using the full plant survey information from 2015 and included the new Jameson cell insta

lled in 2014.  Using this as the baseline recovery it was estimated that the recovery would decrease at an average rate of ~ 0.8 per cent for both copper and gold per metal unit above 9 tph of copper feed to Concentrator 1. Given metal units were predicted to peak at an excess of 12 tph from FY17 the expected recovery losses with no further upgrade were estimated to be in excess of 2.6 per cent for both copper and gold. A comparison of the predicted cleaner block recovery for Concentrator 1 with and without the installation of the proposed flowsheet is shown in Figure 22. 

The final installation included the following equipment: 

- 1 x B5400/18 Jameson cell; 

- 1 x E2532/6 Jameson cell; 

- 6 x e50 Outotec tank cells; 

- 1 x VTM-650 Metso Vertimill; 

- 1 x FLSmidth hydrocyclone cluster (8 cyclones); 

- 1 x Falcon SB2500 gravity unit; and 

- 1 x final concentrate trash screen. 

Based on the nominal flow sheet in Figure 20, the existing T3 rougher concentrate is diverted to a new regrind circuit. The product of the regrind circuit feeds a new 18 downcomer Jameson cell producing a final concentrate. The tail of this cell feeds 3 Outotec e50 cleaner cells followed by 3 Outotec e50 cleaner scavenger cells. The cleaner concentrate then feeds a 6 downcomer Jameson cell with the tail recirculating back to the head of the cleaners. The cleaner scavenger concentrate reports to the regrind circuit and cleaner scavenger tail reports to the head of the T3 roughers.  This circuit layout is similar to that proposed and supported by Huynh et al, 2012. 

Concentrate grade was also expected to increase from the cleaner expansion, as all final concentrate from Cadia would be produced from Jameson cells, ensuring maximum fluorine and non-sulphide gangue

###### **Concentrator 2 cleaner upgrade** 

Concentrator 2 at Cadia was initially designed to treat Ridgeway ore, a sublevel cave and later a block cave operated at Cadia from 2002 until going into care and maintenance in March 2016. From this point the plant transitioned to also being fed with ore from the Cadia East block cave. A clear opportunity existed to implement Jameson cell technology to manage the fluorine levels in the Cadia East ore reporting to the concentrate. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

In January 2016, capital expenditure was approved to install a Jameson cell (E3432/8) as a recleaner in the Concentrator 2 circuit with the prime objectives

being: 

1. Rejection of fluorine from the flotation concentrate with a target fluorine grade below 400ppm; and 

2. Rejection of approximately 75 per cent of the NSG (non-sulphide gangue) reporting to the flotation concentrate with an expected increase in the concentrate grade by 3.5 per cent, an improved net smelter return through reduced concentrate transport costs, TCRCs and a higher payable metal rate. 

Potential benefits in metal recovery were also considered likely from the upgraded cleaner flowsheet, however recovery uplift was not included in the financial evaluation. This was principally on the basis that the improvement in concentrate grade and fluorine rejection alone presented a robust business case for capital expenditure. 

The installation of the Concentrator 2 Jameson cell as a final recleaner (refer to Figure 23) as opposed to a cleaner feed scalping unit was based on: 

1. Sufficient existing cleaner capacity; and 

2. Experience from the first Jameson cell installation in Concentrator 1 suggested excellent fluorine rejection (surveyed upgrade ratio 0.25). 

A model was developed on the proposed flowsheet based on Concentrator 2 survey data and early Jameson pilot test work recoveries. This process identified the need to modify the existing circuit in order to maximise the Jameson cell attributes, specifically: 

- Installation of froth crowders in the existing conventional recleaners (OK8), to reduce the surface area by approximately 50 per cent and subsequently increase the recovery and mass pull from these cells; and 

- Modifications to the existing cleaner circuit to convert the first cleaner scavenger into an additional cleaner cell. 

Learnings from the installation of the Jameson cell in Concentrator 1 highlighted the importance of designing a flotation concentrate handling system to manage high froth factors. In order to mitigate issues experienced with the Concentrator 1 installation the following design considerations were applied to Concentrator 2: 

- The physical positioning of the cell allowed Jameson cell concentrate to gravity flow to the existing final concentrate hopper rather than transfer by pump; and 

- A bespoke de-aeration hopper was installed ahead of the final concentrate pump with the intent of breaking down the froth prior to it discharging into the hopper; and 

- Internally designed spray bar on the feed box at the Jameson cell prevented the feed box overflowing into the tails box. 

On completion of the Concentrator 2 cleaner upgrade, fluorine grade in the flotation concentrate was reduced to less than 250 ppm. The Jameson cell increased the Concentrator 2 flotation concentrate grade by 4.4 per cent at a >99 per cent confidence interval by rejection of non-sulphide gangue with no loss to copper or gold recovery (compared to 3.5 per cent estimated in the original business case).

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The application of Jameson cells into the Cadia flowsheets successfully improved both recovery and concentrate grade. The various upgrades also achieved the objective of removing the entrained fluorite reporting to the concentrate via conventional flotation technology. Several lessons were learnt progressively though the individual upgrades to Concentrator 1 and Concentrator 2, particularly regarding the concentrate handling system. Modelling the proposed circuit flowsheets proved critical to achieving the business case goals for recovery, concentrate grade and reduction of deleterious elements in the concentrate. Mineralogical analysis was used as the basis for, and subsequent proof of the investment and a fundamental mechanism to optimise circuit performance.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Asanko Gold Mine in Ghana started processing ore from the Nkran pit in January 2016 at a production nameplate of 3 Mt/a.  The flowsheet is a conventional SAG, ball mill and pebble crusher (SABC) with gravitygold and carbon-in-leach (CIL) recovery. The nameplate production was comfortably achieved within 3 months, so much so, that it was clear the SABC circuit was capable of processing more than the downstream section of the plant. Consequently, a program of de-bottlenecking was initiated to rectify volumetric capacity constraints. This program was later referred to as ‘Project 5 Million’ (t/a) or P5M. Having completed the debottlenecking exercise, it became evident that the SABC circuit could not reach 5 Mt/a solely on hard rock from Nkran. The new challenge was therefore to increase the capacity of the milling circuit through a focused comminution initiative that would address the following: geometallurgical treatment plan; upfront fragmentation requirements; installation of feed and mill monitoring equipment; and integration of a knowledge-based control strategy. 

This paper takes the reader through the various measures implemented to increase the milling rates and to create a stable/ sustainable control philosophy. As a result of the implementation of advanced mill performance monitoring technology (MillSlicer) and the collaboration between a team of experts in comminution, control and operations, the Asanko Gold Mine process plant feed tonnage has successfully increased from 3 Mt/a

to 5 Mt/a. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

As part of the upgrade of the Asanko Gold Mine processing plant from 3 Mt/a to 5 Mt/a, an optimisation initiative was formulated through a detailed definitive feasibility study (DFS) and front end engineering design (FEED). The exercise identified sections of the plant that would require upgrades in the form of either equipment volumetric increases or gravity-circuit upgrades. The modifications included the following: 

- cyclone overflow and thickener underflow pipe diameter increases, 

- the addition of one extra Knelson concentrator in the milling circuit, 

- the upgrade of the cyclone feed pumps, 

- an additional tailings line and pump train to the tailings storage facility, 

- an increase in screen aperture for the inter tank carbon-in-leach (CIL) screens, and 

- an additional oxygen plant. 

Despite all of these modifications being implemented, from the mill discharge to the tailings line, the required mill feed rate could not be consistently achieved for two main reasons: 

- considerable variation in the ore hardness and feed size distribution, and 

- ineffective over- or under-predicted corrections and interventions made by SCADA operators. 

In effect, the mill throughput decreased. Consequently, a detailed, focused program was initiated to optimise the mill throughput and take full advantage of the newly modified processing plant. This paper details the reasoning and actions taken by the implementation team to increase the milling rates and to create a stable/ sustainable control philosophy.

###### **CIRCUIT OPTIMISATION STEPS** 

###### **Ore feed variability – development of the geo-matrix** 

It became apparent that the SABC circuit is very sensitive to variations in ore hardness and feed fragmentation. These factors needed to be better understood in the context of maintaining stable circuit performance and higher capacity than name-plate. 

The Nkran pit, along with neighbouring satellite pits have been frequently tested for comminution variability as the mine development progressed. Typically, the Bond Ball Work Index (BBWi) is taken for rapid turn-around and benchmarking purposes.  Various comminution studies were undertaken to develop a milling model that can effectively describe the SABC circuit performance.  The most influential test-work in this regard involved the DRA grind mill apparatus at ALS Perth, from which the Dynamite Hill satellite deposit and Esaase-Obotan deposits’ composite results were used to describe the breakage rates trend (through energy-based population balance modelling) in relation to top size, for a particular ore hardness (Hinde _et al_ , 2001). Figure 1 shows the variation extrapolated to ascertain the peak specific breakage rates at typical SAG mill feed top sizes. 

A number of plant audits were then undertaken to assess the validity of the milling model which showed that

the Obotan circuit could achieve better performance and higher capacity through optimisation and improved controls. 

Figure 2 shows a database of the BBWi sample population, which was gradually accrued over time, and is used to describe the variation in hardness that may be encountered.  Later on, certain hardness’ were attributed to specific ore facies and mapped across the Nkran pit to develop a comminution geo-matrix that could assist with production forecasting by estimating future development blocks and plant feed hardness. 

The degree of variation in hardness S-curve is typically between 10~20 kWh/t, approximately a 10 kWh/t spread which is a two-fold order of magnitude, but not necessarily weighted similarly in terms of actual production tonnes. 

Taking into account this latitude of variation, it was clear that the plant’s capacity would be affected by changes in hardness, but also by the effect of fragmentation reporting to the SAG mill. Through the resultant simulations, a validated mill model was created, which included pebble crushing performance, and gave way to a simple formula that estimates potential feed capacity using hardness and fragmentation (% -80 mm).  The relationship between BBWi and forecast SABC tonnage was found to be linear for a typical jaw crushed run-of-mine (ROM). Each shift this information is relayed into a crusher feed plan which assists with blending based on hardness (BBWi) and predicts tonnage to be achieved for that shift. 

The team realised that the percentage of minus 80 mm material could be improved by secondary crushing a proportion of the feed. In this way, the SAG mill throughput could be increased and a healthy SAG mill charge could still be maintained.  A series of mobile crusher pilot projects were undertaken to prove this theory and to establish the full-scale potential requirements. 

It was also apparent that it was necessary to operate the SAG mill at peak power in order to achieve optimal performance. To this end, the MillSlicer instrument provided by Pro-Op Industries was selected to monitor the SAG mill load position and to optimise the SAG mill power condition.
