###### **MILL POWER AND CONTROL SYSTEM OPTIMISATION** 

###### **Principles of the MillSlicer** 

MineralScan MillSlicer is a mill performance monitoring instrument (Gugel and Forguson, 2018). The MillSlicer effectively determines the average mill load toe angle relative to the 12 o’clock position of rotation, which can then be used to manipulate the load characteristics to obtain the optimal angle.  According to Hogg and 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Fuerstenau (1972) and Morrell (1992), for empirical mil

l power draw estimates to converge under most operating conditions, the optimal angle for peak power should be 123.9° from the vertical. After a period of operation, it was realised that the mill load toe angle was responding in a manner similar to Figure 3, which could then be used as a rules-based mechanism to adjust the mill feed tonnage to achieve the optimum charge toe angle. An angle below 123.9° means that the mill is going into an overload condition and well above this is an under-loaded condition. The primary objective of the control system is to control the mill toe angle in order to optimise the mill throughput. In order to control the mill toe angle, the system has three basic parameters, assuming mill speed is fixed: 1. Total feed rate into the mill. 2. Percentage feed rate split between the two apron feeders. 3. Water feed into the mill. The control system controls the total feed rate automatically by adjusting the material throughput on each of the two apron feeders feeding from the coarse ore stockpile. The percentage feed ratio of each feeder rate is controlled manually by the operator as it strongly depends on the size of the material on the stockpile. Material segregation depends on the mining method, origin of the material and also crushing deployed before material is tipped on the stockpile. For this site, the larger rocks are on the outer end of the stockpile and are mostly fed via the outer feeder (Feeder #2) nearest to the mill. Smaller material is commonly fed from the inner feeder (Feeder #1). The operator can adjust this ratio manually according to visual inspection of the material segregation. The mill water is also controlled manually and is calculated from a function using the type of material fed into the SAG mill. In essence, the moisture content is controlled by this function. Rotational energy polar plot extracted from Digital Control Lab brochure (Gugel and Forguson, 2018). ###### **Development of the rules-based system control philosophy** The first observation made when the control optimisation was attempted was the long reaction time of the mill after a throughput change. Any attempt to adjust the PID loop was impossible, not only due to the long timeconstants (2-4 hours), but also because of the inconsistent size and type of materials which would change several times a day. Changing the material composition has a significant impact on the control parameters of the system. Operators tried to optimise the feed rate through audio observations and making judicious adjustments. The output of this methodology strongly depe

nded on the operator’s experience and interpretation of the process. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Regular stoppages of the mill were experienced to take samples and to determine the actual state of the mill through visual inspection.  Over-zealous adjustments caused overloads and regular mill grind outs resulting in loss of production. 

Subsequently, a rules-based system (RBS) was implemented which continuously attempts to optimise the SAG mill throughput by adjusting the maximum allowed material feed rate. 

The RBS is used as the primary control loop and the original PID loop is only used to control the feed rate when the toe angle overshoots the toe angle set point.  The practical observed reasoning behind this is that once the toe angle set point is breached, the mill goes into a grind out phase.  A grind out phase reduces the feed rate significantly (commonly, down to 40 per cent of optimal) for up to 45 min before a feed equilibrium is re-established, shown in Figure 4a. 

In order to achieve a sustainable throughput without ‘knowing’ the material segregation and material type, several control limits and time constants were introduced as part of the RBS.  A waiting period taken to note the impact of several consecutive lateral changes further improved the stability of the system and prevented the overloading condition of the mill. In conjunction with the slow reactive time of the above scenario, the RBS also introduced a fast acting mode for when the mill is overloaded or in a grind-out state. This function drastically reduces the maximum feed rate increment by up to 20 per cent and assists the mill to get out of the grind-out scenario much faster, with less production impact.  Once the mill recovers and the toe angle exceeds a toe angle set-point, which is defined as one of the set-point bands, the control again enters the normal control mode, but with a reduction in maximum permissible feed rate being set as the new starting point of control. Monitoring the trends of the toe angle and keeping step-wise adjustments conservative over longer time intervals proved to be good strategy to optimise the mill throughput. 

In order to assist the RBS, a maximum calculated feed rate for each shift was also introduced.  This maximum feed rate is calculated from the metallurgical properties of the stockpile material (Geomet model). The RBS uses this as a basis for its calculations and continuously adjusts the maximum feed rate depending on the rules specified for the specific band and rate of change. 

The result of the RBS, where the toe angle is used as primary process variable, is a significant improvement in control stability where physical measures are used to improve the mill throughput strategy, shown in Figure 4b.  Furthermore, little or no human interpretation and intervention are required to control the mill feed rate. The overall result was a sustained and substantial improvement in the

SAG mill throughput and efficiency.

At very low ball loads the mill slicer response was dull and unresponsive. A SAG mill feed rate set-point algorithm was developed to ‘drive and maintain’ the highest feed rate possible and slaved to achieve the desired toe angle, given: 

- the limitations and constraints of the circuit as a rules-based monitoring system, and

- the response characteristics shown in Figure 3. 

Over time, the filters and response intervals for the set-point changes were finely tuned and eventually a good control strategy was developed.  The maximum feed rate set-point possible (or Upper Clamp UC), was preset daily and kept in-line with the geomet model formula derived from knowing the BBWi and %-80 mm of the incoming feed stream.  Typically, a mining block campaigned for production has its BBWi determined according to the geomet model. 

Early findings indicated that the plant was achieving 96 to 99 per cent of theoretical throughput when under MillSlicer automated control.  This predictability was used to formulate the milling budget based on the hardness of each rock type to be processed during that particular year.  Using the ore type mix based on the mining schedule, one can predict the tonnage which can be processed at that point in time.  Milling rates are predicted based on hardness and required fragmentation into the mill. 

Following a full shell relining, mill power development is physically reduced and limited as a consequence of reduced effective mill diameter (typically 600kW ~ 800kW less).  The degree of scatter of load toe-angle measurement also increases and attenuates over time as the liners wear-in. Given this well-known phenomenon, the nearness of operating close to the optimum angle with little to no liner wear meant that the toe-angle set-point could be set just below the optimum angle position and safely pulled out of an overload condition due to the aggressiveness of the newer lifter profile. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Northern Star Resources Limited Jundee Gold Mine in Western Australia operates a comminution circuit that consists of a primary crusher, 3.85 MW semi-autogenous grinding (SAG) mill, 1.8 MW ball mill and pebble recycle crusher. In 2017, a secondary crushing circuit was installed to remove the SAG mill throughput bottleneck and increase production of highly competent underground ore from 1.35 to a minimum of 1.7 Mt/a. 

This paper discusses the findings from the trial phase, the circuit design, project delivery, site optimisation, and the plant performance. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

During the Jundee operations mine life the open pit feed ore sources have been depleted and the plant feed has transitioned to 100 per cent underground ore. The underground ore is more competent than the open pit ore and throughput has subsequently decreased. 

Previous expansions added a secondary ball mill and a SAG mill recycle crushing circuit to partially offset the reduction in plant throughput. 

The Jundee Expansion Project (JEP) was designed as part of an overall solution for the mines transition to 100 per cent hard rock underground ore. The JEP maximised the capacity of the existing infrastructure and ensured major equipment throughput bottlenecks would not result from the expansion. The original plant was designed

for processing oxide and transitional ore. The grinding circuit design throughput was 250 t/h, and the crushing circuit design throughput was 500 t/h. 

The JEP was designed to achieve gold production guidance of 245 000 to 265 000 ounces in FY2018. To achieve the gold production guidance, the underground ore plant throughput was required to increase from a FY2017 budget of 1.35 Mt/a to FY2018 budget of 1.7 Mt/a. 

Mobile secondary crushing was introduced in November 2016 to trial the effect of feed size reduction on the primary mill throughput. The trial concluded that while target plant throughput was achievable, it was only sustainable on an instantaneous basis due to stability issues in the SAG mill. Mobile secondary crushing continued until the commissioning of fixed secondary crushing in September 2017. 

A SAG mill control expert system was installed to improve the SAG mill stability with resulting increases in plant throughput. The expert system uses mill weight and power to manipulate throughput and displays mill sound as a reference. 

In January 2018, the annualised throughput rate was 1.9 Mt/a. 

###### **PROJECT DEVELOPMENT** 

The Jundee Expansion Project was designed to achieve gold production guidance of 245 000 – 265 000 oz in FY2018, an increase from 233 566 oz produced in FY2017. A reduction in operating costs in FY2018 is also being realised, as in FY2017 mobile secondary crushing was utilised to reduce the feed size to the grinding circuit. To achieve the gold production guidance, the underground ore plant throughput was required to increase from 1.35 Mt/a to FY2018 budget of 1.7 Mt/a. 

In terms of competency, as measured by the JKtech A*b index, the Jundee ore is in the top 20th percentile of ore competency worldwide. The average A*b and typical A*b range of Jundee ores is presented in Figure 1.

Due to the competency of the ore, the grinding circuit was SAG mill constrained and secondary crushing was determined by mobile secondary crushing trials to be a suitable option to increase SAG mill throughput. 

Grinding circuit modelling and mobile secondary crushing operation indicated that between 210 t/h and 250 t/h could be achieved depending on the ore competency and grinding circuit product size target used in calculations. 

The process design for the JEP was completed in-house with third-parties used to validate designs. The design considered the FY18 production requirements, but also considered possible future production growth.

The crushing circuit flowsheet was developed to provide a consistent feed to the coarse ore stockpile, to allow partial or full secondary crushing, to minimise plant downtime for brownfield tie-ins, and allow for maintenance with minimal mobile crane requirements.

###### **Crushing circuit** 

Instability in the SAG mill operation due to secondary crushing occurred during the mobile crushing trials, therefore closed circuit crushing and flexibility in varying the feed size to the grinding circuit was specified in the design. 

Partial secondary crushing is provided to allow coarse product to be added to the SAG mill feed. Partial secondary crushing is achieved by spile bar arrangement splitting the crusher screen o

versize product and directing to either the stockpile or the secondary crusher, a range of 15-60 per cent secondary crusher bypass can be achieved. 

A 500 kW secondary crusher was selected to allow 100 per cent secondary crushing, and it is expected that 100% secondary crushing is required to achieve consistent grinding throughput rates closer to 250 t/h. The secondary crusher was provided with a coarse chamber due to the limited data on feed particle top size. The coarse chamber feed opening is 279 mm. 

The crushing product quality is maintained by crushing in closed circuit with a double deck banana screen. The crusher screen was designed in line with the feed conveyor to allow inline feeding of the screen and improve the distribution across the screen. The screen width was limited to 2.4 m wide to negate the need for a screen feeder. A banana screen was selected due the higher capacity per screen area. The top deck is required for protection of the bottom deck panels from large rocks and the screen panel apertures are 70 mm x 100 mm. The bottom deck screen panel apertures are 25 mm x 50 mm, and depending on the percentage of screen oversize bypassing the secondary crusher the circuit P80 ranges from 20 mm to 45 mm. 

A semi-portal crane was provided for secondary crusher maintenance with the ability to directly load and unload from a truck. A davit crane is provided for screen maintenance activities. 

The transfer chute from the primary crusher discharge conveyor to the stockpile feed conveyor modifications required the largest timeframe for tie-in. The stockpile feed conveyor was shortened by relocating the tail drum and the primary crusher discharge conveyor chute were modified to feed the secondary crusher circuit (Figure 3). 

A surge bin and vibration feeder were provided for the secondary crusher feed to manage ore feed fluctuations and provide a constant feed to the secondary crusher. 

The existing primary crusher discharge belt magnet was retained, and due to the high proportion of steel reporting from the underground workings, additional magnets were provided for the secondary crusher feed and the stockpile feed conveyor. This ensured the ore had to pass through at least two magnets prior to reaching the stockpile. 

To minimise tie-in duration and downtime risk a standalone switch room was provided for the new electrical equipment.

###### **Grinding circuit** 

The low-aspect SAG mill dimensions at Jundee were not ideal for processing single stage crushed competent ore as the pebble recycle rate was less than 10 per cent with 65 mm pebble ports. The pebble

recycle rate was insufficient to obtain the expected reduction in circuit efficiency when utilising pebble crushing. 

The HP100 pebble crusher feed top size with a coarse liner is limited to 70 mm, and therefore larger pebble ports were not considered.

The reduction in feed size due to secondary crushing results in the operation returning to a primary mill duty, and the pebble recycle increasing to 25 per cent of the feed rate. The SAG mill design ball charge of 20% v/v is favourable to operating with a secondary crushed feed. Rock charge was estimated to be less than 5% v/v, for a total charge of less than 25% v/v. 

The installed power split between the SAG mill (3.85 MW) and ball mill (1.8 MW) was unsuited for the new flowsheet design as secondary crushing increases the product transfer size from the SAG mill to the ball mill. Therefore, it would be difficult to maintain the required circuit P80 of 106 µm. 

Historical operation in SAG mill only mode was reviewed including superficial velocity and pulp lifter volumetric throughput rates and it was determined that negligible slurry pooling occurred. Therefore, the option to recycle cyclone underflow to the SAG mill was provided. The cyclone underflow split is controlled by an orifice plate in the ball mill feed line. 

Additional equipment component optimisation required in the grinding circuit includes SAG mill discharge grate size reduction, SAG mill lifter angles, SAG mill trommel aperture, pebble recycle liner design and closed side setting. 

###### **PROJECT DELIVERY** 

###### **Safety** 

Safety was managed by the engineering, procurement, and construction management contractor with oversight for site occupational health and safety team. The construction contractor provided a field safety officer. During the project 35,360 hours were expended on site with 3,568 leading indicators recorded. There were no lost time injuries. 

###### **Schedule** 

Evaluation studies commenced in November 2016, a pre-feasibility study (PFS) was completed and submitted to the Board in late February 2017 and the capital expenditure request subsequently approved. 

The secondary crusher circuit was commissioned by the end of September 2017, resulting in a seven-month project timeline from approval. The PFS schedule estimate was seven to nine months. The short schedule timeframe was achieved with the aid of the following: 

- Timely design decisions and review of detailed design data. 

- Involvement of site personnel in the design and review process. 

- Assigning Site Project Managers to interface between the construction project and operations. 

- Separating structural and plate work packages. 

- Incentivising suppliers by weighting payments to delivery to site dates. 

- Incentivising lead contractor with safety, cost and schedule bonuses. 

The main schedule related issues encountered during the project were: 

- Late delivery of steel work due to paint curing times because of cold weather. 

- Crusher and screen late delivery times. The crusher due to export delays from France, and the screen due to quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) failures. 

###### **PERFORMANCE** 

Grinding performance challenges were faced during the application of s

econdary crushing, these challenges included: 

- mill power draw and mill weight instability, 

- poor control of the grinding circuit, and 

- variable feed size distribution. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The accumulation of critical size material (+40 mm to 90 mm) forced the mill into a cyclic status of overload and recovery from overload scenario. The mill experienced high power draw and high mill weight events accompanied by the rapid loss of mill weight as the mill recovered from the overload condition. In the process of recovery there was insufficient rock charge in the mill to protect the liners which caused plate and lifter bar damage in the primary mill. 

To aid rock retention in the mill the 100 per cent, 40 mm x 50 mm discharge grates replaced a mix of 50 per cent, 40 mm x 50 mm and 50 per cent, 65 mm x 65 mm pebble ports to aid maintaining rock charge and mill weight. 

The poor control of the grinding circuit was aided by refining the primary mill expert system which measures mill power and load and manipulates throughput. Since commissioning in April 2017, the expert control system enabled an increased awareness of the mill performance on the power-load curve. 

The mill expert control system improved grinding stability, however, it was the removal of +40 mm material which considerably improved the grinding stability issues and cyclic events. The magnitude of the peaks and troughs decreased proportionally with the reduction in particle size due to an increase in secondary crushed material. 

Coarse ore stockpile segregation contributed to the cyclic events. The cyclic events occurred when finer material converged into the middle of the stockpile whilst coarse rock segregated to the outside of the stockpile. Stockpile reclaim feeder speeds were adjusted based on the segregation to feed a favourable F 80 to the SAG mill. 

The feeder speed strategy was used as a temporary measure in lieu of supplying the ideal particle size distribution to the coarse ore stockpile through the variation of secondary crusher closed side setting and secondary crusher feed ratio combinations. 

###### **Mobile versus fixed crushing** 

Prior to mobile secondary crushing, the average plant throughput was 138 t/h with a standard deviation of 21.5. Plant throughput increased to an average of 202 t/h with a standard deviation of 18.1 for mobile secondary crushing. Mobile secondary crushing was effective in increasing throughput within three weeks of operation, however, the cost of processing run-of-mine material was A$6.50 per tonne. Mobile secondary crushing allowed for greater stability in milling rates which is indicated by the standard deviation decrease from 21.5 to 18.1. 

Fixed secondary crushing commenced in October 2017 and has provided additional benefits to mobile secondary crushing. The quality control, as measured by the crushing circuit P 80, of secondary crushed material improved, which su

bsequently improved stability in the grinding circuit. Fixed secondary crushing provided greater flexibility to reduce the particle size distribution of the crushing circuit product at an average of $1.20 per tonne crushed. This resulted in an increased in plant throughput to 216 t/h with a standard deviation of 13.1 from commissioning to the end of January 2018. ###### **Operational philosophy** 

The ratio of crusher screen oversize material crushed has been a key control variable for particle size distribution to the primary SAG mill. Secondary crushing has been successful in increasing the plant throughput. The operational focus has been on stabilising the mill throughput to enable the circuit to operate closer to the maximum design. 

The main parameter impacting stability of the SAG mill operation is the percentage of +40 mm rock in the feed. The closed side setting (CSS) of the secondary crusher is set to a minimum of 25 mm and the pebble crusher CSS target is 12 mm to maximise crushing power draw and reduce critical size material in the mill feed. 

The Jundee crushing circuit features a spile bar bypass arrangement on the crusher screen oversize chute to the crusher screen product conveyor and secondary crusher feed conveyor (Figure 2). Individual spile bars are inserted or removed which allows for the ratio of secondary crushed material to be changed. Partial secondary crushed material can be varied to maintain sufficient autogenous media in the feed to assist SAG milling. 

Two operational strategies were implemented to control the feed size to the SAG mill, varying feeder speeds of the stockpile reclaim circuit to the primary mill and varying the ratio of secondary crushed material to the coarse ore stockpile. Greater success was accomplished by varying the ratio of secondary crushed material using the bypass arrangement rather than simulating a finer mill feed size by varying the coarse ore stockpile feeder speeds to the primary mill. The percentage of secondary crushed material was steadily increased to 85 per cent, reducing quantity of +40 mm material reporting to the coarse ore stockpile. The feeder speeds were fixed to improve circuit stability which subsequently lead to increased quality control of particle feed size distribution to the coarse ore stockpile. 

The design of the spile bar bypass chute throat dimension allows for a maximum of 85 per cent secondary crushed material in the closed-circuit operation without causing bridging or blockages. 85 per cent secondary crushed ratio has produced the most stable mill throughput. 100 per cent secondary crushed material has been tested, however, this has not been a full time operational plan. The operation is currently changing the primary mill lining design to enable the capability of continuously crushing 100 per cent of the mill feed. 

The power split between the SAG mill and ball mill can be controlled by a split of cyclone underflow to the SAG mill and operating without the pebble crusher. The ball mill feed pipe features an orifice plate which 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

controls the flow to the ball mill, the ball mill power is maintained at 1720 kW. The excess cyclone underflow slurry is directed back to the SAG mill. 

The cyclone underflow and gravity screen oversize a

re directed to a tri-directional box which flows to the ball mill or SAG mill for regrind. During commissioning, there were flow issues related to design where a baffle plate was installed to reduce the wear inside the box. The baffle plate and tri box design caused flow and wear issues and there was a high sanding velocity in the recirculation pipe to the SAG mill. This was overcome with water addition to the SAG recirculating line and ceramic tiling of the box. The orifice plate in the ball mill feed line allows for ball mill power to be maximised but not be forced into an overload situation. 

###### **Scheduled upgrades** 

Progressing to 100 per cent secondary crush and consistent 250 t/h milling rates depends on specific upgrades to the newly commissioned plant and downstream equipment including: 

- Installation of HP6 medium liner to achieve choke fed operation and further reduce crusher product size. 

- SAG mill composite shell lifters and liners to prevent liner damage during periods of mill instability during the transition to 100 per cent secondary crush. 

- Reduction in SAG trommel aperture to 10 mm x 35 mm to reduce ball mill scatting and increase pebble crusher utilisation. 

- Reduction in SAG mill discharge grate apertures to 15 mm x 35 mm with 45 mm x 50 mm ports allow rock charge to be maintained and utilise available installed power. 

- VVVF variable speed drive for improved mill control and liner performance throughout serviceable life. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The Jundee Expansion Project selected installation of a secondary crushing circuit to reach the production target minimum of 1.7 Mt/a due to the high ore competency of the Jundee underground ore. Mobile secondary crushing was used to prove a reduction in the particle size distribution to the primary SAG mill would be an effective step change for de-bottle necking the grinding circuit. The operation since increased plant throughput by 40 per cent from 138 t/h to 216 t/h. 

The Jundee low aspect SAG mill is not ideal for crushing competent ore and the power split between the SAG and ball mill required additional equipment component optimisation. This was a focus of the Jundee Expansion Project to balance the power split between the SAG and ball mill. 

Grinding circuit stability was achieved by commissioning a SAG mill control expert system and changing components of the mill liner design. 

The implementation of fixed secondary crushing has improved quality control of secondary crushed material and the ratio of secondary crushed material has increased to 85 per cent. 85 per cent secondary crushed material has produced the most stable throughput; however, 100 per cent secondary crushed material is to be trialled with future upgrades to the comminution circuits. The quantity of critical size and coarse material accumulation in the primary mill has decreased proportionally with the particle feed size distribution to the mill. 

The grinding circuit specific energy has

reduced by 30 per cent to 40 per cent since the installation of the secondary crusher and the grind size achieved is now consistently closer to the target of 106 µm. This has been an effect of increased stability in the grinding circuit associated with the particle size reduction.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Newmont Boddington Gold (NBG) processing plant was designed for 35Mt/y with ball mills expected to deliver a combined new mill feed rate of 4837 tonnes/hr. Since beginning commercial production in late 2009, the plant has steadily increased throughput to meet design capacity in 2014 and reached 37 Mt/y in 2015. Through improved efficiencies, changes to the milling circuit have taken place since commissioning to take the plant beyond its design to an actual throughput of 39.0 Mt in 2017 and a budgeted throughput of 39.4 Mt/y this year. 

The NBG milling circuit has four parallel ball mills, each consisting of a 7.9 x 13.4 m ball mill with twin 7.5 MW fixed speed motors in closed circuit with twelve 650 mm cyclones. Each mill is fed by two wet screens with the undersize gravitating to a mill discharge hopper where it is combined with the ball mill discharge and pumped to hydrocyclones for classification. The cyclone underflow is re-ground to a target P80 of 150 µm. 

This paper will focus on process improvements made to the NBG milling circuit which include cyclone reconfiguration, fine screen panel redesign, implementation of an expert control system, mill power draw increase and grinding media changes to take NBG beyond its design throughput. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Newmont Boddington Gold is situated 12 km north-west of the town of Boddington and 130 km south-east of Perth in Western Australia. Gold was discovered at Boddington in 1980. Production from the oxide material began in August 1987 at a throughput rate of 3.0 Mt/y. Oxide ore treatment continued with circuit expansions and the addition of a facility to treat supergene and high-grade basement ores until 2001, at which time the operation was placed under care and maintenance. The current mining operations at NBG commenced in 2008, and commissioning of the processing plant started in the latter half of 2009. It has since been ramping up to its nameplate design of 35 Mt/y with mill production reaching design capacity in 2014, then 37 Mt/y by 2015, 37.9 Mt/y by 2016 and 39.0Mt/y by 2017. In order to achieve these gains in processing rate, small incremental

in-house projects were completed such as cyclone component reconfiguration, fine screen panel redesign, implementation of an expert control system, mill power draw increase and grinding media changes. 

###### **Comminution circuit** 

The NBG primary crushing circuit comprises two 1.5 x 2.9 m XHD primary gyratory crushers located at the edge of the mine with a nominal capacity of 3670 t/h each at an open side setting (OSS) of 175 mm. The crushed product (nominal P80 of 150 mm) is conveyed 2.5 km to the coarse ore stockpile (COS) located at the plant facility. The COS has a live capacity of 40 000 t and a total capacity of nearly 400 000 t, when bulldozed to the side. Coarse ore is reclaimed via any one of three reclaim feeders onto the secondary crusher feed conveyor. The secondary crushing circuit comprises six secondary crusher feed surge bins and six secondary (MP1000) cone crushers. Un-scalped ore drawn from the COS is fed to the secondary crushers which are in closed circuit with four 3.6 x 7.3 m single deck banana screens with an aperture of approximately 50 mm. The secondary crusher closing screen undersize is sent to the tertiary crushing circuit. The tertiary crushing circuit comprises four feed bins and four 2.4 m diameter by 1.65 m wide high pressure grinding rolls (HPGRs) each fitted with two 2.8 MW variable speed drives. The HPGR product is conveyed to and stored in four fine ore bins with a combined live capacity of 20 000 t (up to four hours of live mill feed surge capacity). The four HPGRs operate in closed circuit with eight 3.66 x 7.93 m wet screens (two per mill). Wet screen oversize is returned to the HPGR circuit and the wet screen undersize reports to the grinding circuit. The circuit is summarised below in Figure 1.

###### **PROCESS IMPROVEMENTS** 

###### **Cyclone reconfiguration** 

Early ball mill performance at NBG was characterised by a high recirculating load with the 650 mm primary cyclones providing a cut size finer than the desired P80 of 150 µm. The design configuration included a 165 mm apex and 255 mm vortex finder. 

Commissioning spares included vortex finders up to 305 mm in size. The vortex finder size were progressively increased using the available commissioning spares to 280 mm at first followed by 305 mm in an attempt to coarsen the grind and reduce the recirculating load. The 305 mm vortex finders were unable to achieve the required coarse cut size and it remained at approximately 50 µm lower than the design. The largest vortex finder able to be fitted into a standard configuration 650 mm cyclone is 305 mm. The standard cyclone model being used by the vendor was predicting the desired cut size would be achieved, but failed to correct for the very low viscosity of the slurry being treated at NBG. 

With the 305 mm vortex finders not yielding the desired plant pe

rformance it was decided to source a modified top plate arrangement that could accommodate larger vortex finders as shown by Figure 2. The modified top plate arrangement had been used at another site previously. A single converted cyclone was trialled with a 355 mm vortex finder and products from it were sampled several times to confirm the desired increase in cut size would be achieved. Understanding the performance may have been biased by the single converted cyclone operating in combination with cyclones with 305 mm vortex finders in the remainder of the cluster an assessment concluded that all 48 cyclones should be modified across the four ball mills as the vortex finder size could readily be reduced from 355 mm should this prove too large.

The conversion kits purchased for this included an increased diameter overflow pipe which reduced the wear causing the smaller overflow pipes to hole. After installation of the 355 mm vortex finders the grind became coarser than target and the amount of oversize being captured by the downstream trash screens became excessive. Upon reviewing the survey conducted during the 355 mm vortex finder trial, a small increase in the fraction of top size material was found. Whilst this represented less than 0.1% of the total mass of mill throughput at NBG, it equated to a significant amount of grit being removed by the trash screens (approximately 5tph or 120tpd). 

The decision was then made to install 330 mm vortex finders and this remains the current configuration. However as the focus was cut size and reducing recirculating load, the initial changes did not consider the lower sections of the cyclone. Specifically in failing to change the apex when changing the vortex finder, the cyclones were placed in a configuration where small changes in feed pressure and/or feed density would result in roping. Upon reviewing the literature, it was found the apex ratio to vortex finder had changed from the originally configured 0.65 to 0.5 and thus was in a region of rope or spray, depending on pressure (Napier-Munn, 2005). With the increase in vortex diameter the required apex diameter was calculated at 200 mm for a ratio of 0.61. Initially there were insufficient 200 mm apex inserts and housings available from the cyclone vendor so both 190 mm and 200 mm apex inserts were purchased to move the ratio back into the desired range. As the 190 mm and 200 mm rubber apex inserts wore they were progressively replaced with 200 mm reaction bonded ceramic units. 

The outcome of the cyclone configuration changes resulted in partial debottlenecking of the classification circuit reducing ball mill recirculating load and increasing ball mill throughput. 

###### **Fine screen panel redesign** 

During commissioning, t

he fine screens at NBG were fitted with 11 x 23 mm slots with flow aperture panels and an open area of 26.3% at the feed end, transitioning to 10.5 mm light duty VR type aperture panels with weirs at the discharge end. Due to high wear rates of the light duty VR type panels which was resulting in weekly fine screen outages, the fine screens were changed to slotted aperture panels across the entire surface to improve the time between maintenance with an accepted loss of screen efficiency as slotted panels are prone to pegging with near size material at the discharge end. In order to utilise a higher proportion of the installed power of the HPGR circuit and reduce the recirculating load in the milling circuit, smaller apertures in the fine screens were trialled. The fine screen panel vendor provided a list of available tooling and panels in stock and from this the most readily available panel with reduced aperture width, similar slot length and the same thickness and working depth was chosen. One ball mill had both fine screens feeding it fitted with 8.5 x 23 mm slots with flow aperture panels. Analysis of the increase in the recirculating load back to the HPGR determined this change across all four ball mills would exceed the capacity of the fine screen oversize conveyor. The data analysis indicated a panel at near the mid-point between 8.5 and 11mm would be required. Tooling was created for a 10mm slotted panel based on the 11mm slotted panel layout. Another trial commenced with a further two fine screens on a second mill fitted with 10 x 23 mm slots with flow aperture panels. Following the success of this trial all fine screens were 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 changed to 10 x 23 mm slotted panels with an open area of 25.1% at the feed end and 8.5 x 23 mm slotted panels at the discharge end. In time it was noted the 8.5 x 23 mm slots were prone to pegging which resulted in the fine screen oversize conveyor becoming a bottle neck. The 8.5 x 23 mm slots were removed from service and the screens fitted with 10 x 23 mm slotted panels across the entire surface. With wear still causing frequent panel changes, and low screen efficiency still resulting in bottlenecks on the fine screen oversize conveyor, as mill throughput was pushed ever higher, a Six Sigma project was undertaken to evaluate the fine screen panel performance. The project resulted in the feed end aperture panels increasing in thickness whilst still retaining the same working depth as shown in Figure 3. This allowed more wear material before the screen fixing pin was reached which would result in the panels dislodging. ###### Keeping up with the Joneses – the value of industry surveys and benchmarking 

###### _T D H McGrath_<sup>_1_</sup> _and W P Staunton_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. Research Fellow, Western Australian School of Mines, Curtin University, GPO Box U 1987, Perth WA 6845. Email: teresa.mcgrath@curtin.edu.au 

2. Adjunct Professor, Western Australian School of Mines, Curtin University, GPO Box U 1987, Perth WA 6845. Email: w.staunton@curtin.edu.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Benchmarking, comparing an operation or process with the industry standard, is known to be a useful method for identifying plant optimisation opportunities, and in many cases providing the pathway to realise the benefits. The difficulty is generating the database of plant data necessary for a benchmarking exercise. Larger companies can benchmark internally; this option is not available to smaller companies, and the full value can only be realised with a comprehensive “industry wide” approach. 

The Gold Technology Group at Curtin University through the AMIRA P420 series of projects has undertaken several comprehensive metallurgical industry surveys in the gold industry over the last two decades. Analysis of these surveys has demonstrated areas where many operations can benefit from re-assessment of their operating practices. 

This paper will review the work undertaken by the Group in this area, in particular the 1999 surveys of gold companies in the Australasian region, and the 2012 international survey of the industry. The challenges of, and opportunities arising from these surveys will be discussed. Some of the highlights from analysis of these databases will be presented as well as noting changes in processing practices observed by the Group over the last 20 years. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Gold Technology Group at Curtin University has been in continuous operation for more than 30 years. During this time, it has operated the AMIRA Gold Processing Technology series of projects (current project AMIRA P420F). 

Initially the P420 research focused on leaching fundamentals and the understanding of the then relatively new carbon in pulp (CIP) process. In the early 2000s collaborative work with Andre Laplante on gravity gold recovery from the milling circuit was added to the project, as well as the development of a series of process

models covering flotation, leaching, gravity recovery and carbon adsorption. 

In the last 20 years there has been an increased focus on plant-based surveys and trials, both in Australia and internationally, recognising the need to ensure a transfer of knowledge between the laboratory and plant practice. 

It was through these series of projects that process recovery models such as the BCC (batch centrifugal concentrator) gravity model and SIMCIL, for modelling leach and adsorption in CIP/CIL, were employed to aid in the optimisation of the recovery circuits. More recently the Group has developed the Integrated Liberation Leach Model (ILLM) which combines the two well-known standalone models (gravity and SIMCIL) to create a robust simulation package encompassing recovery for both individual gravity and leach circuits as well as overall recovery. 

The Group has conducted two industry practices surveys for benchmarking in 1999 (AMIRA P420 Gold Technology Project, 1999) and 2012 (AMIRA P420 Gold Technology Project, 2012). In 1999, more than 60 Australasian operations were asked questions focused on leaching, carbon adsorption, acid washing, elution, electrowinning and sampling. Not surprisingly for a voluntary survey, even with direct follow up to resolve missing, ambiguous or perceived erroneous answers, the surveys were completed with varying levels of thoroughness. 

The second, much more intensive, international industry practices survey comprised of nearly 570 questions and was offered online in 2012. Topics included comminution, gravity recovery, leaching and adsorption, elution, electrowinning, carbon management, carbon regeneration, gold room, tailings, flotation, refractory ore treatment processes, cyanide recovery and water. This survey involved 20 companies with 59 sites from 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Australiasia, Africa and the Americas responding. Again, while much data was collected, there were fairly significant gaps in data entry as could be expected with such an onerous task. 

In addition, the Group has built up a database on process plant practices and outcomes from its work of the last 30 years. Operators are encouraged to take part in benchmarking exercises such as these, even though they require a commitment of resources, ultimately most sites find them worthwhile. Knowing where an operation fits on a curve gives the site information about obvious opportunities to improve, allows the site to determine if it is operating at ‘industry best practice’ level and enables insight as to possible improvements that can be implemented when attempting to achieve best practice. 

Access to all this information, including years of laboratory test work, plant surveys and trials, process models and benchmarking surveys provides a unique opportunity to evaluate gold processing trends, strategies for optimisation, a context for ongoing research and development, opportunities to identify

professional development/training requirements and framework for investigating future technologies. In agreement with the participating sites, the data are presented anonymously so an individual site cannot be identified without their acknowledgement. Please note the data and figures presented have been converted to $USD for the given time period unless otherwise stated. ###### **COST OF PRODUCTION** Using the data from industry practices surveys we can investigate the increased cost of production between the two survey periods. The data in Figure 1 show that the cost to produce an ounce of gold has risen from an average of $300 in 1999 to $488 in 2012. Even after taking into account inflation, which increases the 1999 cost of production to $393 in 2012 terms, there is still a 24 per cent increase. This suggests the cost of processing, power, reagents, permitting, labour, etc. has increased noticeably. And, as the 2012 data reveals in Figure 2, Africa and Australia tend to be costlier for production. Although the cost to produce an ounce of gold has risen for the surveyed sites, the production of gold has not decreased as a result, as can be seen in Figure 3. The average annual throughput, given in Figure 4 has also increased from 1.9 Mtpa in 1999 to 4.48 Mtpa in 2012. This 135 per cent increase in tonnages being processed is roughly twice the resulting 77 per cent increase in ounces produced. The data then suggest that head grades have decreased by half on average, barring any changes that may have resulted from optimisation in recovery processes between the two survey periods. 1600

Cyanide consumption is partially based on the ore and partially based on the cyanide management strategy. Though uptake of the technology was initially slow, industry best practice for the last 20 years has been to automate monitoring and control for cyanide levels in the leach circuit, so as to minimise cyanide consumption once reasonable set points have been determined. In 1999 ~42 per cent of responding mine sites reported using an automated system for cyanide management, this time period was within about 10 years of the introduction of the technology into the market. Australia was a leader in this area in the 1990s and despite early concerns with maintenance by 2012 79 per cent of the global sites reported using the device. The trends for cyanide consumption as a function of automated or manual measurement and control can be seen in Figure 5. In the 2012 data set there is a 50 per cent reduction in the cyanide addition by employing automated cyanide control, reducing the average from 1.1 to 0.5 kg/t of ore treated between the manual and automated sites, respectively. For comparison, the average cyanide addition was 0.9 kg/t 1999 for the primarily free milling Australian gold ores, so in many respects the industry has gotten smarter about cyanide additions, particularly using targeted set points and automated control systems. Improved cyanide control can also be enhanced by the frequency and accuracy of the measurements taken. Automated cyanide measurements are generally more accurate than manual titrations and they are also taken about six times more often than the manual measurements according to the 2012 survey data given in the AMIRA 2012 survey. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 3.5

This has resulted from both increased pressure to process more tonnes of ore as well as the observation that many ores do not require the finer grind to achieve acceptable recoveries. Oftentimes, a minimal loss in recovery can easily be tolerated due to energy savings and increased throughput. The return in popularity of gravity recovery devices for gold recovery (not as a pre-con

centration or gangue rejection device) over the past few decades comes as much as a consequence of the trend for coarser ore processing rather than by mineralogy. 

Gravity devices such as the batch centrifugal concentrators (BCCs) do not have an innately high single pass efficiency so closed loop milling circuits rely on the cyclones to keep the gravity recoverable gold (GRG) in the milling circuit until the particles are either captured by the BCC or ground fine enough to leach completely within the residence time of the given leach circuit. Some P420 classification survey data from various operations around the world are given in the AMIRA 1999 and 2012 surveys. The data show that cyclone partition performance for ore is often poor, with a flat slope of m <2. It can also be seen that there is a consistent relationship between the ore and the GRG partition, so as m decreases there is a lowered chance of maintaining the GRG in the circulating load. 

Figure 6 offers a comparison of gravity recovery as reported by the responding sites in the 1999 and 2012 industry practices surveys. The most obvious factor to notice is the pronounced movement towards more efficient secondary gravity recovery by intensive cyanidation in 2012 as compared to just one operation using intensive cyanidation in 1999. 

It also seems that there is an overall improvement in gravity gold recovery when transitioning to intensive cyanidation shown by the 1999 responding sites achieving, on average, 27.8 per cent of their gold recovery by tabling which had increase to an average of 29.1 per cent in 2012 when processed by intensive cyanidation. The argument could be made that the sites are different, and the ores are not the same but a counter argument could also easily be waged that the ores being treated today are generally harder to process and contain less free gold. 

Furthermore, the 2012 data show that the sites using intensive cyanidation are achieving an average of 29.1 per cent while those still tabling are average only 8.9 per cent gold recovery by gravity. While there may be a good reason for tabling at those sites (ie, high levels of native copper) the 20.2 per cent difference would be worth investigating, and trends in secondary recovery suggest that intensive cyanidation is becoming more common for just that reason.

A low residence time indicates a relatively low carbon inventory and should be an indication of good carbon activity. Very low residence times (< 5 days) are often associated with the processing of preg-robbing ores. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 A high residence indicates a relatively high carbon inventory, and most likely a low carbon activity. Most recently the Gold Group reviewed a site with a residence time of 72 days. ###### **CARBON CONSUMPTION** In CIP/CIL carbon is recirculated many times in the circuits during its life. However, there is inevitable loss of carbon via physical attritioning, or thermal loss in the regeneration kiln. Figure 9 summarises the reported carbon consumptions from the 1999 and 2012 surveys. While there can be good reasons for higher carbon consumption (e.g. in preg-robbing ores where carbon is passed through the circuit much more rapidly to maintain high activity), high carbon losses more often reflect poor carbon handling and transport factors. Both surveys show that the typical carbon loss is 20-40 g/t. However, some sites report much higher losses, which should be some cause for concern. Figure 9 – Reported carbon consumption in 2012. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 ###### **CONCLUSIONS** It is widely understood that changes in ore bodies and processing technologies have changed the gold industry over the past 30 years, some more drastic than others. Comprehensive and detailed reviews of industry practices help to establish best practice and allow for benchmarking of individual sites. It has been demonstrated that the average cost of production has increased whil

e the actual metal units produced has decreased. All of this despite huge increases in throughput, suggesting a decrease in grade as well as an increase in complexity and refractory nature of the ores. 

With higher throughputs being pushed through undersized mills the resulting increased grind size has made gravity recovery an important unit operation and sites employing intensive cyanidation as opposed to low G gravity devices are realising major benefits in terms of increased gold recovery by gravity and ultimately increased overall recovery. 

The move towards automation in both measurement and control strategies has seen a decrease in the cyanide consumption and tightening of set points around leach circuits worldwide. The resulting savings in reagent costs and labour can then be allocated to other operational requirements. 

While there have been improvements in decreasing carbon consumption between the surveys the industry still is fairly poor on average at regenerating carbon, which is problematic because experience and data have demonstrated that the most important factor in recovery from the leach circuit is the activity of the carbon. 

It can be expected that gold processing will continue to see a shift towards automation and optimisation which leads to decreased costs and higher staff availability and productivity. Benchmarking will continue to play an important role realising these benefits. In an industry that performs relatively well, small improvements are all that can be anticipated until another paradigm shift occurs, similar to that of the introduction of carbon adsorption and the CIP process, or even the use of cyanide in leaching, allowing for the processing of difficult and currently uneconomic ores that increasingly comprise a large portion of future ores.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Mount Carlton project in Queensland's North East sits on a high-sulphidation epithermal style deposit rich in gold, copper and silver. 

Mt Carlton is an open pit mining operation with ore processed using a primary crusher, single stage SAG mill and flotation to produce a concentrate for sale. Orway Mineral Consultants (OMC) was involved in the original design of the comminution circuit and the project was commissioned in late 2012, with first concentrate shipped in March 2013. When Evolution sought to optimise the project in 2015, OMC was invited to assist by undertaking a circuit review to identify opportunities for the optimisation. 

During 2016, the Mt Carlton site team implemented the optimisation strategies developed in conjunction with OMC. These included reconfiguring the SAG mill discharge arrangement, reducing the average ball diameter and allowing the mill to operate at higher speed and under more autogenous conditions. Cyclone operation was changed to constant pressure and the vortex finder size was decreased. 

The combined strategies improved energy efficiency and allowed higher SAG mill power utilisation. The additional power has been used to increase throughput by 2.4 per cent while achieving a 27µm reduction in product size (P80) to gain downstream recovery improvements. The reduction in grind size has been achieved with only 6.8 per cent increase in specific energy consumption because of a 6.5 per cent increase in grinding efficiency. The circuit product size is also notably more consistent due to the improvements made to the cyclones, providing benefit to the downstream flotation circuit. A significant decrease in ball consumption was also gained, saving hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in operating cost. 

This paper will discuss the circuit design, start up and will detail the changes made during the optimisation and why these were successful. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Mt Carlton Gold-Silver-Copper project is owned by Evolution Mining and is located in the Central North of Queensland (Figure 1). 

The project was discovered in 2006 and commissioned in December 2012 with first concentrate produced in March 2013. This paper looks at some of the decision making during the design of the primary crushingsingle stage SAG (SS SAG) circuit with recycle cr

ushers, the performance post commissioning and following optimisation. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 Figure 1 – Location of Mt Carlton. ###### **GEOLOGY** The Mt Carlton project is a high-sulphidation epithermal style deposit with mineralisation occurring within felsic volcanic rocks on the northern margin of the Permian Bowen Basin. The project comprises gold, silver and copper primarily as copper arsenic sulphides (enargite) and silver arsenic sulphides (tetrahedrite/polybasite) and some native gold (within pyrite). The Mt Carlton deposit comprises two discrete zones: the large gold dominant V2 deposit and the smaller, silver rich A39 deposit. The V2 deposit is flat lying and situated 20 m to 180 m below surface and is 70 m thick with a 500 m by 500 m areal extent. The two deposits are located 200 m apart. Initially both deposits were mined and processed in 3 monthly campaigns, mining and processing of the A39 deposit was completed in August 2014, production now coming solely from the V2 deposit. The main rock types are from an intrusive and extrusive felsic volcanic metamorphic ore complex. Sulphide veins dipping at moderate to steep angles to the NW host a majority of the known economic mineralisation. The ore lithology is predominately Rhyodacite with varying degrees of brecciation and silicification. ###### **HISTORIC TESTWORK SUMMARY** Twenty samples with geographical details were subjected to comminution variability testing during the study phases of the project (Table 1). ###### **CIRCUIT SELECTION AND DESIGN** 

Through a number of design reviews the following findings are noted: 

- Two-stage grinding such as SAB or SABC is not recommended by OMC for the processing of these ore types as a result of the very high variation in power requirement in both SAG and ball mills. Mill selection for this large operating power range would not be practical. In addition, the grinding circuit will not be stable with two-stage grinding for these ore types. 

- A tertiary crushing and ball milling circuit was also considered for increased processing stability. However, due to the high abrasiveness of the material, extreme wear rates on the secondary and tertiary crusher liners were predicted. Of the tested samples from Mt Carlton, the average Ai is 0.5 and the 85th percentile is 0.64, which reflect the 84th and 94th percentile of the OMC testwork database (+3,000 samples) respectively. The stability achieved would therefore come at a high maintenance and capital cost (low availability or a requirement for standby units). For these reasons the tertiary crushing circuit configuration was not selected. 

- Following investigations and discussions on the use of different comminution circuit configurations, the use of single stage SAG milling was determined to be the best option for the Mt Carlton project. This configuration is best suited for high variability ore characteristics. It also provides the simplest flowsheet with the smallest foot print and minimises material handling. This combined with the expectation that this circuit will have the lowest operating cost has led to the recommendation of a single stage SAG mill circuit with recycle crusher.

**2000 - 2703**| Table 4 – Power Utilisation – Single Stage SAG Mill. ###### **Process description** Ore at Mt Carlton from open pit mining is truck dumped or fed by front-end loader (FEL) into the run-of-mine (ROM) bin. The ROM bin has a static grizzly to protect the jaw crusher from oversize lumps. Ore is withdrawn from the ROM bin by a vibrating grizzly feeder. The grizzly oversize cascades into the jaw crusher before being discharged and conveyed to the coarse ore stockpile. The grizzly undersize discharges onto the same conveyor as the jaw discharge for transport to the stockpile. Primary crushed ore is reclaimed from the stockpile by two apron feeders onto the SAG mill feed belt to feed the SAG mill. SAG mill feed is combined with recycle crusher product, cyclone underflow and inlet dilution water to achieve the correct milling density. The SAG mill discharges over a trommel with the undersize material reporting to the cyclone feed hopper. The trommel oversize passes through magnets to remove tramp metal while being conveyed to a pebble crusher feed bin. Pebbles are withdrawn by one of two feeders into one of the pebble crushers or overflow the bin and bypass the crushers. The crushed and uncrushed pebble

s are conveyed back onto the mill feed conveyor. 

The mill trommel undersize is diluted with water to achieve the correct density prior to pumping to the cyclones. The cyclones classify the ground slurry with the cyclone overflow at the target grind size reporting as product to the trash screen. The coarse underflow gravitates back to the SAG mill for further size reduction. 

###### **COMMISSIONING AND RAMP-UP** 

Commissioning was originally anticipated to be complete in early 2012, however due to delays during the engineering and construction phases, commissioning was delayed until December 2012. The mill discharge configuration was modified in December 2012 by replacing two of the twenty-four grate segments with pebble ports as it was believed the mill would not be able to achieve design throughput without achieving the design pebble crushing rate. The commissioning ore selected was low grade ore from the silver rich A39 deposit to optimise available ROM stocks, considering the mining schedule and need to meet concentrate supply requirements 

The crushing circuit was effectively commissioned in January 2013 with approximately 3,500t of commissioning ore crushed, then suspended until March 2013 whilst the remainder of the plant was completed. Ore commissioning of the remainder of the plant commenced on 20<sup>th</sup> March 2013. The grinding, flotation and filtration circuits were all commissioned by the end of March 2013, with saleable concentrate being produced within the month. The regrind circuit was commissioned in July 2013, however not operated until September 2013. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Ramp up to design targets was scheduled to take four weeks following commissioning, with budget feed to commence in Week 3 and a throughput of 100t/h forecast by Week 4. The plant was scheduled to treat two discrete orebodies in three monthly campaigns, there were ramp up allowances factored into the first campaign of V2 ore scheduled for July 2013. Plant utilisation was the largest single factor preventing the plan being achieved, as shown in Figure 2. The grinding circuit performed well during the ramp up phases, although design mill throughput was not able to be achieved on a consistent basis due to downstream process issues of which the concentrate bagging system had the largest impact on both utilisation and mill throughput rate.  Modifications to the concentrate bagging system in June 2013 realised a significant improvement in mill utilisation, however the milling rate was still detrimentally impacted by the bagging system capacity with further improvements made in 2014. Consistent mill throughput rates of 100t/h were achieved for short periods in September 2013; however it was not until June 2014 that the design throughput rate of 100t/h was sustainably achieved. The grind was however coarser than design. 

The first concentrate shipment of A39 concentrate was dispatched on the 15<su

p>th</sup> of May 2013, with the first campaign of A39 ore ceasing on 30<sup>th</sup> June 2013. The first campaign of V2 ore commenced 2<sup>nd</sup> July 2013 and whilst similar issues with the bagging system capacity were experienced; the ore performed better than expected. Saleable concentrate was produced from the start of the campaign with the first shipment of V2 concentrate dispatched in August 2013.

###### **OPTIMISATION** 

A site visit and circuit performance review was undertaken by OMC in November 2015. This involved a review of production data, operating philosophy and a grinding circuit survey conducted on the 21<sup>st</sup> of November, 2015. 

The production data suggested that the design throughput (100 t/h) was being achieved at an average COF P80 of 120 µm. The ore treated during the survey was found to be softer than the design, although within the historical testwork range for the fresh ore. The survey data was used to fit a JKSimMet model in order to verify recommendations made during the site visit. 

The following were the key points and recommendations of the optimisation study: 

- OMC uses an ‘f SAG’ efficiency factor (Siddall, Henderson & Putland, 1996) for determining total grinding circuit specific energy. The power required for the grinding circuit standardised to an F 80 of 150 mm and P80 of 75 µm is compared to the Bond BWi based power that is theoretically needed to effect comminution from the same size range.  The ratio of the two values is referred to as the ‘f SAG’ efficiency or design factor. To determine the efficiency of an operating grinding circuit, OMC compares the actual f SAG of the plant to the theoretical value calculated using testwork results. The power consumption of the SAG mill compared to the theoretical power consumption based on the test work shows that the circuit was operating inefficiently, with f SAG values over 1.4, compared to the predicted 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

f SAG of 1.25 for the ore surveyed (see Table 5). This indicates that the circuit was using approximately 22 per cent more energy than it should be for the duty, or possibly the tested ore characteristics were not representative of the processed ore. A high fines content was observed in the cyclone overflow, indicating that sliming may be contributing to the observed inefficiency. 

- SAG mill speed was not used as much as it should be due to the operating conditions in the SAG mill, where the pebble ports were resulting in too much of the rock media being extracted and crushed. Without the ability to sustain a sufficient rock load, it was not possible to increase the speed as this would result in the charge striking the shell plates of the mill. A suggested grind and load based control philosophy was provided for use in conjunction with the recommended set point changes. It is worth noting that the survey ore character

istics were notably softer than the design characteristics, particularly survey the Axb value of 37 compared to the design value of 24.9. As such, a high pebble extraction rate is not needed to maintain throughput for the current ore type, however this may need to be re-assessed if the feed blend becomes more competent in the future. 

- At the time of the OMC site visit, the SAG mill was operating at a low speed of 67 per cent Nc, couple with a relatively high ball charge of 12.5 per cent to compensate for the reduced power draw at the low speed. The total load was low at 18-25 per cent. These conditions result in operation at close to the maximum rotor current (maximum power draw for the operating speed). The drawn power at 2.6 MW was just enough to achieve the target throughput and grind, however, it limited the operating range for the mill and contributed to much higher than design media consumption rates (actual 3 kg/t vs predicted 1.9 kg/t). Following the assessment of the survey data, it was also suspected that operating at such a low speed is contributing to the observed energy inefficiency. It was recommended to move away from the current mode of operation by reducing the ball charge and increasing the operating mill speed. This required a reduction in the current kinetics of coarse rock breakage in the SAG mill to ensure that a sufficient rock load can be maintained in the mill at the higher speed. 

- To reduce the coarse rock breakage kinetics, it was recommended that the two pebble port sections be removed to limit the amount of fine media being removed. This would reduce the average diameter of the balls in the mill. If this was not sufficient, the amount of 105 mm media was to be increased gradually in the top-up blend (base case blend was 50 per cent 105 mm, 50 per cent 125 mm). 

- Simulations indicated that under the above conditions, the ball charge may be reduced to 9 per cent, and by increasing the speed to 75 per cent, the current throughput and grind could be maintained with an adequate load level in the mill. This is a significant reconfiguration of the circuit and required a gradual transition with the mill speed increased only as the charge facilitated to prevent destruction of the load and liner damage. 

- It was not recommended that recycle crushing was utilised, as the throughput was higher than design and the target grind coarser. Recycle crushing is typically used in SS SAG circuits to assist in coarsening the grind where coarser grinds are targeted, however if the rock is competent it is more inclined to hold up in the mill and over-grind. Recycle crushing could be required in the future when harder ore closer to the design range is treated, however was not currently required. 

- Reducing the ball charge to 9 per cent and removing the ported sections of the mill was predicted to reduce the media consumption rate by 36 per cent, a significant operating cost saving. While it was also envisaged that energy efficienc

y would improve, it was not possible to estimate this effect with the current model. It was recommended that a second survey be conducted following the implementation of the above changes to provide a new benchmark for further optimisation. - The data collected during the survey showed that the shape of the overflow PSD is somewhat unconventional, as there appeared to be excessive fines generation in the circuit with a poor water split to overflow. The cyclones were achieving a relatively efficient cut based on a reduced efficiency curve when the effect of the water split was removed. A fitted alpha value of 2.94 was produced using the survey data, although a fishhook was observed in the partition curve (Figure 3). - Increasing the recirculating load could assist in reducing sanding in the discharge hopper. The circulating load was 130 per cent at the time of the survey. By reducing the vortex finder to 110 mm and maintaining a spigot size of 90mm, the recirculating load could be increased to 200 per cent with 3 cyclones operating. The Vortex to spigot ratio was low in this case which is not typically ideal for optimal performance. Alternatively, if the overflow density can be reduced to 40 per cent solids w/w, the same effect can be achieved without changing the vortex finder, which would allow for better classification efficiency. The current overflow density was much higher than design at 48-50 per cent solids. Increasing the recirculating load should also assist in reducing the sliming that was observed in the circuit, improving the milling efficiency. A combination of the two approaches, three cyclones with a smaller reduction in vortex finder size and reduced overflow density would provide the best outcome. 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 - A constant feed flow (constant pressure) control philosophy was recommend for be implementation to improved circuit stability. |**Parameters**|**Units**|**Design**|**Model**

###### Figure 3 – Mt Carlton Partition Curve. During 2016 site personnel did excellent work implementing most of the

optimisation strategies developed with OMC, which had a significant impact on plant performance. Pebble ports where removed from the grates, reducing the average ball size diameter and consumption in the mill. The smaller ball diameter reduced impact breakage, allowing the mill to operate at higher speed and under more autogenous conditions. This increased efficiency and utilised more installed SAG mill power. The cyclone operation was changed to constant pressure and the vortex finder size was decreased improving cyclone performance. The removal of the pebble ports has facilitated a change in the mill operating speed from an average of 62.5 per cent Nc to 70.4 per cent Nc after the change. This allows higher SAG mill power utilisation. Before the change, the SAG mill power utilisation was about 65.1 per cent. This increased to 72.4 per cent post the grate change. An analysis of production data following the change in 2016 showed 80 per cent SAG mill power utilisation. Looking at the production data, it can be seen that the product size was more variable before the pebble ports were removed. The grind size then became even more consistent following the change to 110 mm vortex finders. After the removal of the pebble ports the circuit product size becomes finer as the liner set wears. This is a result of decreased impact breakage as the effectiveness of the lifters diminishes. The grinding action becomes more abrasive over the life of the lifters. The operating work index also appears to 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 increase dramatically towards the very end of the- lifter life. Removing the pebble ports has reduced the average ball size in the mill, preserving rock media, which has allowed the mill to run 12.7 per cent faster with an 11.3 per cent increase in power draw when combined with a slight reduction in ball charge. This additional power has been used to grind 2.4 per cent more throughput while achieving a 27 µm reduction in product size. This reduction in grind size has been achieved with only a 6.8 per cent increase in specific energy consumption because of the 6.5 per cent average increase in grinding efficiency as expressed by the operating work index. The energy efficiency is now only slightly higher than would be expected based on the last

plant survey ore characteristics. An improvement in the water split to overflow in the cyclones would be expected to reduce fines generation further, bringing the grinding efficiency in line with theoretical. 

Before the pebble port change, the grinding media consumption was 3.02 kg/t, over twice that of the design. After the change the ball consumption has been 2.16 kg/t. This represents savings close to a million dollars per annum. In the later months of 2016 ball consumption levelled out at around 2.4 to 2.5 kg/t. This higher value is a result of the higher average power draw being sustained (2890 kW compared to 2345 kW) and subsequently the finer grind size. Ball consumption is technically defined and calculated as kg/kWh, where kg per tonnes depends on how fine the grind is and the consumed specific energy. This ball consumption rate is still a considerable savings at around 20 per cent. If the equivalent power draw could have been drawn under the pre-operating conditions (which it can’t because of rotor current restrictions), the ball consumption would be expected to be well over 3.5 kg/t based on the historical consumptions rates. The blend of 50 per cent 125 mm and 50 per cent 105 mm steel balls currently being used appears adequate for the current duty. If a higher throughput and a coarser grind were to be targeted, a higher portion of 125 mm balls could be used as the SAG mill is now close to being lump rock limited. 

The SAG mill is currently not the circuit bottleneck, achieving the design capacity at a finer than design grind size. Ball consumption and energy efficiency have been optimised at the current plant capacity. 

Further optimisation is still ongoing with a number of new initiatives identified in the review following the original optimisation study. These initiatives may include: 

- Implementation of expert control for the grinding circuit (feed rate and SAG mill speed), including a historian for the SCADA system. 

- Review and optimisation of the SAG mill liner design. 

- Consideration of a change to water addition to control the discharge hopper level and a move to operation at a lower cyclone overflow density. Water addition is currently adjusted to achieve the target cyclone overflow density. This change will improve the water split to underflow and reduce overgrinding (fines content in the overflow PSD). This could be trialled and the grinding circuit re-surveyed. This will provide an updated baseline for a second round of optimisation. Given the importance of the selected overflow density to both grinding and flotation, two surveys maybe undertaken; one at the current overflow density (+42 per cent solids) and one at the overflow density optimal for comminution, circa 35 per cent solids. The high cyclone overflow density is being driven by flotation requirements. As such sampling of the flotation circuit at the same time is being considered.
