###### **MONITORING OF LINER WEAR** 

It is a well know adage that without measurement you cannot improve performance. However, this is poorly implemented with regard to mill liners. The introduction of 3D laser scanning to monitor liner wear, the application of which is described by Franke (2008), has revolutionised this. However, the cost has limited its use to large SAG mills, leaving hundreds of smaller mills around the world with grossly inadequate wear monitoring. As an integral part of embedding good liner practice through ongoing monitoring, the site were provided with a simple monitoring tool and on-site training. This step of making the site personnel an integral part of the liner optimisation process is seen as essential to successful implementation. The objective was to enable ongoing monitoring of liner profile along the mill and on the end liners. The output data is: 

- Liner profiles 

- Wear rates

   - mass loss kg/day 

- change in lifter face angle as the liner wears 

- high wear areas 

- point in liner life when the liner wear rate accelerates 

- prediction of liner life and required change-out date

###### **Method** 

A simple pin mechanical wear gauge was provided. This is custom-designed to hold the pins firmly while allowing easy movement to position them; provide sufficient resolution through 10 mm spacing of pins; is easy to keep clean; is light enough to handle easily and fits across a full row of mill liners. In this case it was made to span the high-low combination so was relatively large, at 840 mm long, so special care was taken in lightening up the aluminium frame. The Gauge is show in action in Figure 11. The liner plate thickness is measured via hammering a nail in the rubber and measuring the protruding length. This is taken at the point where the leg of the gauge rests, so as to provide an accurate reference thickness for the full profile. A logsheet was dra

wn up for logging the data as it is measured. The liner is measured during routine mill inspections, taking about 1 hour each time. 

The liners are measured in the same longitudinal position for each liner ring on a monthly basis. The inlet and discharge liners are also monitored, but not as rigorously in this first implementation.

Based on this the liner profile could be updated prior to manufacture of the replacement liners. It was found that issues with the feed system (arising from vibratory feeders and a mis-positioned feed weightometer) compounded by manual mill control, led to significant fluctuations in mill filling, down to as low as 25%. This has given rise to accelerated wear, but the influence of these low filling periods cannot be quantified. A further complicating factor in this application is that the mill functionality was changing over the period of this first liner. The circuit had pre-crushing added, which resulted in a consistent mill filling of below 25%, as the mill could not hold a rock load with a finer feed top-size. Fortunately this was in the latter half of the liner life, so the issue of liner impact were reduced due to the lifters being partially worn. Again, the impact of this could not be quantified. The updated design was based on holding a filling of 30%. The key recommendation were: - Use slightly higher lifters, adding 40 mm to both the high and low lifters. This will extend both the lifter and plate lives. The plate behind the low lifter requires a higher lifter in front of it, so any increase in the plate thickness must maintain the added 40 mm to the low lifter – this is relevant as the low lifter is integral to the plate in this design. - Apply a 30° angle to the discharge end lifters, so as to prevent projection of balls onto the end of the shell, causing the high wear issues of ring 6 (Figure 15). The discharge end lifter was split into an inner segm

ent with a steep face (as this takes the most wear) and an outer section with the high angle as this has a lower wear and is responsible for projecting the balls on the liner. 

- Once the mill operation can be stabilised, based on a new apron feeder allowing improved control of mill feed and the activation of the simple mill filling logic, then the angle of the lifter bars can be steepened to further improve liner life. 

- As the mill operation was then transitioned to a full pre-crush, the liner design will be modified to suit the new milling conditions. Operating measures indicate a mill filling of consistently below 25%, so the lifter profile should now be modified to suit this new operating condition.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A program of was implemented to dramatically improve the liner life and reliability for the SAG mill at the Pustynnoye site of JSC Altynalmas mines. This included redesigning the liner, selecting a new liner supplier, working with the supplier on the updated design detailing, reviewing relining practice, site monitoring the liner wear, updating the liner design based on the monitoring outcomes, and identifying mill control issues. 

Controlling and simplifying the liner wear monitoring when using a manual gauge is an area being addressed. It is planned to include fixed moulded in (or inserted post-production into the rubber) reference points for the legs of the liner gauge. This will ensure consistent measurements of the same liners at each measurement. These reference studs will be directly behind the high lifter, as this is a non-wearing point in the liner. 

The site are following up on the opportunities to dramatically reduce relining time, based on a business case around increased annual production for the mill being the bottleneck. A good working relationship between the site personnel, liner supplier and independent liner expert has allowed a rapid improvement in liner life linked to mill operation. 

The first iteration of the new liner increased the liner life from an original 2-3 months up to 5-6 months, over a 50% increase. Based on the wear data, it is expected that the updated design, which has been implemented for the next installation, should achieve the desired 6-month life along the full mill. However, the excessive wear of the last ring has not yet been resolved. 

The monthly production data presented in Figure 3 and Table 4 shows that the mill throughput has increased by 26%, principally with improved liner design. The feed also became slightly finer with a 2% increase in minus 12.5 mm, but the SSE across the ball mill showed no decrease, indicating the ore competence remained constant. The SSE across the SAG mill decreased, showing that the efficiency of the SAG mill had increased. The concurrent increase in liner life and mill production demonstrate that productivity does not need to be compromised to achieve increa

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The development and optimisation of mill discharge trommels, and specifically their screen panels, can be a neglected area in the complex operation of a minerals processing plant. Trommels are often seen as a ‘set and forget’ component of the circuit, even when significant improvements in design are possible. A redesigned trommel and panel arrangement has simplified and added flexibility to the plant shutdown schedule at Kirkland Lake Gold’s Fosterville Gold Mine in Central Victoria. 

Prior to the trommel redesign, the shutdown frequency was determined by the expected life of trommel panels at 14 weeks. Planning downtime around this item led to higher maintenance costs and wastage in other areas of the plant. This was particularly disruptive with respect to mill lining change-outs, which were forced out of sequence and often changed prematurely. 

Fosterville Gold engaged Metso Australia Limi

ted to propose a new trommel design that would better suit the site. The new trommel was engineered to balance simplicity with performance, and incorporated the latest in Modular trommel design, modelling and Finite Elemental Analysis (FEA). Modular Panels and Spiral Segments achieve significantly longer life, and allow in-situ panel change outs, flexibility in spiral and dam positioning and an improvement in classification performance. Trommel panel life has significantly increased from 14 to 71 weeks in the trommel’s highest wearing zone. The new design has eliminated some risks to safety by reducing manual labour and lifting requirements during shutdowns. There is greater flexibility with respect to shutdown requirements. The site is no longer at the mercy of trommel panel lifespan, which allows for better optimisation of wear components in the circuit. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The trommel screen coupled to the discharge trunnion of a SAG mill is a simple and robust classification device used to separate the mill discharge stream into separate size fractions. Combined with a baffling system and water sprays, trommels have the potential to efficiently classify material and produce a clean, consistent flow of oversize that can be removed for recycling or secondary processing. Furthermore, this coarse screening serves a secondary purpose by offering protection to downstream equipment. This may include minimising damage to brittle ceramic cyclone components or eliminating blockages caused by coarse material and worn grinding media. Trommels are often selected for their low capital cost and ease of fitment into the comminution circuit. A trommel does not require changes to the mill deck, unlike a screen installation would for example. Although trommels can be a cost effective solution in many cases, they can be a constraining factor in high throughput circuits leading to a reduction in classification efficiency (Mosher, 2016) 

Along with mill liner replacement, the change out of a trommel, or its panels can be a major contributor to mill downtime. Along with mill liner replacement, the change out of a trommel, or its panels can be a major contributor to mill downtime. Improving the availability of the trommel screen and simplifying its maintenance may be a quick-win opportunity in improving the overall availability of the grinding circuit. 

Fosterville Gold Mine recognised the design of their existing trommel and wear components to be a limiting factor on their plant uptime schedule. With significant repairs required to this existing unit as a consequence of long-term wear, an investigation into new design were initiated. Fosterville Gold Mine, located in central Victoria, 25 km North East of the historic gold mining city of Bendigo, is owned by Kirkland Lake Gold. With workings dating back to 1894, with the initial discovery, the Fosterville Goldfield is in the Bendigo Zone of the Whitelaw Terrane in the Lachlan Fold Belt. The Bendigo Zone co

mprises a sequence of folded and faulted Cambrian to Ordovician turbidites underlain at depth by Cambrian basalts. Primary gold mineralisation at Fosterville is refractory, occurring as ultra-fine grained particles or solid solution within fine grained,

disseminated arsenopyrite and zoned pyrite crystals (Perseverance, 2008). The occurrence of visible gold has become increasingly significant at Fosterville and is observed more frequently with depth and down-plunge within the Lower Phoenix Mineralized Zones (Fuller, 2017). 

The processing circuit commences with a single stage of crushing, followed by a single stage Metso SAG mill, closed with hydrocyclones, which produces a product size of 70-90 micron. The SAG Mill is of ш 20’ x 20’ Effective Grinding Length, with an installed power of 3500 kW _._ Mill speed is variable, between 12 to 16 rev/min. 

A flash flotation cell is utilized in the grinding circuit to recover coarse liberated sulphides. The Cyclone overflow reports to a flotation circuit where a rougher and cleaner concentrate is produced and combined with the flash flotation concentrate. A gravity gold recovery circuit consisting of a Knelson concentrator and two Gemini tables has recently been commissioned to create a secondary final product. The overall combined flotation concentrate is ground to 15-20 micron in a regrind mill before reporting to the BIOX® leach circuit and further processing to create a final product. 

The first sulphide gold pour was in April 2005, with the one millionth ounce poured in January 2016. The plant however has a nominal capacity of 700 000 tonne per annum, however is constrained by ore supply. 

###### **INCUMBENT TROMMEL** 

###### **Engineering Design** 

The original trommel was supplied by Metso with the SAG mill in 2004 The trommel design was not focused on long term maintenance requirements, primarily due to limited funds at the pre-start stage of the project. Secondly, maintenance practices were difficult to predict in detail as the plant had no production history. The initial trommel panel design was a classic 15 mm thick rubber mat, punched, and installed on a fabricated steel frame (rubber lined), with eight beams, as shown in Figure 1. Three rings of dam segments were installed inside the inner surface with the purpose of retarding slurry flows along the trommel. 



Figure 1 – Incumbent trommel design, with punched panels. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The main benefits of this design were reduced capital expenditure and low cost for replaceable components. The disadvantages of this design were an unfavourable shape of the slots, shorter wear life of the screen mat and increased labour requirement for panels replacement. These

factors would go on to impact equipment availability and maintenance requirements. 

###### **Operational Issues** 

The scheduling of major process maintenance shutdowns at the Fosterville concentrator has historically been at the mercy of periodic trommel refurbishments. The trommel refurbishment was a complicated activity that involved the following at every shutdown. 

- The complete removal of the spray bars, trommel cover and trommel frame 

   - The trommel was required to be removed from service to complete the reline due to the panels being very large and required fixing from external to the trommel. The workers may have also been exposed to working at heights risks. Also, due to the extended time taken to change out the panels there was the possibility of interference with other work groups and the inching of the mill during relines. 

- Transportation of the trommel frame to the process maintenance workshop and return 

- Complete strip of all trommel wear components, regardless of the wear pattern. The screen panels showing minor wear were required to be changed out along with the wear limiting panels even if a further life cycle could be achieved. Heavy wear was often experienced on the trommel frame in areas of slurry flow which required repeated rubber lining repairs 

- Installation of new wear components, including screen panels, spirals, dams and baffles 

- Installation of the refurbished trommel to the discharge trunnion of the mill and fitting of the cover and spray bars 

This ongoing process lead to an elevated cost of trommel maintenance and extended plant downtime. A trommel change-out was typically required every 14 weeks. The scope of the job required approximately $30,000 of materials at each interval. On top of this, 60 hours of labour and additional crane hire led to a further $20,000 of costs per shutdown. This work also presented a greater risk to personnel safety on site during these periods. 

The operational life of the incumbent trommel was limited to 14 weeks due to continual panel failures when pushed beyond this point. The shutdown schedule was therefore driven by trommel maintenance, rather than other big-ticket items, often leading to mill lining change outs being forced out of sequence. The flexibility in improving the design of the mill lining was also reduced. Any change in mill lining design aimed at improving wear life would need to extend lining operation by a full trommel life cycle of 14 weeks. A redesign of this nature would require significant design changes to the lining and potential process risks. Investigations were conducted to increase the thickness of the trommel panels, however there was a risk of pegging issues. 

Process upsets were often experienced with the original trommel design. Once a screen panel wore through and failed, it may not have been realised for extended periods of time, with the cyclone spigots becoming blocked with coarse scats. This lead to coarse material reporting

to the flotation circuit and thus resulting in gold losses to the tails. Samples taken of the coarse material lost to the tails during a panel failure and cyclone blocking event revealed a grade of 49.1 g/t Gold in the greater than 106 micron size range. 

Historically the gold grade associated with scats was usually <2.0 g/t, however with current ore change and associated high grade, scats grade can be as high as 6.0 gt/ Au. Visually, the trommel oversize scats were wet and coated by fine particles due to inefficient classification. 

###### **MODULAR SAG MILL DISCHARGE TROMMEL** 

###### **Desired Outcomes** 

An opportunity for replacing the trommel with an optimised design was presented when engineering inspections revealed heavy damage to the incumbent frame’s rubber lining. The option of a long-term repair to the rubber lining proved to be undesirable, due to the significant downtime required to remove and reinstall the trommel, transport to an appropriate vendor with sufficient autoclaving facilities and the completion of significant rubber relining. An understanding of the issues surrounding the incumbent trommel had been developed by Metso Australia’s personnel whilst supporting Fosterville’s mineral processing requirements, specifically mill lining. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Moving forward, the design aspirations for the new trommel were to significantly increase the trommel screen panel life without any detrimental effect on the operational performance. The ultimate objective was to remove the trommel as a driver for plant shutdowns and thus increasing the flexibility in scheduling and reducing wastage in other areas of the plant. The maintenance process needed to be simplified, with _in situ_ panels replacement. It was expected, that with these improvements a significant cost saving would be observed. A further goal was to reduce the exposure of maintenance personnel to the risks of heavy lifting operations and repetitive manual labour. 

###### **Engineering Design** 

The alternative design proposed for consideration was a modular, snap-on system, with smaller panel screens. Three important design constraints were: provision of the same operating capacity, installation on the existing mill flange and fitment within the space provided by the existing discharge chute and covering. The last dimensional constraint proved to be much more difficult to satisfy than initially anticipated, and required that final design have an uneven number of beams (eleven) which resulted in asymmetrical cross bracing. 

###### _Trommel Frame_ 

The frame is a lightweight, but robust, welded steel structure covered with vulcanised rubber to protect the steel structure from abrasion. It is designed to resist the effects of fatigue using Finite Element Analysis 

- Trommel Frame was configured for Metso’s Trellsnap Fixing System. 

- Overall trommel frame dimensions of 3165 mm long x 1985 mm diameter.

The overall frame dimensions were constrained to the design of the installed SAG discharge trunnion, chute and trommel cover 

Additional to the design features above, an allowance was made for the inclusion of sacrificial wear bars on the inner faces of the cross braces of the trommel frame. Historically, significant wear was observed on the incumbent trommel frame in the areas exposed to the slurry flow through the screening panels and was required to be continually patched. Ultimately it was in this area that the significant structural damage occurred, leading to the requirement for replacement. A layout of the trommel frame is shown in Figure 2, with the sacrificial wear bars evident on the diagonal cross braces of the frame. 



Figure 2 – Updated modular SAG Mill trommel designed for Fosterville Gold Mine. The sacrificial wear bars visible on the diagonal braces. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### _Trommel Panels and Spirals_ 

This design included the application of Trellsnap moulded rubber trommel panels. The moulded panels proposed are significantly thicker, compared to a punched panel at 15 mm. Wear life improvements were expected, with an estimated life more than double that of punched panels, due to the increased thickness and heavier durability of the moulded panels. Pegging of the panels is avoided due to the tapering of the apertures; a relief angle of 5° is an inherent design property of the moulded panels. 

This design was prepared with a 12x20 mm aperture size as per the incumbent design. This was reviewed and is considered the correct design; however, this is easily altered as required with ongoing technical processing review. A spiral has been selected to allow a controlled discharge of scats from the trommel and improved separation. 200 mm high Trommel spiral segments were included. Some benefits of the Trellsnap system are as follows: 

- Light-weight panels that are easily handled. 

- They can be replaced quickly using simple tools. A small Jimmy bar is all that is needed to remove the panels from position and a rubber mallet to reinstall. See Figure 3. 

- There is no need to remove the trommel housing cover for maintenance as all panel replacements are completed from inside the trommel. 

- The snap-on system offers flexibility; blind panels and panels with different aperture sizes or materials of construction can be combined within the same unit 

- For installation flexibility, one spiral is bolted to each screen panel on the spiral path. These spiral panels may also be easily adjusted to any position in the trommel and furthermore parallel or perpendicular to the slurry flow to create baffles or dams respectively. 

- The panels in areas of elevated wear can be individually replaced, whilst low wear zones can remain untouched. 



Figure 3 – Fixing system for Trellsnap Panels.

Early measurements of the panels showed minimal wear of the trommel panels of the full length. At week 14, comparable to the reline date of the previous trommel, the highest wear reading was 5 mm of rubber. Therefore, already indicating the new design would allow a significant panel life improvement. Using a conservative change out limit of 15mm remaining rubber thickness, the new panels had worn 14% of their working thickness at an equivalent operational period for the former panels to fail. Subsequent inspections revealed a distinct high wear zone becoming evident at rings four and five, between the two rings of spiral segments, with a wear rate of 0.49 mm per week. The lowest wear rates were evident in rings one, two and three at 0.14 to 0.21 mm per week. Visual inspections were recorded for the wear on the spiral segments and as at the latest inspection there was only minor scalloping on the leading face. It was during the November shutdown, at 71 weeks post install, that the first maintenance works were required on the trommel system. A selective replacement of trommel screen panels was completed, with rings four and five almost completely replaced with new panels. As planned, the change out was completed _in situ_ and in a very short time frame of three hours with a minimal labour requirement and risk to personnel. The inclusion of additional wear protection to the frame with the fitting of the sacrificial wear bars has shown its value in the early stages of the frame’s life. Minor wear of the wear bars was evident at the November 2017 inspection. This wear would have historically manifested on the rubber coating of the frame itself and lead to potential compromise of the frame’s structure. A somewhat unexpected benefit has also manifested with the ongoing operation of the trommel, with an increased life of the rubber lining in the trommel underflow hopper being observed. Historically the lining suffered from areas of isolated wear causing periodic remedial works. The flow from the updated trommel has appeared to be more evenly spread and has therefore decreased this isolated wear occurring. ###### **Scheduling Flexibility** Following the installation and operation of the new trommel, not one downtime event has been attributed the failure or planned shutdown of the trommel. The typical three monthly major shut routine is still maintained, however, is not determined by the need to repair the trommel. The uptime period can now be extended if required with confidence in trommel panel integrity. 14th AusIMM Mill

Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

###### **Process** 

There have been no failure events for the trommel panels since installation of the modular trommel. This has allowed a level of confidence in the integrity of the system. Blocked SAG circuit cyclones have become a very rare occurrence, with attributed coarse gold losses to tails avoided. 

The expected pegging issues with the thicker panels did not eventuate due to the mitigating design characteristics of the aperture relief angle. Milling rates have been reduced in the recent 12 months however, the scat production rate has clearly reduced. Cleaner, with less fine particle, scats are being produced, leading to a decrease in expected gold losses. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The design and selection of the discharge trommels for a SAG mill should not be overlooked in the complex operation of a minerals processing operation. In this case, the trommel panels had operated as the limiting wear component of the grinding circuit and as such had determined the plant shutdown schedule. A high cost was borne in maintaining the trommel and wastage was observed in other areas of the plant. The additional benefits of a safer system can also not be ignored. The removal of a major maintenance activity and the elimination of heavy lifting operations has decreased exposure of personnel to significant risks. 

The updated SAG discharge trommel for Fosterville Gold Mine has delivered several benefits over the former OEM trommel. Principally, the increase in component wear life without any process upsets, has allowed flexibility in the maintenance schedule and the opportunity to pursue significant design changes to the SAG mill lining design.

###### 21st century relining – the path to greater mine site profitability 

P Rubie and J Russell 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper looks at the past, present and not too distant future of grinding mill relining. 

Since the adoption of autogenous grinding (AG) mills and sem

i-autogenous grinding (SAG) mills as the primary ore reducing devices in the comminution circuit, plant shutdown frequency and duration has largely been driven by the liner maintenance requirements of these mills. 

The past 30 years have seen the introduction of many technologies to reduce relining times and frequencies. Advanced relining systems have been developed which include single and twin Mill Relining Machines, capable of placing large (up to 8000 kg) liners, high energy recoilless THUNDERBOLT Hammers, and high capacity Feed Chute Transporters. 

Despite these advances, today many of the hazards associated with mill relining remain and reline times still vary considerably between mine sites. A sophisticated discrete event simulation program, designed to analyse the mill relining process, has revealed the dominant influences on reline times of crew performance and of the need for safe access to larger segments of the mill. 

A new generation of advanced and semi-automated technologies is currently being tested that will address these remaining challenges.  These technologies remove people from the hazardous environment inside the mill and will allow techniques used in modern advanced manufacturing to provide a near-future step change in mill relining safety and performance. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Technical options for improving existing concentrator _commercial performance_ are limited to: 

- higher throughput rates (tonnes per hour) while maintaining grind performance (particle size distribution) and recoveries (percent) and / or 

- reducing concentrator down time, planned and unplanned. 

Neither option is easy to achieve. 

Increasing throughput rate generally degrades grind performance and, subsequently, recoveries (Powell, Smit, Radziszewski, Cleary, Rattray, Eriksson and Shaeffer. 2006). 

Planned maintenance shutdowns are necessary. Grinding mill relining requirements usually dictate major shutdown timing and duration. These major shutdowns account for most of the planned concentrator downtime. 

Grinding mill relining is known to be dangerous and is considered an unfortunate fact-of-life in concentrator operations. Much effort is applied to maximising mill liner life with the attractive and seemingly logical goal of minimising mill relining / major shutdown events. 

However, long-life liners can degrade mill performance (Yahyaei, M.; Powell, M.S.; Toor, Paul; Tuxford, Andrew; Limpus, Andrew. Nov 2015). 

This paper references the proven _overall commercial benefit_ of a concentrator profit-maximising strategy where less aggressive, shorter life mill liners, are exchanged more frequently (Russell, J. 2006). 

At face value, more relines per year seems an unattractive proposition. 

Major new developments in grinding mill relining technology provide vastly improved levels of safety and promise significantly reduced reline times. The last 18 months has seen a Cambrian like explosion in the evolution of mill relining technolog

y with a large number and variety of new technologies being spawned by Russell Mineral Equipment (RME). Technologies that have been theorised for some time are now progressing from the prototype testing and validation phase and are gradually finding their way into the relining ecosystem. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

As a result, one or two additional liner exchanges per year are no longer to be feared. More relines, conducted at much higher safety levels, will deliver an improved overall safety outcome. More relines, but at much faster liner exchange rates, means no annual increase in mill relining related downtime. 

The subsequent improvement in concentrator _commercial performance_ , with no plant capacity expansion, will soon be entirely possible. 

###### **DISCUSSION** 

RME’s goal is to provide the means to reline grinding mills with no-one inside the mill, a situation which, as demonstrated by our investigations, allows for significantly faster relining speeds. 

Such capability provides the ultimate in mill relining safety and the ultimate in improved commercial performance for the concentrator. 

Risk is an inherent feature of the mining environment so our industry’s decision makers are understandably conservative. The authors appreciate that attempting to convince concentrator owner / operators to make the giant leap from today’s practices to today’s possibilities will most likely meet with responsible conservatism and ultimately some resistance. 

Fortunately, a measured, gradual process enabling transition from today’s practices toward today’s possibilities exists. This process includes the option for concentrator management to stop and enjoy the improved safety and relining performance at any step along the way in this transition. 

Machine design improvements, including automation to provide relining efficiencies, are not enough to create the changes required. Even the most automated process will still require personnel to enter the mill; technicians or metallurgists will need to inspect the installed mill liners, for example. Automated technologies could perhaps drop a worn liner during liner removal, requiring a relining crew member to enter the mill to facilitate conventional mill liner recovery. 

Since personnel will always be required to enter the mill, albeit less frequently in the future, improved safety technologies for people entering and working in the mill will always have a place. 

The first and simplest steps along the path to safer and faster relines are the new safety technologies and processes. 

The discussion component of this paper comprises three parts: 

1. Part One outlines the opportunity for an improved commercial outcome for the concentrator through an _innovative mill relining strategy_ . Part One summarises and references work which confirms that grinding mill liners and liner exchange schedules, which are optimised for profit, vary considerably to t

hose strategies which seek maximum mill liner life and a minimum of mill relining / major shutdown events. 

2. Part Two details the afore-mentioned range of new grinding mill relining _safety technologies and processes_ which deliver vastly improved levels of safety for: 

(a) mill relining crews who line mills using conventional relining methods in which personnel are working constantly inside the mill, and 

(b) advanced, semi-automated or automated relines, during which personnel enter the mill only occasionally. These technologies and processes deliver a paradigm shift in relining crew safety by removing the need for mill relining crews to work inside the mill. 

3. Part Three details a range of new grinding mill relining _performance technologies_ which reduce the time taken to exchange liners. They directly support the safety advances referred to in Part Two. 

###### **Innovative mill relining strategy, optimised for improved concentrator profits, not for long liner life** 

Metallurgists operating large mineral concentrators, equipped with one or more large SAG mills, commonly observe differences in plant throughput as SAG mill liners wear (Yahyaei, M.; Powell, M.S.; Toor, Paul; Tuxford, Andrew; Limpus, Andrew. Nov 2015). The difference can be most marked either side of a SAG mill reline shutdown. The grinding performance of new liners during the first week of operation can be as low as 80% of the final week’s grinding performance on now well-worn liners (Yahyaei et al 2015). 

RME personnel first became aware of this characteristic through engagement with concentrator metallurgists and management during mill relining equipment commissioning and use. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

Further confirmation of this characteristic was sought by RME, resulting in a series of academic papers which highlighted the importance of this characteristic to the maintenance planning and effective operation of grinding mills. The idea of designing liners for performance was proposed by John Russell in 2006 (Russell 2006). His hypothesis was that, despite the requirement for more frequent relining, designing liners for performance would enhance the mill’s throughput and increase plant revenues.  These additional revenues represented a significantly higher profit margin since all mine site overheads would have already been paid and only direct operating costs associated with the extra throughout would detract from the additional revenue. 

This hypothesis caught the attention of the University of Queensland’s Julius Kruitschnitt Mineral Research Centre (JKMRC), leading to formal research by Toor, Franke, Powell, Bird, and Waters (2013). Their study was based on the 32 ft. SAG mill at Newcrest’s Cadia Valley Operation (CVO). 

A further investigation was conducted by (Yahyaei, Powell, Toor, Tuxford, & Limpus, 2015) to estimate the effect on throughput and hence profitability by designing liners for performan

ce with more frequent, optimised relines. Yahyaei et al (2015) predicts a 3.7% increase on average in throughput per annum. Although the proposed strategy will increase the cost of liners plus relining by 31.5% (i.e. A$ 548,000), the increase in plant throughput is estimated to yield A$ 20.1 M of additional revenue based on data for 12 months to 30 June 2014 from the plant quarterly report. 

However, a decade after the initial observations, RME observes an increasing trend toward ever thicker, longer-lasting liner designs in SAG mills. The probable reasons for this are: 

- Relining is hazardous, disruptive and often unpredictable. Gains can only be realised when relines are optimised and predictable (Powell, Hilden, & Weerasekara, 2012) . 

- Benefits in reline throughput can be masked by the variability that exists in the ore and the comminution process. 

- Focussing on reducing the number of relines has the very quantifiable benefit of reduced downtime and reducing exposure to risk. 

Personnel responsible for liner design and development and shutdown planning have little or no visibility of concentrator plant metallurgical performance and may not be aware that the SAG mill shell liners, which may last for six months, have turned the site’s 40’ / 12.2m SAG mill into a 37’ / 11.3m SAG mill with 1’6” / 460mm deep shell liners. In addition, new thick liners require reduced mill speed in order to avoid ball strike beyond the toe of the charge. Factors such as these conspire to reduce SAG mill throughput with new thick, ‘highlift’, liners. 

Organising major shutdowns requires intensive coordination and mill relining is recognised as the most dangerous maintenance activity within the concentrator. These factors understandably provide incentive to develop long-life liners, regardless of the documented benefits of the ‘liners for performance’ theory (Yahyaei et al, 2015). 

There is a commercial argument for an intermediate shutdown, primarily to replace performance-optimised shell liners and half the discharge grates but with the opportunity to simultaneously complete other minor maintenance tasks in the concentrator. Competing with this argument is a safety argument to not expose personnel to extra relining events. 

The balance of this paper proposes an environment in which these additional throughput benefits could be realised; an environment where relines are significantly safer, of short duration and are predictable. The possibility of such an environment is beginning to emerge. 

This paper promotes the concept of two large and two small shutdowns per year at possibly three month spacing. New performance and safety technologies eliminate concerns regarding extra downtime and safety risks to mill relining crews. 

###### **Safety technologies and processes** 

A range of new grinding mill relining _safety technologies and processes_ has been developed to deliver vastly improved levels of safety to reliners and, importantly, peace of mind to t

he concentrator personnel responsible for the safety of contract relining crews. 

###### **_Safety technology: recovery of injured personnel from within the mill_** 

In the unfortunate event of an accident inside the mill, safe lifting of the injured relining crew member from the charge to the Mill Relining Machine (MRM) beam can be difficult. Conditions inside the mill at the time of an accident are usually required to be preserved which requires isolation of the MRM, preventing it from being used for rescue. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

An independent rescue jib and stretcher system, designed to enable fast and easy deployment, has been developed by RME. All components are stored in a locked metal box outside the mill in close proximity to the MRM. A key is housed in a ‘break glass to access’ container mounted to the lid of the box, ensuring that it, and the components in the box, are available when needed. The three parts that make up the rescue jib and stretcher system (Rescue Raise) are light and can be hand carried into the mill for erection. The mast is placed into a permanent socket on the MRM and the jib and winch are then assembled to the mast. ###### **_Safety technology: avoiding injury inside the mill: ‘see and be seen’ technologies_** 

One of the greatest in-mill dangers associated with conventional relining (that is, relining with personnel working inside the mill), is the risk of crush injury; crew members being crushed between a transported liner or the Mill Reline Machine structure and the mill shell. The first line of defence is to see and be seen by other crew members or by ‘devices’. There are four see and be seen technologies. 

- Improved in-mill lighting makes people more visible, either by direct line-of-sight or by camera. Adequate lighting is also essential for conventional relining work or automated relining. 

Lighting levels inside the mill are often inadequate, falling below the minimum levels recommended for transit areas and areas where general work is conducted. The MRMs are fitted with focused lighting that illuminates the area around the grapple to acceptable levels but does not provide high level general illumination. A diffused light has been trialled at RME’s R&D facility and at site during several relines. A single light in a large 40’ diameter mill was found to provide excellent general illumination of the transit and general work areas. Reline crew members commented that the single light provided th

e best in-mill visibility that they had experienced. 

Lighting is often located over the MRM turntable such that when personnel on the charge look at the operator, as is often required, the intensity of the light is uncomfortable and results in momentary blindness when looking away. An advantage of this new light is that the level of diffusion allows it to be looked at directly, without discomfort, and there is no temporary blindness when looking away. Also the large diameter of the diffuser reduces the size and sharpness of shadows, providing a clearer work environment. The new lights are fitted as a pair to the MRM’s Safety Portal.

To improve the MRM operator’s view of other relining personnel in the mill, all new RME MRM are fitted with two ‘visibility aid’ cameras and have a display screen at the MRM operator’s console. This camera and screen system provides the operator with clear images of other relining crew personnel in the mill. ###### • Proximity detection within the mill 

RME has developed a proximity detection system for use during mill Relining. The system provides an additional layer of crushing hazard risk reduction that is independent of the MRM operator. The sensing technology has long been deployed in underground mines and other industrial situations to detect the presence of workers that may not be visible to, or noticed by, a machine operator. The technology provides an alert to the person in the hazardous zone and to the MRM operator. All personnel in the mill are required to wear a smart tag that senses the proximity of the MRM. Once sensed, the tag transmits a signal to the proximity controller on the MRM and provides the alerts. RME has designed a machine control system that integrates with the controller and responds to the sensor al

ert by slowing or stopping the MRM when a person enters the warning and danger zones. The size of the zones and response of the MRM are configurable. 

The system has been fitted to RME’s R&D MRM for functional testing and also to a customer’s MRM for validation during a reline. 

With traditional relines, personnel are often required to be in close proximity to the MRM while it is still in motion. Site testing is essential to understand the zone and machine response parameters that will reduce exposure to the crushing hazard, while allowing the reline to continue. One full reline has been conducted with the system installed and work practices were generally able to be adapted to accommodate safe manmachine interactions. 

Good lighting, improved visibility of other crew members via cameras and the ultimate protection of the proximity system (which forces the MRM to stop) are all _see and be seen_ benefits for the crew inside the mill. 

- The in-mill surveillance camera extends this _see and be seen_ philosophy to observers outside the mill. 

The mill relining environment, inside the mill, is a dangerous work site. There are a large number of individual hazards, all of which can place the crew members’ safety at risk. 

The risk appetite of mill relining crews differs from company to company, as do skill levels in this unregulated environment. If there were no reported injuries during the last reline, this crew would be deemed to be acceptable. In practice, there is no guarantee that the same ‘safe’ crew members would be available for the next reline. 

Visibility of activities inside a mill, from outside the mill, is virtually impossible. There is only one entry portal, the feed end trunnion, and it is largely filled by a MRM. Access by non-relining crew personnel, to the interior of the mill, is discouraged and requires various endorsements including a valid confined space qualification. 

The confined space of the mill often presents a visual barrier for managers wishing to enforce safe work practices that are consistent with site standards. Most concentrator personnel therefore do not enter the mill during a reline; it is simply too much trouble. Monitoring of safety standards and safe practices inside the mill by concentrator personnel, 24 hours a day for three or four days, is extraordinarily difficult. Also, contract relining crews can behave better during the short periods of inspection. 

RME’s experience demonstrates that a widespread belief is held amongst contract relining crews that reporting injuries to mine site personnel (that is, their customer) jeopardises future work prospects. 

RME personnel have witnessed, and at times filmed, some terribly dangerous mill relining practices. 

All mining companies would support uniform safety standards across the entire site. The practical difficulties of monitoring practices, inside the mill, confound the safety aspirations of mining companies. 

RME installs cameras inside and outside mi

lls to gather data for our mill RELINE DIRECTOR discrete-event simulation software for the purpose of optimising mill relining performance. These cameras gather the data required for optimisation but analysis of the data also reveals the frequency and magnitude of dangerous relining practices inside the mill. 

To provide visibility, without the requirement for mill access, a surveillance camera system with external high resolution screen was developed. A 360 degree High Definition IP camera is positioned high above the MRM cantilevered off the Safety Portal, providing 360 degree vision of the inside of the mill. After successful testing at RME’s R&D facility, the surveillance camera system was installed on an operational Mill Reline Machine for use during a reline. The system proved to be very popular not only with managers but also external crew members wishing to observe reline progress. The system allows for many days of continuous high resolution recording, allowing review of the footage in the event of an incident. This surveillance system removes the need for concentrator management or concentrator safety personnel to enter the mill. 

It is believed that the presence of this surveillance camera would materially lift mill relining crew safety standards and practices. Safety-conscious, collaborative reline crews will understand the safety benefits that such a surveillance system provides to site and to the crew.

###### **_Safety technology: mill entry and exit travel safety_** 

There is a personnel movement transition zone between ‘inside the mill’ and ‘outside the mill’ to which RME has given particular attention. Outside the mill is a relatively safe environment which deteriorates quite rapidly as the mill is entered, with personnel immediately working at heights and traversing quite narrow beam walkways. 

The single greatest impediment to successful mechanisation and optimisation of grinding mill relining is the diameter of mill entry at the feed end of the mill. Smaller entry diameters limit the size and capacity of the MRM and, ultimately, the physical size of liners. Entry diameter is often driven by the lowest cost (smallest, albeit adequate) mill trunnion bearing. 

Smaller entry diameters also increase the difficulty for relining personnel to enter and exit the mill. 

Typically, the MRM necessarily consumes the entire bottom half of the available mill entry, leaving the top half open for passage of liners and personnel. This entry space can be quite low; a 900mm high x 1800mm wide semi-circular s

pace for an 1800mm clear entry diameter mill. 

When personnel enter the mill, often on their hands and knees, they make the transition from broad, safe platform area, outside the mill, to the relatively narrow top surface of the MRM’s outer beam. 

Once in the mill, relining crew members are required to make the transition from ‘hands and knees’ to ‘standing’ position on a relatively narrow beam with significant fall heights, each side, to the mill’s charge level. 

To overcome this risk, RME has developed a range of safe travel or securing aids to secure personnel against falling from heights during this transition between inside and outside the mill. 

For RUSSELL TWIN MRMs, the safe travel aid takes the form of a travelling post and lanyard device which provides a third point of contact (two feet and one hand) and, in the unlikely event of a fall, has the certified strength to arrest the falling crew member. 

For single RUSSELL MRMs, the safe travel aid takes the form of a personal lanyard and hook which is easily attached to a horizontal line attached to the Safety Portal while the reliner is outside the mill. See Figure 6 below.

Today, mills are very big as are their liners. Individual liners of 5,000kgs are not uncommon. Mill relining equipment has advanced from a reliner’s back, through to 3-axis liner handler cranes, to today’s 7/8-axis MRMs.

###### **_Safety technology and process: a paradigm shift_** 

INSIDEOUT Technology is the name given to a group of technologies and features that facilitate relining to be performed outside the hazardous mill environment. 

All of these concepts have now been materialised through the development of prototype technologies. Many have progressed beyond prototype to production status. 

The mill is a confined space with an uneven floor and with the potential for falling objects. The atmosphere is often hot and humid with the potential for falling objects. Crew members are currently required to work in close proximity to a powerful MRM that is often carrying suspended loads and, for some tasks, crew members resort to working at height on ladders or by climbing up the liners. Removing the requirement for people to be in the mill is a safety imperative. 

INSIDEOUT Technologies falls into two main groupings; INSIDEOUT Placement and INSIDEOUT Removal. 

###### **_INSIDEOUT Placement_** 

INSIDEOUT Placement technologies are designed to allow the installation of new liners without the need for reline crew members to be in the mill, on the mill charge. 

The two main tasks that are currently performed in the mill, in close proximity to the loaded MRM, during liner installation are: 

- Liner alignment – a crew member on the charge looks through the

liner bolt hole in the liner and provides direction to the MRM operator who manipulates the liner until the bolt hole in the liner is precisely aligned with the hole in the shell. 

- Bolt insertion – once the liner is in position, the crew member inserts bolts through the hole from the inside of the mill. A nut and washer are then screwed onto the bolt from outside the mill. 

Testing has shown that with the correct communication headset and standardised commands, a person on the outside of the mill looking back through the mill bolt hole, can direct the MRM operator to bring the liner into accurate alignment. Liner orientation has proven less easy to judge from outside the mill. One solution that is undergoing field tests consist of two sensor modules; one module is affixed to the mill shell, outside the mill, in line with the bolt holes and the other is affixed to the liner or grapple on a flat surface perpendicular to the bolt axis. The sensors communicate via Wi-Fi and a display provides direct visual feedback of the liner’s orientation, relative to the bolt hole, to the MRM operator. 

Bolt installation is aided by thorough preparation. It is achieved by placing the bolts into the liner bolt holes outside the mill and temporarily securing them in the liner using patented clips, the design of which are dictated by the bolt and liner. A feature of the clips is that they hold the bolt securely in the liner but release when impacted. The end of the liner bolt is drilled and tapped and a specialised cap is fitted to the end of the bolt, prior to installation in the liner. When the liner has been accurately positioned by the MRM and the bolt holes are aligned, a crew member on the outside of the mill attaches the end of the BOLTBOSS Slide Hammer tool to the specialised cap on the liner bolt and then uses this tool to impact the bolt, releasing it from the clip. The bolt is then extracted through the mill shell. A nut and washer are then released via a cam action from the BOLTBOSS Slide Hammer tool and slid and hand-screwed onto the end of the bolt. The Slide Hammer tool is then released from the bolt cap. 

This INSIDEOUT Placement methodology has been successfully tested at RME’s R&D facility. Successful site trials have been performed during 2017 and 2018.The methodology described above is applicable to shell liners, feed end liners and Pulp Lifters. Liners that are secured with long bolts such as grates require a different approach. An external bolting solution has been successfully used in RME’s R&D liners however no site testing has yet been carried out as liner casting and fastener modifications are required for its implementation.

###### **_INSIDEOUT Removal_** 

INSIDEOUT Removal technologies are designed to allow the removal of liners without personnel in the mill. 

RME’s preferred approach for liner removal is to capture the liners directly from the mil

l shell rather than from the mill charge. The traditional, widely practiced approach to liner removal, which involves knocking all accessible liners onto the mill charge, has come about as a result of the need for the mill to be evacuated while THUNDERBOLT Hammers are in use. The result is that liners that were neatly ordered on the mill shell are converted to a random pile on the charge or in some cases still stuck to the mill shell. These liners must be levered, turned and slung from the mill by the MRM and reline personnel. During this ‘knock-in’ phase, the MRM sits idle with no liner removal from the mill occurring. 

To achieve RME’s objective of capturing liners directly from the mill shell, it is first necessary to enable the accurate control of the MRM from outside the mill. 

This has been achieved by the development of the VU (Virtual You) 3D headset and Gimbal. Initial experiments with commonly available Virtual Reality (VR) headsets and camera systems proved disappointing, with high latency and poor image quality. These systems were adequate for gaming but were not capable of transmitting or displaying true, real-time, high-quality, 3D imagery.  RME’s Technology Group developed a robust Gimbal suitable for the mill environment. Two Gimbals are located inside the mill in positions that provide clear vision of the liner. The Gimbals mimic the movements of the operator’s head, allowing natural viewing of the MRM and environment. The dual cameras and headset provide a near eyeresolution 3D image. The VU has now been tested and proven to allow the accurate driving and positioning of the MRM by an operator located outside of the mill. 

To capture a worn liner, to allow its extraction directly from the mill shell, requires two ‘handles’. Handles are achieved by a simple liner design change and a special threaded liner bolt sleeve. 

A senior RME engineer working in the development team proposed that if the hole in the liner could be made smaller than the hole in the mill shell, then an object could pass through the hole from the outside of the mill and lock in the liner. The object could then be gripped by the MRM, providing secure attachment to the liner. This proposed concept evolved into the idea that sleeves could be added to the end of the liner bolt that were small enough to pass through the mill shell but be caught in the smaller bolt hole in the liner. These sleeves could be screwed onto the bolt after the nut and washer were removed and prior to the bolt being knocked in. This solution would have the added benefit of preventing the bolt from becoming a projectile and would remove the need for bolts to be picked up from the mill charge prior to inching the mill. 



Figure 7 – Photograph of the Steve Sleeve fitted to the end of a liner bolt 

These became known as Steve Sleeves after the engineer, Steve Waters, who proposed the concept. The head of the bolt provides an ideal shape for engagement by a tool. It was found during testin

g that the sleeve swaged itself into the liner hole when impacted by the THUNDERBOLT Recoilless Hammer, preventing the

Investigation showed that the hole in the liner is usually the same diameter or a larger diameter, than the hole in the mill. This is because of the tolerances required when casting liners due to shrinkage distortion. The general tolerance of both the hole diameter and hole centre distances for cast liners is +/- 1.5mm. 

In order that this concept could be tested without liner modification, a hole insert was designed that could be placed in the liner hole, reducing its diameter prior to the installation of the liner. These inserts were tested by trying to drive a bolt with a sleeve through them using a THUNDERBOLT 1500 Hammer. It was found that the sleeve could survive between 7 and 10 blows of the Hammer which was considered adequate.

###### **THUNDERBOLT SKYWAY** 

In late 2016 and early 2017, a prototype THUNDERBOLT SKYWAY system was designed, manufactured and assembled at RME’s Research and Development facility. This prototype consists of a single tower and beam, a platform and a semi-automated THUNDERBOLT 1500 module. 

The R&D mill shell was used to test the guidance accuracy of the control system and the full facility was used to help establish the relining practices that are appropriate for such a technology. 

The SKYWAY prototype has undergone significant durability testing having been subjected to the equivalent of 30 arduous full relines to date. The majority of the THUNDERBOLT impacts have been performed against a liner mass resulting in maximum stress on the system components. Testing will continue until the equivalent of 60 full relines have been performed, equating to at least ten years of service at a multi-mill concentrator. 

SKYWAY consists of an elevated rail structure that forms a halo around the mill. The rails are supported by vertical columns that provide a small floor-level footp

rint during mill operation. 

Standard elevating platform modules (refer Figure 10) and THUNDERBOLT 1500 modules are installed onto the elevated rail at the commencement of the reline and are removed at the end of the reline. When a site has multiple mills, an elevated rail is permanently installed at each mill.  Because the Platform and THUNDERBOLT modules are removed following a reline, they are able to service multiple mills. The elevated rail has many advantages: it occupies a space that is generally available at most sites and allows the platform module and THUNDERBOLT Hammer module to navigate obstructions that are usually encountered around a mill.

###### **_LEAN one piece flow and automation_** 

The removal of personnel from the mill using the INSIDEOUT methodologies opens up the possibility for a totally new approach to relining. INSIDEOUT and removing people from the mill allows: 

- the Lean principal of creating flow; making it possible to implement One Piece Flow 

- automation or semi-automation of the MRM 

Lean manufacturing, since its emergence in the late 1980s, has had a profound and lasting effect on all advanced manufacturing companies. 

Two Lean principles that have had a significant effect on RME’s factory efficiency and productivity are: 

- Flow - ‘creating continuous flow to bring problems to the surface’ (Liker, 2004, pp. 87-103). The practical expression of this principal at RME was the introduction of One Piece Flow or Takt to the MRM production process in 2009. 

- Standardisation – ‘Standardised Tasks are the Foundation for Continuous Improvement and Employee Empowerment’ (Liker, 2004, pp. 140-148). 

Takt is a German word for rhythm or meter. It is the rate of customer demand; the rate at which the customer is buying the product. In the case of MRMs for RME in 2009, this was on average one machine every ten working days. 

The principle of One Piece Flow and Takt requires that companies st

rive to manufacture goods one at a time, at the rate of customer demand, balancing the work throughout the Production Line so that the tasks and resources assigned to each process are matched to the Takt rate. Once a balanced work flow is achieved, work is standardised and variances become the focus of increased attention. 

The concept of introducing One Piece Flow or Takt to mill relining was proposed in 2015 (Rubie et al 2015). Current relining practices use a batch methodology during liner knock-in. As described earlier, during knockin, every member of the crew occupies a zone around the mill and using whatever equipment is available in that zone, removes nuts and washers and knocks all accessible bolts and liners into the mill. 

Problems with this approach include: 

- It is not clear what the critical path activity is during knock-in, so difficulties with one liner can be covered up by activities on another liner 

- The role of all reline personnel changes for knock-in, interrupting the flow of work 

- It is not possible to standardise work as the tasks required to address the chaos created inside the mill is unique for each inching cycle and for each liner 

- Automation of liner removal is not possible 

With a Takt or One Piece Flow approach, a single liner would be unfastened and gripped by the MRM, removed from the shell and transported to the liner cart. The MRM would then return to the next liner requiring removal from the shell. 

Using this methodology: 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

- The roles of each person can remain constant throughout the reline 

- Problems are made visible and are brought to the surface for solving 

- People become specialised at their tasks 

- Standardisation of processes can be achieved 

- Waste and bottlenecks are made very visible 

If a Takt time was assigned to individual liner movements into and out of the mill, problems that interfered with achieving the Takt rate would receive the focus they deserve. 

Simply adopting this mindset when practicing liner placement and removal at RME’s testing facility spawned many ideas as to how significant time could be removed from relines. In the idealised environment of the R&D facility, a Takt rate of 2.5 minutes for each liner movement in and out of the mill was achieved. 

The benefits of semi-automating the MRM movements, to eliminate the time wasted trying to achieve the correct geometry for both liner placement and liner removal, became very obvious.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Rock breakage is a major component of all mining and mineral processing operations with the particle size distribution linked to productivity through the comminution chain. Optimisation and automatic control of comminution, material handling, and agglomeration processes is a complex task with large potential for gains in productivity, and energy efficiency. A key factor in realising these gains is the requirement for fullyautomated online particle size distribution measurement to provide the necessary feedback and input for control. Moreover, to enable automatic control system it is necessary to provide a consistent, reliable size distribution measurement that avoids the significant errors resulting from under-sizing overlapped particles and over-sizing clusters of fine particles. Published literature and observation of commercial systems indicate a body of predominantly 2D photographic based particle size measurement systems that suffer from a number of significant errors except in the simplest case of a monolayer of particles under good illumination with limited colour variation in the material. 

In order to overcome these limitations a university and industry collaboration developed three-dimensional particle measurement (3DPM) between 2006 and 2012, based on 3D surface profile measurement of the visible material on conveyor. 3DPM avoids particle delineation errors due to variation in material colour and shadows, detects overlapp

ing versus non-overlapping particles, and identifies areas of fine particles as fines and not large rocks. 3DPM measures: the visible material and calculates its particle size distribution, bulk volume, detects boulders, and conveyor belt fill factor in an automated consistent manner. Furthermore, 3DPM’s advanced algorithms allow observation of particle variation that would otherwise be undetected without the capacity to identify visible areas-of-fines and overlapped particles. Boliden Mines has installed 3DPM at three operations for measurement between the stockpile silo and grinding mill, and measurement after the primary crusher. Fragmentation measurements across multiple years of measurement are presented with some observations of plant behaviour. In the future 3DPM results will be incorporated into automatic control strategies for plant optimisation. 3DPM is used across a wide range of material types and applications that also includes; limestone aggregate for quality control in manufacturing, agglomerates for closed-loop automatic control in chemical production, and measurement of coke for size-based blending feed control to the blast furnace in steel production. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

###### **Boliden** 

Boliden is a Swedish exploration, mining and metallurgy company providing mining, refining and recycling of base and precious metals. Boliden's open pit and underground mines are some of the world’s most productive in part due to a constant focus on the development of new techniques and methods for exploiting resources. Boliden invests heavily in technology and modernisation to streamline the design, planning and management of its mines to further raise quality. Boliden continues to actively pursuing the development of automation in mines with the dual goals, of improved safety and non-stop production. Boliden incorporates nine mines in Sweden, Finland and Ireland, and five smelters across Sweden, Finland and Norway. 

Boliden is one of the world's premier zinc producers and the leader in Europe when it comes to the production of copper and nickel. Boliden main products are zinc and lead ingots, copper cathodes, gold bars 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

and silver granules. In 2016 Boliden’s mines had a combined operating profit of SEK 3447 M (approximately AUD 540 M) 

As part of this drive for modernisation and automation Boliden commissioned installations of an automated online particle size distribution measurement system on conveyor belt using 3D surface imaging called 3DPM. Boliden has previously used a number of Split-Online (2D photographic based) systems but when considering a new system 3DPM was chosen as it provides consistent automated fragmentation assessment that negates many of the disadvantages of 2D techniques (detailed further below in the _Particle size distribution measurement_ section). 3DPM is installed at three Boliden operations, namely Aitik, Garpenberg and T

ara. The Aitik mine in the north of Sweden is Europe's largest open pit mine and the world’s most efficient open-pit copper mine, processing 36 M tonnes of ore in 2016. Garpenberg, in central Sweden is a highly productive underground zinc mine with silver, lead, copper and gold, contributing an operating profit in 2016 of SEK 2063 M, and Tara in Ireland is Europe’s largest zinc mine with lead and silver. 

###### **Goals** 

Boliden’s goal is to improve comminution efficiency and production. To that end, automated, online size distribution measurement is performed and recorded. 3DPM provides operator feedback and data that can be investigated and compared to plant operation and it is in this capacity that 3DPM is currently used. Furthermore, it provides a reliable frequent measurement that can be used as a reference point for material size between the mine and the mill. Improving understanding of how the size distribution impacts milling, and crushing will enable the next step to developing automated control strategies that use the size distribution as input, both for automation of individual crushers and mills, but also automated control across the comminution process. It is primarily within this context of measurement and big data for understanding that 3DPM is currently used. Boliden’s vision for applying 3DPM is covered by the following areas. 

###### _Root cause analysis_ 

The ore size distribution in the mill is essential for autogenous grinding. The mill throws material in a cascading motion and relies on impact breakage when large rocks impact back on the main charge breaking the larger particles with compression grinding applying to the finer particles. If the proportion of sufficiently large rocks is too small, impact breakage will not occur and then less efficient compression grinding will dominate thereby reducing the overall efficiency of the mill and decrease throughput. Within this context, a 3DPM installation on the mill feed can serve two purposes. The first purpose applies to the case of decreased mill efficiency where the data provided by the 3DPM gives valuable information on the material feed to the engineers that investigate the root cause of the deviation. The second purpose applies if the mill has dual feed where a larger fraction can be fed to the mill from a separate storage of larger rocks. If 3DPM indicates insufficient larger rocks, the operator or a control system could feed more to the mill. 

###### _Crusher control_ 

At all Boliden mining operations, the ore is crushed and stockpiled in a silo before feeding to autogenous grinding (AG) mills. Feeding an AG mill with too small material decreases the mill throughput due to the resulting lack of grinding media. This indicates that there is an optimal size distribution in the feed and that controlling it would be beneficial. Measurement of the rock size distribution directly after the crushers is a key enabler for implementing a crusher control strategy to optimize

the feed to the AG mills. Primary crushing is removing overly large fractions and could be controlled to target production of more suitably sized grinding media. At Boliden mines there are ore silos after crushing and before the mills with multiple outlet feeds providing an ore mixing function. Alternating periods of fine or coarse crushing could be used to provide a more desirable overall size distribution in the silo with sufficient rocks for crushing media and more fines to increase throughput. 

###### _Feed control_ 

3DPM facilitates feed control to the mill. To even-out variations in the feed to the mill from the crushers, an ore storage is located between the mill and the crushers. The size of the storage is designed to handle most unexpected disturbances in the crushers, which at the Aitik mine is approximately one day of mill production. Each ore storage is simply designed as a large silo where incoming crushed material is fed at the top and a number of individually controllable feeders underneath extracts ore to the conveyor belt that feeds the mills. Inherent to this design is the segregation of particle sizes in the silo, which means that each of the outlets will produce material with a different size distribution. As the material is extracted from the silo and new material enters, the size distribution from each of the outlets will change over time. Continuous size distribution measurements with 3DPM on each outlet would allow control of the feed size distribution to the mill to better suit autogenous grinding and increase throughput.

###### **Particle size distribution measurement** 

In the mining industry many processes affect, or are affected by the material particle size distribution, including blasting, cave design, comminution, and agglomeration. As a result, significant effort goes into measuring or estimating the size distribution of particulate material in order to evaluate and optimise production in terms of production rate and costs. Mine and quarry operators want to measure the particle sizing results of these activities but the standard measurement technique of sieving/screening is often an impractical assessment tool due to slow feedback, quantity of material, and typically infrequent measurement. 

As a result, particle size measurement using machine vision has been the subject of research and development since the 1980’s (Carlsson and Nyberg 1983, Ord 1988) due to the opportunity for online, noncontact, fully automated measurement to facilitate evaluation and optimisation of particle processes. However, the bulk of published literature and commercial systems for fragmentation measurement rely on 2D photographic-based imaging. 2D systems have a range of error sources and limitations outlined in detail by Sanchidria et al. (2009), Noy (2013) and Thurley (2014). These limitations include particle delineation errors due to uneven or inco

nsistent lighting, excessive or variable shadowing, and, colour and texture variation in the material. Additionally, they lack a direct measure of scale, suffer from perspective distortion, lack the capability to distinguish between overlapped and non-overlapped particles (resulting in under-sizing bias) and do not detect areas of fines in a meaningful way (typically resulting in an over-sizing bias). As a result, photographic-based 2D systems typically require extensive manual editing of the particle delineation to provide a reasonable estimation, although this introduces operator bias. Whilst manual editing may be passable for a non-time-critical assessment such as a blasted muckpile, it is unsuitable for process control. Photographic-based systems such as Split and Wipfrag also perform a distribution transformation based on a user specified sieve size distribution, transforming the particle size results from the images into the expected sieve size distribution. However, it appears common that this transformation is required to be performed at regular intervals to keep the system ‘calibrated.’ Re-calibrating at intervals eliminates data consistency making it inappropriate to compare results collected before and after the calibration, which is unsuitable for collecting and analysing trends over long periods of time. 

Potts and Ouchtenlony (2005) reviewed the Split commercial photographic-based 2D system and expressed strong reservations saying that 2D _“imaging has a certain but limited usefulness when measuring fragment size distribution in a muckpile or from a belt in an accurate way. It could probably detect rough tendencies in fragmentation variations, if the lighting conditions do not vary too much.”_ In addition, they report that for their application, the system erroneously _“causes the truncated, bimodal distributions (of rock) to, in a misleading way, show up as unimodal curves. This implies a strong limitation of the system’s ability to detect changes in the form of the fragment size distribution.”_ Potts and Ouchterlony (2005) were attempting to measure the size distribution of blasted rock with a high proportion of fines and large sizes meaning the size distribution curve had two peaks (bimodal) instead of one peak (unimodal) where the later has the highest proportion of material is in the middle size classes. Using a fragmentation measurement system that cannot detect a bimodal size distribution of material will prevent detection of one when it is present. The choice of a fragmentation measurement system comes down to how much one can trust a system if it forces a type of size distribution instead of representing the actual fragmentation of the particles visible at the time of measurement. 

3DPM measures the size of the particles that were visible on the surface of the conveyor belt at the time of measurement. It reports the size distribution of these visible particles as well as bulk volume, detects boulders, and the conveyor bel

t fill factor, in an automated consistent manner. 3DPM is based on the research of Thurley (2002, 2014), Thurley and Andersson (2007), and uses a 3D surface profile measurement laser sensor that overcomes many of the issues related to 2D and photographic based methods. It is a ruggedized industrial measurement system based on laser triangulation (a projected laser line and measurement camera) collecting highly accurate 3D point profiles of the laser line across the rock pile on conveyor. Figure 1 (left) shows the laser triangulation measurement sensor, Figure 1 (middle) shows a false colour image of the 3D data of the rocks on conveyor, and Figure 1 (right) shows the automatic particle delineation of that same 3D data.
