The 3D surface profile image data allows 3DPM to perform particle delineation without problems due to lighting, shadows or colour variation of the material. It enables automated analysis without the need for manual editing and provides direct measurement of the material size avoiding scaling or perspective distortion errors. Furthermore, 3DPM’s algorithms classify delineated particles as areas-of-fines, overlapped and non-overlapped particles mitigating significant sizing errors due to under-sizing overlapped particles, and over-sizing areas-of-fines are large rocks. Areas-of-fines are sized based on their visible area, and individual particles are sized based on the width of the best-fit-bounding-rectangle around the particle. 

3DPM uses the predominantly non-overlapped rocks for which the visible portion is a reliable estimate of size, and the areas-of-fines to calculate the size distribution results. Each individual particle is sized based on the width of the best-fit-rectangle as it provides a good estimate of the particle sieve size (Thurley 2002, Thurley and Andersson 2007). Size results are collated into a size distribution using one size class for detected areas-of-fines, and then incorporating each individual rock into the size distribution.  The size distribution is them typically binned into size classes specified by the customer. This does not have to be particularly coarse. For example, the 2006 implementation (Thurley and Andersson, 2007) for iron ore pellets used size classes of 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12.5, 13, 14 and 16+ mm based on a 3D point resolution of 0.5mm. 

Figure 2 (Thurley, 2014) shows an example of the sizing results for 500 measurements (over 4 hours) for material that has passed through a primary crusher. The raw measurement curves are shown in light grey, and a polynomial smoothing is shown in the following colours; black, blue, light blue, green for the D80, D50, D20 and D10 percent passing values respectively. One can clearly see significant variation in the size classes, most particularly in the D10 value.

However, if 3DPM’s advanced algorithms to detect fines and overlapped particles are turned off, then the results become smoother, and particularly the D10 and D20 become close to featureless horizontal lines, losing their capacity to discriminate significant variation in the output from the crusher (as shown in Figure 3 from Thurley, 2014). By turning off these algorithms, two opposing errors are added to the results with areas-of-fines mis-sized as large rocks, and overlapped rocks mis-sized as small rocks, making the measurement unreliable and unrepresentative of the size and size variation of the visible material.

As with any vision-based measurement technique (photographic or 3D profile), one can only measure the visible surface of the material meaning that the size estimations are subject to surface bias such as from material segregation due to vibration. It is important to consider measurement in a location where material segregation does not catastrophically bias the visible surface.  Size estimations are also dependent on the scan resolution which will define a lower limit, below which it is not possible to delineate and size individual particles. However, as already noted, areas of visible fines are detected and classified as fines in the resultant particle size distribution. All of these factors mean that vision-based methods are not the same as sieving/screening for measuring the particle size distribution. However, the issue is not whether the

###### **RESULTS** 

Difficulties in stabilising the mill and flotation processes are a key concern for Boliden. Typically, one can quickly determine that fluctuations in these processes are not caused by something in the concentrator, such as reagents or mill wear, and therefore it is likely changes in the ore. Variations in the material size distribution is a key parameter for autogenous mills and therefore a key area of disagreement between the mine and mill when production difficulties occur. With the installation of 3DPM, size distribution results can now confirm whether or not the rock size distribution correlates with mill production and therefore if it is a casua

l factor in reduced productivity focusing problem solving efforts in the right direction.  In the case of the Tara installation in 2012, 3DPM settled the dispute between the mine and mill by establishing that variations in the material size distribution did not correlate with reduced productivity in the mill. Subsequently it was established that regions in the mine with harder mineral composition and therefore harder to grind was the key casual factor in reduced mill productivity at that time. 

Size distribution results are shown in graphs of size versus time. Each point in the graph represents an hourly average of 3DPM measurements. This typically means each point is an average of about 120 measurements as 3DPM calculates the size distribution approximately every 30 seconds in the installations presented here. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Boliden has installed four 3DPM systems for automated online size distribution measurement based on 3D profile imaging in a range of operations for measurement of mill feed and crusher output. These systems provide reliable and consistent size distribution measurement over years and provide the necessary big data for subsequent root cause analysis of mill and crusher behaviour in relation to material size. Specifically, in the case of the Tara installation and the difficulties during 2012, 3DPM resolved disagreement between the mine and mill and established that material size was not correlating with the mill productivity problems at that time. 3DPM provides a useful base line measurement between the mine and the mill, providing a reference for discussion and setting of size related targets for the supplier (the mine) and the customer (the mill). It is immediately useable for blending and feed control if there are multiple feed sources available to the operator or control system. 3DPM is a reliable long-term measurement system having been in operation for six years at the Tara mine. Looking forward, further work on identifying size related features useful for control and implementing autonomous control strategies will be undertaken. 

3DPM provides size data that avoids a number of significant errors common to traditional 2D photographic based sizing systems. It avoids particle delineation errors due to variation in material colour and shadows, avoids scaling and perspective distortion errors, detects overlapping versus non-overlapping particles preventing mis-sizing overlapped rocks as small rocks, and identifies areas of fine particles a

s bulk fines and not large rocks. 3DPM measures the visible material and calculates; its particle size distribution, bulk volume, detects boulders, and conveyor belt fill factor in an automated consistent manner. 3DPM is used across a wide range of material types both in precious metals and other applications including; limestone aggregate for quality control in manufacturing, agglomerates for closed-loop automatic control in chemical production, and measurement of coke for size-based blending feed control to the blast furnace in steel production.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Philsaga Mining Corporation (Philsaga) had three main aims in converting their lining system from steel to metal cap. They wanted to increase mill availability, minimise localised high wear and optimise particle breakage to deliver increased efficiency within the milling circuit. Combining Discrete Element Method (DEM) modelling and empirical interpretation of liner wear resulted in a rigorous approach to understanding the impact of mill liners on overall mill performance. This new understanding was subsequently used to not only derive a new lining design to optimise performance and thereby improve overall plant economics, but also to guide further lining development. 

In this work, detailed DEM modelling, developed from actual plant data, together with optimising liner design for wear paved the way towards the installation of a Metal Cap lining system at Philsaga’s Ш6100 mm SAG Mill. The results were a reported increase in SAG mill throughput of 16 – 20 per cent due to improved breakage through more efficient use of installed power, a reduction in localised high liner wear with overall increase in liner life and reduction in liner replacement time. Site also reported an increased gold recovery of 2 per cent which the improved breakage might have contributed to. 

This paper will present the design challenges and compare the Metal Cap lining systems performance against Steel lining system. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Whilst liners play an important role in protecting the mill shell from the aggressive milling environment, they also play a critical role in delivering the input power to the charge, thereby greatly impacting the mill charge motion  (Powell, _et al_ , 2012).  For a mill with identical operating conditions, a different lifter design will change the charge profile and consequently the mechanism of grinding (Powell & Nurick, 1996a, b, c). 

The motion of grinding media and the energy distribution have a profound influence on the comminution of ore particles in tumbling mills. The DEM modelling allows numerical simulation of the dynamic interaction of the mill charge media with the mill liners and lifters. It allows calculation of the trajectories of individual entities in the entire grinding charge as they move in the mill and collide with one another and the mill shell. The resulting impact energy and force distributions can be used to calculate the grinding rate in mills, as presented by some workers in this area (Mishra and Rajamani 1994, Cleary 2001, Datta and Rajamani 2002, Mishra and Rajamani 1994, Powell, Govender, and McBride, 2008, Herbst, 2004). Detail review of the application of DEM in this ar

ea can be found in Weerasekara _et al_ (2013).  The DEM modelling could help to study charge motion and energy in detail (Weerasekara, Liu and Powell, 2016). 

Based on years of research in the field of comminution and SAG milling, it has been observed during SAG milling operation that a wide distribution of energy events (collision) is generated. Consequently, designs based on the concept of single high energy impact breakage events in the toe region do not reflect the reality of the collision environment that actually exists within the mill. A broader range of breakage mechanisms, including ones that operate at very low impact energies, are involved in comminution in a SAG mill. Typically, five dominant breakage mechanisms are identified (compiled in Weerasekara _et al_ , 2013): 

1. Abrasion: reduction in diameter by shear interactions. 

2. Rounding: change in shape (reduction in aspect ratio and angularity) by preferential frictional sliding on corners and high curvature parts of the particles surfaces. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

3. Chipping: preferential removal of corners and edges by normal impacts (leading to shape change). 

4. Impact breakage: single impact breakage due to high energy normal interactions. 

5. Incremental damage: cumulative damage from normal impacts leading to body breakage. This is a critically important mechanism, particularly in SAG mills where there are many weak collisions. 

Philsaga assets are located in Central Eastern Mindanao in the Republic of the Philippines and are accessed by the national highway north of Davao City.  The new ‘Co-O’ Mill, based on a SAG mill with capacity of approximately 2500 tpd, was commissioned in the March quarter 2014 as a Carbon-In-Leach (CIL) circuit. The plant incorporates some upgraded leaching circuits from the old mill. Philsaga had three main aims in converting their lining system from steel to metal-cap. They were to increase mill availability, minimise localised high wear and optimise particle breakage to deliver increased efficiency within the milling circuit. 

This paper presents the work carried out, and some of the modern tools used, to convert the existing steel lining system to optimized metal-cap lining system at Philsaga’s concentration plant, both to improve grinding efficiency and to decrease liner wear. This work presents the improvements achieved. 

###### **MATERIALS AND METHODS** 

###### **Charge particle trajectory predications** 

In order to determine the charge trajectory, software called MillTraj® was used, an approach developed by Powell (1991). This provides a quick and easy way of initially identifying and comparing charge trajectory for a given lining system under a given set of operating conditions. The design of the liner and the operation of the mill need to ensure that there are no direct steel on steel impacts above the toe region, otherwise the liners and balls will suffer severely accel

erated wear and there is a risk of major breakage and damage to liners and lifters. 

###### **DEM Modelling** 

DEM solves Newton’s equations of motion to resolve particle motion and incorporates a contact law to resolve inter-particle contact forces (Figure 1). Forces are typically integrated explicitly in time to predict the time history response of the material using an appropriate quadrature method. A detail description of the mathematical models can be found in early work of (Cundall and Strack 1979, Cundall, 1988) and publications since then. 

###### _Impact Specific Energy_ 

The impact specific energy is a cumulative value of the total normal contact energies experienced by a particle divided by its mass. The impact component refers to a normal collision event as depicted in Figure 2. For example, the regions which exhibit high impact collision events are those primarily underneath the cascading throw of the particles in the charge and also those generally under the bulk mass of the charge. 

###### _Shear Specific Energy_ 

The shear specific energy is a cumulative value of the total shear contact energies experienced by a particle divided by its mass. The shear collision event is depicted in 

Figure 3. For example, the regions which exhibit high shear collision events are those primarily in the upper and lower regions of the dead-zone of the charge.

###### _Collision energy spectrum_ 

Using these DEM simulations, the energy dissipation associated with different particle interactions can be calculated. Frequency distributions of energy, both in the normal and shear directions can be determined from all the individual collision events. Spectra can be calculated for each type of collision event and for each ball and rock size class. The collision energy is expressed as a specific energy (Ecs). This energy density is noted by researchers and practitioners in comminution to be the key driver in rock fracture. Thus, although a large rock may experience a large absolute collision energy, the dissipation of that energy throughout the rock can result in little damage due to its large mass. For the same absolute impact energy, a small rock one tenth of the diameter will experience 1000-fold energy density of the large rock and may shatter from the resultant high intensity stress waves. 

The simulations for SAG/AG mills are revealing that the conditions for breakage are different to those traditionally assumed and reported by existing breakage tests (Weerasekara _et al_ , 2013).  This is evident from the primary output of the DEM simulations, the calculated particle energy spectra shown in Figure 4. 

The DEM calculated energy spectrum for a SAG mill indicates that most of the particle impacts are occurring at v

ery low energy (Weerasekara _et al_ , 2013). In fact, this energy level is well below that required for a typical ore to break.  In general, for a single impact breakage to occur, the energy need would be above 0.5 kWh/t, however the figure indicates that less than 0.1 per cent of impacts are in this range.  A further 2 per cent of impacts are sufficient to cause incremental damage and breakage through repeated impact events. The majority of the impacts in a SAG mill do not cause particle breakage for the rocks (plus 15 mm) in the mill. Most impacts are of low energy and are more likely to cause attrition than fragmentation. Therefore, these interactions have to be taken into account in the design process such that the target throughput and product size (P80) can be achieved.

###### **SAG Mill operation** 

The Philsaga SAG mill is 6.1 m Ч 7.32 m with a 20° conical angle (to vertical) of feed and discharge heads. This SAG mill is used to grind a feed nominally passing of 130 mm. It is driven by a 1400 kW motor coupled with a variable frequency (VF) drive designed to run at 13.2rpm (ie 76 per cent critical speed). The mill currently runs at a constant 11.5 rpm which is 67.5 per cent of critical speed (the speed at which media or balls would be pinned to the mill shell by centripetal forces). 

###### _Steel system_ 

During the life of the Steel SAG mill shell, before conversion to the Metal-Cap system, three sets of steel shell liners were installed at different time intervals. The first, two sets of shell liners were from Supplier #1 and third set was from a Supplier #2. All three sets had the same high-low lifter design using steel, while Supplier #1 provided 70 mm thick liner plates and Supplier #2 provided 85 mm thick liner plates. The mill shell is lined with 36 rows of lifters. Specifications of lifter/liners used are shown in Table 1 and Figure 5. The mill is typically run at 25 per cent total filling, with 11 per cent ball and 14 per cent ore filling. 

###### _Metal cap system_ 

Steel systems are generally heavier compared to rubber based composite systems. This means in a SAG mill every tonne of weight saved in the lining system is another potential tonne of ore or media charge that can be put into the mill. Leveraging of this and capitalising on the synergy brought about by utilising the unique wear properties of rubber and metal for specific areas a composite system was considered. This lead to the design of a composite rubber and Chrome Moybdenum (CrMo) steel metal cap system. 

Chrome Moybdenum (CrMo) steel is an industry standard for highly abrasive grinding duties generally found in SAG Mill applications. Weir Minerals has developed a range of CrMo Casting Inlays that have shown clear benefits in mill lining systems where they have been adop

ted. The philosophy adapted is based on proven concepts that suit the milling environment. The mill lining systems are individually designed to meet the grinding criteria and requirements, rather than providing an off the shelf standard product and solution. In this design, the CrMo is strategically located in areas that will see high abrasive contact. This construction adds to the overall component properties by allowing high energy impacts to be absorbed and deflected, delivering an increase in service life while retaining the face angle for an extended period. The benefit of retaining the face angle for a longer period is that impact breakage is high through the liner life and therefore milling efficiency is sustained. ###### _Collision Energy Spectra_ 

The collision energy spectra provide the opportunity to better understand the various contributions to the overall energy distribution within the mill, which cannot otherwise be estimated using charge trajectory analysis. Knowledge of the changes in these spectra with operational and geometric mill attributes may create the possibility of improving the energy efficiency of size reduction by shifting energy from less useful types of collisions to more useful ones through the change of mill operating conditions. 

It is evident for Figure 8 that the metal-cap system has a higher frequency of collision across the possible energy range generated in the mill compared to the steel system. On average this translates to a 20 per cent increase for the 45° and 26 per cent increase for the 35° metal cap system. This increase in collision frequency translates into a higher probability of particle breakage events which will translate into an increase in throughput. 

Resolving the collision frequency into both impact and shear frequencies showed that both impact and shear collisions increase relative to the steel system as can be seen in Figure 9.  High energy, low frequency impact collision will generally contribute to body breakage while the low energy, high frequency impacts will cause surface damage (Figure 10a). High energy, low frequency shear will promote attrition and low energy, high frequency shear will result in abrasion (Figure 10b). Therefore, any increase in these collision events wi

ll enhance the grinding process.

###### _Collision energy by size_ 

The collision energies were mass-averaged as collision specific energy (Ecs) (kWh/ton) and plotted against particle size distribution for each mill system (Figure 11). Specific energy (Ecs) can be considered as average intensity (energy density) of a collision event in the mill. As described above, this energy density is noted by researchers and practitioners in comminution to be the key driver in rock fracture, and a way of quantifying applied energy as explained earlier. 

Figure 11 clearly shows that metal-cap systems have higher Ecs relative to the steel system. This is about a 23 to 27 per cent increase for 45° and 30° respectively compared to the steel system. This means that the Metal cap system will, on average, transfer the input energy more efficiently to the breakage process than the steel system. It is also evident that this is achieved through similar amount of input power (energy use) (Figure 12) or approximately 2 per cent less than the steel system.

This in combination with selection of specific materials to optimise liner wear has proven to be successful in designing and selecting an appropriate lining system for a specific milling duty. Philsaga’s mine wanted to increase SAG mill availability, minimise localised high wear and optimise particle breakage to deliver increased efficiency within the milling circuit. Application of the above approach has resulted in these objectives being met through design of composite rubber and met

al-cap lining system. 

It was seen from the DEM modelling that a 20 to 26 per cent increase in frequency of collisions across the entire energy range for metal cap 45° and 30° respectively compared to the steel system could be achieved. The Metal cap systems further showed a 23-27 per cent increase in collision energy intensity (Ecs) relative to the steel system. The combination of an increase in collision frequency and energy intensity (energy density) contributes to increased probability of breaking a rock particle and this will translate to increased throughput. Resolving the collision frequency into both impact and shear frequencies showed that both impact and shear collisions increase relative to the steel system. High energy, low frequency impact collision will generally contribute to body breakage while the low energy, high frequency impacts will cause surface damage. High energy, low frequency shear will promote attrition and low energy, high frequency shear will result in abrasion. Therefore, any increase in these collision events will enhance the grinding process. This means that the metalcap system will, on average, transfer the input energy (motor power) more efficiently for the breakage process than the steel system.   Following on from these results it was reported that the site has increased gold recovery by 2 per cent, increased SAG mill throughput by 16-20 per cent while improving liner service life by 40 per cent and has reduced liner system replacement time by more than 60 per cent. 

Liner design has a dramatic impact on both mill availability and grinding efficiency. By optimising the design through materials of construction, significant improvements can be made to not only enhance wear resistance but also to reduce relining times, thereby positively improving availability. ###### What category cyclone is devastating your plant? 

###### _B Wong_<sup>_1_</sup> _and T G Vizcarra_<sup>_2_</sup> 

1. AusIMM, Operations Manager, JKTech Pty Ltd, Brisbane QLD 4113. Email: b.wong@jktech.com.au 2. Process Specialist, JKTech Pty Ltd, Brisbane QLD 4113. Email: t.vizcarra@jktech.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Optimisation projects are regularly undertaken without knowing the root cause of an issue. It is all well and good to trial a multitude of flotation reagents, change the operating characteristics of your flotation cells, or add more media into your ball mills, but time and again, root cause analysis traces issues back to the performance of hydrocyclones. In JKTech's experience, hydrocyclones are poorly operated and maintained (in both primary grinding and regrind circuits), exacerbating issues that many operations commonly experience. 

Recent case studies are presented where JKTech has been engaged to improve the process only to discover that the hydrocyclones were the main issue. At one operation it was found that the hydrocyclone feed density gau

ge was reading significantly lower to the actual density. Following re-calibration of the gauge, and with further improvement of cyclone operational and design parameters using JKSimMet, a significantly sharper efficiency curve was achieved. This resulted in improvements to downstream recoveries while alleviating pumping capacities that were previously constrained by fines and water caught up in recirculating loads. 

Several other case studies are presented which may seem to be relatively basic, but many basics seem to be getting lost in the day-to-day responsibilities of the modern plant metallurgist. Simple fixes to hydrocyclones can result in significant production increases, but more focus is needed in monitoring these to sustain the benefits. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

In Australia, north Queensland, northern Western Australia and the Northern Territory are prone to tropical cyclones each year, some causing massive destruction and millions of dollars of damage. In mineral processing plants, it could be said that hydrocyclones (referred to as cyclones herein) can follow the same pattern as their meteorological namesake. They are generally used to classify mineral particles after grinding, but in JKTech's experience, cyclones are poorly operated and maintained in both primary grinding and regrind circuits, causing very inefficient classification and exacerbating issues that many operations commonly have. Poorly operated cyclones are destructive to mineral recovery. 

Optimisation projects are regularly undertaken by operations without knowing the root cause of an issue. Many times, the issue can be mitigated by improving cyclone performance. Without knowing the root cause, costly changes such as trialling flotation reagents, modifying operating strategies, changing the operating characteristics of flotation cells, or even adding more media into ball mills will often be trialled. More destructively, some of these changes could entail capital expenditure or even exacerbate further recovery losses. 

It appears the modern-day metallurgist is becoming too busy to focus on their core job – improving the metallurgy of the plant. This could be due to many reasons that have been highlighted in many other papers (Munro and Tilyard, 2009; Drinkwater et al, 2011) and discussions but is not the focus of this paper. 

JKTech assisted several clients in recent years where the cyclones were one of the predominant issues that required attention. Sometimes these were known and yet nothing was done to improve them, while sometimes the issue was unknown but simple to mitigate. This paper describes case studies together with how to monitor and improve the operation of cyclones. Getting back to basics, simple yet effective. 

###### **CYCLONES – WHAT THEY ARE DESIGNED TO DO** 

Cyclones are generally used in most mineral processing plants to classify the ground product of the mills in preparation for downstream processes such as flotation and leaching. Cyclones

are generally considered to be more cost effective to classify particles due to their lower footprint, higher utilisation and lower capital and operating costs when compared to other classifying equipment such as screens. They are also (meant to be) easier to operate. 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

The "cut size" of the cyclones relies on centrifugal forces that are generated by tangential flow velocities introduced by the cyclone feed. The cut size can be altered by changing the diameter of the spigot (apex) and vortex finder. The finer, less dense material is forced upwards along an internal column of air and out through the vortex finder creating the overflow, which is generally the feed to downstream separation processes such as flotation and/or leaching. The coarser, high density material becomes the underflow that is generally ground in a mill before being recycled to the cyclones for further classification. The cyclone pressure is the most common control variable, altered by volumetric feed flowrate and the number of operational cyclones. 

The operation of the cyclone can be visually assessed as shown in Figure 1: when the cyclone is overloaded, the underflow will exhibit roping conditions indicating that the air column in the vortex has collapsed and lost the ability to classify effectively; when the cyclone is "underloaded", the underflow will flare out and is most easily observable during a plant start-up when water is being flushed through the system. 



Figure 1 – Cyclone underflow shapes (Napier-Munn et al, 1999). 

It is very common for cyclones within a pack to be unevenly loaded. Figure 2 shows snapshots of two underflows, and size distributions of the corresponding overflows, at a copper operation in South-East Asia. The target P80 was 90 µm, and it is evident one cyclone was cutting excessively fine, while the other was sending a coarser-than-desired sizing to flotation.

###### **HOW TO MEASURE CYCLONE PERFORMANCE** 

###### **Cyclone surveys** 

The only way to effectively measure the efficiency of cyclones is to conduct a sampling survey, collecting the cyclone feed, underflow and overflow. Samples need to be representative, defined by Napier Munn et al in 1999 as “all particles present in the stream have an equal chance of being selected in the sample by the sampling device”. 

In reality, this can be difficult to obtain, however to ensure a sample is as representative as possible the following should be taken into account: 

14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 

- Ensure that the plant is operating “as steady as possible” so that the samples collected are reflective of the operation: mill throughput, number of operating cyclones, cyclone pressure, density and flow should at least be consistent; 

- Clean/hose/knock off any build up a

s spigots and vortex finders wear over time. It is very important that the metallurgist be involved with cyclone inspections, and not just leave it up to the maintenance department. This is also relevant for other key pieces of equipment such as crushers, mills and flotation cells. There are commonly cases where metallurgical performance is sacrificed for wear life; not intentionally, but due to a lack of knowledge. Cyclone inspections should be routinely performed at the beginning of each major planned plant shutdown so that the appropriate maintenance action can be performed during the shutdown, or the cyclone tagged out of use before plant start-up. Check that the internal components have not worn excessively; an inspection of the apex and spigots should be undertaken for measurements, wear, blockages etc. If Figure 4 occurs, it is too late. 

2. Do not perform sampling with significant build up around cyclones. Build up around cyclones is common to all plants (Figure 5). Prior to any sampling, the area should be thoroughly cleaned to prevent build up material falling into the sampler, causing contamination. If this occurs, the sample needs to be discarded and taken again. 

3. Do not use "cup samplers". Operators will commonly do their rounds a few times each day, and at the cyclones, the density of the cyclone overflow will be measured by collecting a sample and using a Marcy Scale. At several operations, the use of “cup samplers” (Figure 6) were prevalent, and not just at the cyclones. This type of sampler is not ideal as slurry can easily splash out of the cup chamber resulting in a non-representative sample. Is it really worth wasting the operators’ time to obtain a meaningless set of data? A properly designed sample cutter that can cut the whole stream is required. These will need to be customised depending on the design, location and convenience of the sample point. ###### **CASE STUDIES** 

The following case studies are from a variety of projects that JKTech was involved in over the past two years. 

###### **Nickel operation in Russia** 

At a nickel operation, JKTech was engaged to improve flotation recovery, specifically to recommend reagents for improved fines recovery. The operation had become bottlenecked at the thickeners, filters were struggling, and concentrate cake moistures had risen from 7 to 11 per cent causing subsequent drying issues at the smelter. The primary grind was reportedly at 65% -45um and the secondary grind was

93 per cent -45um. Particle size distribution data was not initially provided. When requested, it was revealed that there was no historical data available and the primary and secondary grind size numbers provided were the design targets. A sample of the flotation feed was taken by the client and measured (Figure 8). It was evident that this was not ideal for flotation as the curve was relatively “flat”, even though they were achieving their grind size target. The size distribution does not have a typical “S” shape, suggesting the efficiency of classification prior to flotation was poor. It was surprising that there was no knowledge about what the actual flotation feed particle size distribution was, and no confirmed primary grind size target in place. It is critical that this be monitored continuously and the provided targets relate to grinding and flotation performance. 100

It is good practice to measure this as it represents the maximum particle size being sent to flotation. This may have required another one or two extra sieve sizes in the particle size analysis. Overgrinding was apparent from the initial observations provided. This would contribute to the following, all of which the operation was experiencing: - It can cause poor settling characteristics in the tailings and concentrate thickeners, resulting in poor underflow density and poor water clarity in the overflow; - It can cause higher concentrate moisture in the filters due to fine particles blinding the filter cloth; - It can waste power in the comminution circuit which would be better utilised to achieve higher mill throughputs; - It can negatively impact metal recovery – excessively fine minerals have slower flotation kinetics; and - It can cause an increase in reagent consumption and more complicated reagent schemes to be used. The shape of the curve and indications of overgrinding highlighted improved operation of the cyclones needed priority over expensive reagent trials to improve recovery (apologies to the reagent suppliers). The operation has since proceeded to investigate both flotation feed size distribution optimisation to reduce overgrinding and flotation reagent screening. Learnings: - Know what your target and actual flotation feed size distributions are; - Optimise and improve upstream where possible before optimising the flotation circuit, as upstream changes inevitably impact downstream improvements; - Ensure the appropriate top size screen is used in all measurements, i.e. there should be no mass

in the top screen. ###### **Bauxite operation in Australia** JKTech was engaged to identify potential improvements to cyclone performance at a bauxite operation in Australia. The objective was to model the cyclones and identify design changes that would be necessary to facilitate an increase in yield. Coarse +300 µm particles are targeted for recovery with gravity separation on the underflow, whereas the -300 µm particles are nominally sent to tailings via the overflow. The surveys revealed that the cyclones were performing very poorly. It was evident from the efficiency curves that only about 20 per cent of fines and water were escaping the circuit via the overflow (Figure 9). Therefore most of the material and water was misreporting to the underflow and overwhelming the gravity circuit, leading to subsequent moisture problems in the concentrate. 100

The root cause of the inefficient classification was identified in the cyclone dilution water, which consisted of tailings from the gravity circuit. The suspended fines in the recycled tailings appeared to be constraining the ability of the process to achieve adequate levels of dilution required for good cyclone performance, with the cyclone feed measured at ~70% solids during the surveys. This was surprising for the operational staff who 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 had expected densities around the ~55-60% range, the discrepancy was due to a poorly calibrated density meter. Discussions with cyclone vendors further confirmed that it was pointless purchasing new cyclones, which would also be ineffective at such high feed densities. Site personnel are currently implementing changes that will facilitate increased fresh water flows to the circuit. The expected benefit is higher capacity in the circuit due to less fines and water recirculation. This will lead to increased throughput and yields in the gravity circuit, due to the alleviation of recirculating loads with the escape of fines and water out of the overflow and into the tailings stream. Learnings: - Check and calibrate your instrumentation on a routine basis; and - Monitor the cyclone efficiency curves on a more regular basis. ###### **Lead-Zinc operation in Australia** A Process Integration project from the mine to flotation plant was conducted at a lead-zinc operation in Australia with the objective of generating optimal particle size distributions for each process/equipment and knowledge throughout the whole value chain. The cyclones were identified as a critical stage to enable successful implementation of several improvements. In general, fine particles tend to follow the flow of water in cyclones, hence recovering wa

ter to the overflow is the basis of allowing fine particles to escape the milling circuit. Water recovery to the overflow is considered a good indicator of classification efficiency, with cyclone efficiency increasing with increasing water recovery to overflow. After initial surveys of the cyclone pack and analysis with JKSimMet, it was identified that the cyclones operated at a very high feed density of 78% solids, and performance could be improved simply by reducing the cyclone feed density. Whilst a simple solution, this would push the capacity of the existing cyclone feed pump slightly beyond its maximum. This was acknowledged by the operations personnel, who were aware about the issue but did not know how to justify making the improvements, so the initiative was put into the “too hard basket”. JKTech assisted in providing critical data for the justification to upgrade the cyclone feed pump. This involved performing the appropriate data analysis, modelling the milling circuit, and simulating various cyclone feed density scenarios. Table 1 shows the initial survey performance together with optimised scenarios from simulations using JKSimMet. In JKTech's experience, cyclones are poorly operated and maintained (in both primary grinding and regrind circuits), exacerbating issues that many operations commonly have, or are unaware of. This can be mitigated by improving the monitoring and assessment of cyclone operations as this is generally not done 14th AusIMM Mill Operators' Conference 2018 / Brisbane, Qld, 29–31 August 2018 well and is one of the basics of metallurgical performance monitoring.
